docs.title: Qwen & Gemma Handbook
docs.text:
Open handbook · Oct 2026

Build, fine-tune and ship Qwen & Gemma agents.

A source-backed, practical handbook for local model training on a 32 GB Apple M1 Pro — agents for authorized Kali Linux work, Java/Quarkus services and React/Tailwind front-ends.

Start here → 2026 LoRA recipe GitHub qwen-kali-agent — make # 1 · environment and memory headroom $ make setup && make check # 2 · validate the training splits $ make data-check # 3 · 8B smoke run, then the 14B adapter $ make train-8b $ make train-14b # 4 · score it on the golden set $ make eval 3specializations 2model families 64chapters 32 GBtarget hardware

docs.title: What is new
docs.text:
29 Oct 2026 Agents, integrated and applied

Eight ways to wire an agent into a product, the run contract and a runnable agent service, then twelve real applications end to end: support, coding in CI, data analysis, incident response, documents, research, sales, e-commerce, helpdesk, pipelines and QA.

28 Oct 2026 New menu: AI Engineer

What it takes to move from software engineering to AI engineering: 19 chapters from vectors and gradients to data preparation, RAG, agents, MCP, agent frameworks, agent integration and real applications, evals, serving and interviews, with on-paper examples and tested code.

28 Oct 2026 Every formula, on paper

129 short examples you can redo with a pencil, one after every formula in chapters 32–42, each number checked by make math-check.

28 Oct 2026 H100 budget corrected

Dense BF16 is ~989 TFLOP/s (1,979 is the sparse figure): Qwen3-14B on 36T tokens is ~2.24M GPU-hours, ~9.3 days and ~$5.6M, not double that.

27 Oct 2026 Gemma 4 E2B and E4B, explained

Per-layer embeddings, KV sharing and the double-wide MLP, read from the checkpoints — and why the E4B cache at 128K outgrows the 12B’s.

27 Oct 2026 Worked examples, grounded

Every formula now starts from a real situation — a next token, a weight row, an eval batch — with a corrected Wilson interval and 64 checked values.

Authorized testing only. A model is not authorization. Use a written scope, a lab you own, and a policy layer that enforces both.

A handbook, not a tested product. Commands were checked against upstream source/docs on 25 Oct 2026, but the MLX runs were not executed on the target Mac. Run the preflight and a smoke test before a multi-day run.

docs.title: The short answer
docs.text: Question Recommendation What do I train locally? Qwen3-14B, 4-bit QLoRA with MLX-LM. Largest Qwen that trains reliably in 32 GB, mature tool calling, 32K native context. Safe fallback Qwen3-8B, 4-bit QLoRA. Faster iteration, same tool format. If you rent a GPU Qwen3.5-9B, or Qwen3.8-27B on 48–80 GB. Much stronger agentic base, 262K context. Teacher / judge Qwen3.8-27B-4bit for quality; Qwen3.6-35B-A3B-4bit for bulk generation. Do not train either on 32 GB. Training framework MLX-LM (mlx_lm.lora), native Apple Silicon, quantized LoRA. 2026 LoRA recipe All layers, rank 16, scale: 2.0 (= PEFT alpha 32), LR 1e-4, effective batch 8, 1–2 epochs. Java track Qwen2.5-Coder-14B, 24/48 blocks, Java 25 + Quarkus 3.40. React track Qwen2.5-Coder-14B, 24/48 blocks, sequence 3K, React 19.3 + Tailwind 4.3. One Qwen3 for all Qwen3-14B + three adapters. One mixed adapter is possible; see 26 — One model for all. Gemma 4 12B Separate adapters, separate ports, same evaluation harness. See 31 — Gemma vs Qwen. Dataset size 2–5M tokens for a first adapter; 10M+ only if evaluation proves it helps. Serving llama-server for tool fidelity, mlx_lm.server for speed, Ollama for convenience. Loopback + SSH only. Agent harness OpenCode + MCP-Kali-Server, or hackingBuddyGPT for a minimal baseline. Evaluation BFCL, KaliBench, Cybench, private golden set, unsafe-action gate.

docs.title: 01 — The Qwen landscape and what to train
docs.text:
Last verified: 25 October 2026.

This chapter is the Kali/agent track. If you are specialising in Java/Quarkus or React/Tailwind, the base model and data are different: start at 18 — Java landscape or 22 — React & Tailwind.

The Qwen family moves fast. This chapter fixes the vocabulary, lays out the open-weight options as they exist today, and explains why the rest of the handbook trains Qwen3-14B locally rather than a newer, larger, or more fashionable model.

The short version: the best model you can train is not the best model you can run. On a 32 GB M1 Pro, the training ceiling is much lower than the inference ceiling, and the newest Qwen architectures are the least mature in MLX's training path.

docs.title: 1. Three generations, two architectures
docs.text:
As of October 2026 there are three relevant generations:

Generation Examples Architecture Training status on MLX Qwen3 (Apr 2025) Qwen3-4B/8B/14B/32B, Qwen3-30B-A3B, Qwen3-Coder-30B-A3B Standard transformer: GQA + dense FFN or MoE Mature. The safest local fine-tuning target. Qwen3.5 / 3.6 / 3.8 (Feb–Aug 2026) Qwen3.5-4B/9B, Qwen3.6-35B-A3B, Qwen3.8-27B Hybrid Gated DeltaNet (GDN) + gated full attention; native vision; 262K context Immature for training. Inference works; LoRA training is experimental on 32 GB. Qwen3-Coder-Next (Jan 2026) 80B total / 3B active Hybrid GDN + 512-expert MoE Inference only on this hardware; 4-bit weights alone are ~45 GB.

The generational jump is real: Qwen3.5-9B beats Qwen3-30B-A3B on agentic benchmarks, and Qwen3.8-27B is a genuinely strong long-horizon agent. But the architecture that makes them efficient at inference (GDN, a linear-attention recurrence) is also the architecture whose backward pass is not yet optimized in MLX. That is the central trade-off of this handbook.

docs.title: 2. The open-weight field
docs.text:
All models below are Apache-2.0 unless noted. Benchmark numbers are vendor-reported and are useful for relative ordering, not for predicting your task.

Model Released Total / active Architecture Native context Notes Qwen3-4B 2025-04 4.0B Dense, 36 layers 32K (131K YaRN) Fast format-iteration model; weaker reasoning. Qwen3-8B 2025-04 8.2B Dense, 36 layers, GQA 32Q/8KV 32K (131K YaRN) Safest training fallback. BFCL-v3 68.1. Qwen3-14B 2025-04 14.8B Dense, 40 layers, GQA 40Q/8KV 32K (131K YaRN) Recommended local training target. BFCL-v3 70.4. Qwen3-32B 2025-04 32.8B Dense, 64 layers 32K (131K YaRN) Inference-only at 4-bit on 32 GB; training does not fit. Qwen3-30B-A3B 2025-04 30.5B / 3.3B MoE, 128 experts, 8 active 32K Inference fits; training is marginal. Qwen3-30B-A3B-Instruct-2507 2025-07 30.5B / 3.3B MoE, 48 layers, non-thinking 262K Strong general/agentic MoE; 4-bit inference ~17–18 GB; no local LoRA. Qwen3-Coder-30B-A3B-Instruct 2025-07 30.5B / 3.3B MoE, 48 layers, non-thinking 262K Strong CLI/coding specialist. 4-bit inference ~17 GB. Gemma 4 12B 2026-06 11.95B Dense, 48 layers, hybrid attention, multimodal 256K Alternative base; Apache-2.0; separate track at 27 — Gemma 4 12B. Qwen3.5-4B 2026-02 4.7B Hybrid GDN, 32 layers, vision 262K Strong small agent; training conditional. Qwen3.5-9B 2026-02 9.7B Hybrid GDN, 32 layers, vision 262K Best quality/time if you rent a GPU. BFCL-v4 66.1, TAU2 79.1. Qwen3.6-35B-A3B 2026-04 36.0B / ~3B Hybrid GDN + MoE, 256 experts 262K Excellent agentic/coding; 4-bit inference 19–24 GB. Qwen3.8-27B 2026-08 27.8B Hybrid GDN, 64 layers, vision 262K Best dense model that fits 4-bit inference; teacher/oracle, not a local training target. Qwen3-Coder-Next 2026-01 79.7B / ~3B Hybrid GDN + 512-expert MoE 262K Too large for 32 GB even at 4-bit (~45 GB).

Terminology. “Total / active” matters for MoE models: Qwen3.6-35B-A3B has 36B parameters but activates ~3B per token, so it generates quickly while still needing ~20 GB of RAM at 4-bit. “Native context” is the trained window; YaRN extension is possible but costs quality and memory.

docs.title: 3. What actually fits
docs.text:
Training needs the weights plus activations, logits, adapter gradients and optimizer state. The table below is the practical conclusion; the derivation is in 02-hardware.md.

Target 4-bit weights Realistic QLoRA peak Verdict on 32 GB Qwen3-8B ~4.6 GB 10–12 GB Yes. Fast, forgiving. Qwen3-14B ~8.3 GB 18–22 GB Yes. The local sweet spot. Qwen3-32B ~18.5 GB >32 GB No. Qwen3.5-4B ~2.6 GB 12–15 GB Conditional; GDN backward is slow. Qwen3.5-9B ~5.4 GB OOM reported at 36 GB No / high risk. Qwen3.6-35B-A3B ~20.2 GB 30–35 GB No. Qwen3.8-27B ~15.6 GB 32–60 GB No. Qwen3-Coder-30B-A3B ~17.2 GB ~28–32 GB Marginal; treat as inference-only. Qwen3-Coder-Next ~44.8 GB — No.

The Qwen3.5/3.8 numbers are not hypothetical. MLX-LM issues report first-backward OOMs for 9B on a 36 GB machine, and 27B peaks of 60–117 GB before a Metal resource-limit failure. The GDN path falls back to a Python recurrence during training because the Metal kernel has no vector-Jacobian product; issue #1956 (Oct 2026) shows step time scaling with the number of trained GDN layers, and the Metal VJP PR #1217 was closed unmerged. Unsloth also advises against 4-bit QLoRA for Qwen3.5 dense/MoE because of quantization sensitivity. See 02-hardware.md §4 and 17 — Fine-tuning update.

The consequence: if you want the newer architecture, rent a CUDA GPU for a day, train there, and bring the merged weights back for 4-bit MLX inference. That is a perfectly good workflow and often cheaper than spending a week fighting the local training path.

docs.title: 4. Why Qwen3-14B is the local default
docs.text:
1. It trains. Standard attention, mature LoRA path, thousands of successful runs. The same cannot be said for GDN models today.
  2. It is large enough to be useful. 14.8B parameters and 32K context are enough for multi-step tool use, Kali CLI vocabulary, and structured output. It is not a frontier reasoner, but the job is pattern-following inside a scaffold, not open-ended exploitation research.
  3. It has native tool calling. Qwen3 was post-trained with tool use; BFCL-v3 70.4 is competitive with much larger 2024 models.
  4. It leaves memory for the rest of the system. At ~18–22 GB peak, macOS, the terminal, and a small Kali VM can coexist. A 27B run leaves nothing.
  5. It is cheap to iterate. An 8B debugging run is ~2× faster; the 14B is the graduation run, not the first run.

When to choose Qwen3-8B instead: your dataset is still changing daily, you have less than 2M tokens, or you need a 4K–8K sequence length. The 8B is also the control in the MLX issue reports — if a training bug appears, test it on 8B first.

When to choose Qwen3.5-9B instead: you will rent an L40S/A100 (or have access to one), you want 262K context, and you care about the strongest possible base. The 9B is a better model; it is just not a better local training model today.

When to choose Qwen3-Coder-30B-A3B: your agent is mostly code/CLI generation and you will use it for inference, not training. It is excellent at terminal work, but 17 GB of weights plus activations leaves little room for a serious QLoRA run.

docs.title: 5. Teacher and oracle models
docs.text:
Even if you train a 14B, a larger local model is useful for:

  • generating candidate trajectories and hard negatives,
  • grading outputs against a rubric,
  • adjudicating disagreements in evaluation,
  • producing a “best-of-N” reference for failure analysis.
Role Model 4-bit memory Why Quality oracle / judge mlx-community/Qwen3.8-27B-4bit 16–23 GB Best dense quality that fits; slow (~8–10 tok/s), so use it selectively. Bulk generator mlx-community/Qwen3.6-35B-A3B-4bit 19–24 GB 40–50 tok/s at short context; 3B active. Good for volume. Coding/CLI specialist mlx-community/Qwen3-Coder-30B-A3B-Instruct-4bit 17–19 GB Strong terminal/code behavior; non-thinking. Cheap formatter Qwen3-8B/14B 5–9 GB Fast, good enough for JSON repair and simple classification.

Do not use a model to judge its own training data without a deterministic check. Execution results, schema validation and human spot checks come first; the LLM judge is a tie-breaker, not ground truth.

docs.title: 6. Base vs instruct vs thinking
docs.text:
• Base models are completion models. Do not fine-tune them for tool calling unless you have a very large, carefully formatted corpus and a reason.
  • Instruct models already follow chat templates and emit tool calls. QLoRA on an instruct model is the practical choice.
  • Thinking mode. Qwen3 supports a reasoning_content block; Qwen3.5/3.6 add preserve_thinking and reasoning-effort controls. Thinking improves hard multi-step tasks but doubles latency and token cost. For a pentest agent, use thinking for planning and disable it for routine tool selection, or train two adapters (fast/no-think and deliberate/think).
  • Template fidelity is more important than raw model quality. A 14B that emits valid JSON every time beats a 27B that emits almost-JSON. Chapter 06-data-format.md is the most important chapter in this repo for that reason.

docs.title: 7. Local vs rented GPU
docs.text:
The local Mac is superb for iteration and inference and mediocre for long training runs. Rough 2026 economics:

Job Local M1 Pro Rent an L40S/A100 1M-token experiment 15–25 hours, $0 ~20–40 minutes, ~$1–3 5M-token adapter 2–4 days ~2–4 hours, ~$5–15 20M-token adapter 8–15 days ~8–15 hours, ~$15–50 Privacy / air-gap Excellent Poor unless dedicated Iteration speed Slow but unlimited Fast, metered

Rule of thumb: if the run is longer than ~24 hours, rent. If the data is sensitive or you need to iterate on the pipeline itself, stay local. The handbook supports both: the same JSONL and the same evaluation harness work with MLX (local) or PEFT/Unsloth/TRL (CUDA).

docs.title: 8. A decision tree
docs.text:
Do you have a CUDA GPU or a $20 budget?
├─ Yes → Is 262K context or the strongest base important?
│         ├─ Yes → Qwen3.5-9B (bf16 LoRA, not 4-bit QLoRA) on L40S/A100
│         └─ No  → Qwen3-14B QLoRA on the rented GPU (faster, same recipe)
└─ No  → Train locally on the M1 Pro
          ├─ First adapter, dataset still moving → Qwen3-8B QLoRA
          ├─ Serious adapter, stable data       → Qwen3-14B QLoRA
          └─ Need newer architecture?           → Rent, or wait for MLX GDN training support

docs.title: 9. Benchmarks are not your task
docs.text:
Vendor benchmark tables compare models on BFCL, TAU, SWE-bench and Terminal-Bench. Those numbers are useful for eliminating bad choices, not for predicting whether a model will run nmap -sV with the right flags on your lab network. A model can score well on BFCL and still fail your tool schemas because:

  • your tool names/descriptions are ambiguous,
  • your arguments use enums or nested objects the model has not seen,
  • your system prompt conflicts with the tool instructions,
  • your context contains 30 tools when the model can reliably choose among 8,
  • the model was trained on a different tool-call syntax.

The only benchmark that matters is a held-out set of your tasks, executed in your lab, with your tools. Chapter 09-evaluation.md builds it.

docs.title: 02 — Hardware reality on a 32 GB M1 Pro
docs.text:
Last verified: 25 October 2026. Numbers marked EST are estimates derived from architecture and published benchmarks, not measurements on this exact machine.

This chapter is the memory accountant's view of fine-tuning. It answers three questions:

  1. Will it fit?
  2. How long will it take?
  3. What will macOS do when it doesn't fit?

If you only read one section, read §3 and §6.

docs.title: 1. The machine
docs.text:
Component M1 Pro (binned 10-core CPU / 16-core GPU) CPU 10 cores (8 performance + 2 efficiency) GPU 16 cores, ~5.2 TFLOPS FP32; FP16/BF16 at the same peak rate (no double-rate half precision) Neural Engine 16 cores (not used by MLX training) Memory 32 GB unified, ~200 GB/s bandwidth Media engine ProRes/ProRes RAW hardware (irrelevant here) OS macOS 26.x (Tahoe or later in 2026) Disk Typically 512 GB–1 TB; keep 100+ GB free

The critical property is unified memory: the CPU and GPU share the same physical RAM. There is no separate VRAM. A model that “fits in 24 GB of VRAM” on a PC does not automatically fit here, because macOS, the window server, the terminal, and any VM are using the same pool.

MLX allocates GPU buffers from this pool and can set a wired limit — the maximum the GPU is allowed to wire. Apple's default is conservative: on a 32 GB machine, mx.device_info()["max_recommended_working_set_size"] typically reports ~21.3 GiB, not 32 GB. You can raise it deliberately, but every gigabyte you wire is a gigabyte macOS cannot compress or swap.

docs.title: 2. The three budgets
docs.text:
There are three different limits, and confusing them is the most common source of “it worked in the demo, then OOM'd”:

Budget Typical value What it governs Physical RAM 32 GB Everything: OS, apps, model, VM. Default GPU working set ~21.3 GiB What MLX will allocate without intervention. Wired limit 0 = default; can be set The hard ceiling for GPU-wired memory.

Check them:

sysctl hw.memsize
sysctl iogpu.wired_limit_mb
python - <<'PY'
import mlx.core as mx
print(mx.device_info())
PY

iogpu.wired_limit_mb=0 means “use the system default”, not “unlimited”. mx.device_info() includes max_recommended_working_set_size in bytes.

Do not set the wired limit to 30 GB on a 32 GB machine. You will starve the OS. The practical ceiling is ~24–26 GB, and only when the Kali VM is shut down and Chrome/Docker/Slack are closed. A kernel panic or a forced reboot in the middle of a 3-day run is worse than a slightly smaller batch.

docs.title: 3.1 The equation
docs.text:
For QLoRA training, peak memory is approximately:

M_peak ≈ M_weights
       + M_lora_params + M_optimizer
       + M_activations
       + M_logits
       + M_temporaries
       + M_runtime (Metal, tokenizer, Python, OS)
Term Approximate size Notes M_weights 4.5 bits/param for MLX 4-bit Includes quantization scales/biases. M_lora_params rank × Σ(in+out) over adapted layers Rank 16 on 16 layers of 14B ≈ 27M params ≈ 107 MB fp32; all 40 layers ≈ 63M ≈ 252 MB. M_optimizer 2–3× adapter params Adam/AdamW moments; still small because the base is frozen. M_activations B × L × N_lora × (c₁H + c₂I) × bytes Dominated by sequence length and adapted layers. M_logits B × L × V × 4 bytes V = 151,936 for Qwen3; ~1.24 GB per 2K sequence in fp32. M_temporaries 10–30% of activations Attention buffers, dequantization, reductions. M_runtime 2–4 GB Metal, Python, tokenizer, fragmentation.

B batch size, L sequence length, N_lora number of adapted layers, H hidden size, I FFN intermediate size, V vocabulary.

docs.title: 3.2 Worked example: Qwen3-14B at 2K
docs.text:
Qwen3-14B: H=5120, I=17408, 40 layers, V=151936.

  • 4-bit weights: ~8.3 GB.
  • LoRA rank 16 on the last 16 layers: ~0.11 GB params, ~0.3 GB optimizer.
  • LoRA rank 16 on all 40 layers: ~0.25 GB params, ~0.7 GB optimizer; the activation term roughly doubles, so peak is ~21–24 GB even with checkpointing.
  • Logits at B=1, L=2048: 1 × 2048 × 151936 × 4 ≈ 1.24 GB (fp32 cross-entropy).
  • Activations without checkpointing: roughly 1 × 2048 × 16 × (10×5120 + 4×17408) × 2 ≈ 7.9 GB.
  • Runtime: ~2–3 GB.

Peak ≈ 19–21 GB — fits under the default 21.3 GiB only if nothing else is running, which is not a safe assumption.

Java/Quarkus note. Qwen2.5-Coder-14B has 48 layers (hidden 5120, intermediate 13824). A 24-block rank-16 adapter is roughly 34M parameters; peak is in the same 18–23 GB range as Qwen3-14B. Adapting all 48 blocks raises activations and can exceed 24 GB, so the Java runbook starts at 24/48.

React/Tailwind note. The same Qwen2.5-Coder-14B at 3,072 tokens peaks around 21–25 GB with 24/48 blocks; the 7B at 4,096 with all 28 blocks is the safer long-context run at 12–16 GB. Front-end examples include component code, styles and tests, so context is the pressure point.

Gemma 4 12B note. 11.95B, 48 layers, 4-bit weights ~6.6–7.6 GB. 24/48 at 2,048 peaks around 16–22 GB; 24/48 at 3,072 around 20–26 GB. Start at 24/48, not all 48. See 27 — Gemma 4 12B.

With --grad-checkpoint:

  • Activations ≈ B × L × N_lora × 2H × 2 ≈ 0.67 GB.
  • Peak ≈ 12–14 GB, plus whatever the recomputation temporaries need. In practice, budget 16–18 GB.

That is why every config in this repo enables gradient checkpointing. It costs ~20–30% throughput and buys 5–7 GB of headroom.

docs.title: 3.3 Worked example: Qwen3-8B at 2K
docs.text:
Qwen3-8B: H=4096, I=12288, 36 layers.

  • 4-bit weights: ~4.6 GB.
  • Logits: 1.24 GB (same vocabulary).
  • Activations without checkpointing: 1 × 2048 × 16 × (10×4096 + 4×12288) × 2 ≈ 5.9 GB.
  • Peak: 12–14 GB without checkpointing, 8–10 GB with it.

The 8B is the “it always fits” option. If a training bug appears, reproduce it here before blaming the 14B.

docs.title: 3.4 Batch size and sequence length
docs.text:
Memory scales linearly with batch and linearly with sequence length, but logits and attention temporaries make long sequences disproportionately expensive. On 32 GB:

Model Seq 1K Seq 2K Seq 4K Seq 8K Qwen3-8B QLoRA, grad-ckpt, B=1 ~7 GB ~9 GB ~13 GB ~21 GB Qwen3-8B QLoRA, grad-ckpt, B=2 ~9 GB ~13 GB ~21 GB OOM Qwen3-14B QLoRA, grad-ckpt, B=1 ~11 GB ~16 GB ~24 GB OOM Qwen3-14B QLoRA, grad-ckpt, B=2 ~16 GB ~24 GB OOM OOM

These are planning estimates, not guarantees. Measure with mx.get_peak_memory() or the trainer's printed peak. Start one row lower than you think you need.

Gradient accumulation is the escape hatch: batch_size=1 with grad_accumulation_steps=8 gives an effective batch of 8 without the activation memory of 8 samples. It is slower (more optimizer steps per token? no — fewer, but each micro-batch is serial), but it fits.

docs.title: 3.5 KV cache is inference-only
docs.text:
Do not add KV cache to the training budget. It matters when serving:

KV bytes/token = 2 (K,V) × layers × kv_heads × head_dim × bytes

Qwen3-14B: 2 × 40 × 8 × 128 × 2 = 163,840 bytes/token = 160 KiB/token.

Context KV cache (fp16) With 4-bit KV 4K 0.67 GB ~0.17 GB 8K 1.34 GB ~0.34 GB 16K 2.68 GB ~0.67 GB 32K 5.37 GB ~1.34 GB

At 32 GB, a 14B 4-bit model (~8.3 GB) + 32K fp16 KV (~5.4 GB) + runtime (~2 GB) ≈ 15.7 GB. That fits. A 27B 4-bit (~15.6 GB) + 32K (~5.4 GB) + runtime ≈ 23 GB — at the edge, especially with a VM running.

docs.title: 4. Training throughput and wall-clock
docs.text:
Training FLOPs are roughly 6 × N × tokens (forward + backward), where N is the number of active parameters. Throughput is effective_TFLOPS / (6N).

M1 Pro peak is ~5.2 TFLOPS, and FP16/BF16 run at the same peak rate as FP32: Apple's GPUs have no double-rate half precision (metal-benchmarks measures ~5.3 TFLOPS for both). Real transformer training with 4-bit dequantization, Python overhead and memory stalls achieves maybe 25–45% of peak, about 1.3–2.3 TFLOPS. For Qwen3-14B (N=14.8B, 6N ≈ 88.8 GFLOP/token):

  • At 1.3 TFLOPS effective: 14.6 tok/s.
  • At 2 TFLOPS: 22.5 tok/s.
  • At 2.3 TFLOPS: 25.9 tok/s.

LoRA skips the weight gradients of the frozen base, so the real cost is closer to 4N per token and these figures are conservative by up to 1.5×. Published anchors are consistent with this range: an M1 Max 32 GB trains Qwen3-8B 4-bit at 92–98 tok/s at 2K with a small number of adapted layers, and the M1 Pro has roughly half the GPU and bandwidth. Budget 20–30 tok/s for 14B and 40–55 tok/s for 8B (EST). If you see 60+ tok/s on a 14B, verify that you are actually training the layers you think you are.

Run Tokens 14B @ 25 tok/s 8B @ 45 tok/s Quick format test 100K 1.1 h 0.6 h Minimal adapter 2M 22 h 12 h Serious first adapter 5M 56 h 31 h Scaled run 10M 111 h 62 h “Just 50M tokens” 50M 23 days 13 days

Interpretation: 50M tokens is not a realistic local run. The research on data-efficient fine-tuning (LIMA and successors) shows that a small, curated set can outperform a much larger noisy one. Plan 1–2M tokens for the first adapter, 3–5M for the second, and only scale after the evaluation says the model is underfitting rather than under-specified.

Tokens/sec is not the only clock. Data loading, tokenization, validation, checkpoint saves and thermal throttling add 10–20%. A 56-hour estimate is realistically 60–70 hours of wall time.

docs.title: 5. Disk, heat and power
docs.text:
• Disk: Qwen3-14B bf16 is ~29.5 GB; 4-bit MLX ~8.3 GB; a fused bf16 model ~30 GB; GGUF Q4_K_M ~9 GB; adapters ~0.1 GB each; checkpoints can add several GB. Reserve 100–150 GB.
  • Heat: a sustained GPU load on a MacBook Pro will throttle after 30+ minutes. A laptop stand and a cool room help; a closed lid with an external display is worse. Expect 10–20% throughput loss on long runs (EST).
  • Power: keep the charger connected. Training on battery will throttle aggressively and may sleep.
  • Sleep: disable sleep for the duration:
sudo pmset -a sleep 0 disksleep 0
# restore later: sudo pmset -a sleep 1 disksleep 10
  • Swap: if vm_stat shows swapouts climbing during training, you are over budget. Reduce batch/sequence length; do not “wait it out”.

docs.title: 6. What to do when it doesn't fit
docs.text:
In order of effectiveness:

  1. Enable gradient checkpointing. Biggest win per line of config.
  2. Reduce max_seq_length. 2048 → 1536 or 1024. Truncation is better than OOM, but fix the data if many examples are long.
  3. Reduce num_layers. All 40 → 24 → 16 → 8. You lose adaptation capacity; tool-format learning usually survives, but evaluate.
  4. Batch size 1 + gradient accumulation. Effective batch without activation memory.
  5. Quantize the base to 4-bit. You should already be doing this. 6-bit/8-bit doubles or quadruples weight memory.
  6. Close everything. Chrome, Docker Desktop, Slack, the Kali VM, photo apps. Check memory_pressure.
  7. Raise the wired limit carefully to 24–25 GB, only after the above. sudo sysctl iogpu.wired_limit_mb=24576.
  8. Move to the 8B. A completed 8B run beats a 14B run that dies at hour 40.
  9. Rent a GPU. For runs over ~24 hours, this is usually the rational choice.

Symptom → likely cause:

Symptom Likely cause [metal::malloc] Resource limit (499000) exceeded Descriptor/handle leak or too many wired buffers; reduce layers/seq, restart, update MLX. kIOGPUCommandBufferCallbackErrorOutOfMemory True GPU OOM; reduce memory. Process killed by macOS, no Python traceback Wired-memory pressure / kernel watchdog. Lower the limit or memory use. Swapouts climbing, UI stutters Overcommitted unified memory; close apps or reduce batch. Loss becomes nan Prompt longer than max_seq_length with --mask-prompt (zero completion tokens), or LR too high. Check the data length distribution. Throughput collapses after 30 min Thermal throttling; improve cooling, reduce sustained load.

docs.title: 7. Recommended machine settings
docs.text:
# Inspect
sysctl hw.memsize
sysctl iogpu.wired_limit_mb
python -c "import mlx.core as mx; print(mx.device_info())"
memory_pressure | head
vm_stat | head

# Optional: give the GPU up to 24 GiB (only for a dedicated training session)
sudo sysctl iogpu.wired_limit_mb=24576

# Restore after training / before normal use
sudo sysctl iogpu.wired_limit_mb=0

A note on the Kali VM. An 8 GB Kali VM plus a 20 GB training process plus macOS does not fit in 32 GB. During training, shut the VM down. During evaluation/serving, the training process is gone, so a 4–8 GB VM is fine. Do not run both.

docs.title: 8. What the numbers mean for the rest of the handbook
docs.text:
• Use Qwen3-8B for the first end-to-end run. It will finish in hours and expose format bugs.
  • Use Qwen3-14B for the adapter you keep. Budget 2–5M tokens and 2–4 days.
  • Keep sequences at 2048 unless the data demands more. Agentic trajectories with 5+ turns can exceed 4K; split them per assistant turn instead of raising the limit.
  • Evaluate on a held-out set before scaling the run. More tokens cannot fix a schema mismatch.
  • If you need Qwen3.5/3.8 quality, train in the cloud. The local inference path for those models is fine; the local training path is not.

docs.title: 9. Sources and measurements
docs.text:
• MLX memory and wired limit — https://ml-explore.github.io/mlx/build/html/python/_autosummary/mlx.core.set_wired_limit.html
  • MLX-LM LoRA memory guidance — https://github.com/ml-explore/mlx-lm/blob/main/mlx_lm/LORA.md
  • Qwen3-8B QLoRA on M1 Max, 92–98 tok/s and 7,936/23,040-token limits — https://pypi.org/project/mlx-train-perf/0.8.0/
  • Qwen3.5-9B first-backward OOM at 36 GB — https://github.com/ml-explore/mlx-lm/issues/1206
  • Qwen3.5-27B / 3.8-27B descriptor leak and 60–117 GB peaks — https://github.com/ml-explore/mlx-lm/issues/1185, https://github.com/ml-explore/mlx-lm/pull/1217
  • M1 Pro inference measurements (9B/14B/27B/35B-A3B) — https://omlx.ai/benchmarks/performance
  • Apple Silicon unified-memory sizing — https://llms-explorer.com/tree/apple-silicon-unified-memory-and-llm-sizing/
  • LIMA (data efficiency) — https://arxiv.org/abs/2305.11206

docs.title: 03 — macOS setup from zero
docs.text:
Target: a clean Apple Silicon Mac (M1 Pro, 32 GB) running macOS 26.x. Last verified: 25 October 2026.

This chapter builds a reproducible environment with uv, a project-local virtual environment, and pinned MLX versions. It ends with a smoke test that proves Metal, the model download, and the chat template all work before you spend time on data.

docs.title: 1. What you need
docs.text:
Requirement Notes Apple Silicon Mac M1 or newer. Intel Macs cannot use MLX. 32 GB unified memory 16 GB can do 4B–8B with care; 32 GB is the minimum for a comfortable 14B QLoRA. 100–150 GB free disk Models, checkpoints, fused weights, datasets. macOS 14+ macOS 26.x recommended for the current MLX/Metal stack. Xcode Command Line Tools Metal compiler and headers. Homebrew For uv, python@3.12, git-lfs, jq, optional llama.cpp. Python 3.11 or 3.12 MLX-LM requires ≥3.11. 3.12 is the tested default here. A Hugging Face account Some datasets are gated; a token also avoids rate limits.

You do not need Docker on the Mac for training. Docker is only for the synthetic-data sandbox and the lab, and it should not run during training.

docs.title: 2. Base tools
docs.text:
# 1. Command Line Tools (accept the GUI prompt)
xcode-select --install

# 2. Homebrew (if not installed)
/bin/bash -c "$(curl -fsSL https://raw.githubusercontent.com/Homebrew/install/HEAD/install.sh)"
# Follow the printed instructions to add brew to your PATH (Apple Silicon: /opt/homebrew/bin).

# 3. Core CLI tools
brew update
brew install uv python@3.12 git git-lfs jq htop
git lfs install

# 4. Optional: GGUF conversion and serving
brew install llama.cpp

# 5. Optional: Ollama app (GUI) — https://ollama.com/download

Verify:

sw_vers
uname -m                 # arm64
xcode-select -p
uv --version
python3.12 --version
llama-server --version 2>/dev/null || true

Why uv? It resolves and installs the MLX/transformers dependency tree in seconds, creates isolated environments, and makes the commands reproducible. pip works too, but you will wait longer and hit resolution conflicts more often.

docs.title: 3. Project layout
docs.text:
mkdir -p ~/work/qwen-kali-agent
cd ~/work/qwen-kali-agent
git clone https://github.com/beniaminp/qwen-kali-agent.git .
# or: unzip the handbook and cd into it

mkdir -p data/{raw,interim,processed,golden} \
         adapters fused mlx_models models logs reports

Set a dedicated Hugging Face cache so models do not fill your system drive unexpectedly:

# ~/.zshrc
export HF_HOME="$HOME/work/hf"
export HF_HUB_ENABLE_HF_TRANSFER=1
export TOKENIZERS_PARALLELISM=false

mkdir -p "$HF_HOME"
source ~/.zshrc

HF_HUB_ENABLE_HF_TRANSFER=1 speeds up large downloads but requires hf_transfer (uv pip install hf_transfer). If it causes errors, unset it.

docs.title: 4. Python environment
docs.text:
cd ~/work/qwen-kali-agent

uv venv --python 3.12 .venv
source .venv/bin/activate

# Pin the stack. Check PyPI for the latest patch before a long run.
uv pip install \
  "mlx-lm[train]==0.32.2" \
  "huggingface-hub[cli]" \
  datasets \
  transformers \
  openai \
  pyyaml \
  jsonschema \
  rich \
  tqdm \
  matplotlib

python -c "import mlx.core as mx; print('mlx', mx.__version__ if hasattr(mx,'__version__') else 'ok')"
python -c "import mlx_lm; print('mlx-lm', mlx_lm.__version__)"

As of 25 Oct 2026, the tested pair is mlx-lm 0.32.2 with mlx 0.32.4 and transformers 5.x. MLX-LM 0.32.x requires transformers>=5.7.0; do not downgrade transformers to 4.x without checking the release notes. If you need a fully frozen environment:

uv pip freeze > requirements.lock.txt

Do not install mlx separately from mlx-lm unless you are debugging. mlx-lm pins a compatible MLX; a mismatched pair produces confusing Metal errors.

docs.title: 5. Hugging Face access
docs.text:
hf auth login
# paste a read token from https://huggingface.co/settings/tokens

For gated datasets (xLAM, some cyber sets), accept the terms on the dataset page first, then:

hf download Salesforce/xlam-function-calling-60k --repo-type dataset --local-dir data/raw/xlam

If a repo returns 401, it is gated or does not exist. The dataset research in 05-datasets.md flags the known gated IDs.

docs.title: 6. Verify Metal and the memory budget
docs.text:
python - <<'PY'
import mlx.core as mx
info = mx.device_info()
for k, v in info.items():
    if isinstance(v, int) and v > 1024**2:
        print(f"{k}: {v/1024**3:.2f} GiB")
    else:
        print(f"{k}: {v}")
print("default device:", mx.default_device())
PY

Expected: device_type: gpu, architecture: metal, and max_recommended_working_set_size around 21–22 GiB on a 32 GB machine. If it says CPU, MLX did not build with Metal — reinstall the wheel for arm64 and check that you are not running under Rosetta (uname -m must be arm64).

Check the wired limit:

sysctl iogpu.wired_limit_mb

0 means default. Do not change it yet; the training chapter explains when raising it helps.

Run the environment checker:

python scripts/check_env.py

It reports macOS version, arch, Python, MLX, free disk, RAM, default working set, and whether the expected model/tooling imports succeed.

docs.title: 7. Smoke test: template before training
docs.text:
Download a tiny model and verify the chat template renders tools correctly. This catches template/tokenizer breakage in minutes instead of after a 20-hour run.

python - <<'PY'
from transformers import AutoTokenizer
tok = AutoTokenizer.from_pretrained("Qwen/Qwen3-0.6B")
messages = [
    {"role": "system", "content": "You are a careful security assistant."},
    {"role": "user", "content": "Scan 10.10.10.5 for open services."},
    {"role": "assistant", "tool_calls": [{
        "id": "call_1", "type": "function",
        "function": {"name": "nmap_scan",
                     "arguments": "{\"target\":\"10.10.10.5\",\"flags\":\"-sV\"}"}
    }]},
    {"role": "tool", "tool_call_id": "call_1", "content": "22/tcp open ssh\n80/tcp open http"},
    {"role": "assistant", "content": "Ports 22 and 80 are open."},
]
tools = [{"type": "function", "function": {
    "name": "nmap_scan",
    "description": "Run an nmap scan against an authorized target.",
    "parameters": {"type": "object",
                   "properties": {"target": {"type": "string"},
                                  "flags": {"type": "string"}},
                   "required": ["target"]}}}]
print(tok.apply_chat_template(messages, tools=tools, tokenize=False))
PY

You should see <|im_start|>system, a <tools> block with JSON, <tool_call> with {"name": ..., "arguments": ...}, and a <tool_response> inside a user turn. If the output is truncated, the assistant content is missing, or the tool block is malformed, stop and fix the template before training. Chapter 06-data-format.md explains every line.

docs.title: MLX server
docs.text:
Already installed with mlx-lm:

mlx_lm.server --help | head -40

docs.title: llama.cpp
docs.text:
brew install llama.cpp
llama-server --version
# Conversion scripts live in the Homebrew share or the repo:
# brew --prefix llama.cpp

If the Homebrew build lacks the Python conversion scripts, clone the repo:

git clone https://github.com/ggml-org/llama.cpp ~/work/llama.cpp
cd ~/work/llama.cpp
cmake -B build -DGGML_METAL=ON
cmake --build build --config Release -j

docs.title: Ollama
docs.text:
Install the app, then verify:

ollama --version
ollama list

Ollama runs a background service on 127.0.0.1:11434. It is convenient for GGUF inference, but it cannot apply an MLX/PEFT adapter directory directly; you must fuse and convert first.

docs.title: React / Tailwind toolchain (optional track)
docs.text:
The front-end track needs Node 24 LTS, npm and Playwright browsers:

brew install node@24
node -v            # 24.x LTS
npm -v

# Chromium for Playwright (and the other browsers if you need them)
npx playwright install chromium

Use the project's package-lock.json and npm ci; do not mix package managers in one repo. TypeScript 7 is the latest compiler, but the ESLint toolchain may need the TypeScript 6 API bridge; see 22-react-tailwind.md §1.3.

docs.title: Java / Quarkus toolchain (optional track)
docs.text:
The MLX environment does not need a JDK, but the Java/Quarkus track does:

# Temurin 25 LTS (or install the JDK 25 package from Adoptium)
brew install --cask temurin@25
brew install maven

java -version      # 25.x
mvn -version       # 3.9+

Quarkus projects should use their Maven wrapper (./mvnw), so the system Maven is only a fallback. The Quarkus CLI is optional:

brew install quarkusio/tap/quarkus
quarkus --version

You do not need the CLI to build or test; ./mvnw quarkus:dev and ./mvnw test are enough.

docs.title: Documentation site
docs.text:
Material for MkDocs is separate from the MLX environment, but installs cleanly into the same venv:

uv pip install -r requirements-docs.txt
mkdocs serve --dev-addr 127.0.0.1:8000
mkdocs build --strict

The site is styled as a GitBook (sidebar, search, grouped parts, edit links) and lives in site/. The live copy is https://beniaminp.github.io/qwen-kali-agent/; .github/workflows/docs.yml publishes to gh-pages.

docs.title: 9. Reproducibility notes
docs.text:
• Pin versions before a long run. Write them into requirements.lock.txt and record the git commit of this repo.
  • Record the model revision. from_pretrained(..., revision="<sha>") or hf download ... --revision <sha>. Qwen occasionally updates tokenizer/config files.
  • Record the dataset manifest. A JSON file with each source ID, revision, row count, hash, license.
  • Do not upgrade mid-run. MLX and transformers both move; a resumed checkpoint may not load.
  • Keep the raw data immutable. All cleaning goes to data/interim and data/processed.

docs.title: 10. Common setup failures
docs.text: Symptom Cause Fix ImportError: No module named 'mlx' Wrong Python/venv, or x86 Python under Rosetta uname -m → arm64; recreate the venv with uv venv --python 3.12; ensure the venv is activated. mlx installs but default_device() is CPU Rosetta or an old wheel Reinstall on arm64; check pip debug --verbose platform tags. xcrun: error: invalid active developer path CLT missing/broken xcode-select --install, then sudo xcode-select -s /Applications/Xcode.app/Contents/Developer if needed. OSError: [Errno 28] No space left on device HF cache on a small volume Set HF_HOME to an external/large volume; delete old models--* blobs. 401 from Hugging Face Gated repo or not logged in Accept terms on the website; hf auth login. transformers version conflict mlx-lm 0.32 requires transformers 5.x Let uv resolve; do not force an old pin. metal::malloc on first model load Wired limit too low or another app hogging GPU Close apps; check mx.device_info(); reboot if a leaked process persists. Extremely slow first run Model download + Metal shader compilation The first generation compiles kernels; subsequent runs are faster.

docs.title: 11. Sources
docs.text:
• MLX-LM installation and training — https://github.com/ml-explore/mlx-lm
  • MLX-LM LoRA guide — https://github.com/ml-explore/mlx-lm/blob/main/mlx_lm/LORA.md
  • MLX device info / wired limit — https://ml-explore.github.io/mlx/build/html/python/_autosummary/mlx.core.set_wired_limit.html
  • uv — https://docs.astral.sh/uv/
  • Hugging Face CLI — https://huggingface.co/docs/huggingface_hub/guides/cli
  • llama.cpp build — https://github.com/ggml-org/llama.cpp/blob/master/docs/build.md
  • Ollama macOS — https://docs.ollama.com/macos

docs.title: 04 — Data strategy: what the model must learn
docs.text:
Last verified: 25 October 2026.

A tool-calling model is not trained by showing it “cybersecurity text”. It is trained by showing it decisions inside an environment: which tool to call, with which arguments, in what order, what to do with the observation, and when to stop. This chapter defines the capability taxonomy, the token budget, the mix, the curriculum, and the quality gates.

The companion chapter 05-datasets.md is the catalog of where to get the data. This chapter is the architecture of the mix.

docs.title: 1. The six capabilities
docs.text:
Every training example should serve at least one of these. If you cannot name which one, delete it.

# Capability What it looks like Failure if missing 1 Tool selection “Given these 8 tools and this request, call nmap_scan, not http_request.” Wrong tool, or a plausible but useless call. 2 Argument construction Valid JSON, correct types, enums, required fields, target from scope. Schema errors, scans against the wrong host. 3 Sequencing recon → enumerate → verify → report; one call at a time or parallel where safe. Random tool spam, repeated calls, no progress. 4 Observation handling Parse stdout/stderr/exit code, notice “connection refused”, adapt. Ignores errors, repeats the same failing command. 5 Recovery Timeout → smaller scan; auth failure → check credentials/scope; no result → try a different service. Gives up, hallucinates results, or escalates destructively. 6 Scope and refusal “That target is outside the authorized scope; I need written authorization.” Scans third parties, runs destructive commands, leaks data.

A dataset that only teaches #1 and #2 produces a model that can call a tool but cannot run a task. A dataset that only teaches #6 produces a model that refuses everything. The mix must cover all six.

docs.title: 2. What “agentic” means here
docs.text:
The target loop is:

system prompt + tools + scope
        │
        ▼
   model plans / decides
        │
        ├── no tool needed → answer
        └── tool call(s) ──► policy layer ──► lab target
                                  │
                                  ▼
                           observation (stdout/stderr/exit)
                                  │
                                  ▼
                         model reflects, repeats

Training data must mirror this loop, not a single-turn Q&A. Concretely, each trajectory should contain:

  • a system prompt that states the role, the authorized scope, and the tool rules;
  • a user task with a target, a goal, and constraints;
  • zero or more assistant tool calls with realistic arguments;
  • matching tool responses (real execution output, not invented);
  • a final assistant answer that summarizes evidence and next steps;
  • optionally, a refusal or clarification when the request is out of scope or ambiguous.

If your data has no role: "tool" messages, it is tool-calling data, not agentic data. Both are useful, but they teach different things.

docs.title: 3. Token budget, not row count
docs.text:
Rows are a bad unit because a row can be 200 tokens or 20,000. Plan in tokens.

Stage Training tokens Purpose Local wall-clock (14B @ 25 tok/s) Format smoke test 50K–200K prove the template, masking, and tool JSON 1–2 h First adapter 1–2M learn the tool surface and domain vocabulary 11–22 h Serious adapter 3–5M add recovery, multi-turn, refusal behavior 33–56 h Scale-up 10M+ only if eval shows underfitting 4–5 days

Build a larger pool than you train on. A 45–90M-token pool lets you sample different mixes and re-run after an evaluation failure. You do not need to train on all of it. Sampling 2–5M high-quality tokens from a 50M pool is normal and desirable.

The 90M-token reference mix in 05-datasets.md is a pool design, not a single local run. Training it end-to-end on this Mac would take weeks. Use it for cloud runs or multi-stage local experiments.

docs.title: 4. The mix
docs.text:
Start with this target, then adjust based on the evaluation failure taxonomy.

Bucket Share What it buys Candidate sources General tool calling 35–40% schema adherence, argument JSON, parallel calls, tool choice xLAM, ToolACE, Hermes, Glaive (filtered), Toucan Multi-turn / agentic 15–20% observe → act, error recovery, long horizons ToolACE, SWE-smith, Nemotron Terminal, OpenThoughts, APIGen-MT (internal only) Cyber QA + Kali CLI 20% vocabulary, flags, procedures, reporting KaliBench train, Trendyol, filtered cyber QA Synthetic verified trajectories 15% your tools, your scope policy, your lab generated with DeepSeek/OpenCode, executed in the sandbox Refusal / scope / no-call 10% authorization checks, ask vs act, abstain When2Call, curated scope dialogues, negative examples

docs.title: Why these proportions?
docs.text:
• General tool calling is the grammar. If the model cannot emit valid JSON or choose among tools, domain knowledge is irrelevant. It gets the largest share because it is the prerequisite.
  • Agentic data is the behavior. A model trained only on single-turn calls will answer “run nmap” with a call and then stop. Multi-turn trajectories teach it to look at the result and continue.
  • Cyber QA is the vocabulary. Kali has 1,600+ tools and thousands of flags. A general model knows some; targeted data fixes the long tail.
  • Synthetic trajectories are the alignment. Public data does not know your tool names, your scope file, or your lab topology. Generate that.
  • Refusal is a capability, not a tax. A pentest agent that scans an out-of-scope host is a liability. Train the refusal explicitly, and evaluate it separately.

docs.title: The minimal viable mix (~2–5M tokens)
docs.text:
Bucket Rows (approx.) Tokens (approx.) General tool calling 8–15k 1.2–2M Agentic 1–3k 0.5–1M Cyber QA + Kali CLI 5–10k 0.5–1M Synthetic trajectories 1–3k 0.5–1M Refusal/scope 2–4k 0.3–0.6M

Do not obsess over exact percentages at this scale. Cover every bucket, keep the quality high, and iterate.

docs.title: 5. Curriculum
docs.text:
A strict multi-stage curriculum is hard to tune at 2–5M tokens. Use a mild easy→hard ramp with a refusal-heavy anneal:

  1. Warm-up (10%). Short, single-turn examples with simple schemas: KaliBench easy rows, Hermes single-turn, a few xLAM rows. Goal: learn <tool_call> syntax and JSON validity.
  2. Bulk (60%). Shuffled multi-turn tool+observation data, terminal trajectories, cyber QA. Shuffle by bucket, not by row, so each batch sees a mix of formats. This prevents catastrophic forgetting of one format.
  3. Cyber-heavy (20%). KaliBench ×2–3, Trendyol, synthetic Kali trajectories, converted explanations. Goal: domain depth.
  4. Anneal (10%). Refusal/scope/no-call examples at a lower learning rate, plus 5% general-tool replay. Goal: end on the behavior you want, without making the model refuse everything.

Sprinkle ~30% of the refusal examples through stages 1–3 as well. If all refusals are at the end, the model may overfit to “refuse” as a global style.

Do not train a “cyber-only” model and then bolt on tool calling. The tool format is the fragile part; it needs constant rehearsal.

docs.title: 6. Licensing strategy
docs.text:
Decide before you download whether the adapter will be published.

Intended release Allowed data Avoid Private / internal only Almost anything you have lawful access to; still respect terms Leaked data, live credentials, unlicensed writeups Public adapter (Apache/MIT) Apache-2.0, MIT, CC-BY-4.0 (with attribution) CC-BY-NC, CC-BY-NC-SA, GPL, “unknown” Commercial product Apache-2.0, MIT, CC-BY-4.0, commercially licensed NC, SA, GPL, unlicensed scrapes

The big traps:

  • APIGen-MT-5k is CC-BY-NC-4.0. It is one of the best multi-turn sets, and it cannot go into a published/commercial model without a separate license. Keep it in an internal ablation.
  • NYU CTF Bench is GPL-2.0. Treat it as evaluation-only; do not redistribute derived data.
  • SecEval's mirror is CC-BY-NC-SA-4.0. The share-alike clause compounds.
  • Mirrors relicense xLAM as MIT/Apache. That does not override Salesforce's CC-BY-4.0. Trace to the origin.
  • “Unknown” means all rights reserved. Do not publish a model trained on it.

Record the license of every source in the dataset manifest. If you cannot identify the license, do not use the source in a release mix.

docs.title: 7. Decontamination
docs.text:
Public benchmarks are contaminated by public training data. If you train on BFCL, KaliBench test, Cybench, NYU CTF or CyberMetric, your evaluation is meaningless.

Minimum procedure:

  1. Hold out the benchmark files physically. Keep them in data/benchmarks/, never in data/processed/.
  2. 13-gram overlap. Normalize whitespace/case, tokenize into 13-grams, and remove any training example with ≥1 overlapping 13-gram with a benchmark item. This is conservative but catches verbatim leakage.
  3. Near-duplicate check. MinHash/SimHash within the training set (threshold ~0.8 Jaccard) and against the benchmark.
  4. Canary strings. Insert a unique canary into each benchmark item and check the model never emits it. Useful for detecting leakage in a published checkpoint.
  5. Report the method and the overlap rate. “0.7% of training rows removed by 13-gram overlap” is a result; silence is not.

KaliBench's public train/test splits have zero exact query overlap, but both are public. A model trained after release may still have seen the test split through other corpora. Use it as a reported benchmark, not as your only holdout.

docs.title: 8. Splits and the golden set
docs.text:
Split Purpose Size Rule train.jsonl optimization 90% of the mix may overlap public training sources valid.jsonl early stopping / model selection 5% same distribution as train, no exact duplicates test.jsonl final internal check 5% held out before any tuning; touch once golden.jsonl behavioral evaluation 200–300 tasks hand-written or lab-generated; never in train benchmarks/ external comparison official sets never in train

The golden set is the most valuable asset in the project. Write it before training, from real lab tasks, with expected tool names/arguments and pass criteria. If you write it after seeing the model's outputs, you will unconsciously make it easy.

A good golden set covers:

  • 60 single-tool tasks (selection + arguments),
  • 60 multi-step tasks (2–6 calls, one recovery),
  • 40 refusal/scope tasks (out-of-scope target, ambiguous authorization, destructive request),
  • 20 no-call tasks (answer from knowledge, no tool needed),
  • 20 malformed-input tasks (bad JSON, missing target, tool error),
  • 20 reporting tasks (summarize evidence, cite the command/output).

docs.title: 9. Dataset manifest and card
docs.text:
Every dataset version gets a manifest:

{
  "version": "2026-10-25.v1",
  "created": "2026-10-25T12:00:00Z",
  "sources": [
    {"id": "Team-ACE/ToolACE", "revision": "abc123", "rows": 11300, "license": "Apache-2.0", "hash": "sha256:..."},
    {"id": "RISys-Lab/KaliBench", "revision": "def456", "rows": 3504, "license": "CC-BY-4.0", "hash": "sha256:..."}
  ],
  "counts": {"train": 48000, "valid": 2500, "test": 2500},
  "tokens": {"train": 4200000, "valid": 210000, "test": 210000},
  "decontamination": {"method": "13-gram", "removed": 312},
  "known_issues": ["APIGen-MT excluded from release mix (CC-BY-NC)"]
}

And a dataset card covering: intended use, out-of-scope use, sources/licenses, collection method, preprocessing, personal/sensitive data, biases, evaluation, maintenance. The scripts/make_dataset_card.py helper generates the skeleton.

docs.title: 10. Common mistakes
docs.text: Mistake Why it hurts Fix Training on 500k rows because “more data is better” Weeks of compute, diluted quality, overfitting to noise Start with 1–2M curated tokens; measure. Mixing tool-call syntaxes in one run Model learns neither format reliably Normalize everything to the target model's template. Using the test split for early stopping Inflates results Three splits + a separate golden set. No refusal examples Agent scans anything it is asked to 10% refusal/scope/no-call, plus a policy layer. Synthetic data without execution Model learns plausible but wrong command output Execute in a sandbox; keep only verified trajectories. Truncating mid-tool-call Teaches malformed JSON Split per assistant turn; filter by token length. Ignoring licenses until release day Cannot publish the adapter License audit before download. No dataset version Cannot reproduce a good run Manifest + git tag + hash.

docs.title: 05 — Datasets: a verified catalog
docs.text:
Last verified: 25 October 2026. Row counts come from the Hugging Face datasets-server where available; token counts are chars/4 estimates and are marked “est.” Gated repos return 401 for both “gated” and “does not exist”, so gated IDs were cross-checked against the author's public listing.

This chapter is the shopping list. It covers general tool calling, agentic trajectories, and cybersecurity/pentest data, with the license, schema, quality and conversion notes you need before downloading anything.

Read 04-data-strategy.md first. This catalog is not a recommendation to train on everything. Most of these sets are raw material; the mix decides what enters a run.

Looking for Java/Quarkus or React/Tailwind data? They have their own catalogs in 19 — Java datasets and 23 — React datasets.

NousResearch/hermes-function-calling-v1 11,578 (5 configs) 21.7 MB; ≈4.1M tok (func_calling) Apache-2.0 conversations, tools, category Qwen-shaped, small, mixed quality. glaiveai/glaive-function-calling-v2 112,960 97 MB; ≈75.9M tok Apache-2.0 system, chat strings 2023-era; trivial calls, format noise. Use sparingly. nvidia/When2Call 15,000 SFT; 9,000 pref; 3,652 MCQ 12.5 MB; ≈5.4M tok CC-BY-4.0 tools, messages Essential for call-vs-ask-vs-abstain. argilla/apigen-function-calling 109,402 60 MB; ≈44.4M tok CC-BY-4.0 answers, query, tools, origin xLAM (60k) + Synth-APIGen (49.4k); needs prep. docs.title: xLAM — breadth, with schema debt
docs.text:
The APIGen pipeline generated 60k samples over 3,673 executable APIs and verified them by format checking, real execution and semantic checks (arXiv:2406.18518). It is excellent for teaching the model to choose among many tools and to produce multi-argument calls.

Its schema is not OpenAI JSON Schema. parameters is a map of param → {type: "str"|"int"|"List", description}, with no top-level "type":"object" and no required array. A sample found 940 of 58,105 tool definitions with a non-object top-level type. Convert:

# Old: {"location": {"type": "str", "description": "..."}}
# New:
{"type": "object",
 "properties": {"location": {"type": "string", "description": "..."}},
 "required": ["location"]}

Never invent a required value; infer it from the reference call's arguments only if the original schema marks it. If the type is ambiguous, drop the field from the schema rather than guess.

xLAM is single-turn and has no tool responses. It teaches selection and arguments, not observation handling.

docs.title: ToolACE — the best open multi-turn set
docs.text:
26,507 APIs, dual rule/model verification, and a formal thinking process (arXiv:2409.00920). The entire tool list sits in system, so rows are long. Calls are not JSON:

[Market Trends API(trend_type="MARKET_INDEXES")]

Tool results are from: "tool" JSON blobs. Tool names contain spaces ("Get Manager Placeholder Image"), and schemas use "type":"dict". Every row needs parsing, name normalization ([A-Za-z0-9_-]), and schema rewriting. It has genuine multi-turn observation loops and chit-chat turns, which help “don't call a tool” behavior.

docs.title: Hermes — Qwen-shaped and small
docs.text: Five configs: single-turn (1,893), multi-turn (1,893), Glaive-derived (5,209), and JSON-mode sets. The format is already Qwen-adjacent: <tools>[...]</tools> in the system message, <tool_call>{"name","arguments"}</tool_call>, <tool_response>. The glaive_* config inherits Glaive's flaws; the json_mode_* configs teach structured output, not tools. Use the clean single/multi-turn configs as a small, cheap supplement.

docs.title: Glaive — volume, not quality
docs.text: 112,960 rows, but 2023-era: system is a "SYSTEM: ..." string, chat uses USER:/ASSISTANT: with <functioncall> {"name":..., "arguments": '{"k":"v"}'} (arguments is a string), and FUNCTION RESPONSE: turns. Single-turn bias, trivial calls, inconsistent refusal behavior, occasional arithmetic errors inside arguments. Filter aggressively; use only as format seasoning.

docs.title: When2Call — the refusal set you need
docs.text: Explicitly benchmarks “when to call, when to ask a follow-up, when to admit the tools cannot answer” (arXiv:2504.18851). This is the single most relevant public set for scope/authorization behavior, and it is CC-BY-4.0 with commercial use stated on the card. Caveat: synthetic and benchmark-shaped; add your own Kali-specific scope dialogues.

docs.title: APIGen-MT-5k — great, but non-commercial
docs.text: Simulated human–agent interplay with clarification questions, function_call/observation turns, and an explicit think tool call (arXiv:2504.03601). 5.2k tokens/row; the best public multi-turn realism. CC-BY-NC-4.0 — internal experiments and evaluation only, never in a model you publish or sell.

docs.title: Toucan — the 2025 scale option
docs.text: 495 real MCP servers, 2,000+ tools, trajectories from Qwen3-32B, Kimi-K2 and GPT-OSS-120B, with LLM-judge quality fields and an irrelevant subset that is effectively negative/no-call data (arXiv:2510.01179). Apache-2.0. Start from the 119k-row SFT config; filter to the top judge bands and trajectories under ~6k tokens.

docs.title: 2. Agentic / terminal / software-agent trajectories

docs.title: Which teach recovery?
docs.text:
• SWE-smith is the strongest open signal: 50k+ injected bugs, failing tests, and 76k full trajectories in three serializations (tool, xml, ticks), MIT (arXiv:2504.21798). The trajectory subset is large; sample it.
  • SWE-Gym adds 2,438 real tasks and 491 curated OpenHands traces (arXiv:2412.21139).
  • Nemotron Terminal Pivot is the most directly transferable to a shell agent: 31k trajectories built around recovery/pivot behavior, bash_command as the tool, terminus-2 prompts.

docs.title: Format warning: terminus-2 vs tool_calls
docs.text:
OpenThoughts, AgentTrove and Nemotron terminal use the terminus-2 JSON convention:

{"analysis": "...", "plan": "...", "commands": [{"keystrokes": "nmap -sV 10.10.10.5\n"}]}

This is not OpenAI tool_calls. Convert commands[] into one bash call per command, move analysis/plan to reasoning_content, and keep environment output in role:"tool". Do not train raw terminus-2 if you also want native <tool_call> reliability — the formats compete.

docs.title: ToolBench / ToolLLM
docs.text: 16,464 RapidAPI tools and DFS-generated solution paths (arXiv:2307.16789). The canonical HF repo did not resolve publicly on 25 Oct 2026 (401; author listing empty), so use the GitHub release or a verified mirror — UNVERIFIED as an HF source. Largely superseded, and its API data is stale.

docs.title: TheAgentCompany
docs.text: A benchmark, not SFT data; only TheAgentCompany/ubuntu_os_images is public. OpenHands/OpenHands-Trajectories and SWE-Gym/SWE-Gym-OpenHands-Trajectories did not resolve publicly on 25 Oct 2026 (UNVERIFIED). The public SWE-Gym trajectory repo is SWE-Gym/OpenHands-SFT-Trajectories.

docs.title: KaliBench — the best CLI set, the weakest attack set
docs.text:
8,504 query–command pairs, 1,642 tools, 23 capability dimensions, documentation-grounded generation, multi-stage verification (LLM, sandboxed execution, human review); NeurIPS 2026 D&B (arXiv:2610.02206).

Measured properties:

  • 3,504 train / 5,000 test, zero exact query overlap;
  • 962 vs 1,642 tools;
  • only 32 train rows (0.9%) use a canonical offensive tool (nmap, sqlmap, hydra, msfconsole);
  • top tools are gdb, mailer, airmon-ng, pwsh, pedis, ld.lld, rva2ofs;
  • 20.1% of commands have no flags;
  • 5.5% are version-style commands;
  • average command length 5.13 tokens;
  • 157 of 962 tools appear once;
  • only 31 use sudo.

It teaches flag/argument fidelity on obscure util-linux binaries, not recon or exploitation sequencing. Both splits are public, so the test set is not a clean holdout for models trained after release.

docs.title: The 322k-row “pentest agent” set is a CVE FAQ
docs.text: All 322,511 rows scanned: 310,428 mention a CVE, only 1,343 (0.4%) contain a fenced code block, mean answer length 59 words, only 714 prompts mention “exploit”, and 69,480 rows (21.5%) are ** RESERVED ** or rejected-CVE placeholders. 310,306 unique CVEs, zero multi-turn rows. Usable only as a filtered CVE subset (drop reserved, require ≥60 words and a reference), never as agentic data.

docs.title: Trendyol is clean but defensive
docs.text: 53,201 rows, zero exact duplicates, two malformed rows, mean 275 words, 0.3% code fences, 1,628 prompts containing offensive terms. Its uniform system prompt is a strong refusal/scope template; copying it verbatim will over-refuse. Paraphrase a shorter policy.

docs.title: Junk is common
docs.text: 0dAI answers a MediaWiki SVG question with fdroid/curl root@x00 gibberish; WNT3D echoes its input; theelderemo tests recognition, not procedure. iselabvn/Kali-tool-calling is the cleanest small set (reasoning_content + tool_calls for exec), but only 790 rows.

docs.title: 4. Licensing and compliance
docs.text:
License Datasets Publishable model? Apache-2.0 ToolACE, Hermes, Glaive, Toucan, OpenThoughts, AgentTrove, Trendyol, Nemotron sets, BFCL, Cybench Yes, with NOTICE/attribution MIT SWE-Gym, SWE-smith, WNT3D (provenance caveat) Yes CC-BY-4.0 xLAM, When2Call, argilla/apigen, KaliBench, CyberMetric (mirror), yatin Yes, with attribution CC-BY-NC-4.0 APIGen-MT-5k, Salesforce APIGen-MT-30k No for a commercial/published model CC-BY-NC-SA-4.0 SecEval mirror No; share-alike compounds GPL-2.0 NYU CTF Bench, ExploitDB Risky; exclude from a publishable mix "other"/custom WhiteRabbitNeo WRN, MITRE ATT&CK Read terms; assume restricted None justinwangx/CTFtime, suryanshp1, resk-fr, XuanwuAI/SecEval, HackTricks No — all rights reserved by default

Three traps:

  1. Non-commercial contagion. APIGen-MT-5k is the best multi-turn set and is CC-BY-NC. Keep it in an internal-only ablation. Whether NC-trained weights are a “derivative” is legally unsettled; treat them as unsafe to publish (UNVERIFIED legal conclusion).
  2. Copyleft data. NYU CTF Bench is GPL-2.0. Training is probably not distribution; redistributing a derived dataset is, and the model-release question is unresolved. ExploitDB is GPL-2.0, which contaminates the 322k set despite its Apache-2.0 tag. theelderemo claims Apache-2.0 over HackTricks/MITRE content, and HackTricks has no SPDX license file (UNVERIFIED). Prefer KaliBench/Trendyol for the cyber core.
  3. License laundering. Mirrors relicense xLAM as MIT/Apache; neither can override Salesforce's CC-BY-4.0. Trace every mirror to the origin and record the origin ID.

Leaked CTF/writeup risk. Challenge files, flags and writeups are copyrighted by organisers; some flags are still live. justinwangx/CTFtime (18,013 writeup chunks, no license) and ethz-spylab/ctf-satml24 (AI-control transcripts, not pentest) should not enter a released model. Generate CTF-style reasoning in your own lab; use Apache-2.0 Docker benchmarks for evaluation only.

docs.title: 5. Benchmarks to hold out
docs.text:
Benchmark Size License What it measures Use BFCL ~2k questions across v3/v4 categories Apache-2.0 function selection, argument validity, parallel/multiple calls, irrelevance primary tool-call holdout KaliBench test 5,000 CC-BY-4.0 NL→Kali command accuracy CLI holdout (public, so report contamination) Cybench 40 CTF tasks, 4 competitions Apache-2.0 end-to-end offensive security in Docker agentic holdout NYU CTF Bench 200 test + 55 dev GPL-2.0 CTF challenge solving evaluation only, not release mix AutoPenBench ~30 scenarios see repo autonomous pentest workflow agentic holdout CyberMetric 80/500/2,000/10,000 MCQ Apache-2.0 (mirror) cybersecurity knowledge knowledge check, not agent behavior SecEval 2,000+ MCQ mirror CC-BY-NC-SA security knowledge evaluation only Terminal-Bench terminal tasks see repo shell agent competence optional

Holdout discipline: put the official files in data/benchmarks/ and never symlink them into data/processed/. Run the 13-gram decontamination from 04-data-strategy.md §7 and report the overlap rate.

docs.title: 6. Recommended downloads
docs.text:
Start with a minimal shopping list. All commands assume hf (Hugging Face CLI) is installed and you are logged in.

mkdir -p data/raw && cd data/raw

# General tool calling
hf download Team-ACE/ToolACE --repo-type dataset --local-dir ToolACE
hf download NousResearch/hermes-function-calling-v1 --repo-type dataset --local-dir hermes-fc
hf download nvidia/When2Call --repo-type dataset --local-dir When2Call
hf download Agent-Ark/Toucan-1.5M --repo-type dataset --local-dir Toucan --include "sft/*"

# Agentic / terminal (sample, do not download all 3 GB unless needed)
hf download SWE-bench/SWE-smith-trajectories --repo-type dataset --local-dir swe-smith-trajectories --include "tool/*"
hf download nvidia/Nemotron-RL-Agentic-Terminal-Pivot-v1 --repo-type dataset --local-dir nemotron-terminal

# Cyber
hf download RISys-Lab/KaliBench --repo-type dataset --local-dir KaliBench
hf download Trendyol/Trendyol-Cybersecurity-Instruction-Tuning-Dataset --repo-type dataset --local-dir trendyol-cyber
hf download iselabvn/Kali-tool-calling --repo-type dataset --local-dir kali-tool-calling

# Gated: accept the terms on the dataset page first
hf download Salesforce/xlam-function-calling-60k --repo-type dataset --local-dir xlam

If a download fails with 401, check the dataset page for a gated agreement. Do not use a mirror that relicenses the data.

docs.title: 7. Conversion recipes
docs.text:
The target format is always:

{"messages": [...], "tools": [OpenAI tool schemas]}

Detailed rules and examples are in 06-data-format.md. The per-dataset mapping:

docs.title: xLAM
docs.text:
query                         → messages[0] user
tools (JSON string)           → tools (parse; repair parameters)
answers (JSON string)         → assistant tool_calls (arguments JSON-stringified)

Repair schema: parameters = {"type":"object","properties":...,"required":[...]}. If answers contains multiple calls, emit multiple tool_calls in one assistant message.

docs.title: ToolACE
docs.text:
system                        → messages[0] system (keep; it contains the tool list)
conversations[from=user]      → user
conversations[from=assistant] → assistant; parse `[Name(arg="v")]` into tool_calls
conversations[from=tool]      → tool (content)

Normalize tool names to [A-Za-z0-9_-]; rewrite the tools array from the system block; "dict" → "object".

docs.title: Hermes
docs.text: Already close. Keep <tools> content as the tools array, parse <tool_call> JSON, map tool responses to role:"tool", and strip the Hermes wrapper tokens (the Qwen template will add its own).

docs.title: Glaive
docs.text:
system "SYSTEM: ..."           → system (strip prefix)
USER: ...                      → user
ASSISTANT: <functioncall> ...  → assistant tool_calls (arguments is a JSON string)
FUNCTION RESPONSE: ...         → tool

Filter rows with arithmetic errors or trivial calls.

docs.title: APIGen-MT
docs.text:
human         → user
gpt           → assistant
function_call → assistant tool_calls
observation   → tool
think         → reasoning_content (or a `think` tool call, depending on the source)

Internal-only because of CC-BY-NC.

docs.title: When2Call
docs.text: Keep the tools + messages structure. Preserve the “ask a follow-up” and “cannot answer with these tools” turns; they are the point. Do not convert every turn into a tool call.

docs.title: Terminus-2 (OpenThoughts, AgentTrove, Nemotron)
docs.text:
analysis/plan → reasoning_content
commands[]    → one `bash` tool call per command (arguments: {"command": "..."})
environment   → tool response

Do not mix terminus-2 and native <tool_call> in the same training run without labeling the format in the system prompt.

docs.title: KaliBench
docs.text:
query                         → user
command + args                → assistant tool_call to `kali_exec`

Use the structured arguments if present; otherwise pass the command string. Hold out the test split. Note that only 0.9% of train rows are offensive tools; supplement with synthetic recon/enumeration trajectories.

docs.title: Trendyol
docs.text: Already system/user/assistant. Keep as cyber QA. Shorten the uniform system prompt; otherwise the model learns to over-refuse.

docs.title: 8. Quality filtering and red flags
docs.text:
General filters:

  • exact duplicate removal (hash of normalized messages),
  • near-duplicate removal (MinHash, Jaccard ≥ 0.8),
  • token length within the chosen max sequence (or split),
  • valid JSON for every tool call,
  • tool names exist in the tools array,
  • required arguments present,
  • no empty assistant messages,
  • no tool response without a preceding call.

Cyber-specific red flags:

  • commands against public IPs/domains that are not lab targets,
  • real credentials, API keys, tokens, hashes of live systems,
  • destructive commands (rm -rf /, mkfs, fork bombs, dd to devices) presented without a lab context,
  • exploit code with no defensive/authorized context,
  • live flags from CTF challenges,
  • personally identifiable data,
  • instructions to evade logging or law enforcement,
  • “scan the internet” / “find vulnerable hosts” style tasks.

Quarantine flagged rows for human review. Do not silently delete them; the quarantine set is useful for training refusal behavior.
