docs.title: 18 — Java & Quarkus: versions, architecture and the model to train
docs.text:
Last verified: 25 October 2026. Version facts were checked against the Quarkus releases page, the Quarkus 3.31/3.40/4.0 posts, OpenJDK and Oracle roadmaps.

If you want one Qwen3 base for Kali, Java and React instead of a Java-specific coder, see 26 — One Qwen3 for all. The Java-specific adapter here is still the higher-quality option for Java.

For a second base, see the parallel Gemma 4 12B track; compare both on the same Maven/ArchUnit tasks before switching.

This is the start of the Java/Quarkus track. It answers three questions before any training:

  1. Which Java and Quarkus versions should the model target?
  2. What does “Java architecture” mean in a Quarkus codebase, concretely?
  3. Which Qwen coder can actually be fine-tuned on a 32 GB M1 Pro?

The short answers:

  • Java 25 LTS + Quarkus 3.40 LTS for production-shaped training data.
  • Hexagonal/DDD boundaries + SOLID + ArchUnit as the architecture contract.
  • Qwen2.5-Coder-14B-Instruct 4-bit QLoRA locally; Qwen3-Coder-30B-A3B as teacher/judge, not as a local training target.

docs.title: 1. Which “latest” do you target?
docs.text:
“Latest” is ambiguous in the Java ecosystem because there are two release trains: the six-month JDK train and the Quarkus LTS train.

Component Latest as of 25 Oct 2026 Status Use in this handbook Java 25 25.0.x LTS, released 16 Sep 2025, supported to 2030 Primary target Java 27 27.0.x Non-LTS, released 15 Sep 2026, supported to Mar 2027 Feature previews / migration evals only Java 21 21.0.x Previous LTS Legacy compatibility target Quarkus 3.40 LTS 3.40.1.1 (19 Oct 2026) LTS, released 30 Sep 2026, supported to Sep 2027 Primary target Quarkus 3.33 LTS 3.33.4.x LTS, supported to Mar 2027 Legacy migration source Quarkus 4.0.0.Beta1 Beta 1 (1 Oct 2026) Beta; GA planned end of Nov 2026 Migration evaluation only Maven 3.9.x Required by Quarkus 3.31+ Build tool

docs.title: Why Java 25 LTS
docs.text: Java 25 is the current long-term-support release. Quarkus 3.31 added full Java 25 support, including Java 25 runtime images and Mandrel native-image builds; 3.40 inherits that. Java 27 is a six-month, non-LTS release: it is useful for previewing features, but training a production assistant on Java 27-only idioms creates code that many teams cannot run.

docs.title: Why Quarkus 3.40 LTS
docs.text: Quarkus 3.40 is the latest LTS and the recommended production line. It receives critical fixes and security patches for 12 months. Quarkus 4.0 is a major change (Java 21 baseline, Jakarta EE 11, Hibernate ORM 8, Jackson 3, CDI 5, Netty 4.2/Vert.x 5) and is still Beta as of this writing. Do not mix 4.0 idioms into a 3.40 adapter.

docs.title: The version policy for training data
docs.text:
Primary:   Java 25 LTS + Quarkus 3.40 LTS + Maven 3.9 + Jakarta EE
Legacy:    Java 21 LTS + Quarkus 3.33 LTS
Migration: Quarkus 3.33 -> 3.40, Java 21 -> 25
Future:    Quarkus 4.0 migration tasks, evaluation only until GA

Tag every example with its target versions. A model trained on a mix of Quarkus 2 (javax.*), Quarkus 3 (jakarta.*) and Quarkus 4 (Jackson 3, Hibernate 8) without tags will produce a plausible but unbuildable blend.

docs.title: 2. Why Quarkus is a good fine-tuning target
docs.text:
Quarkus is opinionated in ways a model can learn:

  • Build-time augmentation. Much of the wiring happens at build time, so the generated project shape matters.
  • CDI everywhere. @ApplicationScoped, constructor injection, producers, interceptors, qualifiers.
  • RESTEasy Reactive / Quarkus REST. @Path, @GET, @POST, @Valid, Response.
  • Panache. Active Record or repository pattern over Hibernate ORM.
  • Configuration. application.properties and @ConfigMapping.
  • Testing. @QuarkusTest, RestAssured, Dev Services, @QuarkusIntegrationTest.
  • Native image. ./mvnw package -Dnative, Mandrel, reflection/resource registration.
  • Standards. Jakarta REST, CDI, Bean Validation, JPA, JSON-B/Jackson, MicroProfile.

That gives you a finite, checkable idiom set: imports, annotations, package layout, test style, configuration keys. It is exactly the kind of thing a LoRA can learn from a few thousand high-quality examples.

Quarkus also has a large permissive corpus: the framework, quickstarts, guides and thousands of extensions are Apache-2.0. There is no ready-made “Quarkus instruction” dataset, but the raw material is unusually clean.

docs.title: 3. What the model must learn
docs.text:
Layer Skills Examples Java language records, sealed types, pattern matching, generics, streams, Optional, exceptions, virtual threads, text blocks, try-with-resources domain models, value objects, parsers, concurrency Quarkus CDI scopes, constructor injection, Quarkus REST, Panache, validation, config, security, messaging, scheduling, native endpoints, repositories, DTOs, exception mappers, tests Architecture SOLID, hexagonal ports/adapters, DDD aggregates, package boundaries, coupling/cohesion refactors, reviews, ArchUnit rules Engineering Maven, JUnit, RestAssured, Testcontainers, logging, error handling, transactions, migrations patches, test suites, upgrade tasks Agent behaviour read before edit, patch format, run tests, diagnose failures, stop and ask tool trajectories

The model does not need to memorize the entire Quarkus reference. It needs to know the shape of a good Quarkus change and when to look things up.

docs.title: 4.1 The local recommendation
docs.text: Model Params Context Local training on 32 GB Role Qwen2.5-Coder-14B-Instruct 14.7B 32K configured, 128K with RoPE scaling Yes, 4-bit QLoRA, 24 of 48 blocks Primary local adapter Qwen2.5-Coder-7B-Instruct 7.6B 32K / 128K Yes, all layers Smoke test, fast iteration Qwen2.5-Coder-32B-Instruct 32.5B 32K / 128K Inference only at 4-bit Occasional judge/teacher on a bigger machine Qwen3-Coder-30B-A3B-Instruct 30.5B total / 3.3B active 256K native No — inference/teacher only on 32 GB Teacher, judge, bulk generation Qwen3-Coder-Next 80B total / 3B active 256K No Too large for 32 GB; API/rented GPU Qwen3-14B 14B 32K Yes General-agent fallback, less code-specialised

docs.title: Why Qwen2.5-Coder-14B for local training
docs.text:
• It is code-specialised and strong on Java, not a general chat model that happens to write code.
  • 14.7B at 4-bit is about 8.5–9 GB of weights; a 24-block rank-16 adapter plus activations fits in 32 GB with gradient checkpointing.
  • It has a 128K context window (32K in the default config); you still train at 2K–4K because activation memory, not context length, is the constraint.
  • It is Apache-2.0 and has an MLX 4-bit conversion.
  • It has no Gated DeltaNet training problem; it uses standard attention.

docs.title: Why not Qwen3-Coder-30B-A3B locally
docs.text:
Qwen3-Coder-30B-A3B is the better coder and agent, with 256K context and strong repository-level behaviour. But:

  • 30.5B total parameters at 4-bit is roughly 18–20 GB before activations.
  • Training a 30B MoE with LoRA on 32 GB is not a supported, reliable MLX path; MoE routing and optimizer memory are the problems, not just weights.
  • It is excellent as a teacher/judge served at 8K–16K context, or as a full fine-tune on a rented 80 GB GPU.

Use it to generate and grade Java/Quarkus data; train the 14B student locally.

docs.title: Why not Qwen3-Coder-Next
docs.text: 80B total, 3B active, 256K context. Even 4-bit weights are far beyond 32 GB. It is an API/rented-GPU model.

docs.title: Memory sketch
docs.text:
Setup Weights Adapter + optimizer Peak estimate Qwen2.5-Coder-7B 4-bit, all 28 blocks, rank 16 ~4.5 GB ~0.2 GB 10–14 GB Qwen2.5-Coder-14B 4-bit, 24/48 blocks, rank 16 ~8.7 GB ~0.4 GB 18–23 GB Qwen2.5-Coder-14B 4-bit, all 48 blocks, rank 16 ~8.7 GB ~0.8 GB 21–26 GB (test) Qwen3-Coder-30B-A3B 4-bit, inference only ~18–20 GB — 22–28 GB at 8K–16K

These are estimates. Measure with mlx_lm.lora and mx.get_peak_memory(); do not trust a table over your own machine.

docs.title: 5. What fine-tuning can and cannot do
docs.text:
It can teach:

  • Quarkus-specific imports, annotations and package layout.
  • The difference between quarkus-rest and legacy quarkus-resteasy-reactive.
  • Constructor injection, records, validation, exception mapping.
  • Panache repository vs Active Record, and where each belongs.
  • SOLID/hexagonal refactors and ArchUnit rules.
  • Your patch format, test command, and “read before edit” policy.
  • Recovery from common Maven/Quarkus failures.

It cannot:

  • Teach Java from zero; the base model already needs to code.
  • Memorize a private repository; use retrieval or long context.
  • Guarantee correctness; compile and test.
  • Replace current documentation; APIs change.
  • Learn Quarkus 4 before its idioms stabilize.

The right architecture is model + repository context + compiler + tests + retrieval, not a model that “knows” everything.

docs.title: 6. Java architecture for a Quarkus codebase
docs.text: The most useful target is not “SOLID slogans” but a package shape the model can reproduce and ArchUnit can check.

docs.title: 6.1 Hexagonal / DDD layout
docs.text:
src/main/java/com/example/orders/
├── domain/
│   ├── Order.java              # aggregate, invariants, no framework imports
│   ├── OrderLine.java          # value object
│   ├── CustomerId.java
│   ├── OrderStatus.java
│   ├── OrderRepository.java    # port (interface)
│   └── DomainException.java
├── application/
│   ├── PlaceOrderService.java  # use case, @ApplicationScoped, @Transactional
│   └── OrderQueryService.java
└── adapters/
    ├── rest/
    │   ├── OrderResource.java
    │   ├── PlaceOrderRequest.java
    │   ├── OrderResponse.java
    │   └── DomainExceptionMapper.java
    └── persistence/
        ├── OrderEntity.java
        ├── OrderLineEntity.java
        ├── OrderEntityRepository.java   # PanacheRepository
        └── PanacheOrderRepository.java  # implements domain port

Dependency rule:

adapters → application → domain

The domain never imports jakarta.persistence, io.quarkus, jakarta.ws.rs or Panache. The application depends on domain ports. Adapters implement those ports and translate DTO/entity types.

docs.title: 6.2 SOLID, mapped to Quarkus
docs.text: Principle In this codebase Smell to reject SRP OrderResource does HTTP; PlaceOrderService does the use case; PanacheOrderRepository does persistence a 400-line resource that validates, persists, maps and logs OCP new DiscountPolicy implementation instead of editing a switch adding an if for every customer type LSP every PaymentGateway implementation returns the same result contract and throws the same domain errors an implementation that returns null where others throw ISP small ports (OrderReader, OrderWriter, PaymentGateway) one OrderService interface with 30 methods DIP domain declares OrderRepository; adapter implements it domain imports PanacheRepository or EntityManager

docs.title: 6.3 Quarkus idioms to train
docs.text:
@ApplicationScoped
public class PlaceOrderService {
    private final OrderRepository orders;
    private final Clock clock;

    public PlaceOrderService(OrderRepository orders, Clock clock) { // constructor injection
        this.orders = orders;
        this.clock = clock;
    }

    @Transactional
    public Order place(CustomerId customerId, List<OrderLine> lines) {
        var order = Order.place(customerId, lines, clock.instant());
        return orders.save(order);
    }
}
  • Constructor injection; no field injection.
  • @Transactional on the use case, not the resource.
  • Records for commands, DTOs and value objects.
  • @Valid at the HTTP boundary; domain invariants in the aggregate.
  • ExceptionMapper for domain errors.
  • @ConfigMapping for typed configuration.
  • @QuarkusTest + RestAssured for HTTP; plain JUnit for the domain.
  • quarkus-rest, not quarkus-resteasy-reactive.
  • jakarta.*, never javax.persistence/javax.ws.rs.

docs.title: 6.4 A minimal domain aggregate
docs.text:
package com.example.orders.domain;

import java.time.Instant;
import java.util.List;
import java.util.Objects;
import java.util.UUID;

public record Order(UUID id, CustomerId customerId, List<OrderLine> lines,
                    OrderStatus status, Instant createdAt) {

    public Order {
        Objects.requireNonNull(id, "id");
        Objects.requireNonNull(customerId, "customerId");
        Objects.requireNonNull(status, "status");
        Objects.requireNonNull(createdAt, "createdAt");
        lines = List.copyOf(lines);
        if (lines.isEmpty()) {
            throw new DomainException("order must contain at least one line");
        }
    }

    public static Order place(CustomerId customerId, List<OrderLine> lines, Instant now) {
        return new Order(UUID.randomUUID(), customerId, lines, OrderStatus.PLACED, now);
    }
}

No @Entity, no @ApplicationScoped, no jakarta.*. It is a plain record you can test in milliseconds.

docs.title: 6.5 The port and the adapter
docs.text:
package com.example.orders.domain;

import java.util.Optional;
import java.util.UUID;

public interface OrderRepository {
    Order save(Order order);
    Optional<Order> findById(UUID id);
}

package com.example.orders.adapters.persistence;

import com.example.orders.domain.Order;
import com.example.orders.domain.OrderRepository;
import jakarta.enterprise.context.ApplicationScoped;

@ApplicationScoped
public class PanacheOrderRepository implements OrderRepository {
    private final OrderEntityRepository entities;

    public PanacheOrderRepository(OrderEntityRepository entities) {
        this.entities = entities;
    }

    @Override
    public Order save(Order order) {
        var entity = OrderMapper.toEntity(order);
        entities.persist(entity);
        return OrderMapper.toDomain(entity);
    }

    @Override
    public java.util.Optional<Order> findById(java.util.UUID id) {
        return entities.findByIdOptional(id).map(OrderMapper::toDomain);
    }
}

The JPA entity stays in adapters.persistence; the domain never sees it.

docs.title: 6.6 The HTTP boundary
docs.text:
package com.example.orders.adapters.rest;

import jakarta.validation.Valid;
import jakarta.ws.rs.*;
import jakarta.ws.rs.core.MediaType;
import jakarta.ws.rs.core.Response;

import java.net.URI;

@Path("/api/orders")
@Consumes(MediaType.APPLICATION_JSON)
@Produces(MediaType.APPLICATION_JSON)
public class OrderResource {

    private final PlaceOrderService service;

    public OrderResource(PlaceOrderService service) {
        this.service = service;
    }

    @POST
    public Response place(@Valid PlaceOrderRequest request) {
        var order = service.place(request.customerId(), request.lines());
        return Response.created(URI.create("/api/orders/" + order.id()))
                .entity(OrderResponse.from(order))
                .build();
    }
}

public record PlaceOrderRequest(
        @jakarta.validation.constraints.NotBlank String customerId,
        @jakarta.validation.constraints.NotEmpty
        java.util.List<@Valid OrderLineRequest> lines) {
}

Use imports rather than fully-qualified annotations in real code; this is compressed for the page.

docs.title: 6.7 ArchUnit: make the architecture executable
docs.text:
package com.example.orders;

import com.tngtech.archunit.core.importer.ImportOption;
import com.tngtech.archunit.junit.AnalyzeClasses;
import com.tngtech.archunit.junit.ArchTest;
import com.tngtech.archunit.lang.ArchRule;
import jakarta.enterprise.context.ApplicationScoped;

import static com.tngtech.archunit.lang.syntax.ArchRuleDefinition.*;
import static com.tngtech.archunit.library.dependencies.SlicesRuleDefinition.slices;

@AnalyzeClasses(packages = "com.example.orders", importOptions = ImportOption.DoNotIncludeTests.class)
class ArchitectureTest {

    @ArchTest
    static final ArchRule domain_is_independent = noClasses()
            .that().resideInAPackage("..domain..")
            .should().dependOnClassesThat()
            .resideInAnyPackage("..adapters..", "..application..", "jakarta..", "io.quarkus..");

    @ArchTest
    static final ArchRule services_are_application_scoped = classes()
            .that().resideInAPackage("..application..")
            .and().haveSimpleNameEndingWith("Service")
            .should().beAnnotatedWith(ApplicationScoped.class);

    @ArchTest
    static final ArchRule persistence_does_not_leak = noClasses()
            .that().resideOutsideOfPackage("..adapters.persistence..")
            .should().dependOnClassesThat().resideInAPackage("..adapters.persistence..");

    @ArchTest
    static final ArchRule no_package_cycles = slices()
            .matching("com.example.orders.(*)..")
            .should().beFreeOfCycles();
}

Add archunit-junit5 in test scope. Run it with ./mvnw -q test. For legacy code, FreezingArchRule.freeze(rule) lets you stop new violations without fixing everything at once.

docs.title: 6.8 Quarkus test
docs.text:
@QuarkusTest
class OrderResourceTest {

    @Test
    void rejectsAnEmptyOrder() {
        given().contentType(ContentType.JSON)
                .body("""
                      {"customerId":"c-1","lines":[]}
                      """)
                .when().post("/api/orders")
                .then().statusCode(400);
    }
}

HTTP validation produces 400; domain errors mapped by DomainExceptionMapper can produce 422. Test both.

docs.title: 6.9 Maven baseline
docs.text:
Use the Quarkus BOM and do not pin extension versions individually:

docs.title: 7. What the adapter should and should not learn
docs.text:
Train it to:

  • produce the package shape above;
  • choose quarkus-rest and jakarta.*;
  • write the test before claiming success;
  • return a diff that applies;
  • explain trade-offs briefly.

Do not train it to:

  • invent Quarkus configuration keys;
  • use javax.* or Spring annotations;
  • put @Entity on domain records;
  • add dependencies silently;
  • claim tests passed when it did not run them;
  • output a 1,000-line “complete rewrite” for a 20-line change.

docs.title: 19 — Java and Quarkus datasets: what exists, what is missing, and how to mix it
docs.text:
Last verified: 25 October 2026. Dataset sizes and licenses were checked against the Hugging Face API and dataset cards; re-check before a large download.

There is no single “Java architecture and Quarkus” dataset. What exists falls into five families:

  1. Raw code corpora — The Stack v3, StarCoderData, CodeSearchNet.
  2. Code instruction data — OpenCodeInstruct, Magicoder, CodeAlpaca.
  3. Repository-level issue resolution — SWE-smith-java, Multi-SWE-bench, SWE-bench Multilingual.
  4. Test generation — Methods2Test.
  5. Quarkus-specific material — the framework, quickstarts and guides, which you must turn into tasks yourself.

The missing piece — SOLID/hexagonal architecture, Quarkus idioms, code review, migration — is exactly what synthetic generation and execution verification are for. See 21 — Java synthetic data.

filter Java

The Stack v3 is the current large corpus (released July 2026). Its training subset is ODC-BY, not “no license”; attribution is required. The full 113.7 TB corpus is gated. Filter Java by the per-file language field and keep the per-file license_type/detected_licenses metadata.

docs.title: 2.1 The Stack v3
docs.text:
• What: 15.9 TB training subset, ~3.6T tokens, 713 languages, 173M repositories; the full corpus is 113.7 TB across 770 languages and 224M repositories.
  • Format: repository rows with inline files (content, path, language, license metadata).
  • Why use it: the cleanest large Java corpus for continued pretraining or for sampling real Quarkus/Jakarta projects.
  • Caveats: ODC-BY attribution; per-file licenses vary; dedup and PII filtering are done but not perfect; gated download; huge.
  • How to use it for SFT: don't train on raw files directly at 3T scale. Sample 50k–200k Java files from repositories that use Quarkus/Jakarta, then generate tasks from them. Or use it for a separate continued-pretraining run on rented GPUs, not for a local LoRA.

docs.title: 2.2 The Stack v2 and StarCoderData
docs.text:
Older but still useful:

  • The Stack v2: 67.5 TB raw, ~900B tokens; permissive-license filter and opt-out; gated.
  • StarCoderData: 783 GB, 86 languages, ~250B tokens, including commits and issues; permissive filter and opt-out; gated.

For a Java LoRA, these are seed corpora, not instruction data. Their Java share is large enough that a small sample is plenty.

docs.title: 2.3 CodeSearchNet
docs.text:
• Java: 1,569,889 functions, 542,991 with documentation.
  • Pairs a method with its Javadoc/comment.
  • Good for: docstring→method, code summarization, code search, “explain this method”.
  • Not good for: architecture, multi-file changes, Quarkus.
  • License: repository MIT; the data itself is tagged other and comes from permissively licensed projects. Keep provenance.

docs.title: 2.4 CodeXGLUE
docs.text: Microsoft's CodeXGLUE is a benchmark suite with Java tasks for code summarization, code translation, clone detection and defect detection. The Hugging Face mirror (microsoft/CodeXGLUE) returned 401 for anonymous access, so use the GitHub release and its task-specific data rather than treating it as a bulk corpus. It is useful for evaluation and for small, well-defined auxiliary tasks; it is not a Quarkus or architecture dataset.

docs.title: 3.1 OpenCodeInstruct
docs.text:
• 5M instruction/answer pairs, ~19 GB, CC-BY-4.0, commercial use allowed.
  • Includes domain, generation_algorithm, unit_tests, tests_execution_status, average_test_score.
  • This is the best large public starting point for code SFT, but it is multilingual and Python-heavy. Filter to Java by language detection or by the prompt/answer containing Java syntax; then prefer rows with passing tests.
  • Its execution metadata is useful as a quality signal, but do not assume every row ran successfully.

docs.title: 3.2 Magicoder
docs.text:
• OSS-Instruct-75K: seed code snippets → diverse instructions; MIT, but generated by GPT-3.5, so OpenAI's usage policy applies.
  • Evol-Instruct-110K: evolves instructions to be harder; Apache-2.0.
  • Good for: diversity and harder reasoning.
  • Weak for: Quarkus, Java 25, repository context, tests.
  • Filter Java; drop Python-only and LeetCode-style puzzles if you want production Java style.

docs.title: 3.3 CodeAlpaca and small Java sets
docs.text:
• CodeAlpaca-20k: CC-BY-4.0, early synthetic instructions; small and dated.
  • Nan-Do/instructional_code-search-net-java: Apache-2.0, Java docstring/instruction pairs; small.
  • XEUIPR/Java-Code-Large-text-only: MIT tag, but provenance is unclear; avoid for a release.
  • dmsovetov/codeparrot-java, hrishizone/Java-GitHub-Codes: no clear license; avoid.
  • semeru/code-code-CodeCompletion-TokenLevel-Java: MIT, token-level completion; niche, not instruction.

Rule: a permissive tag is not a provenance audit. Prefer datasets with a paper, a maintainer, and per-row license metadata.

docs.title: 4.1 SWE-smith-java
docs.text:
• 7,470 task instances, 1.4 GB, from Java repositories; each row has a patch, FAIL_TO_PASS, PASS_TO_PASS, image_name, repo, problem_statement.
  • This is the closest public analogue to “fix a real Java issue and prove it with tests”.
  • The SWE-smith project is MIT; the Java dataset card is untagged, so verify before redistribution.
  • Use it for: bug-fix trajectories, recovery, test-driven repair, agent tool use.
  • Caveat: synthesized bugs can be artificial; mix with real PRs.

docs.title: 4.2 Multi-SWE-bench
docs.text:
• 1,632 instances across seven languages; Java repos include alibaba/fastjson2, elastic/logstash, mockito/mockito.
  • CC0 for the dataset, but the underlying repositories have their own licenses.
  • Evaluation only. It is a benchmark; do not train on it. The Java subset is small, so use it as a held-out signal, not a training set.

docs.title: 4.3 SWE-bench Multilingual
docs.text:
• 300 tasks, Java among them; MIT.
  • Evaluation only. Public and likely in pretraining; report the caveat.

docs.title: 4.4 What repository-level data teaches
docs.text:
• Read a file tree, find the relevant class, change multiple files.
  • Keep tests green.
  • Recover from a failed compile or a failed assertion.
  • Produce a patch, not a lecture.

These are the behaviours a “coding agent” needs, and they are underrepresented in single-file instruction datasets.

docs.title: 5. Test-generation data
docs.text:
Methods2Test is the strongest public Java test corpus:

  • 780k focal-method/JUnit-test pairs from 91k open-source projects.
  • Variants add class name, constructor signatures, method signatures and fields.
  • MIT license.
  • Good for: “write a JUnit 5 test for this method”, edge cases, assertions.
  • Caveats: old JUnit style, no Quarkus, no Mockito guarantees, tests may be weak or flaky.

Use it to teach test shape, then generate Quarkus-specific tests synthetically and execute them.

docs.title: 6. Quarkus-specific data: build it
docs.text:
There is no public Quarkus instruction dataset of meaningful size. The raw material is good:

  • quarkusio/quarkus — framework code, tests, extensions.
  • quarkusio/quarkus-quickstarts — runnable feature examples.
  • quarkus.io/guides — reference guides with code snippets.
  • code.quarkus.io — generated project skeletons.
  • Quarkus blog posts — release notes and migration guides.
  • Your own Quarkus repositories — the highest-value data, if you have the rights.

docs.title: 6.1 Turn a quickstart into tasks
docs.text:
For each quickstart module:

  1. Read pom.xml, the main resource, the service/repository, and the tests.
  2. Create a task that removes one behaviour (an endpoint, a validation rule, a repository method, a test).
  3. Keep the original code/test as the gold patch.
  4. Run ./mvnw -q -DskipITs test at the base commit and after the patch.
  5. Keep only tasks where the base fails and the gold passes.

This produces execution-verified feature tasks with a real Quarkus shape.

docs.title: 6.2 Turn a guide into Q&A and review tasks
docs.text:
Guides are good for:

  • “Which extension provides X?”
  • “Why does Quarkus do Y at build time?”
  • “What is the correct annotation for Z?”
  • “Review this code against the guide's recommended pattern.”

Do not train on the guide text verbatim; generate a task, then verify the answer against the guide and a build.

docs.title: 6.3 Turn commits into issue tasks
docs.text:
Use scripts/mine_java_commits.py:

python scripts/mine_java_commits.py \
  --repo ~/src/quarkus-quickstarts \
  --out data/java/interim/quickstart-commits.jsonl \
  --limit 300 --only-with-tests --license Apache-2.0

Each seed has a base commit, a commit message, changed files, the gold patch and a test command. Then ask a teacher to write a problem statement from the commit message and a new solution patch; apply, test, keep passes. This is how you get scale without training on the gold patch itself.

docs.title: 7. Architecture and SOLID data: the gap
docs.text:
There is no public dataset that reliably labels “this refactor improves SRP/DIP” or “this package violates hexagonal boundaries”. The honest approach:

  1. Mine real refactors from permissive repositories (git log for commits touching interfaces, package moves, dependency inversion).
  2. Generate refactor tasks from a working baseline: “move persistence behind a port; keep tests green; add ArchUnit rules”.
  3. Verify with the compiler, tests and ArchUnit, not an LLM's opinion.
  4. Review with a rubric for SRP/OCP/LSP/ISP/DIP, coupling, cohesion and readability.
  5. Keep a human-labeled slice to calibrate the rubric.

ArchUnit is the closest thing to an executable definition of architecture. A refactor that passes the old tests and the new rules is a much stronger training example than a prose “SOLID” answer.

docs.title: 7.1 Example architecture task
docs.text:
{
  "task": "Refactor the order feature so the domain does not depend on Quarkus, Panache or Jakarta persistence. Add ArchUnit rules for domain independence and package cycles. Keep the existing HTTP tests green.",
  "constraints": [
    "Java 25 LTS, Quarkus 3.40 LTS",
    "jakarta.* only",
    "no behavior change",
    "return a unified diff",
    "run ./mvnw -q verify"
  ],
  "acceptance": [
    "ArchitectureTest passes",
    "OrderResourceTest passes",
    "no class in ..domain.. imports ..adapters.., io.quarkus.. or jakarta.."
  ]
}

This is a task, not a training row. The training row is the verified diff plus the test output.

docs.title: 8. The mix
docs.text:
For a first Java/Quarkus adapter, aim for 2–4M tokens (roughly 2,000–5,000 examples after truncation):

Bucket Share Source Why Quarkus feature/API implementation 25% quickstarts, guides, synthetic teaches the framework shape Repo bug fix / recovery 20% SWE-smith-java, commits, synthetic teaches multi-file reasoning SOLID/hexagonal refactor 15% synthetic + ArchUnit teaches architecture Test generation 15% Methods2Test, synthetic teaches verification Code/architecture review 10% PR comments, synthetic teaches critique Migration/upgrade 5% 3.33→3.40, 21→25 teaches version hygiene Refusal/uncertainty/security 5% synthetic negatives teaches boundaries General Java/code replay 5% OpenCodeInstruct/Magicoder limits forgetting

A mature adapter can grow to 8–12M tokens. Do not scale the same prompt 10×; scale the task families and verify.

docs.title: 9. Java-specific quality filters
docs.text:
Run these before tokenization:

  • Compiles with javac --release 25 or ./mvnw -q -DskipITs test.
  • Tests pass, and the test actually exercises the change.
  • No legacy imports: javax.persistence, javax.ws.rs, javax.inject, javax.enterprise, javax.transaction, javax.validation.
  • No Spring idioms (org.springframework, @Autowired) in Quarkus rows.
  • No legacy RESTEasy coordinates (quarkus-resteasy-reactive) when quarkus-rest is expected.
  • Version tag: Java 25, Quarkus 3.40.x; reject rows that mix 3.x and 4.x without a migration label.
  • No secrets in code, config, logs or test data.
  • No System.out/printStackTrace in production examples; use JBoss Logging or SLF4J.
  • No TODO/FIXME in the final answer.
  • Patch applies with git apply --check to the base commit.
  • License metadata present; reject unknown/copyleft for a release mix.
  • Deduplicate exact and near-duplicate patches; split by repo/commit.

scripts/validate_java_dataset.py automates the static checks. It is not a compiler.

docs.title: 10. Contamination and evaluation hygiene
docs.text:
• Hold out MultiPL-E Java, HumanEval-X Java, Multi-SWE-bench Java and SWE-bench Multilingual Java.
  • Run 13-gram overlap between training rows and every benchmark.
  • Split by repository and base commit, never by random row.
  • Hold out entire Quarkus modules or releases for a time-based test.
  • Keep a private golden set of 100–200 tasks written from your own repositories.
  • Report the base model and adapter on the same prompts, at temperature 0, with the same tools and system prompt.

A model that memorizes quarkus-quickstarts will look good on a quickstart test and fail on your codebase. The private golden set is the only cure.

docs.title: 11. Canonical rows
docs.text:
A single-file Java task:

{
  "messages": [
    {"role": "system", "content": "You are a senior Java/Quarkus engineer. Target Java 25 LTS and Quarkus 3.40 LTS. Use jakarta.* imports, constructor injection and tests."},
    {"role": "user", "content": "Write a Java 25 record `Money` with a non-negative amount and an ISO-4217 currency. Reject nulls and invalid currencies."},
    {"role": "assistant", "content": "```java\npackage com.example.money;\n\nimport java.math.BigDecimal;\nimport java.util.Objects;\n\npublic record Money(BigDecimal amount, String currency) {\n    public Money {\n        Objects.requireNonNull(amount, \"amount\");\n        Objects.requireNonNull(currency, \"currency\");\n        if (amount.signum() < 0) throw new IllegalArgumentException(\"amount must be >= 0\");\n        if (!currency.matches(\"[A-Z]{3}\")) throw new IllegalArgumentException(\"currency must be ISO-4217\");\n    }\n}\n```"}
  ],
  "meta": {
    "repo": "java-domain-example",
    "license": "Apache-2.0",
    "category": "java-domain",
    "test_command": "./mvnw -q -DskipITs test"
  }
}

A repository patch task with tools: see data/examples/java-train.example.jsonl. For Qwen2.5-Coder, tool arguments must be objects, not JSON strings:

{"name": "read_file", "arguments": {"path": "src/main/java/com/example/OrderResource.java"}}

The Qwen2.5-Coder template applies tojson to arguments; a string becomes an escaped JSON string and the model learns the wrong shape. Use prepare_dataset.py --arguments-format dict.

docs.title: 20 — Fine-tuning a Qwen coder for Java and Quarkus
docs.text:
Last verified: 25 October 2026 against mlx-lm 0.32.2 and the Qwen2.5-Coder tokenizer template. The training commands were not executed on the target Mac in this environment.

This is the runbook for the Java/Quarkus track. It assumes:

  • macOS Apple Silicon with MLX installed (03-macos-setup.md);
  • a JDK 25 and Maven 3.9+ for building the training/eval projects;
  • Java data in data/java/processed/{train,valid,test}.jsonl (19-java-datasets.md);
  • 32 GB unified memory.

The default is Qwen2.5-Coder-14B-Instruct 4-bit QLoRA, adapting 24 of its 48 blocks. The 7B is the smoke test; the all-layer 14B is an experiment, not the first run.

docs.title: 0. The recipe in one table
docs.text:
Choice Value Why Base mlx-community/Qwen2.5-Coder-14B-Instruct-4bit code-specialised, Apache-2.0, fits 32 GB Method 4-bit QLoRA, lora base frozen; adapter small Blocks 24 of 48 memory-safe starting point Rank / scale 16 / 2.0 PEFT alpha=32 equivalent LR 1e-4 standard LoRA range with scale=2 Effective batch 8 (1 × 8 accumulation) LoRA prefers 8–16 Sequence 2048 measure p99 first Iterations 300 ~1.5–2 epochs over 2M tokens Masking mask_prompt: true train only the final assistant turn Checkpoint every 50 short run; keep options

Expected wall clock: 35–55 hours on an M1 Pro at ~20–25 tok/s for 3–4M tokens. The 7B smoke run is 15–25 hours; do a 100k-token subset first.

docs.title: 1. Preflight
docs.text:
cd ~/work/qwen-kali-agent
source .venv/bin/activate

java -version          # expect 25.x
./mvnw -version        # expect Maven 3.9+
python scripts/check_env.py

Checklist:

  • java -version reports 25.
  • ./mvnw -version reports Maven 3.9+.
  • ./mvnw -q -DskipITs test passes on the reference project.
  • MLX sees the GPU (mx.device_info()).
  • 100+ GB free disk.
  • Docker is available if @QuarkusTest uses Dev Services.
  • The Java data exists and is non-empty.
  • No secrets in data/java/.
  • You have a baseline evaluation of the base model.

The JDK is only for data generation and evaluation. MLX training itself does not need a JDK, but you cannot verify Java data without one.

docs.title: 2.1 Mine seeds from a permissive repository
docs.text:
mkdir -p data/java/{raw,interim,processed,golden}

python scripts/mine_java_commits.py \
  --repo ~/src/quarkus-quickstarts \
  --out data/java/interim/quickstart-commits.jsonl \
  --limit 300 --only-with-tests --license Apache-2.0

Each row has a base commit, task text, changed files, gold patch and a test command. It is a seed, not a finished training row. Use 21 — Java synthetic data to turn it into a verified task and a new solution.

docs.title: 2.2 Normalize and split
docs.text:
Qwen2.5-Coder requires tool arguments as objects:

python scripts/prepare_dataset.py \
  data/java/interim/all.jsonl \
  --out data/java/processed \
  --arguments-format dict \
  --split 0.9 0.05 0.05

Why: its chat template does tool_call.arguments | tojson. A JSON string becomes an escaped string; a dict becomes a JSON object. Qwen3's template expects the string form. Do not use one dataset for both without re-rendering.

docs.title: 2.3 Validate
docs.text:
python scripts/validate_dataset.py data/java/processed/train.jsonl \
  --tools examples/java/tools.json

python scripts/validate_java_dataset.py data/java/processed/train.jsonl \
  --tools examples/java/tools.json --require-dict-arguments --strict

The Java validator catches:

  • legacy javax.* imports;
  • Spring idioms;
  • legacy RESTEasy coordinates;
  • wrong Quarkus/Java version tags;
  • System.out/printStackTrace;
  • TODO/FIXME;
  • probable secrets;
  • tool arguments stored as strings instead of objects.

It is a linter, not a compiler. The real filter is ./mvnw test.

docs.title: 2.4 Measure tokens
docs.text:
python scripts/token_stats.py data/java/processed/train.jsonl \
  --model Qwen/Qwen2.5-Coder-14B-Instruct

Choose max_seq_length at the 99th percentile, rounded to 256. Java repository tasks are longer than single-function tasks; if p99 is 3,500, use 3,072 and split the long rows, not 4,096 by default.

docs.title: 2.5 A useful dataset size
docs.text:
• First adapter: 1.5–3M tokens, 2,000–5,000 examples.
  • Mature adapter: 5–10M tokens, 10k+ examples.
  • Do not dump 100k raw files; the model learns style from a few thousand verified tasks.

Mix from 19-java-datasets.md §8: 25% Quarkus features, 20% bug fixes, 15% SOLID refactors, 15% tests, 10% review, 5% migration, 5% refusal, 5% general replay.

docs.title: 3.1 7B smoke — configs/qwen2.5-coder-7b-java.yaml
docs.text:
model: mlx-community/Qwen2.5-Coder-7B-Instruct-4bit
train: true
data: data/java/processed
fine_tune_type: lora
optimizer: adamw
num_layers: -1
batch_size: 2
iters: 300
val_batches: 25
learning_rate: 1.5e-4
steps_per_report: 10
steps_per_eval: 100
save_every: 100
max_seq_length: 2048
grad_checkpoint: true
grad_accumulation_steps: 4
mask_prompt: true
adapter_path: adapters/qwen25-coder-7b-java
seed: 42
lora_parameters:
  rank: 16
  dropout: 0.05
  scale: 2.0
lr_schedule:
  name: cosine_decay
  warmup: 30
  arguments: [1.5e-4, 300, 1.0e-6]
optimizer_config:
  adamw:
    weight_decay: 0.01

All 28 blocks fit comfortably. Use it to validate the data/template, not to judge final quality.

docs.title: 3.2 14B default — configs/qwen2.5-coder-14b-java.yaml
docs.text:
model: mlx-community/Qwen2.5-Coder-14B-Instruct-4bit
train: true
data: data/java/processed
fine_tune_type: lora
optimizer: adamw
num_layers: 24
batch_size: 1
iters: 300
val_batches: 25
learning_rate: 1.0e-4
steps_per_report: 10
steps_per_eval: 100
save_every: 50
max_seq_length: 2048
grad_checkpoint: true
grad_accumulation_steps: 8
mask_prompt: true
adapter_path: adapters/qwen25-coder-14b-java
seed: 42
lora_parameters:
  rank: 16
  dropout: 0.05
  scale: 2.0
lr_schedule:
  name: cosine_decay
  warmup: 30
  arguments: [1.0e-4, 300, 1.0e-6]
optimizer_config:
  adamw:
    weight_decay: 0.01

24 of 48 blocks is the memory-safe default for a 48-layer model. It covers the last half, including the layers closest to the output.

docs.title: 3.3 14B all layers — configs/qwen2.5-coder-14b-java-all-layers.yaml
docs.text: Same as 3.2 but num_layers: -1, LR 8e-5, 250 iterations. Peak memory may exceed 24 GB. Run it only after the 24-layer adapter is evaluated; drop to 32 blocks if it OOMs.

docs.title: 3.4 14B long context — configs/qwen2.5-coder-14b-java-longctx.yaml
docs.text: num_layers: 24, max_seq_length: 4096, LR 8e-5, 250 iterations. 4K roughly doubles activation memory versus 2K. Only use it if token_stats shows a real need.

docs.title: 4. Verify what the adapter actually covers
docs.text:
Before spending hours:

python scripts/check_lora.py \
  --model mlx-community/Qwen2.5-Coder-14B-Instruct-4bit \
  --num-layers 24 --rank 16 --scale 2

Expected:

  • 24 adapted blocks of 48;
  • 7 projections per block (q_proj, k_proj, v_proj, o_proj, gate_proj, up_proj, down_proj);
  • ~168 LoRA modules;
  • roughly 34M trainable parameters for 24 blocks (about 69M for all 48).

The exact numbers depend on the MLX version and the model's embedding handling. If you see only q_proj/v_proj, stop.

For a Qwen2.5-Coder-14B all-layer run, expect ~336 modules and ~69M trainable parameters.

docs.title: 5. Smoke run on 7B
docs.text:
Start with a 100k-token subset and 50 iterations:

# make a subset (example: first 2,000 rows)
head -n 2000 data/java/processed/train.jsonl > data/java/processed/train.smoke.jsonl
mkdir -p data/java/processed-smoke
cp data/java/processed/train.smoke.jsonl data/java/processed-smoke/train.jsonl
cp data/java/processed/valid.jsonl data/java/processed-smoke/valid.jsonl

mlx_lm.lora --config configs/qwen2.5-coder-7b-java.yaml \
  --data data/java/processed-smoke --iters 50 --save-every 25 \
  --adapter-path adapters/qwen25-coder-7b-java-smoke

Check at iteration 1–20:

  • loss is finite and falling;
  • tokens/sec is 35–45 for 7B;
  • peak memory is 10–14 GB;
  • the rendered sample contains <|im_start|>user, <tool_call> and <tool_response> where expected.

Then fuse and run a smoke test:

mlx_lm.fuse \
  --model mlx-community/Qwen2.5-Coder-7B-Instruct-4bit \
  --adapter-path adapters/qwen25-coder-7b-java-smoke \
  --save-path fused/qwen25-coder-7b-java-smoke-4bit

mlx_lm.server --model fused/qwen25-coder-7b-java-smoke-4bit \
  --host 127.0.0.1 --port 8080 --max-tokens 2048 --temp 0.2

Then send the prompts from examples/java/ and check that:

  • the model emits a Java/Quarkus answer, not Python or Spring;
  • javax. does not appear;
  • a tool call uses an object argument shape (Qwen2.5);
  • it says “I did not run the tests” when it did not.

Do not proceed to 14B until the 7B adapter is at least plausible on 20 hand-written tasks.

docs.title: 6. The 14B run
docs.text:
mlx_lm.lora --config configs/qwen2.5-coder-14b-java.yaml

Expected first lines:

Loading pretrained model
Loading datasets
Training
Trainable parameters: 0.2xx% (34.xxxM/14.7B)
Iter 1: Val loss ..., Val took ...s
Iter 10: Train loss ..., Learning Rate ..., It/sec ..., Tokens/sec ..., Trained Tokens ..., Peak mem ... GB

Healthy signals:

Metric Healthy Warning Train loss falls to 0.3–0.7 stuck >1.0 after 200 iters Val loss tracks train rises for 2+ evals Tokens/sec 20–25 (14B, 24 layers) <12 = memory/thermal Peak memory 18–23 GB >26 GB = danger It/sec stable collapses = swap/thermal

Code loss is naturally lower than chat loss because code is predictable; do not compare absolute values across datasets. Compare the adapter to the base on the same Java tasks.

docs.title: 6.1 If it OOMs
docs.text:
In order:

  1. num_layers: 24 → 16.
  2. max_seq_length: 2048 → 1536.
  3. Confirm grad_checkpoint: true and batch_size: 1.
  4. Close Docker, the Kali VM, Chrome and the IDE.
  5. Move to the 7B.

Do not start by shrinking the dataset. A completed 7B adapter beats a 14B run that dies at hour 40.

docs.title: 6.2 If loss is nan
docs.text:
• A prompt is at or over max_seq_length; with --mask-prompt the completion is empty. Check token_stats and drop/split.
  • The LR is too high. Halve it; keep scale: 2.0.
  • The data has an empty assistant message or a broken tool call. Run the validators again.

docs.title: 7. Checkpoints and resume
docs.text:
mlx_lm.lora --config configs/qwen2.5-coder-14b-java.yaml \
  --resume-adapter-file adapters/qwen25-coder-14b-java/0000200_adapters.safetensors \
  --iters 100 \
  --adapter-path adapters/qwen25-coder-14b-java-resume

Only weights are restored; optimizer state, LR schedule position and iteration count are not. Use a new adapter path and a fresh short cosine schedule.

Checkpoints are ~100–250 MB each for 14B. Delete old ones after evaluation.

docs.title: 8.1 The golden set
docs.text:
Build 100–200 tasks from your own repositories before training. Categories:

Category Count What it measures Quarkus REST endpoint 25 correct annotations, validation, status codes Panache/repository 20 transaction boundary, mapping, query SOLID/hexagonal refactor 25 package boundaries, no behavior change Test generation 20 tests compile, pass, actually assert Bug fix 25 multi-file reasoning, recovery Code review 20 finding quality, no invented issues Migration 15 3.33→3.40, 21→25 Refusal/uncertainty 15 no unsafe or invented claims

Each task has repo, base_commit, task, constraints, test_command and expect. See data/examples/java-golden.example.jsonl.

docs.title: 8.2 Grading
docs.text:
For each task:

  1. Copy the repo to a temp directory and check out base_commit.
  2. Prompt the model with the system prompt, repo context and task.
  3. Extract the diff from the response.
  4. git apply --check, then git apply.
  5. Run test_command in the sandbox with a timeout.
  6. Run arch_check if the task changes boundaries.
  7. Record compile, test, ArchUnit and review results.

A minimal harness:

import json, shutil, subprocess, tempfile
from pathlib import Path

def grade(task, model, repo_dir):
    with tempfile.TemporaryDirectory() as tmp:
        work = Path(tmp) / "repo"
        shutil.copytree(repo_dir, work)
        subprocess.run(["git", "checkout", task["base_commit"]], cwd=work, check=True)
        prompt = task["task"] + "\n\nConstraints:\n" + "\n".join(task.get("constraints", []))
        answer = model.complete(system=SYSTEM, user=prompt, tools=TOOLS)
        diff = extract_diff(answer)
        (work / "model.patch").write_text(diff)
        check = subprocess.run(["git", "apply", "--check", "model.patch"], cwd=work,
                               capture_output=True, text=True)
        if check.returncode != 0:
            return {"pass": False, "reason": "patch_does_not_apply", "stderr": check.stderr}
        subprocess.run(["git", "apply", "model.patch"], cwd=work, check=True)
        test = subprocess.run(task["test_command"], shell=True, cwd=work,
                              capture_output=True, text=True, timeout=900)
        return {"pass": test.returncode == 0, "reason": "tests",
                "stdout": test.stdout[-4000:], "stderr": test.stderr[-4000:]}

shell=True is safe only because test_command comes from your trusted golden set, inside a disposable sandbox. Never run model-generated shell commands this way.

docs.title: 8.3 Metrics
docs.text:
Metric Definition First target Mature target Compile rate generated files compile / tasks >0.90 >0.98 Patch apply rate diffs that apply / tasks >0.90 >0.98 Test pass rate tasks with green tests / tasks >0.45 >0.65 ArchUnit pass refactors passing rules / refactors >0.80 >0.95 Review precision valid findings / all findings >0.75 >0.90 Unsafe/invented rate false claims or unsafe changes / tasks 0 0 p95 latency seconds per task <180 <120

Report Wilson intervals. A 5-point difference on 100 tasks is not significant.

docs.title: 8.4 Benchmarks
docs.text:
• MultiPL-E Java — function-level generation; public; contamination caveat.
  • HumanEval-X Java — 164 tasks in the Java subset; public.
  • Multi-SWE-bench Java — real issue resolution; evaluation only.
  • SWE-bench Multilingual Java — real issue resolution; evaluation only.
  • Your Quarkus golden set — the decision-maker.

Do not tune on the benchmarks. Report them once per candidate, with the version/commit and contamination method.

docs.title: 8.5 Release gates
docs.text:
• compile rate ≥ 0.90;
  • patch apply ≥ 0.90;
  • test pass ≥ 0.45 (first) / 0.65 (mature);
  • ArchUnit pass ≥ 0.80 on refactors;
  • no javax.*, Spring or legacy RESTEasy coordinates;
  • no secrets/PII;
  • unsafe/invented rate = 0;
  • benchmark contamination reported;
  • 30 human-reviewed trajectories and 20 failures inspected.

docs.title: 9. Fuse, serve and wire the agent
9.1 Fuse
docs.text:
mlx_lm.fuse \
  --model mlx-community/Qwen2.5-Coder-14B-Instruct-4bit \
  --adapter-path adapters/qwen25-coder-14b-java \
  --save-path fused/qwen25-coder-14b-java-4bit

docs.title: 9.2 Serve with MLX
docs.text:
mlx_lm.server \
  --model fused/qwen25-coder-14b-java-4bit \
  --host 127.0.0.1 --port 8080 \
  --max-tokens 4096 --temp 0.2 \
  --prefill-step-size 512

Qwen2.5-Coder has no thinking block, so do not pass enable_thinking. Its template supports tools and tool responses, but mlx_lm.server's parser support can lag the template. Verify a real tool_calls response with curl. If it returns prose, serve the same GGUF with llama-server --jinja (below); the model format is not the problem.

docs.title: 9.3 Serve with llama.cpp
docs.text:
# GGUF conversion needs an unquantized HF-format directory.
mlx_lm.fuse \
  --model mlx-community/Qwen2.5-Coder-14B-Instruct-4bit \
  --adapter-path adapters/qwen25-coder-14b-java \
  --save-path fused/qwen25-coder-14b-java-bf16 \
  --dequantize

python3 ~/work/llama.cpp/convert_hf_to_gguf.py \
  fused/qwen25-coder-14b-java-bf16 \
  --outtype f16 --outfile models/qwen25-coder-14b-java-f16.gguf

~/work/llama.cpp/build/bin/llama-quantize \
  models/qwen25-coder-14b-java-f16.gguf \
  models/qwen25-coder-14b-java-Q4_K_M.gguf Q4_K_M

llama-server -m models/qwen25-coder-14b-java-Q4_K_M.gguf \
  --host 127.0.0.1 --port 8080 -c 16384 -ngl 99 -fa auto --jinja

(--dequantize produces a ~30 GB bf16 directory; delete it after conversion. See 10-export-serving.md for the full path.)

docs.title: 9.4 Agent loop
docs.text:
Use examples/java/tools.json and examples/java/system-prompt.md. The loop is:

read task
  → search_code / read_file
  → plan
  → apply_patch or write_file
  → run_maven test
  → if fail: read error, diagnose, patch again (max 2)
  → arch_check for boundary changes
  → git_diff
  → final answer with test evidence

The model should call run_maven itself, but the harness enforces the allowlist, timeout and working directory.

docs.title: 9.5 OpenCode
docs.text:
examples/java/opencode.json points OpenCode at the local server and enables edits. For generation, run it inside a disposable clone:

opencode run -m local/qwen25-coder-14b-java --format json \
  "Add a validated POST /api/orders endpoint; run ./mvnw -q -DskipITs test; return a diff."

Do not give it host network, Docker socket or production credentials. See 21 — Java synthetic data for the full sandbox.

docs.title: 10. Experiment matrix
docs.text:
# Run Purpose Cost 1 7B all layers, 50 iters, 100k tokens validate data/template 2–4 h 2 7B all layers, 300 iters baseline 15–25 h 3 14B, 24 layers recommended 35–55 h 4 14B, all layers capacity test 45–65 h 5 14B, 24 layers, LR 5e-5 vs 1e-4 LR sensitivity 2 × 40 h 6 14B, 24 layers, +2M synthetic data scaling 50–70 h

Stop when the golden-set gain is within noise. Do not run the whole matrix; run #2, #3, then one variable at a time.

docs.title: 11. Checklist
docs.text:
Before:

  • Java 25 + Maven 3.9+ verified;
  • data/java/processed validated;
  • arguments are dicts for Qwen2.5;
  • token p99 fits max_seq_length;
  • check_lora.py shows MLP projections;
  • 100+ GB free;
  • VM/Docker off for training;
  • baseline saved.

After:

  • best checkpoint chosen by golden set, not train loss;
  • compile/test/ArchUnit measured;
  • unsafe/invented rate = 0;
  • fused model loads;
  • tool calls parse;
  • GGUF path tested if needed;
  • model card + dataset manifest written.

docs.title: 12. Sources
docs.text:
• Qwen2.5-Coder-14B-Instruct — https://huggingface.co/Qwen/Qwen2.5-Coder-14B-Instruct
  • MLX-LM LoRA — https://github.com/ml-explore/mlx-lm/blob/main/mlx_lm/LORA.md
  • MLX-LM lora.py — https://github.com/ml-explore/mlx-lm/blob/main/mlx_lm/lora.py
  • Qwen2.5-Coder tokenizer template — https://huggingface.co/Qwen/Qwen2.5-Coder-14B-Instruct/blob/main/tokenizer_config.json
  • Quarkus testing — https://quarkus.io/guides/getting-started-testing
  • Quarkus REST — https://quarkus.io/guides/rest
  • Hibernate ORM with Panache — https://quarkus.io/guides/hibernate-orm-panache
  • ArchUnit — https://www.archunit.org/
  • MultiPL-E — https://github.com/nuprl/MultiPL-E
  • Multi-SWE-bench — https://huggingface.co/datasets/ByteDance-Seed/Multi-SWE-bench
  • 17 — Fine-tuning update
  • 21 — Java synthetic data

docs.title: 21 — Generating Java/Quarkus training data with another LLM
docs.text:
Last verified: 25 October 2026. The pipeline uses the DeepSeek API and OpenCode from 07 — Synthetic data; the Java-specific prompts and verification rules are new.

Public Java datasets teach syntax and single-file coding. They do not teach your Quarkus conventions, your package boundaries, your test command, or the difference between a plausible diff and one that compiles. Synthetic data fills that gap only when every candidate is executed.

This chapter describes a repo-grounded pipeline:

permissive repo + docs + commits
        │
        ▼
teacher proposes a task (JSON)
        │
        ▼
teacher proposes a patch + tests (JSON)
        │
        ▼
validator: schema, scope, Java/Quarkus rules
        │
        ▼
sandbox: git apply --check → ./mvnw test → ArchUnit
        │
        ▼
judge + human spot check → keep / repair / discard
        │
        ▼
canonical JSONL (Qwen2.5-Coder arguments as objects)

The teacher can be DeepSeek V4.1 Flash/Pro, a local Qwen3-Coder-30B-A3B, or a larger API model. The verifier is not an LLM: it is Maven, the compiler, the tests and ArchUnit.

docs.title: 1. What synthetic data must add
docs.text:
Gap in public data Synthetic task Quarkus 3.40 idioms REST endpoint, Panache repository, validation, config, test Java 25 style records, sealed types, pattern matching, virtual threads SOLID/hexagonal refactor behind ports, add ArchUnit rules, keep tests green Repository context multi-file changes, read before edit, patch format Recovery inject a compile/test failure, ask for a fix, verify Review find real smells with file/line evidence Migration 3.33→3.40, 21→25, legacy javax→jakarta Safety refuse secrets, auth bypass, destructive changes, invented test results

Do not generate 10,000 paraphrases of “write a Quarkus endpoint”. Generate a matrix: phase × layer × difficulty × failure mode.

docs.title: 2. Teacher choices
docs.text:
Teacher Where Best for Caveats DeepSeek V4.1 Flash API bulk tasks, patches, tests, reviews cheap; validate JSON; thinking tokens cost output DeepSeek V4-Pro API hard architecture, migration, judge ~3–4× price; reserve for hard slices Qwen3-Coder-30B-A3B-Instruct 4-bit local MLX/llama.cpp private code, offline generation ~18–20 GB weights; 8K–16K context practical; slower Qwen3-Coder-Next API/rented GPU hardest repo tasks 80B; not local Qwen3.8-27B 4-bit local judge/reviewer slow; good quality A frontier API API gold examples, rubric calibration cost/terms; do not send proprietary code without permission

Use Flash for volume, Pro for the hard 10–20%, and a strong local model for private repositories.

docs.title: 3. Seed sources
docs.text:
Use only code you have the right to use:

  • quarkusio/quarkus-quickstarts (Apache-2.0).
  • quarkusio/quarkus (Apache-2.0).
  • Quarkus guides (site says CC BY 3.0; check each guide).
  • Your own Quarkus repositories (with permission).
  • The Stack v3 Java files whose license_type/detected_licenses are permissive (ODC-BY attribution).
  • Real PRs/commits from permissive repos.

Do not seed from proprietary code, GPL/AGPL code for a commercial release, leaked data, or repositories with no license.

docs.title: 4. The eight generation strategies
docs.text: # Strategy Output Verification 1 Repo-grounded feature task + patch + test compile + tests 2 Bug injection / recovery broken commit → fix failing test then green 3 SOLID/hexagonal refactor behavior-preserving diff + ArchUnit tests + ArchUnit 4 Test generation JUnit/Quarkus tests tests compile and pass; mutation/coverage optional 5 Code/architecture review findings with file/line rubric + human spot check 6 Migration 3.33→3.40 / 21→25 diff build + tests 7 Architecture Q&A explanation grounded in docs citation + human check 8 Negative examples refusal/uncertainty rubric; no tool call

docs.title: 4.1 Repo-grounded feature
docs.text:
Input: a file tree, pom.xml, 3–8 relevant files, existing tests, and a task. Output: a diff that adds the feature and tests that pass.

This is the highest-value bucket. It teaches the exact package shape, imports, annotations and test style.

docs.title: 4.2 Bug injection / recovery
docs.text:
Take a working commit, inject a realistic bug (null handling, transaction boundary, missing validation, wrong HTTP status, N+1 query), keep the test failing, and ask for a fix. Or use SWE-smith-java seeds.

The training row should include the failing output and the diagnosis, not just the final patch. That is how the model learns recovery.

docs.title: 4.3 SOLID/hexagonal refactor
docs.text:
Start from a working “big ball of mud” slice. Ask for:

  • a domain port;
  • an adapter that implements it;
  • no JPA entity leaking;
  • ArchUnit rules that fail on the old structure;
  • behavior preserved.

Verify with the old tests plus the new architecture tests. A refactor that passes both is a strong example; a prose “this is more SOLID” is not.

docs.title: 4.4 Test generation
docs.text:
Use Methods2Test for shape, then generate Quarkus tests:

  • @QuarkusTest + RestAssured for HTTP;
  • plain JUnit for domain;
  • @TestTransaction or Dev Services for persistence;
  • no Thread.sleep;
  • assertions that fail on the old behavior.

Run the tests. Reject tests that pass on the broken code (they assert nothing).

docs.title: 4.5 Review
docs.text:
Ask for findings by severity with file/line, principle, issue and minimal fix. The judge checks:

  • Is the finding real?
  • Is the line plausible?
  • Is the fix minimal?
  • Does it avoid invented APIs?

Review data is weaker than executed patches; keep it a small slice and label it.

docs.title: 4.6 Migration
docs.text:
Two separate tasks:

  • Quarkus 3.33 → 3.40: BOM, plugin, deprecated APIs, quarkus-rest coordinates, test fixes.
  • Java 21 → 25: compiler release, language features, build/tooling, native image.

Do not mix Quarkus 2 javax migration with 3.x tasks unless the task explicitly says “legacy migration”. Quarkus 3 already uses jakarta.*.

Quarkus 4 migration is a separate future bucket; it is Beta and changes Jackson, Hibernate, CDI and the Java baseline.

docs.title: 4.7 Architecture Q&A
docs.text:
Generate questions from Quarkus guides and your architecture docs:

  • “Why does Quarkus do X at build time?”
  • “Which extension provides Y?”
  • “Where should this transaction boundary live?”
  • “Why is a JPA entity in the domain a problem?”

Require a citation (guide section or file) and a short answer. This is knowledge/style data, not a substitute for tests.

docs.title: 4.8 Negative examples
docs.text:
At least five families:

  1. Unsafe: auth bypass, credential logging, rm -rf, disabling TLS verification.
  2. Under-specified: “fix the bug” with no repo, no failing test, no expected behavior.
  3. Out of scope: modify a dependency, change the license, add a paid service.
  4. Invented API: uses a Quarkus annotation that does not exist.
  5. False claim: “all tests pass” without running them.

Teach the model to ask, refuse, or say “I did not run it” — not to bluff.

docs.title: 5. Prompt templates
docs.text:
The reusable files live in examples/java/:

  • teacher-system.md — global rules.
  • task-prompt.md — task taxonomy.
  • prompts/solver.md — plan + patch + tests.
  • prompts/test.md — JUnit/Quarkus tests.
  • prompts/refactor.md — SOLID/hexagonal.
  • prompts/review.md — findings.
  • prompts/migration.md — version upgrades.

docs.title: 5.1 Task generation with DeepSeek
docs.text:
export DEEPSEEK_API_KEY="..."
python scripts/generate_synthetic.py \
  --mode tasks --tasks 300 --batch 10 \
  --model deepseek-flash \
  --system-file examples/java/teacher-system.md \
  --prompt-file examples/java/task-prompt.md \
  --out data/java/interim/tasks.jsonl

The script uses JSON-object mode, retries, and tracks token cost. It does not execute anything and does not solve the tasks.

docs.title: 5.2 Solving a task
docs.text:
Use the OpenAI-compatible API with prompts/solver.md and the repo context. A minimal loop:

import json
import os
from pathlib import Path
from openai import OpenAI

client = OpenAI(api_key=os.environ["DEEPSEEK_API_KEY"], base_url="https://api.deepseek.com")
template = Path("examples/java/prompts/solver.md").read_text()

for task in tasks:
    prompt = (template
              .replace("{task}", task["task"])
              .replace("{repo_context}", task["repo_context"])
              .replace("{constraints}", json.dumps(task["constraints"]))
              .replace("{acceptance}", json.dumps(task["acceptance"]))
              .replace("{test_command}", task["test_command"]))
    r = client.chat.completions.create(
        model="deepseek-flash",
        messages=[{"role": "system", "content": Path("examples/java/teacher-system.md").read_text()},
                  {"role": "user", "content": prompt}],
        response_format={"type": "json_object"},
        temperature=0.3,
        max_tokens=8192,
    )
    candidate = json.loads(r.choices[0].message.content)
    # validate schema, apply patch, run tests, keep only verified

Use .replace, not .format: the prompt contains JSON braces.

docs.title: 5.3 A solver response
docs.text:
{
  "plan": ["read OrderResource", "add POST", "map DomainException to 422", "add test"],
  "patch": "diff --git a/src/main/java/... b/src/main/java/...\n...",
  "tests": ["src/test/java/com/example/orders/OrderResourceTest.java"],
  "commands": ["./mvnw -q -DskipITs test"],
  "risks": ["validation status may be 400 vs 422"],
  "notes": "uses quarkus-rest and jakarta.validation"
}

Validate the patch with git apply --check before applying. Reject responses with prose outside JSON.

docs.title: 5.4 Repair loop
docs.text:
If the build fails:

  1. Capture the first 100 lines of the Maven error.
  2. Send the task, patch, and error back to the teacher: “Here is the real compiler/test output; produce a minimal fix.”
  3. Max 2 attempts.
  4. Keep the final verified trajectory, including the failed attempt if it teaches recovery.

Do not let the teacher “fix” by deleting the failing test.

docs.title: 6.1 Build the lab image
docs.text:
docker build -t java-lab -f examples/java/Dockerfile.java-lab .

The image has JDK 25, Maven 3.9 and git. Mount a Maven cache at $HOME/.m2; the examples set HOME=/tmp and mount the host cache at /tmp/.m2.

docs.title: 6.2 Run a candidate
docs.text:
rm -rf /tmp/java-work && cp -a ~/src/quarkus-orders /tmp/java-work
cd /tmp/java-work
git checkout <base_commit>

# apply candidate patch (from JSON)
git apply --check model.patch && git apply model.patch

docker run --rm \
  -u "$(id -u):$(id -g)" -e HOME=/tmp \
  -v /tmp/java-work:/workspace \
  -v "$HOME/.m2":/tmp/.m2 \
  -w /workspace java-lab \
  ./mvnw -q -DskipITs test

For Quarkus @QuarkusTest with Dev Services (PostgreSQL, Kafka), the container needs Docker-in-Docker or an external service. Simpler:

  • use H2 for tests (quarkus-jdbc-h2, test profile), or
  • run a Postgres service on the lab network and set quarkus.datasource.jdbc.url, or
  • disable Dev Services and use Testcontainers with a reachable Docker socket (less isolated).

Pick one and pin it. A test harness that needs Docker-in-Docker is fragile.

docs.title: 6.3 Offline builds
docs.text:
1. Run one online build to populate /tmp/.m2 (the mounted cache).
  2. Re-run with -o (offline).
  3. Pin plugin and dependency versions; no snapshots.
  4. Use a Maven mirror/proxy if the sandbox has no internet.

docs.title: 6.4 ArchUnit
docs.text:
docker run --rm -u "$(id -u):$(id -g)" -e HOME=/tmp \
  -v /tmp/java-work:/workspace -v "$HOME/.m2":/tmp/.m2 \
  -w /workspace java-lab \
  ./mvnw -q -Dtest=ArchitectureTest test

A refactor is only “architecture-verified” if the rule fails on the base commit and passes after the patch. Check both.

docs.title: 6.5 Safety
docs.text:
• No host mounts other than the temp repo and the Maven cache.
  • No Docker socket, SSH keys, cloud credentials or .env.
  • No --network host.
  • Per-command timeout (300–900 s).
  • Copy the repo; never edit the original.
  • Scan for secrets before sending code to any API.
  • Treat model output as hostile until it compiles and tests.

docs.title: 7. OpenCode as the agent in the loop
docs.text: OpenCode can read files, edit them, run Maven, and emit JSON events. It is useful when you want a multi-step transcript rather than one-shot JSON.

docs.title: 7.1 Configure
docs.text:
examples/java/opencode.json:

{
  "provider": {
    "local": {
      "npm": "@ai-sdk/openai-compatible",
      "options": {"baseURL": "http://127.0.0.1:8080/v1", "apiKey": "local"},
      "models": {"qwen25-coder-14b-java": {"name": "Qwen2.5-Coder-14B Java"}}
    }
  },
  "model": "local/qwen25-coder-14b-java",
  "permission": {"bash": "ask", "edit": "allow", "webfetch": "deny"}
}

For a DeepSeek teacher, use the provider block from 07 — Synthetic data.

docs.title: 7.2 Add project rules
docs.text: OpenCode reads AGENTS.md from the repository. Put your Java/Quarkus rules there (or use a skill): Java 25, Quarkus 3.40, jakarta.*, quarkus-rest, constructor injection, domain boundaries, ./mvnw test, no new dependencies without asking.

docs.title: 7.3 Run headless
docs.text:
cd /tmp/java-work
opencode run -m local/qwen25-coder-14b-java --format json \
  "Add a validated POST /api/orders endpoint. Read the existing resource and tests first. Run ./mvnw -q -DskipITs test. Return a diff."

For unattended runs, do not enable --auto globally; define an agent whose bash permission allows only ./mvnw and whose edit root is the temporary clone.

Parse the event stream into OpenAI-style messages:

  • assistant text → content;
  • tool call → tool_calls;
  • tool result → role: "tool";
  • reasoning → drop for Qwen2.5-Coder (no thinking template).

Normalize tool arguments to objects for Qwen2.5-Coder. Reject transcripts that claim tests passed without a run_maven result.

docs.title: 7.4 What OpenCode is good and bad at
docs.text: Good: multi-step repo navigation, edits, test-fix loops, generating a transcript. Bad: bulk throughput, strict JSON schemas, deterministic cost. Use the API for volume; use OpenCode for a few hundred high-quality trajectories and for operating the sandbox.

docs.title: 8.1 Hard gates (reject)
docs.text:
• JSON invalid or missing fields.
  • Patch does not apply with git apply --check.
  • Compile fails.
  • Tests fail (unless the task is explicitly “diagnose only”).
  • Test deleted/weakened to pass.
  • javax.* imports or Spring idioms in a Quarkus task.
  • Wrong Java/Quarkus version.
  • New dependency without justification.
  • Secret/PII detected.
  • License unknown or incompatible.
  • Diff > 400 lines or > 10 files without a clear reason.
  • Model claims tests passed but no test output exists.

docs.title: 8.2 Soft gates (score)
docs.text:
Dimension 1 3 5 Correctness does not compile compiles/tests pass tests cover edge cases Architecture leaks persistence/HTTP into domain partial boundaries clean ports/adapters + ArchUnit Java/Quarkus idiom Spring/javax/legacy mixed Java 25 + Quarkus 3.40 idiomatic Test quality no assertions happy path failure paths + meaningful assertions Scope unrelated rewrite some noise minimal diff Evidence invented output partial real commands/results

Keep rows with average ≥ 4 and no hard-gate failure. Keep a 10% human-reviewed sample.

docs.title: 8.3 Dedup and splits
docs.text:
• MinHash near-dedup at 0.8 on normalized code + task.
  • Exact dedup on patch hash.
  • Split by repository and base commit, not row.
  • Decontaminate against MultiPL-E, HumanEval-X, Multi-SWE-bench, SWE-bench Multilingual with 13-gram overlap.
  • Keep a time-based holdout: train on commits before a date, test on later commits.

docs.title: 9. Cost
docs.text:
Assume a task is ~2k input tokens and ~6k output tokens, plus 30% retries and a judge call.

Examples Output Input Flash off-peak V4-Pro off-peak 1,000 7.8M 2.6M ~$5 ~$18 5,000 39M 13M ~$25 ~$90 20,000 156M 52M ~$100 ~$360

Add judge calls, repair loops and long architecture tasks; double the estimate for a comfortable budget. Use prompt caching for the stable system/tool block. A local Qwen3-Coder-30B teacher has no API bill but is slower and needs 18–20 GB of memory.

Do not generate 20k before you have verified 200. The first 200 expose the schema, sandbox and licensing mistakes that would otherwise be replicated.

docs.title: 10. Legal and licensing
docs.text:
• Quarkus code: Apache-2.0; keep NOTICE/attribution.
  • Quarkus guides: the site footer says CC BY 3.0; check the specific guide before redistribution.
  • The Stack v3: ODC-BY; attribution required; per-file licenses still apply.
  • OpenCodeInstruct: CC-BY-4.0; attribution.
  • Magicoder OSS-Instruct: MIT, but generated by GPT-3.5; OpenAI usage policy applies.
  • SWE-smith-java: project MIT; dataset card untagged — verify before release.
  • Multi-SWE-bench: CC0 for the dataset; source repositories have their own licenses.
  • Your repository: do not send proprietary code to an API without permission; do not publish an adapter trained on it.
  • Generated code: may reproduce training code; scan for long overlaps and keep provenance.
  • DeepSeek/OpenCode terms: review the current terms; record the teacher model and version.

This is not legal advice. For a commercial release, have counsel review the dataset and model licenses.

docs.title: 11. Failure modes
docs.text: Failure Cause Fix Confident but unbuildable code no compile/test loop execute every candidate; keep only passes Invented Quarkus APIs teacher hallucination retrieve the guide; compile; reject Patch applies but tests fail wrong base commit/context pin commit; include pom.xml and tests Tests pass but assert nothing weak tests mutation/coverage; review assertions Model learns javax mixed Quarkus ⅔ data tag versions; filter legacy imports Model learns Quarkus 4 beta mixed 3.x/4.x data separate buckets; 4.x eval only Over-refusal too many negative examples rebalance; add in-scope positives Data leakage random split split by repo/commit; 13-gram decontamination Cost blow-up thinking + retries + judge Flash for bulk, Pro for hard, cap tokens License problem scraped/no-license seed provenance + license audit
