  • axe-core/playwright — https://github.com/dequelabs/axe-core-npm/tree/develop/packages/playwright
  • Webdev-Bench — https://huggingface.co/datasets/Roy-DOU/Webdev-Bench
  • Design2Code — https://huggingface.co/datasets/SALT-NLP/Design2Code
  • 17 — Fine-tuning update
  • 25 — React synthetic data

docs.title: 25 — Generating React/Tailwind training data with another LLM
docs.text:
Last verified: 25 October 2026. The API and OpenCode mechanics are shared with 07 — Synthetic data; the front-end prompts, browser verification and visual gates are new.

Public React datasets teach syntax and toy apps. They do not teach your design tokens, your component architecture, your responsive breakpoints, your accessibility bar, or the difference between a plausible screenshot and a working interface.

This chapter describes a repo-grounded pipeline:

permissive React repo + design tokens + commits
        │
        ▼
teacher proposes a task (JSON)
        │
        ▼
teacher proposes a patch + tests (JSON)
        │
        ▼
static validator: schema, versions, a11y, security
        │
        ▼
sandbox: npm ci → typecheck → lint → test → build
        │
        ▼
browser: Playwright flows → screenshots → axe → responsive
        │
        ▼
human/VLM visual review → keep / repair / discard
        │
        ▼
canonical JSONL (Qwen2.5-Coder arguments as objects)

The teacher can be DeepSeek V4.1 Flash/Pro, a local Qwen3-Coder-30B-A3B, or a larger API model. The verifier is not an LLM: it is TypeScript, ESLint, Vitest, Vite, Playwright and axe.

docs.title: 1. What synthetic data must add
docs.text:
Gap in public data Synthetic task React 19 idioms Actions, useActionState, ref as prop, use, View Transitions Tailwind 4 tokens @theme, semantic classes, dark mode, variants Component architecture primitives/patterns/features/pages, composition Repository context multi-file changes, read before edit, patch format Recovery inject a type/test/visual failure, ask for a fix, verify Accessibility keyboard, focus, labels, axe, target size Design quality hierarchy, spacing, typography, states, responsive Migration React 18→19, Tailwind 3→4, Router 7→8, TS 6→7 Safety refuse secrets, XSS, client-only auth, destructive changes

Do not generate 10,000 paraphrases of “build a dashboard”. Generate a matrix: layer × task family × difficulty × failure mode × viewport.

docs.title: 2. Teacher choices
docs.text:
Teacher Where Best for Caveats DeepSeek V4.1 Flash API bulk tasks, components, tests cheap; validate JSON; thinking tokens cost output DeepSeek V4-Pro API hard pages, refactors, reviews ~3–4× price; reserve for hard slices Qwen3-Coder-30B-A3B-Instruct 4-bit local MLX/llama.cpp private code, offline generation ~18–20 GB; 8K–16K practical; slower Qwen3-Coder-Next API/rented GPU hardest repo tasks 80B; not local Qwen3.8-27B 4-bit local judge/reviewer slow; good quality A VLM (Qwen3-VL class) local/API screenshot → design spec not the student; text-only coder cannot see images A frontier API API gold examples, rubric calibration cost/terms; no proprietary code without permission

Use Flash for volume, Pro for the hard 10–20%, and a local model for private repositories. Use a VLM only to turn images into text specs or to judge visual output.

docs.title: 3. Seed sources
docs.text:
Use only code you have the right to use:

  • shadcn-ui/ui (MIT) — components, tokens, Radix patterns.
  • tailwindlabs/tailwindcss (MIT) — v4 idioms and tests.
  • facebook/react (MIT) — React 19 patterns and tests.
  • radix-ui/primitives (MIT) — accessibility primitives.
  • TanStack/query (MIT) — server-state patterns.
  • storybookjs/storybook (MIT) — stories and a11y.
  • microsoft/playwright (Apache-2.0) — test patterns.
  • cfahlgren1/react-code-instructions (MIT) — complete-app shape.
  • The Stack v3 JS/TS/TSX with permissive license_type (ODC-BY).
  • Your own product, with permission.

Do not seed from proprietary code, leaked data, unlicensed repositories, paid component libraries (Tailwind Plus), or real brand sites you do not have rights to replicate.

docs.title: 4. The ten generation strategies
docs.text:
# Strategy Output Verification 1 Component spec component + variants + stories + tests typecheck, Vitest, axe 2 Page/route brief page + layout + states build, Playwright, responsive 3 Design-system refactor tokens/CVA extraction, no visual drift tests + screenshot diff 4 Tailwind 3 → 4 migration CSS-first config, renamed utilities build + visual diff 5 React 18 → 19 migration Actions, ref as prop, remove legacy tests + build 6 Accessibility audit/fix semantic HTML, focus, labels, keyboard axe + keyboard test 7 Test generation Vitest/RTL/Playwright tests run and assert 8 Bug injection/recovery broken commit → diagnosis → fix failing test then green 9 Design-to-code via VLM spec design.md → React + Tailwind screenshot similarity + rubric 10 Review/critique findings with file/line and fixes rubric + human spot check

Plus a negative slice: unsafe, under-specified, out-of-scope, invented API, false claim.

docs.title: 4.1 Component spec
docs.text:
Input: design tokens, 2–5 existing components, a test file, and a task. Output: a component with typed props, variants, states, accessible markup and tests.

This is the highest-value bucket. It teaches the component shape, tokens, CVA, focus styles, and test style.

docs.title: 4.2 Page/route brief
docs.text:
Input: routes, layout primitives, a data hook, a design brief. Output: a page with hierarchy, responsive layout, loading/empty/error/content states.

Require all four states. A page with only a happy path is a failed example.

docs.title: 4.3 Design-system refactor
docs.text:
Start from a working screen with raw palette classes, duplicated buttons, inconsistent radii. Ask for:

  • semantic tokens;
  • a CVA primitive;
  • direct imports, no barrel;
  • no visual change.

Verify with tests + before/after screenshots. A refactor that changes pixels without a reason is not behavior-preserving.

docs.title: 4.4 Tailwind 3 → 4 migration
docs.text:
Take a v3 page:

  • @tailwind base/components/utilities → @import "tailwindcss";
  • tailwind.config.js → @theme;
  • shadow-sm → shadow-xs;
  • rounded → rounded-sm;
  • outline-none → outline-hidden (or a real focus ring);
  • bg-opacity-50 → bg-black/50;
  • flex-shrink-* → shrink-*.

Verify with build + screenshot diff. This is a high-value migration task because the model otherwise blends v3 and v4.

docs.title: 4.5 React 18 → 19 migration
docs.text:
• ReactDOM.render → createRoot;
  • forwardRef → ref as prop where appropriate;
  • useFormState → useActionState;
  • propTypes/defaultProps on function components → TypeScript props;
  • class components → function components only when the task asks;
  • Context.Provider → <Context>.

Verify with typecheck, tests and build. Do not mix Next.js/RSC into a Vite SPA migration.

docs.title: 4.6 Accessibility audit/fix
docs.text:
Take a component with real issues:

  • div with onClick;
  • icon-only button without a label;
  • missing alt;
  • focus ring removed;
  • low contrast;
  • 16px target;
  • dialog without focus trap;
  • form error not linked.

Ask for a minimal fix. Verify with axe, keyboard navigation and a screen-reader spot check.

docs.title: 4.7 Test generation
docs.text:
Generate:

  • Vitest + Testing Library for behavior via roles;
  • Playwright for critical flows and responsive;
  • axe assertions;
  • visual snapshots for stable pages.

Reject tests that pass on the broken baseline (they assert nothing), use Thread.sleep/arbitrary timeouts, or assert implementation details.

docs.title: 4.8 Bug injection/recovery
docs.text:
Inject a realistic bug:

  • stale closure in a form;
  • missing key;
  • controlled/uncontrolled input switch;
  • race between two queries;
  • layout shift from an unsized image;
  • missing error state;
  • focus lost after a dialog closes;
  • Tailwind class conflict from cn misuse.

The training row should include the failing output and the diagnosis, not just the final patch.

docs.title: 4.9 Design-to-code via a VLM spec
docs.text:
A text coder cannot see a screenshot. Use a VLM to produce a structured design.md:

# Design spec — Billing settings

## Product and audience
B2B SaaS admin; needs to change plan and payment method quickly.

## Layout
Two-column: settings nav (240px) + content (max 720px). Mobile: stacked.

## Hierarchy
H1 "Billing"; plan card primary; invoice table secondary; danger zone last.

## Palette
Canvas #FAFAFB; surface #FFFFFF; ink #1F2430; muted #6B7280; brand #6D28D9;
success #15803D; danger #B91C1C.

## Typography
Inter; H1 28/36 semibold; H2 18/28 semibold; body 14/22; caption 12/16.

## Components
PlanCard, PaymentMethodRow, InvoiceTable, ConfirmDialog, Button, Badge.

## States
loading skeleton; empty invoices; error retry; success toast; disabled while pending.

## Responsive
>=1024 two columns; 768 one column; 320 no horizontal scroll; 44px targets.

## Accessibility
Landmarks; one H1; labels; focus-visible; 4.5:1; dialog focus trap; reduced motion.

## Copy
Real plan names and prices; no lorem ipsum.

## Acceptance
typecheck, lint, test, build; axe zero serious/critical; screenshots at 320/768/1440.

Then ask the coder for React + Tailwind. Verify by rendering and comparing to the reference screenshot (SSIM/CLIP + human/VLM pairwise), not by asking the same teacher “does it look good?”.

If you need image input end-to-end, train a VLM (Qwen3-VL class or Design2Code-style) separately. Do not put images into a Qwen2.5-Coder row.

docs.title: 4.10 Review/critique
docs.text:
Ask for findings by severity with file/line, principle, issue and minimal fix. The judge checks:

  • Is the finding real?
  • Is the line plausible?
  • Is the fix minimal?
  • Does it avoid invented APIs?
  • Does it distinguish “taste” from “bug”?

Review data is weaker than executed patches; keep it a small slice and label it.

docs.title: 5. Prompt templates
docs.text:
Reusable files live in examples/react/:

  • teacher-system.md — global rules.
  • task-prompt.md — task taxonomy.
  • prompts/solver.md — plan + patch + tests.
  • prompts/component.md — component + variants + stories.
  • prompts/page.md — page + states + responsive.
  • prompts/test.md — Vitest/Playwright.
  • prompts/refactor.md — design system.
  • prompts/review.md — findings.
  • prompts/migration.md — React/Tailwind/Router/TS upgrades.
  • prompts/a11y.md — audit/fix.
  • prompts/design.md — design spec / visual critique.

docs.title: 5.1 Task generation with DeepSeek
docs.text:
export DEEPSEEK_API_KEY="..."
python scripts/generate_synthetic.py \
  --mode tasks --tasks 300 --batch 10 \
  --model deepseek-flash \
  --system-file examples/react/teacher-system.md \
  --prompt-file examples/react/task-prompt.md \
  --out data/react/interim/tasks.jsonl

The script uses JSON-object mode, retries and token accounting. It does not execute anything and does not solve the tasks.

docs.title: 5.2 Solving a task
docs.text:
Use the OpenAI-compatible API with prompts/solver.md and repo context:

import json
import os
from pathlib import Path
from openai import OpenAI

client = OpenAI(api_key=os.environ["DEEPSEEK_API_KEY"], base_url="https://api.deepseek.com")
template = Path("examples/react/prompts/solver.md").read_text()

for task in tasks:
    prompt = (template
              .replace("{task}", task["task"])
              .replace("{repo_context}", json.dumps(task["repo_context"]))
              .replace("{constraints}", json.dumps(task["constraints"]))
              .replace("{acceptance}", json.dumps(task["acceptance"]))
              .replace("{test_command}", task["test_command"]))
    r = client.chat.completions.create(
        model="deepseek-flash",
        messages=[{"role": "system", "content": Path("examples/react/teacher-system.md").read_text()},
                  {"role": "user", "content": prompt}],
        response_format={"type": "json_object"},
        temperature=0.3,
        max_tokens=12000,
    )
    candidate = json.loads(r.choices[0].message.content)
    # validate schema, apply patch, run checks, keep only verified

Use .replace, not .format: the prompt contains JSON braces. For a full page, 12k output tokens is often needed; for a component, 6–8k is enough.

docs.title: 5.3 A solver response
docs.text:
{
  "plan": ["read tokens", "read Button", "add SettingsPage", "add states", "add tests"],
  "patch": "diff --git a/src/routes/settings.tsx b/src/routes/settings.tsx\n...",
  "files": ["src/routes/settings.tsx", "src/features/settings/components/ProfileForm.tsx"],
  "tests": ["src/features/settings/components/ProfileForm.test.tsx"],
  "commands": ["npm run typecheck", "npm run lint", "npm test -- --run", "npm run build"],
  "risks": ["focus management after save"],
  "notes": "uses design tokens; no new dependencies"
}

Validate the patch with git apply --check before applying. Reject responses with prose outside JSON.

docs.title: 5.4 Repair loop
docs.text:
If the build fails:

  1. Capture the first 80 lines of the TypeScript/ESLint/Vitest/Playwright error.
  2. Send the task, patch and error back: “Here is the real compiler/test output; produce a minimal fix.”
  3. Max 2 attempts.
  4. Keep the final verified trajectory, including the failed attempt if it teaches recovery.

Do not let the teacher “fix” by deleting the failing test or adding @ts-ignore.

docs.title: 6.1 Build the lab image
docs.text:
docker build -t web-lab -f examples/react/Dockerfile.web-lab .

The image is based on the official Playwright image (Chromium installed). Check node -v once; Vite 8 needs Node 20.19+ or 22.12+. It has no application dependencies; npm ci installs them.

docs.title: 6.2 Run a candidate
docs.text:
rm -rf /tmp/react-work && cp -a ~/src/my-app /tmp/react-work
cd /tmp/react-work
git checkout <base_commit>

git apply --check model.patch && git apply model.patch

docker run --rm \
  -u "$(id -u):$(id -g)" -e HOME=/tmp \
  -v /tmp/react-work:/workspace \
  -v "$HOME/.npm":/tmp/.npm \
  -w /workspace web-lab \
  bash -lc 'npm ci --prefer-offline && npm run typecheck && npm run lint && npm test -- --run && npm run build'

Playwright:

docker run --rm -u "$(id -u):$(id -g)" -e HOME=/tmp \
  -v /tmp/react-work:/workspace -v "$HOME/.npm":/tmp/.npm \
  -w /workspace web-lab \
  npx playwright test

Axe and screenshots are part of the Playwright suite.

docs.title: 6.3 Offline builds
docs.text:
1. Run one online npm ci to populate the cache.
  2. Use npm ci --prefer-offline or --offline with a complete cache.
  3. Pin package-lock.json; no latest ranges in test repos.
  4. Do not let the model add dependencies; if it must, require a justification and record it.

docs.title: 6.4 Playwright config
docs.text:
import { defineConfig, devices } from "@playwright/test";

export default defineConfig({
  testDir: "./e2e",
  fullyParallel: true,
  forbidOnly: !!process.env.CI,
  retries: process.env.CI ? 1 : 0,
  use: {
    baseURL: "http://127.0.0.1:4173",
    trace: "on-first-retry",
    reducedMotion: "reduce",
  },
  webServer: {
    command: "npm run preview -- --port 4173",
    url: "http://127.0.0.1:4173",
    reuseExistingServer: !process.env.CI,
  },
  projects: [
    { name: "mobile", use: { ...devices["iPhone 13"] } },
    { name: "tablet", use: { ...devices["iPad Mini"] } },
    { name: "desktop", use: { ...devices["Desktop Chrome"], viewport: { width: 1440, height: 900 } } },
  ],
});

reducedMotion: "reduce" makes screenshots and motion tests deterministic. Disable animations in toHaveScreenshot.

docs.title: 6.5 Axe and responsive checks
docs.text:
import AxeBuilder from "@axe-core/playwright";
import { expect, test } from "@playwright/test";

test("settings page is accessible and does not overflow", async ({ page }) => {
  await page.goto("/settings");

  const results = await new AxeBuilder({ page })
    .withTags(["wcag2a", "wcag2aa", "wcag22aa"])
    .analyze();

  const severe = results.violations.filter(
    (v) => v.impact === "serious" || v.impact === "critical",
  );
  expect(severe).toEqual([]);

  const overflow = await page.evaluate(
    () => document.documentElement.scrollWidth - document.documentElement.clientWidth,
  );
  expect(overflow).toBeLessThanOrEqual(1);
});

docs.title: 6.6 Keyboard and focus
docs.text:
test("dialog traps focus and returns it", async ({ page }) => {
  await page.goto("/settings");
  await page.getByRole("button", { name: "Delete workspace" }).click();
  await expect(page.getByRole("dialog")).toBeVisible();
  await page.keyboard.press("Escape");
  await expect(page.getByRole("button", { name: "Delete workspace" })).toBeFocused();
});

Manual keyboard checks are still required; Playwright can prove focus order, not screen-reader quality.

docs.title: 6.7 Visual regression
docs.text:
await expect(page).toHaveScreenshot("settings-desktop.png", {
  fullPage: true,
  animations: "disabled",
  maxDiffPixelRatio: 0.01,
});

For refactors, capture the baseline before the patch, apply the patch, capture after, and compare. For new pages, compare against a reference design with a rubric and a human/VLM pairwise check; pixel diff is not meaningful without a baseline.

docs.title: 7. OpenCode as the agent in the loop
docs.text: examples/react/opencode.json points OpenCode at the local MLX/llama.cpp server.

docs.title: 7.1 Project rules
docs.text: OpenCode reads AGENTS.md from the repository. Put the React/Tailwind rules there: React 19, Tailwind 4.3, TypeScript 7-compatible source, semantic tokens, accessible primitives, npm run typecheck, no new dependencies without asking.

docs.title: 7.2 Run headless
docs.text:
cd /tmp/react-work
opencode run -m local/qwen25-coder-14b-react --format json \
  "Build a responsive billing settings page. Read the design tokens and existing form primitives first. Include loading, empty and error states. Run typecheck, lint, test and build. Return a diff."

Parse the event stream into OpenAI-style messages:

  • assistant text → content;
  • tool call → tool_calls;
  • tool result → role: "tool";
  • reasoning → drop for Qwen2.5-Coder (no thinking template).

Normalize tool arguments to objects. Reject transcripts that claim checks passed without a run_npm or run_playwright result.

docs.title: 7.3 What OpenCode is good and bad at
docs.text: Good: multi-step repo navigation, edits, browser/test loops, generating a transcript. Bad: bulk throughput, strict JSON schemas, deterministic cost. Use the API for volume; use OpenCode for a few hundred high-quality trajectories and for operating the sandbox.

docs.title: 7.4 Playwright MCP
docs.text: If you use a browser MCP server, give it only localhost URLs in the disposable container. Do not expose the host browser, cookies, corporate SSO or the open internet. The agent needs the rendered app, not your session.

docs.title: 8.1 Hard gates (reject)
docs.text:
• JSON invalid or missing fields.
  • Patch does not apply with git apply --check.
  • Typecheck fails.
  • Lint fails on errors.
  • Unit or E2E tests fail (unless the task is explicitly “diagnose only”).
  • Test deleted or weakened to pass.
  • vite build fails.
  • axe serious/critical violations remain.
  • Horizontal overflow at 320px.
  • @tailwind base, bg-opacity-*, flex-shrink-*, dynamic class construction.
  • ReactDOM.render, useFormState in a React 19 task.
  • dangerouslySetInnerHTML unsanitized; secrets; client-only auth.
  • New dependency without justification.
  • Diff > 400 lines or > 10 files without a clear reason.
  • Model claims checks passed but no output exists.

docs.title: 8.2 Soft gates (score)
docs.text:
Dimension 1 3 5 Correctness does not typecheck typecheck/build pass tests cover edge cases Architecture one giant component some separation primitives/features/pages + composition Design system raw palette, inconsistent partial tokens semantic tokens + CVA + dark mode Visual quality broken hierarchy acceptable clear hierarchy, rhythm, restraint Accessibility keyboard traps labels/focus axe zero + keyboard + semantics Responsive overflow works at one width 320/768/1440 + container queries Tests none/weak happy path failure paths + roles + E2E Evidence invented output partial real commands/screenshots

Keep rows with average ≥ 4 and no hard-gate failure. Keep a 10% human-reviewed sample.

docs.title: 8.3 Dedup and splits
docs.text:
• MinHash near-dedup at 0.8 on normalized code + task.
  • Exact dedup on patch hash.
  • Perceptual hash for near-identical screenshots.
  • Split by repository and base commit, not row.
  • Decontaminate against Webdev-Bench, Design2Code, SWE-bench Multilingual, Multi-SWE-bench and SWE-bench Multimodal with 13-gram overlap.
  • Keep a time-based holdout: train on commits before a date, test on later commits.

docs.title: 9. Cost
docs.text:
Assume a task is ~2k input tokens and ~8k output tokens, plus 30% retries and a judge call.

Examples Output Input Flash off-peak V4-Pro off-peak 1,000 10.4M 2.6M ~$6 ~$22 5,000 52M 13M ~$30 ~$110 20,000 208M 52M ~$125 ~$440

Add browser/CPU time: 1–5 minutes per task; 5,000 tasks is 80–400 CPU-hours. Run Playwright in parallel, but cap workers so a single Mac or CI runner does not thrash.

Do not generate 20k before verifying 200. The first 200 expose the schema, sandbox, design-token and licensing mistakes that would otherwise be replicated.

A local Qwen3-Coder-30B teacher has no API bill but is slower and needs 18–20 GB of memory. Use it for private code, not for bulk volume.

docs.title: 10. Legal and licensing
docs.text:
• The Stack v3: ODC-BY; attribution; per-file licenses apply.
  • OpenCodeInstruct: CC-BY-4.0; attribution.
  • Magicoder OSS-Instruct: MIT, but generated by GPT-3.5; OpenAI usage policy applies.
  • react-code-instructions: MIT; generated apps may imitate brands; do not ship clones.
  • WebSight: CC-BY-4.0; synthetic, but contains real images; check image provenance.
  • Design2Code: ODC-BY; evaluation only; real webpages and brands.
  • Webdev-Bench: MIT; evaluation only.
  • SWE-bench Multilingual: MIT; evaluation only.
  • Multi-SWE-bench: other; source repositories have their own licenses.
  • SWE-bench Multimodal: no dataset license tag; source repositories; evaluation only.
  • shadcn/ui, Tailwind, React, Radix, TanStack, Storybook: MIT.
  • Playwright: Apache-2.0.
  • Tailwind Plus / paid component libraries: do not train on them.
  • DeepSeek/OpenCode terms: review the current terms; record the teacher model and version.

Do not train on proprietary screenshots, customer data, or a real brand's site without permission. Replicating a trademarked interface can raise copyright/trade-dress issues even if the code is generated.

This is not legal advice. For a commercial release, have counsel review the dataset and model licenses.

docs.title: 11. Failure modes
docs.text: Failure Cause Fix Confident but unbuildable UI no typecheck/build loop execute every candidate; keep only passes “Looks fine” but broken mobile no viewport tests Playwright at 320/768/1440; overflow assertion Tailwind classes do nothing v3 directives in a v4 project, dynamic classes version tags; validator; build + screenshot Generic AI look no design spec/reference design.md, tokens, rubric, human review Accessibility regressions axe not run axe gate + keyboard tests Tests pass but assert nothing weak tests mutation/coverage; review assertions Visual diff flaky animations, fonts, dynamic data reduced motion, disable animations, seed data, mask Model learns div buttons low-quality seed data validator + a11y examples Over-refusal too many negatives rebalance; add in-scope positives Data leakage random split split by repo/commit; 13-gram decontamination Cost blow-up long pages + retries + judge Flash for bulk, Pro for hard, cap tokens License problem scraped/branded seeds provenance + license audit

docs.title: 26 — One Qwen3 model for all three tracks
docs.text:
Last verified: 25 October 2026 against the Qwen model cards, the Qwen3 technical report, the Qwen3-Coder repository and MLX-LM 0.32.2.

Considering Gemma 4 12B as a second base? See 27 — Gemma 4 12B and 31 — Gemma vs Qwen. The Qwen recommendation here is unchanged.

The handbook now has three tracks:

  • Kali/agent — tool calling, scope, recovery, refusal.
  • Java/Quarkus — Java 25, Quarkus 3.40, architecture, Maven.
  • React/Tailwind — React 19.3, Tailwind 4.3, design systems, Playwright.

They currently use two bases: Qwen3-14B for Kali and Qwen2.5-Coder-14B for Java/React. The obvious question:

Is there one Qwen3 model that can do all three?

The short answer:

  • One local base you can fine-tune for all three: Qwen3-14B. Use one base and three LoRA adapters, not one mixed adapter, unless you deliberately want the simplicity trade-off.
  • One model you can serve for all three without training: Qwen3-Coder-30B-A3B-Instruct for code-heavy work, or Qwen3-30B-A3B-Instruct-2507 if you need more general/security breadth and 262K context. Both fit 4-bit inference on 32 GB; neither is a reliable local LoRA target.
  • Do not pick Qwen3.5/3.6/3.8 for local 32 GB training. They are stronger models, but the Gated DeltaNet training path in MLX is still immature. Rent a GPU if you want them.

docs.title: 1. What “for all” can mean
docs.text:
Goal Best answer Why One base to fine-tune locally for all three Qwen3-14B, three adapters Only Qwen3 dense model that is both strong enough and reliably trainable in 32 GB One adapter for all three Qwen3-14B, mixed data Simpler serving; expect per-track regressions One model to serve, no training Qwen3-Coder-30B-A3B or Qwen3-30B-A3B-2507 30B-class quality, 3.3B active, 4-bit fits 32 GB; MoE is inference-only here Best quality, training on a rented GPU Qwen3.5-9B or Qwen3.8-27B 262K context, vision, stronger agentic/coding; not local 32 GB Best code-only model Qwen3-Coder-30B-A3B Code-specialised, 256K, agentic tool use Best general/security breadth Qwen3-30B-A3B-Instruct-2507 262K, non-thinking, general instruction and tool use

“For all” is therefore a base-model question, not a single-adapter question. A 14B adapter has limited capacity; three small adapters on one frozen base give you specialization without three copies of the weights.

docs.title: 2. The Qwen3 candidates
docs.text:
All are Apache-2.0 except where noted. Vendor benchmarks are useful for relative ordering, not for predicting your task.

Model Params Layers Native context Local training on 32 GB Local inference Role Qwen3-8B 8.2B 36 32K / 131K YaRN Yes, all layers Fast Unified fallback Qwen3-14B 14.8B 40 32K / 131K YaRN Yes, 24/40 or all 40 15–17 tok/s Recommended base for all Qwen3-32B 32.8B 64 32K / 131K No Slow Inference/teacher Qwen3-30B-A3B 30.5B / 3.3B 48 32K Marginal / not recommended Yes, ~17–18 GB 4-bit General MoE Qwen3-30B-A3B-Instruct-2507 30.5B / 3.3B 48 262K No Yes, ~17–18 GB 4-bit General/long-context MoE Qwen3-Coder-30B-A3B-Instruct 30.5B / 3.3B 48 262K No Yes, ~17–18 GB 4-bit Code/agentic specialist Qwen3.5-4B 4.7B 32 262K Conditional Yes Small multimodal agent Qwen3.5-9B 9.7B 32 262K No / high risk Yes Rent a GPU to train Qwen3.6-35B-A3B 36.0B / ~3B 48 262K No Yes, 19–24 GB Agentic coding MoE Qwen3.8-27B 27.8B 64 262K No Yes, ~15–17 GB 4-bit Teacher/oracle Qwen3-Coder-Next 79.7B / ~3B — 262K No No (~45 GB 4-bit) API/rented GPU

The Qwen3-14B is the only row that is simultaneously:

  • dense and standard-attention (no GDN/MoE training surprises);
  • strong at tool calling and instruction following;
  • small enough for 4-bit QLoRA on 32 GB;
  • large enough to be useful for Java and React after fine-tuning;
  • Apache-2.0 with an official MLX 4-bit conversion.

docs.title: 2.1 Why not Qwen3-8B as the “one for all”?
docs.text: It fits more comfortably and trains all 36 layers, but it has less capacity for three domains. It is the right debug model and the right fallback if the 14B will not fit your context needs. It is not the best final base.

docs.title: 2.2 Why not Qwen3-Coder-30B-A3B as the local training base?
docs.text:
Because it is a 30.5B MoE, not a 14B dense model:

  • 4-bit weights alone are ~17–18 GB; gradients, activations and optimizer state push past 32 GB.
  • MoE routing and expert gradients are not a reliable MLX LoRA path on this machine.
  • It is excellent served at 4-bit with 8K–32K context, and excellent as a teacher/judge.

Use it for inference and data generation, not for a local adapter.

docs.title: 2.3 Why not Qwen3-32B?
docs.text: 32.8B dense at 4-bit is ~18.5 GB of weights; LoRA training does not fit in 32 GB. It is an inference/teacher model.

docs.title: 2.4 Why not Qwen3.5/3.6/3.8?
docs.text:
They are newer and stronger, but they use hybrid Gated DeltaNet (GDN) plus gated attention. The MLX training path is still immature: first-backward OOMs, Metal descriptor leaks and step time scaling with trained GDN layers have been reported on 32–36 GB machines, and the Metal VJP PR was closed unmerged. Unsloth also advises against 4-bit QLoRA for Qwen3.5.

If you rent a 48–80 GB GPU, Qwen3.5-9B is the best quality/time balance and Qwen3.8-27B is the strongest dense option. That is a separate training track, not a 32 GB local one.

docs.title: 3. Recommendation: one base, three adapters
docs.text:
Qwen3-14B-4bit (frozen)
├── adapters/qwen3-14b-kali     # tool calling, scope, recovery, refusal
├── adapters/qwen3-14b-java     # Java 25, Quarkus 3.40, architecture
└── adapters/qwen3-14b-react    # React 19.3, Tailwind 4.3, a11y

Why this is better than one mixed adapter:

Three adapters One mixed adapter Per-track quality Highest Diluted Interference None Kali refusal vs coding style; Java vs React syntax Disk ~0.3–0.8 GB total ~0.2–0.4 GB Serving Three ports or per-request adapter One model, one port Evaluation Per-track clean Must check every track Data mixing None Ratios, mode tokens, caps Updating one track Retrain one adapter Retrain everything

LoRA adapters are cheap. Three adapters on one base is the pragmatic “one model for all” answer: one base model to download, quantize, and serve; three small specializations.

docs.title: 3.1 Training order
docs.text:
1. Kali adapter first. It teaches the tool-call contract, recovery and scope/refusal behaviour.
  2. Java adapter second. It teaches repository editing, Maven and architecture.
  3. React adapter third. It teaches component/design-system/browser verification.

They do not share an adapter; the order only affects when you have a usable model. If you want one base checkpoint and three adapters, train each from the same Qwen3-14B-4bit, not adapter-on-adapter.

docs.title: 3.2 Serving
docs.text:
Option A — three fused models on three ports (simplest, most robust):

mlx_lm.fuse --model mlx-community/Qwen3-14B-4bit \
  --adapter-path adapters/qwen3-14b-kali --save-path fused/qwen3-14b-kali-4bit
mlx_lm.fuse --model mlx-community/Qwen3-14B-4bit \
  --adapter-path adapters/qwen3-14b-java --save-path fused/qwen3-14b-java-4bit
mlx_lm.fuse --model mlx-community/Qwen3-14B-4bit \
  --adapter-path adapters/qwen3-14b-react --save-path fused/qwen3-14b-react-4bit

mlx_lm.server --model fused/qwen3-14b-kali-4bit  --port 8080
mlx_lm.server --model fused/qwen3-14b-java-4bit  --port 8081
mlx_lm.server --model fused/qwen3-14b-react-4bit --port 8082

Run only the adapter you need at a time on 32 GB; one 14B 4-bit server plus a browser is already a lot of memory. Three servers at once is a bad idea.

Option B — one server, per-request adapter:

mlx_lm.server accepts --adapter-path and a per-request adapters field. This is convenient for a router, but client support varies. If your OpenAI client cannot send adapters, use Option A or restart the server with the right adapter.

Option C — llama.cpp for GGUF and better tool-call fidelity:

Convert each fused model to GGUF, quantize to Q4_K_M, and serve with llama-server --jinja on separate ports. See 10-export-serving.md.

docs.title: 3.3 Routing
docs.text:
A small router is better than asking one model to infer the domain from a vague prompt:

if request touches authorized hosts / scan / exploit / report:
    port 8080, Kali system prompt + Kali tools + scope file
elif repository contains pom.xml / build.gradle / .java:
    port 8081, Java system prompt + repo tools + Maven
elif repository contains package.json / .tsx / tailwind:
    port 8082, React system prompt + repo/browser tools
else:
    ask the user which mode, or use the base model without an adapter

Do not rely on the model to choose between three tool schemas. Pass only the relevant tools.

docs.title: 4. If you insist on one mixed adapter
docs.text: Sometimes one adapter is genuinely better: one endpoint, one deployment, one model card, simpler ops. It can work if you accept a quality trade-off and design the data carefully.

docs.title: 4.1 Mixed data layout
docs.text:
data/unified/
├── raw/                 # optional snapshots
├── interim/             # per-track rows before mixing
├── processed/
│   ├── train.jsonl
│   ├── valid.jsonl
│   ├── test.jsonl
│   └── manifest.json
└── golden/              # per-track golden sets, never trained on

Build it from the three track splits:

python scripts/mix_datasets.py \
  --source kali=data/processed/train.jsonl \
  --source java=data/java/processed/train.jsonl \
  --source react=data/react/processed/train.jsonl \
  --weights kali=0.40,java=0.30,react=0.30 \
  --out data/unified/processed \
  --arguments-format string

--arguments-format string is mandatory: Qwen3 expects OpenAI-style JSON strings, while the Java/React rows were prepared for Qwen2.5-Coder with objects. The mixer converts them and records the choice in manifest.json.

docs.title: 4.2 Ratios
docs.text:
Bucket Share Why Kali/agent 40% Tool contract, scope/refusal, recovery; smallest public data, highest risk Java/Quarkus 30% Repository edits, Maven, architecture React/Tailwind 30% Components, design tokens, browser checks Cross-domain included Repo navigation, test-failure recovery, refusal, instruction following

A ⅓ split is also reasonable. Do not let Java/React dominate because their rows are longer; weight by examples, then check tokens per track in manifest.json and token_stats.py.

docs.title: 4.3 Mode token
docs.text:
Put an explicit mode at the top of the system prompt:

MODE: KALI

or

MODE: JAVA

or

MODE: REACT

Then the task. The model learns to switch behaviour without a separate router. At inference, the harness sets the mode and supplies the matching tools.

Do not encode the mode only in the user text (“this is a Java task”) and then expect it to generalize; make it a stable system-level field.

docs.title: 4.4 Tools per row, not a mega-schema
docs.text:
A unified adapter does not need one tool schema containing Kali, Maven and Playwright tools. Each training row carries only its track's tools:

  • Kali: 6–10 typed tools (scope_check, nmap_scan, http_probe, …).
  • Java: read_file, search_code, apply_patch, run_maven, arch_check, git_diff.
  • React: read_file, search_code, apply_patch, run_npm, run_playwright, screenshot, axe_check, git_diff.

At inference, pass only the relevant set. A 14B model with 30 tools will choose worse than the same model with 8.

docs.title: 4.5 Training
docs.text:
mlx_lm.lora --config configs/qwen3-14b-unified.yaml

The config uses:

  • Qwen3-14B 4-bit;
  • 24 of 40 blocks;
  • rank 16, scale: 2.0;
  • LR 1e-4, effective batch 8;
  • sequence 2,048;
  • mask_prompt: true.

Start with 1–2 epochs (~200–300 iterations for 2–3M tokens), not a fixed 600. Evaluate every track before scaling.

Verify the adapter before the run:

python scripts/check_lora.py \
  --model mlx-community/Qwen3-14B-4bit \
  --num-layers 24 --rank 16 --scale 2

Expect 24 adapted blocks of 40, seven projections per block (168 modules) and roughly 36M trainable parameters. All 40 blocks is ~60M and ~280 modules; test it only after the 24-block adapter is evaluated.

docs.title: 4.6 The quality trade-off
docs.text:
Expect one or more of:

  • Java/React code style drifts toward the base Qwen3 style; fewer Quarkus/Tailwind idioms.
  • Kali refusal becomes less crisp if coding rows dominate.
  • The adapter spends capacity on three vocabularies; per-track loss is higher than a dedicated adapter.
  • A single sequence budget must fit three very different row shapes.

A reasonable acceptance bar:

Track Dedicated adapter Unified adapter tolerance Kali tool-call validity >0.95 ≥0.90 Kali unsafe-action rate 0 0 Java compile rate >0.90 ≥0.85 Java test pass >0.45 ≥0.40 React typecheck/build >0.90 ≥0.85 React axe serious/critical 0 0

If the unified adapter misses these, keep the three-adapter design.

docs.title: 5. Thinking mode
docs.text:
Qwen3-14B has hybrid thinking:

  • default enable_thinking=True;
  • /think and /no_think soft switches;
  • enable_thinking=False for a hard non-thinking mode.

With MLX --mask-prompt, the completion starts at assistant\n and includes the think block, so the adapter learns to emit <think>…. Train and serve with the same setting:

  • Thinking on (default): better reasoning, more tokens, more latency; use sequence 2,048+ and check truncation.
  • Thinking off: shorter, faster; requires patching the local tokenizer_config.json to default enable_thinking=False before training, because mlx_lm.lora has no chat-template flag. Do not train thinking-on and serve thinking-off; you get a duplicated or empty think block.

For a unified adapter, thinking on is the simpler, safer default. If you need no-think for code latency, train a separate no-think adapter from a patched tokenizer config; do not mix the two.

docs.title: 6. What to evaluate
docs.text: A unified adapter must be evaluated per track, not on an average:

docs.title: Kali
docs.text:
• tool-call validity;
  • tool/argument accuracy;
  • multi-step task success;
  • unsafe-action rate (must be 0);
  • scope/refusal precision.

Use 09-evaluation.md and the private 240-task golden set.

docs.title: Java
docs.text:
• ./mvnw -q -DskipITs test;
  • compile rate;
  • ArchUnit pass rate;
  • review precision;
  • no javax.*/Spring/legacy RESTEasy.

Use 20-java-finetuning.md §8.

docs.title: React
docs.text:
• tsc --noEmit, vite build;
  • Vitest/Playwright;
  • axe serious/critical = 0;
  • no horizontal overflow at 320/768/1440;
  • visual rubric and requirement satisfaction.

Use 24-react-finetuning.md §8.

docs.title: The decision rule
docs.text:
Keep the unified adapter only if:

  1. no track loses more than ~5 points versus its dedicated adapter;
  2. the unsafe/security gates still pass;
  3. the operational simplicity is worth the loss.

Otherwise, one base + three adapters is the better “one model for all”.

docs.title: 7. What not to do
docs.text:
• Do not train Qwen3-Coder-30B-A3B locally on 32 GB. It is a 30.5B MoE; use it as teacher/judge/serving.
  • Do not train Qwen3-32B locally. 32.8B dense does not fit.
  • Do not mix Qwen2.5-Coder arguments objects with Qwen3 strings. Re-render the rows with mix_datasets.py --arguments-format string.
  • Do not put all domain tools in one schema. 6–10 tools per request.
  • Do not train Qwen3.5/3.6/3.8 LoRA on this Mac. GDN training is not reliable in MLX yet.
  • Do not evaluate only the average. A unified model can look fine on average and fail safety or Java compilation.
  • Do not serve three 14B models at once on 32 GB. One adapter at a time.

docs.title: 8. Cost and time
docs.text:
Plan Training Wall clock (est.) Disk Three adapters, 2M tokens each 3 × ~1 epoch 45–75 h 0.5 GB adapters + 3 × 8.5 GB fused (optional) One mixed adapter, 4M tokens ~1.5 epochs 50–70 h 0.3 GB adapter + one fused model Qwen3-8B unified, 3M tokens all 36 layers 20–30 h 0.3 GB Qwen3-Coder-30B inference only none minutes to start ~18 GB 4-bit

The three-adapter plan costs more wall clock but gives you a usable model earlier (after the Kali adapter) and avoids a full retrain when one track changes.

docs.title: 9. The answer in one table
docs.text:
If you want… Use Train locally? One Qwen3 base for all three, best local quality Qwen3-14B + 3 LoRA adapters Yes One adapter, simplest ops Qwen3-14B + mixed data Yes, with trade-offs One model to serve all three, no training Qwen3-Coder-30B-A3B (code-heavy) or Qwen3-30B-A3B-2507 (general) No Best code quality Qwen3-Coder-30B-A3B No Best Java/React adapter quality Qwen2.5-Coder-14B track adapters Yes Best overall with a rented GPU Qwen3.5-9B or Qwen3.8-27B Rented GPU

Bottom line: Qwen3-14B is the “one Qwen3 for all” on this machine. It is the only Qwen3 dense model that trains reliably in 32 GB and is strong enough for all three domains. Keep one base and three adapters; use a mixed adapter only when operational simplicity matters more than per-track quality.

docs.title: 27 — Gemma 4 12B: the alternative track
docs.text:
Last verified: 25 October 2026 against the Gemma 4 model card, the Hugging Face config and chat template, MLX-LM 0.32.2, and the MLX community 4-bit checkpoint.

This is the start of a separate Gemma 4 12B track. It does not replace the Qwen tracks. The point is to run both:

  • Qwen3-14B for the Kali/agent track;
  • Qwen2.5-Coder-14B for the specialised Java and React adapters;
  • Gemma 4 12B as a second base for comparison, and as the strongest choice for vision-heavy React work.

The Qwen files, configs, adapters and docs stay exactly as they are.

docs.title: 1. What Gemma 4 12B is
docs.text:
Property Gemma 4 12B Release 3 June 2026; model card current 30 July 2026 Parameters 11.95B dense Layers 48 Hidden / intermediate 3,840 / 15,360 Attention 16 query heads / 8 KV heads; hybrid sliding-window + global attention Context 256K native Vocabulary 262,144 Modalities Text, image, audio in; text out; encoder-free “Unified” architecture Tool calling Native function calling, <|tool_call> format Thinking <|channel>thought … <channel|>; enabled by <|think|> License Apache-2.0 MLX 4-bit mlx-community/gemma-4-12b-it-4bit, ~6.6–7.6 GB

“Unified” means Gemma 4 12B has no separate vision or audio encoder. Raw image patches and audio waveforms are projected directly into the decoder’s embedding space through linear layers. That is elegant for inference and fine-tuning, but it also means the text-only MLX loader strips the vision/audio weights; image training is a separate mlx-vlm path.

The architecture is a hybrid: most layers use a 1,024-token sliding window, with periodic full-attention layers; global layers use p-RoPE and unified K/V. For LoRA this matters because full-attention layers omit a separate v_proj. Do not assume every block has the same seven projections.

docs.title: 2. Gemma 4 12B vs the Qwen bases
docs.text:
Gemma 4 12B Qwen3-14B Qwen2.5-Coder-14B Parameters 11.95B 14.8B 14.7B Layers 48 40 48 Native context 256K 32K (131K YaRN) 128K Vision Yes No No Tool calling Native, custom syntax <tool_call> JSON <tool_call> JSON Thinking Channel-based <think> None License Apache-2.0 Apache-2.0 Apache-2.0 Local 4-bit QLoRA Yes, 24/48 Yes, 24/40 Yes, 24/48 Best role React/vision, A/B Java Kali/agent Java/React code specialist

Do not read this table as “Gemma wins”. It has newer training, more context and vision. Qwen2.5-Coder is code-specialised and its tool format is simpler. The only reliable comparison is your own golden set.

docs.title: 3.1 React and design-to-code
docs.text:
Gemma 4 12B can see a screenshot. That is a genuine capability Qwen2.5-Coder lacks. It opens two options:

  1. Text-only LoRA — train on design.md → React/Tailwind; use Gemma as a VLM to produce the design spec, then the adapter writes the code.
  2. Multimodal LoRA — train image → code with mlx-vlm and a separate dataset. This is more complex and not covered by the text mlx_lm.lora configs here.

Even the text-only path benefits from the 256K context: a page, its components, tests and a design brief fit more comfortably.

docs.title: 3.2 Java/Quarkus
docs.text: Gemma 4 12B is a newer, strong coding base. It may beat Qwen2.5-Coder on some tasks and lose on others. The Quarkus target is unchanged: Java 25 LTS + Quarkus 3.40 LTS, verified by Maven and ArchUnit.

docs.title: 3.3 Kali/agent
docs.text: Gemma 4 has native function calling and a real improvement over Gemma 3. But Qwen3 has the stronger documented tool-calling record in this handbook, and Gemma’s tool format is unusual (call:name{key:<|"|>value<|"|>}). Treat Kali as an A/B experiment, not a default switch.

docs.title: 3.4 One base for all
docs.text: Gemma 4 12B is a credible single base: Apache-2.0, 12B, 256K, vision, native tools. The trade-off is the same as with Qwen: one base + three adapters beats one mixed adapter for quality. See 31 — Running both and comparing.

docs.title: 4. What fits on 32 GB
docs.text:
These are planning estimates. Measure with mlx_lm.lora and mx.get_peak_memory().

Setup Weights Adapter/optimizer Peak estimate Gemma 4 12B 4-bit, inference ~6.6–7.6 GB — 10–14 GB at 8K 24/48 blocks, seq 2,048 ~6.6–7.6 GB ~0.3 GB 16–22 GB 24/48 blocks, seq 3,072 ~6.6–7.6 GB ~0.3 GB 20–26 GB 16/48 blocks, seq 4,096 ~6.6–7.6 GB ~0.2 GB 20–26 GB all 48 blocks, seq 2,048 ~6.6–7.6 GB ~0.6 GB 22–28 GB

Start at 24/48, seq 2,048. If it is comfortable, raise sequence before layers. If it OOMs, drop to 16/48 or 2,048; do not start by shrinking the dataset.

mlx_lm.lora uses the last N blocks. All 48 is an experiment, not the first run.

docs.title: 4.1 Expected trainable parameters
docs.text:
The exact number depends on the MLX version and on v_proj being absent in full-attention layers:

  • 24/48, rank 16, scale: 2.0: roughly 30–35M trainable parameters.
  • all 48: roughly 60–70M.
  • modules: about 5–7 per block, not always 7, because of K=V in full-attention layers.

Run scripts/check_lora.py on the Mac. If it reports fewer than four modules per adapted block, stop.

docs.title: 5. Tool format: the part that breaks naive ports
docs.text:
Gemma 4 does not use Qwen’s JSON tool-call format.

Qwen3:

<tool_call>{"name":"read_file","arguments":{"path":"src/App.tsx"}}</tool_call>

Gemma 4:

<|tool_call>call:read_file{path:<|"|>src/App.tsx<|"|>}<tool_call|>

Consequences:

  1. Tool arguments must be JSON objects (mappings) in the canonical messages. A string makes the Gemma template raise: tool_calls[].function.arguments must be a JSON object (mapping), not a string.
  2. Use prepare_dataset.py --arguments-format dict.
  3. Tool results use role: "tool" with a tool_call_id; Gemma resolves that id to the function name.
  4. The template emits native <|tool_call> blocks; do not put Qwen-style <tool_call> JSON in assistant content.
  5. Tool names should match [A-Za-z_][A-Za-z0-9_-]*.

Modern mlx-lm includes a Gemma 4 parser (mlx_lm/tool_parsers/gemma4.py). The old failure mode — tool calls landing in content with an empty tool_calls array — is fixed, but verify on your exact version:

curl -s http://127.0.0.1:8083/v1/chat/completions \
  -H 'Content-Type: application/json' \
  -d '{"model":"gemma4-12b-kali","messages":[{"role":"user","content":"Read src/App.tsx"}],"tools":[...]}' |
  python3 -m json.tool

If tool_calls is empty, use llama-server --jinja or update mlx-lm; do not train an agent on unparsed tool text.

docs.title: 6. Thinking mode
docs.text:
Gemma 4 uses a channel:

<|channel>thought
...reasoning...
<channel|>final answer
  • Thinking is enabled by <|think|> at the start of the system prompt; enable_thinking=True in the template adds it.
  • The canonical MLX mlx_lm.lora path applies the tokenizer template with its default; for Gemma 4 that is thinking off.
  • With thinking disabled, Gemma 4 still emits an empty thought block. Do not mix a no-think adapter with a template that injects a different block.
  • reasoning_content in a message is rendered as the thinking channel.
  • Do not keep previous turns’ thinking in history, except in tool-call turns. Gemma 4 expects historical assistant messages to contain final answers.

The practical rule: train and serve with the same thinking setting. The configs here target the default no-think path; if you want a thinking adapter, verify the template first and keep a separate adapter.

docs.title: 7. Vision and audio are separate
docs.text:
mlx_lm is the text path. Its Gemma 4 loader strips vision_tower, multi_modal_projector, audio_tower and related weights. That is fine for text-only LoRA.

For image or audio:

  • use mlx-vlm and the multimodal Gemma checkpoint;
  • train a separate adapter, with image content in the messages;
  • do not put images into a mlx_lm.lora row;
  • expect a different memory profile and a slower run.

The text-only React adapter can still use Gemma as a captioner or design-spec writer: render a screenshot, ask for a structured design.md, then train the coder on text → code.

docs.title: 8. The track layout
docs.text:

docs/29-gemma4-finetuning.md   full MLX runbook

The Qwen directories are untouched. You can run the same task against both stacks and compare.

docs.title: 9. Recommendation
docs.text:

docs.title: 28 — Gemma 4 12B datasets
docs.text:
Last verified: 25 October 2026. Sizes and licenses were checked against the Hugging Face API and dataset cards; re-check before a large download.

The raw material is largely the same as the Qwen tracks. What changes is the template, the tool-call format, and the option of using Gemma as a vision model.

This chapter is the Gemma-specific shopping list. The full catalogs are:

  • 05 — Datasets — general tool calling, agentic, cyber.
  • 19 — Java datasets — Java/Quarkus.
  • 23 — React datasets — React/Tailwind, design-to-code.
  • 07 — Synthetic data, 21 — Java synthetic, 25 — React synthetic.

docs.title: 1. What changes for Gemma
docs.text:
Topic Qwen Gemma 4 12B Tool arguments Qwen3: JSON string; Qwen2.5-Coder: object Object/mapping Tool call syntax <tool_call>{"name":...}</tool_call> <|tool_call>call:name{key:<|"|>value<|"|>}<tool_call|> Tool result role: tool, id ignored by Qwen3 template role: tool, id resolved to name Thinking <think>…</think> <|channel>thought…<channel|> Thinking history final assistant may include think block drop previous thoughts, except tool-call turns Vision no (text model) yes, but text mlx_lm strips vision weights Context 32K (Qwen3) / 128K (Coder) 256K

The canonical data shape is still messages + optional tools. The template does the rendering. Do not store Gemma-rendered strings; they are brittle and impossible to re-template.

docs.title: 2. Text datasets that are worth using
2.1 Raw code
docs.text:
Dataset Size License Gemma use HuggingFaceCode/stack-v3-train ~3.6T tokens / 15.9 TB ODC-BY seed repos; filter TS/TSX/Java bigcode/starcoderdata 250B tokens / 86 languages gated; per-file optional; older code_search_net 1.86M JS functions repo MIT; data other docstring→code; low priority

Do not train raw files as SFT. Sample repositories and generate tasks with a verifier.

docs.title: 2.2 Code instructions
docs.text:
Dataset Size License Gemma use nvidia/OpenCodeInstruct 5M / ~19 GB CC-BY-4.0 large instruction base; filter Java/TS/React ise-uiuc/Magicoder-OSS-Instruct-75K 75K MIT (GPT-3.5 output; OpenAI policy) diversity ise-uiuc/Magicoder-Evol-Instruct-110K 110K Apache-2.0 harder tasks cfahlgren1/react-code-instructions 74,428 / ~907 MB MIT complete-app shape; React 18/Tailwind 3 era

Rebuild and retag React examples to React 19/Tailwind 4; do not train the raw 2024-era apps as if they were current.

docs.title: 2.3 Design and visual
docs.text:
Dataset Size License Gemma use HuggingFaceM4/WebSight v0.2 1,922,671 / ~285 GB CC-BY-4.0 screenshot + HTML/Tailwind; text subset for HTML/Tailwind style SALT-NLP/Design2Code 484 / ~69 MB ODC-BY evaluation only; screenshot→HTML SALT-NLP/Design2Code-hf 484 ODC-BY HF-format version princeton-nlp/SWE-bench_Multimodal 480 test + 100 dev no dataset license tag; source repos eval only; screenshots/mockups Roy-DOU/Webdev-Bench 40 tasks / 1,125 checks MIT eval only; multi-round front-end

Gemma’s vision advantage: you can use WebSight/Design2Code/SWE-bench Multimodal as image input with mlx-vlm, not just text. But a text-only mlx_lm.lora run strips the vision tower; those images are then only references for a written spec.

docs.title: 2.4 Java/Quarkus
docs.text:
Reuse the sources in 19 — Java datasets:

  • The Stack v3 Java subset.
  • OpenCodeInstruct and Magicoder Java rows.
  • Methods2Test for test generation.
  • SWE-smith-java, Multi-SWE-bench Java, SWE-bench Multilingual Java for repair.
  • Quarkus quickstarts and Quarkus repos for framework idioms.
  • Maven/ArchUnit verification.

Gemma-specific filter: compile with Java 25, Quarkus 3.40 LTS, jakarta.*, quarkus-rest; reject javax.*, Spring, legacy RESTEasy.

docs.title: 2.5 Kali/agent
docs.text:
Reuse 05 — Datasets:

  • general tool calling: xLAM, ToolACE, Hermes, Toucan;
  • agentic: SWE-smith, Nemotron Terminal, OpenThoughts;
  • cyber: KaliBench train, Trendyol cyber QA, filtered security QA;
  • refusal/scope: When2Call and your own scope dialogues.

Gemma’s tool parser accepts \w- names and native calls. Test tool-call validity on your exact tool schema before trusting a large Kali mix.

docs.title: 3. The Gemma row shape
docs.text:
{
  "messages": [
    {"role": "system", "content": "MODE: REACT\nYou are ..."},
    {"role": "user", "content": "Add a StatCard ..."},
    {"role": "assistant", "content": null, "tool_calls": [
      {"id": "call_1", "type": "function",
       "function": {"name": "read_file", "arguments": {"path": "src/components/ui/StatCard.tsx"}}}
    ]},
    {"role": "tool", "tool_call_id": "call_1", "content": "..."},
    {"role": "assistant", "content": "```tsx\n...\n```"}
  ],
  "tools": [
    {"type": "function", "function": {
      "name": "read_file", "description": "Read a file.",
      "parameters": {"type": "object", "properties": {"path": {"type": "string"}}, "required": ["path"]}
    }}
  ],
  "meta": {"track": "react", "license": "MIT", "test_command": "npm run typecheck && npm test -- --run"}
}

Rules:

  • arguments is an object; a string is a hard error in the Gemma template.
  • Tool call id is required if a tool result follows.
  • tool_call_id must match a preceding call.
  • content can be null on a tool-call assistant turn.
  • reasoning_content is optional; it renders as a thinking channel.
  • Keep only the current turn’s thinking; drop previous thoughts except tool-call turns.
  • The first message should be system or developer.
  • Do not include Qwen’s <tool_call> JSON in content.

docs.title: 4.1 Kali
docs.text:
Bucket Share Source General tool calling 35–40% xLAM, ToolACE, Hermes, Toucan Multi-turn/agentic 15–20% SWE-smith, Nemotron Terminal, synthetic Cyber QA + Kali CLI 20% KaliBench train, Trendyol, filtered QA Verified synthetic trajectories 15% DeepSeek/OpenCode + lab Refusal/scope 10% When2Call, private scope dialogues

Target 2–4M tokens for the first adapter. Do not train on BFCL, KaliBench test, Cybench, NYU CTF or CyberMetric.

docs.title: 4.2 Java
docs.text:
Reuse 19 — Java datasets §8. Target 2–4M tokens:

  • 30% repository edits/repair;
  • 20% feature implementation;
  • 15% tests;
  • 15% review/architecture;
  • 10% migration/refactor;
  • 10% negative/security.

docs.title: 4.3 React
docs.text:
Reuse 23 — React datasets §8. Target 2–4M tokens:

  • 20% components/primitives;
  • 15% pages/layouts;
  • 15% data/forms;
  • 10% design system;
  • 10% accessibility;
  • 10% testing;
  • 10% bug fix;
  • 5% migration;
  • 5% negative/security.

docs.title: 4.4 Unified
docs.text: 40% Kali / 30% Java / 30% React, plus a mode token. Use 31 — Running both for the comparison method.

docs.title: 5. Gemma-specific quality gates
docs.text:
Run these in addition to the filters in 23 — React datasets §9 and 19 — Java datasets §9:

  • arguments is a mapping on every tool call.
  • Every tool call id is unique and every tool result resolves.
  • Tool names are [A-Za-z_][A-Za-z0-9_-]*.
  • No Qwen-style <tool_call> JSON in assistant content.
  • No previous-turn thinking, except tool-call turns.
  • Render one row with the Gemma tokenizer; confirm <|tool_call>call: appears.
  • Render one row with tools and confirm the system/tool block is well formed.
  • mlx_lm.server returns tool_calls, not raw text in content.
  • Text-only rows contain no image placeholders.
  • The source license is recorded; no unlicensed/branded seeds.
  • Token p99 fits max_seq_length (2,048 or 3,072), not 256K.
  • 13-gram overlap against Webdev-Bench, Design2Code, SWE-bench Multilingual/Multimodal and Multi-SWE-bench.

The static validator is:

python scripts/validate_gemma4_dataset.py data/gemma4/react/processed/train.jsonl \
  --tools examples/react/tools.json --strict

It catches string arguments, broken ids, undeclared tools, Qwen call syntax, secrets and missing metadata. It does not compile or render; the real verifier does.

docs.title: 6. Multimodal data (separate track)
docs.text:
If you want Gemma to consume screenshots directly:

  1. Use the multimodal checkpoint (google/gemma-4-12B-it or an MLX-VLM build).
  2. Build rows with image + text content, not text-only messages.
  3. Use mlx-vlm training, not mlx_lm.lora.
  4. Hold out Design2Code/WebSight and evaluate rendered similarity + human/VLM pairwise.
  5. Do not mix multimodal rows into a text adapter; the weights and template differ.

A practical middle ground: use Gemma as a VLM spec writer to turn screenshots into design.md, then train the text adapter on spec → code. That keeps the training path simple and gives the text coder a fair input.

docs.title: 7. Licensing
docs.text:
Same rules as the Qwen tracks:

  • The Stack v3: ODC-BY; per-file licenses.
  • OpenCodeInstruct: CC-BY-4.0.
  • Magicoder: MIT; GPT-3.5 output subject to OpenAI policy.
  • react-code-instructions: MIT; generated apps may imitate brands.
  • WebSight: CC-BY-4.0; synthetic with real images; check provenance.
  • Design2Code: ODC-BY; evaluation only.
  • Webdev-Bench: MIT; evaluation only.
  • SWE-bench Multilingual: MIT; evaluation only.
  • Multi-SWE-bench: other; source repos have their own licenses.
  • SWE-bench Multimodal: no dataset license tag; source repos; evaluation only.
  • shadcn/ui, Tailwind, React, Radix, TanStack, Storybook: MIT.
  • Playwright: Apache-2.0.
  • Gemma 4 weights: Apache-2.0.

Do not train on proprietary code, customer data, paid component libraries or real brand sites without permission. This is not legal advice.

docs.title: 29 — Fine-tuning Gemma 4 12B
docs.text:
Last verified: 25 October 2026 against MLX-LM 0.32.2 and the Gemma 4 12B config/chat template. The commands were not executed on the target Mac in this environment.

This is the runbook for the Gemma track. It does not touch the Qwen configs or adapters.

The default is 24 of 48 blocks, rank 16, scale: 2.0, sequence 2,048, effective batch 8. The React config raises sequence to 3,072; the all-layer path is an experiment.

docs.title: 0. The recipe in one table
docs.text:
Choice Value Why Base mlx-community/gemma-4-12b-it-4bit 11.95B, 48 layers, 4-bit, text-only loader Method 4-bit QLoRA, lora base frozen; adapter small Blocks 24 of 48 memory-safe default Rank / scale 16 / 2.0 PEFT alpha=32 equivalent LR 1e-4 standard LoRA range with scale=2 Effective batch 8 (1 × 8 accumulation) LoRA prefers 8–16 Sequence 2,048 (React 3,072) component/code rows fit; 256K is a serving feature, not a training budget Iterations 300 ~1–2 epochs; adjust to tokens Masking mask_prompt: true train only the final assistant turn Checkpoint every 50 short run; keep options

Gemma 4 12B is smaller than Qwen3-14B, but it has 48 layers and a 262K vocabulary. Do not assume it is faster just because it has fewer parameters; measure.

docs.title: 1. Preflight
docs.text:
cd ~/work/qwen-kali-agent
source .venv/bin/activate

python -c "import mlx_lm, mlx.core as mx; print(mlx_lm.__version__); print(mx.device_info())"
python scripts/check_env.py

Checklist:

  • mlx-lm>=0.32.2 (the Gemma 4 tool parser and gemma4_unified mapping).
  • mlx-community/gemma-4-12b-it-4bit downloads and loads.
  • mx.get_peak_memory() works.
  • 100+ GB free disk.
  • The Gemma data exists and is non-empty.
  • No secrets in data/gemma4/.
  • Qwen adapters and configs are untouched.
  • You have a baseline evaluation of the base Gemma model.
python - <<'PY'
from mlx_lm import load
model, tok = load("mlx-community/gemma-4-12b-it-4bit")
print(type(model).__name__, len(model.layers))
PY

If this fails, fix the MLX/model version before touching the data.

docs.title: 2. Render the template before training
docs.text:
This is the step that catches most Gemma mistakes. Use the multimodal processor for the canonical template:

from transformers import AutoProcessor

processor = AutoProcessor.from_pretrained("google/gemma-4-12B-it")

messages = [
    {"role": "system", "content": "MODE: REACT\nYou are a senior React/Tailwind engineer."},
    {"role": "user", "content": "Read src/App.tsx."},
    {"role": "assistant", "content": None, "tool_calls": [
        {"id": "call_1", "type": "function",
         "function": {"name": "read_file", "arguments": {"path": "src/App.tsx"}}}
    ]},
    {"role": "tool", "tool_call_id": "call_1", "content": "export default function App() {}"},
    {"role": "assistant", "content": "I read the file."},
]

tools = [{
    "type": "function",
    "function": {
        "name": "read_file",
        "description": "Read a repository file.",
        "parameters": {
            "type": "object",
            "properties": {"path": {"type": "string"}},
            "required": ["path"],
        },
    },
}]

print(processor.apply_chat_template(
    messages, tools=tools, tokenize=False,
    add_generation_prompt=True, enable_thinking=False,
))

Expect:

  • a <|turn>system block containing <|tool>…<tool|>;
  • <|tool_call>call:read_file{path:<|"|>src/App.tsx<|"|>}<tool_call|>;
  • <|tool_response>…<tool_response|>;
  • an empty <|channel>thought\n<channel|> when thinking is disabled.

If you see an error about arguments must be a JSON object, your row used a string. Convert with:

python scripts/prepare_dataset.py ... --arguments-format dict

docs.title: 2.1 Thinking
docs.text:
mlx_lm.lora has no enable_thinking switch. The Gemma template defaults to thinking off (enable_thinking=false). The no-think path still emits an empty thought block. Train and serve with the same setting.

If you want a thinking adapter, patch the local model's tokenizer_config.json to default enable_thinking=true (or use a wrapper that passes it) and verify the rendered sample. Do not train thinking-on and serve thinking-off; you get a mismatched channel.

docs.title: 3.1 Build a track
docs.text:
mkdir -p data/gemma4/{kali,java,react,unified}

# Normalize for Gemma: arguments are mappings
python scripts/prepare_dataset.py data/gemma4/kali/interim/all.jsonl \
  --out data/gemma4/kali/processed --arguments-format dict \
  --split 0.9 0.05 0.05

python scripts/prepare_dataset.py data/gemma4/java/interim/all.jsonl \
  --out data/gemma4/java/processed --arguments-format dict

python scripts/prepare_dataset.py data/gemma4/react/interim/all.jsonl \
  --out data/gemma4/react/processed --arguments-format dict

docs.title: 3.2 Validate
docs.text:
python scripts/validate_dataset.py data/gemma4/react/processed/train.jsonl \
  --tools examples/react/tools.json

python scripts/validate_gemma4_dataset.py data/gemma4/react/processed/train.jsonl \
  --tools examples/react/tools.json --strict

The Gemma validator catches:

  • string arguments (the template will reject them);
  • broken/unknown tool_call_id;
  • undeclared tool names;
  • Qwen-style <tool_call> JSON in content;
  • previous-turn thinking in history;
  • secrets and missing metadata.

docs.title: 3.3 Token stats
docs.text:
python scripts/token_stats.py data/gemma4/react/processed/train.jsonl \
  --model google/gemma-4-12B-it

Use the 99th percentile, rounded to 256. Do not confuse the 256K serving context with the 2K–3K training budget; long rows cost memory and time.

docs.title: 3.4 Unified mix
docs.text:
python scripts/mix_datasets.py \
  --source kali=data/gemma4/kali/processed/train.jsonl \
  --source java=data/gemma4/java/processed/train.jsonl \
  --source react=data/gemma4/react/processed/train.jsonl \
  --weights kali=0.40,java=0.30,react=0.30 \
  --out data/gemma4/unified/processed --arguments-format dict

dict is mandatory for Gemma. string is for Qwen3; mixing them is the most common template error.

docs.title: 4.1 Kali — configs/gemma4-12b-kali.yaml
docs.text:
model: mlx-community/gemma-4-12b-it-4bit
train: true
data: data/gemma4/kali/processed
fine_tune_type: lora
optimizer: adamw
num_layers: 24
batch_size: 1
iters: 300
val_batches: 25
learning_rate: 1.0e-4
steps_per_report: 10
steps_per_eval: 100
save_every: 50
max_seq_length: 2048
grad_checkpoint: true
grad_accumulation_steps: 8
mask_prompt: true
adapter_path: adapters/gemma4-12b-kali
seed: 42
lora_parameters:
  rank: 16
  dropout: 0.05
  scale: 2.0
lr_schedule:
  name: cosine_decay
  warmup: 30
  arguments: [1.0e-4, 300, 1.0e-6]
optimizer_config:
  adamw:
    weight_decay: 0.01

docs.title: 4.2 Java — configs/gemma4-12b-java.yaml
docs.text: Same shape, data/gemma4/java/processed, adapter adapters/gemma4-12b-java, sequence 2,048.

docs.title: 4.3 React — configs/gemma4-12b-react.yaml
docs.text: Same shape, data/gemma4/react/processed, adapter adapters/gemma4-12b-react, sequence 3,072. If it OOMs, drop to 2,048 before dropping layers.

docs.title: 4.4 Unified — configs/gemma4-12b-unified.yaml
docs.text: Same shape, data/gemma4/unified/processed, adapter adapters/gemma4-12b-unified.

docs.title: 4.5 How many iterations?
docs.text:
iters ≈ epochs × dataset_tokens / (batch_size × grad_accumulation_steps × avg_tokens_per_sample)

A 2.5M-token dataset, average 1,800 tokens, effective batch 8, one epoch:

iters = 2,500,000 / (8 × 1,800) ≈ 174

So 200 is one epoch; 300 is ~1.5 epochs. Use validation loss and the golden set, not a fixed 600.

docs.title: 5. Verify the adapter
docs.text:
python scripts/check_lora.py \
  --model mlx-community/gemma-4-12b-it-4bit \
  --num-layers 24 --rank 16 --scale 2

Expected:

  • 48 blocks total; 24 adapted.
  • q_proj, o_proj, gate_proj, up_proj, down_proj at minimum; k_proj and sometimes v_proj depending on full vs sliding attention.
  • Roughly 30–35M trainable parameters for 24/48 at rank 16.
  • ~60–70M for all 48.

Do not expect exactly 7 modules per block: Gemma 4 uses K=V in full-attention layers, so v_proj is absent there. check_lora.py only warns if fewer than four modules per adapted block.

If you see only q_proj/v_proj, stop.

docs.title: 6. Smoke run
docs.text:
Create a 100k-token subset and 40 iterations:

head -n 1500 data/gemma4/react/processed/train.jsonl > data/gemma4/react/processed/train.smoke.jsonl
mkdir -p data/gemma4/react/processed-smoke
cp data/gemma4/react/processed/train.smoke.jsonl data/gemma4/react/processed-smoke/train.jsonl
cp data/gemma4/react/processed/valid.jsonl data/gemma4/react/processed-smoke/valid.jsonl

mlx_lm.lora --config configs/gemma4-12b-react.yaml \
  --data data/gemma4/react/processed-smoke --iters 40 --save-every 20 \
  --adapter-path adapters/gemma4-12b-react-smoke

Check:

  • finite loss, falling;
  • tokens/sec — budget 18–28 for 12B at 2K, lower at 3K;
  • peak memory 16–26 GB;
  • rendered sample contains <|tool_call>call: and <|tool_response>;
  • no arguments must be a JSON object error.

Fuse and test:

mlx_lm.fuse \
  --model mlx-community/gemma-4-12b-it-4bit \
  --adapter-path adapters/gemma4-12b-react-smoke \
  --save-path fused/gemma4-12b-react-smoke-4bit

mlx_lm.server --model fused/gemma4-12b-react-smoke-4bit \
  --host 127.0.0.1 --port 8083 --max-tokens 4096 \
  --temp 0.2 --top-p 0.95

Send 20 tasks. Check:

  • React 19 function components, no class components or jQuery;
  • Tailwind 4 (@import "tailwindcss", @theme), not v3 directives;
  • semantic tokens, not raw hex;
  • loading/empty/error states;
  • actual tool_calls, not raw text;
  • honest “I did not run the tests” when it did not.

Do not launch the 14B/12B full run until the smoke output is plausible.

docs.title: 7. The main runs
docs.text:
# Kali
mlx_lm.lora --config configs/gemma4-12b-kali.yaml

# Java
mlx_lm.lora --config configs/gemma4-12b-java.yaml

# React
mlx_lm.lora --config configs/gemma4-12b-react.yaml

# One mixed adapter
mlx_lm.lora --config configs/gemma4-12b-unified.yaml

Healthy signals:

Metric Healthy Warning Train loss falls to 0.3–0.7 stuck >1.0 after 200 iters Val loss tracks train rises for 2+ evals Tokens/sec 18–28 (2K) <10 = memory/thermal Peak memory 16–26 GB >27 GB = danger It/sec stable collapses = swap/thermal

Code loss is lower than chat loss; compare the adapter to the base on the same tasks, not across datasets.

docs.title: 7.1 If it OOMs
docs.text:
1. max_seq_length: 3072 → 2048.
  2. num_layers: 24 → 16.
  3. Confirm grad_checkpoint: true, batch_size: 1.
  4. Close Docker, Chrome, the IDE and the Kali VM.
  5. Move to a smaller model or a rented GPU.

Do not start by shrinking the dataset.

docs.title: 7.2 If loss is nan
docs.text:
• A prompt is at or over max_seq_length; with mask_prompt the completion is empty.
  • The LR is too high; halve it.
  • The data has an empty assistant message or a string arguments (the template would usually error first).
  • Run the validator and the template render again.

docs.title: 8. Checkpoints and resume
docs.text:
mlx_lm.lora --config configs/gemma4-12b-react.yaml \
  --resume-adapter-file adapters/gemma4-12b-react/0000200_adapters.safetensors \
  --iters 100 \
  --adapter-path adapters/gemma4-12b-react-resume

Only weights are restored; optimizer state, LR schedule position and iteration count are not. Use a new adapter path and a fresh short cosine schedule.

Checkpoints are ~100–250 MB each. Delete old ones after evaluation.

docs.title: 9.1 Kali
docs.text:
Use the Kali golden set and the 09/31 harness:

  • tool-call validity;
  • tool/argument accuracy;
  • multi-step success;
  • unsafe-action rate = 0;
  • scope/refusal precision.

docs.title: 9.2 Java
docs.text:
Use the 20 harness:

  • ./mvnw -q -DskipITs test;
  • compile rate;
  • ArchUnit pass;
  • review precision;
  • no javax.*/Spring/legacy RESTEasy.

docs.title: 9.3 React
docs.text:
Use the 24 harness:

  • tsc --noEmit, vite build;
  • Vitest/Playwright;
  • axe serious/critical = 0;
  • no horizontal overflow at 320/768/1440;
  • visual rubric and requirement satisfaction.

docs.title: 9.4 Release gates
docs.text:
Use the same gates as the Qwen tracks. For Gemma, add:

  • tool_calls populated by mlx_lm.server;
  • no arguments string errors in a 100-row render;
  • no previous-turn thinking leakage in multi-turn rows;
  • if multimodal, a separate mlx-vlm evaluation.

docs.title: 10. Fuse and serve
docs.text:
mlx_lm.fuse \
  --model mlx-community/gemma-4-12b-it-4bit \
  --adapter-path adapters/gemma4-12b-react \
  --save-path fused/gemma4-12b-react-4bit

mlx_lm.server \
  --model fused/gemma4-12b-react-4bit \
  --host 127.0.0.1 --port 8083 \
  --max-tokens 4096 --temp 0.2 --top-p 0.95

Gemma’s recommended sampling for general use is temperature 1.0, top-p 0.95, top-k 64. For deterministic code and security work, a lower temperature (0.2) is reasonable; keep it fixed across the comparison.

docs.title: 10.1 Tool-call check
docs.text:
curl -s http://127.0.0.1:8083/v1/chat/completions \
  -H 'Content-Type: application/json' \
  -d '{
    "model": "gemma4-12b-react",
    "messages": [{"role": "user", "content": "Read src/App.tsx"}],
    "tools": [{"type": "function", "function": {
      "name": "read_file", "description": "Read a file.",
      "parameters": {"type": "object", "properties": {"path": {"type": "string"}}, "required": ["path"]}
    }}]
  }' | python3 -m json.tool

Check choices[0].message.tool_calls; if empty and the content contains <|tool_call>, update MLX or use llama-server --jinja.

docs.title: 10.2 GGUF path
docs.text:
Gemma 4 12B uses the new gemma4_unified architecture. Verify that your llama.cpp build and convert_hf_to_gguf.py support it before relying on GGUF; if conversion fails, use the MLX path. A GGUF build is not required for the comparison.

mlx_lm.fuse \
  --model mlx-community/gemma-4-12b-it-4bit \
  --adapter-path adapters/gemma4-12b-react \
  --save-path fused/gemma4-12b-react-bf16 \
  --dequantize

python3 ~/work/llama.cpp/convert_hf_to_gguf.py \
  fused/gemma4-12b-react-bf16 \
  --outtype f16 --outfile models/gemma4-12b-react-f16.gguf

~/work/llama.cpp/build/bin/llama-quantize \
  models/gemma4-12b-react-f16.gguf \
  models/gemma4-12b-react-Q4_K_M.gguf Q4_K_M

llama-server -m models/gemma4-12b-react-Q4_K_M.gguf \
  --host 127.0.0.1 --port 8083 -c 16384 -ngl 99 -fa auto --jinja

--dequantize creates a ~24 GB bf16 directory; delete it after conversion. See 10 — Export & serving.

docs.title: 11. Run both stacks
docs.text:
Stack Base Ports Qwen Kali Qwen3-14B 8080 Qwen Java Qwen2.5-Coder-14B 8081 Qwen React Qwen2.5-Coder-14B 8082 Gemma Kali/Java/React Gemma 4 12B 8083–8085 Gemma unified Gemma 4 12B 8086

Do not run all of them at once on 32 GB. Run one adapter per stack, compare, then stop it. Use 31 — Running both and scripts/compare_models.py.

docs.title: 12. Checklist
docs.text:
Before:

  • mlx-lm>=0.32.2;
  • Gemma template renders;
  • data uses --arguments-format dict;
  • validator strict passes;
  • token p99 fits;
  • check_lora.py shows MLP projections;
  • 100+ GB free;
  • Docker/VM/Chrome off;
  • baseline saved;
  • Qwen stack untouched.

After:

  • best checkpoint by golden set;
  • tool calls parse;
  • typecheck/build/tests/axe on React;
  • Maven/ArchUnit on Java;
  • Kali unsafe rate = 0;
  • fused model loads;
  • GGUF path tested;
  • model card + dataset manifest written;
  • comparison report vs Qwen.
