docs.title: 33 — How Qwen was built
docs.text:
Last verified: 25 October 2026 against the Qwen2.5, Qwen2.5-Coder and Qwen3 technical reports, the Qwen3-Coder and Qwen3.5 releases, and the model cards.

This chapter reconstructs the Qwen pipeline from public information. It separates what is disclosed (architecture, token counts, training stages, some RL details) from what is not (exact data mixture, exact hyperparameters, full RL recipe).

Read with: 37 — Architecture anatomy for the shape-level view and 38 — Derivations and proofs for the math behind GRPO, distillation and attention.

docs.title: 1. The family tree
docs.text:
Generation Models used here What changed Qwen2.5 0.5B–72B dense, 30B-A3B MoE 18T tokens, 1M+ SFT samples, strong multilingual/coding Qwen2.5-Coder 0.5B–32B continued pretraining on 5.5T code tokens; file + repo level; FIM Qwen3 0.6B–32B dense, 30B-A3B / 235B-A22B MoE 36T tokens, 119 languages, thinking/non-thinking fusion, strong RL Qwen3-Coder 30B-A3B, 480B-A35B, Coder-Next 7.5T tokens 70% code, 256K, agentic RL Qwen3.5 / 3.6 dense 0.8B–27B, MoE 35B-A3B / 122B-A10B / 397B-A17B hybrid GDN + gated attention, native multimodal, 256K–1M Qwen3.8 27B dense, larger MoE newer generation; not the local training target here

The local handbook uses Qwen3-14B for agents and Qwen2.5-Coder-14B for specialised code adapters because both train reliably in 32 GB. The newer Qwen3.5/3.6/3.8 models are stronger but their GDN training path is immature in MLX on this machine.

docs.title: 2. Qwen2.5: the base recipe
docs.text:
The Qwen2.5 report describes:

  • 18 trillion pretraining tokens, up from 7T in Qwen2.
  • Dense and MoE variants, 0.5B–72B.
  • 1M+ supervised fine-tuning samples.
  • Strong multilingual, coding, math and structured-output data.
  • A base architecture that Qwen3 and Qwen2.5-Coder inherit: GQA, SwiGLU, RoPE, RMSNorm with pre-norm, QKV bias in Qwen2 (removed in Qwen3).

Qwen2.5 is important because it establishes the data and post-training philosophy: large-scale pretraining, then a large SFT mixture, then preference optimisation. The exact mixture is not public.

docs.title: 3. Qwen2.5-Coder: continued pretraining on code
docs.text: Qwen2.5-Coder is not trained from random weights. It starts from Qwen2.5 and continues pretraining on a code-heavy corpus.

docs.title: 3.1 Data
docs.text:
• 5.5 trillion tokens total.
  • 5.2T file-level tokens at sequence length 8,192, with next-token prediction and FIM (fill-in-the-middle).
  • 300B repo-level tokens extending context to 32,768 for repository understanding.
  • Final mixture 70% code, 20% text, 10% math.
  • Sources: public GitHub repositories, web-crawled code text, synthetic code data, code-related documents.
  • Cleaning: dedup, quality filtering, language balancing, license filtering.

docs.title: 3.2 FIM objective
docs.text:
Fill-in-the-middle trains the model to complete a span given a prefix and suffix. With special tokens <fim_prefix>, <fim_suffix>, <fim_middle>:

\[ \mathcal{L}_{\text{FIM}} = -\sum_{t\in\text{middle}} \log p_\theta(x_t\mid \text{prefix},\text{suffix},x_{<t}). \]

On paper

A tiny Python infill: the prefix is def sq(x):, the suffix is print(sq(3)), and the middle return x*x is three tokens that the model predicts with probabilities \(\tfrac12\), \(\tfrac12\) and \(\tfrac14\). Use \(\ln2\approx0.693\).

\[ \begin{aligned} \mathcal{L}_{\text{FIM}} &=-\big(\ln\tfrac12+\ln\tfrac12+\ln\tfrac14\big)\\ &=4\ln2\approx2.77 \end{aligned} \]

The prefix and suffix tokens are context only and add nothing to the sum; a perfect infill (all three probabilities 1) would score 0.

Longer version: 43 §1.

This is why code models are good at editing inside a file, not just continuing at the end.

docs.title: 3.3 Architecture
docs.text:
Model Params Layers Heads (Q/KV) Context Vocab Qwen2.5-Coder-7B 7.6B 28 28 / 4 128K 151,646 Qwen2.5-Coder-14B 14.7B 48 40 / 8 128K 151,646 Qwen2.5-Coder-32B 32.5B 64 40 / 8 128K 151,646

The 14B has \(d=5{,}120\), \(d_{\text{ff}}=13{,}824\), 48 layers, GQA 40/8, untied embeddings. Apache-2.0.

docs.title: 3.4 Post-training
docs.text:
• SFT on code instructions, repo tasks, code repair, tests, documentation.
  • DPO/preference optimisation for helpfulness and correctness.
  • Instruction data includes file-level and repo-level tasks, not just isolated functions.

The result is a code-specialised model with strong FIM, repair and repository reasoning, but a narrower general-agent profile than Qwen3.

docs.title: 4.1 Architecture
docs.text:
Qwen3 uses a Llama-style decoder with:

  • GQA;
  • SwiGLU;
  • RoPE;
  • RMSNorm with pre-norm;
  • QK-Norm for stability;
  • no QKV bias (removed from Qwen2);
  • BBPE tokenizer, vocabulary 151,669.

Dense family:

Model Layers Heads (Q/KV) Tie embedding Context Qwen3-0.6B 28 16 / 8 Yes 32K Qwen3-1.7B 28 16 / 8 Yes 32K Qwen3-4B 36 32 / 8 Yes 128K Qwen3-8B 36 32 / 8 No 128K Qwen3-14B 40 40 / 8 No 128K Qwen3-32B 64 64 / 8 No 128K

MoE family:

Model Layers Heads (Q/KV) Experts (total/active) Context Qwen3-30B-A3B 48 32 / 4 128 / 8 128K Qwen3-235B-A22B 94 64 / 4 128 / 8 128K

The report’s “128K” is the architecture’s extended context; pretraining’s long-context stage trains to 32,768, and YaRN/DCA extend inference to 128K. The model card’s “32K native / 131K YaRN” is the practical statement.

Qwen3-14B has \(d=5{,}120\), \(d_{\text{ff}}=17{,}408\), 40 layers, 14.8B total, 13.2B non-embedding.

docs.title: 4.2 Pretraining data: 36T tokens, 119 languages
docs.text:
Qwen3 is trained on 36 trillion tokens covering 119 languages and dialects:

  • web documents, books, code, STEM, reasoning, multilingual text;
  • synthetic data generated by Qwen2.5, Qwen2.5-Math and Qwen2.5-Coder;
  • PDF text extracted with Qwen2.5-VL, then refined with Qwen2.5;
  • additional multilingual data.

docs.title: 4.3 Three pretraining stages
docs.text:
1. General stage — about 30T tokens at 4,096 context, building broad knowledge.
  2. Reasoning/STEM stage — knowledge-intensive data, more STEM and code, faster LR decay.
  3. Long-context stage — hundreds of billions of tokens at 32,768; 75% of samples 16K–32K, 25% 4K–16K. RoPE base raised from \(10^4\) to \(10^6\) with ABF; YaRN and Dual Chunk Attention give 4× inference extension.

The three-stage structure is the template to copy if you build a small model: general → reasoning/code → long context.

docs.title: 4.4 Post-training: four stages
docs.text: Qwen3’s post-training is the most instructive part.

docs.title: Stage 1 — Long-CoT cold start
docs.text:
Curate math, code, logic and STEM problems with verified answers or test cases. Filter:

  • queries that are not easily verifiable;
  • queries the model can answer without CoT;
  • responses with wrong answers or bad format.

The report uses 3,995 query–verifier pairs for the reasoning RL stage. Cold-start SFT teaches the format of long reasoning before RL.

docs.title: Stage 2 — Reasoning RL
docs.text:
Qwen3 uses GRPO (Group Relative Policy Optimisation). For a query \(q\), sample \(G\) outputs \(\{o_i\}\), score them with a verifier \(R_i\), and compute:

\[ \hat A_i = \frac{R_i - \operatorname{mean}(R)}{\operatorname{std}(R)}, \] \[ r_i(\theta) = \frac{\pi_\theta(o_i\mid q)}{\pi_{\text{old}}(o_i\mid q)}, \] \[ \mathcal{J}_{\text{GRPO}}(\theta) = \mathbb{E}\left[ \frac{1}{G}\sum_{i=1}^{G} \min\left( r_i(\theta)\hat A_i,\; \operatorname{clip}(r_i(\theta),1-\epsilon,1+\epsilon)\hat A_i \right) -\beta\,\operatorname{KL}(\pi_\theta\|\pi_{\text{ref}}) \right]. \]

On paper

One maths query, \(G=4\) sampled answers. The verifier scores them \(R=(1,0,1,0)\), so \(\operatorname{mean}(R)=0.5\) and, with the population standard deviation, \(\operatorname{std}(R)=0.5\). Take \(\epsilon=0.2\), \(\beta=0.04\) and a KL estimate of 0.25.

\(i\) \(R_i\) \(\hat A_i\) \(r_i(\theta)\) \(\operatorname{clip}(r_i)\) \(\min(\ldots)\) 1 1 +1 1.5 1.2 1.2 2 0 −1 0.5 0.8 −0.8 3 1 +1 1.0 1.0 1.0 4 0 −1 1.0 1.0 −1.0 \[ \begin{aligned} \tfrac14(1.2-0.8+1.0-1.0)&=0.1\\ \mathcal{J}_{\text{GRPO}}&=0.1-0.04\cdot0.25=0.09 \end{aligned} \]

Answer 1 is already 50% more likely than under \(\pi_{\text{old}}\) and answer 2 has halved. In both rows the min picks the clipped value, which is a constant, so this step pushes neither of them further; answers 3 and 4 get the full update.

The group baseline replaces a learned value function. The KL term keeps the policy near the reference. Qwen3 reports large-batch, many-rollout, off-policy training and entropy control as important for stability.

docs.title: Stage 3 — Thinking mode fusion
docs.text:
The goal is one model that can think or answer directly. Qwen3:

  • builds SFT data with and without reasoning paths;
  • uses chat templates with /think and /no_think;
  • adds a thinking budget to cap reasoning tokens;
  • trains the model to follow the mode token.

This is why Qwen3 can serve both “reasoning” and “chat” from one checkpoint, unlike separate QwQ/Qwen chat models.

docs.title: Stage 4 — General RL
docs.text:
A reward system over 20+ tasks:

  • instruction following, format following, preference alignment;
  • tool use, agentic tasks, long-horizon decision making;
  • RAG factuality, specialized scenarios;
  • rule-based, model-based and human feedback rewards.

docs.title: Strong-to-weak distillation
docs.text:
Smaller Qwen3 models are trained by distilling the flagship:

\[ \mathcal{L}_{\text{KD}} = \operatorname{KL}\left( p_{\text{teacher}}(\cdot\mid x) \;\|\; p_{\text{student}}(\cdot\mid x) \right), \]

often on on-policy student samples. The report says distillation is more efficient than RL for small models and uses about 1/10 of the GPU hours of the four-stage recipe. The student learns both thinking and non-thinking behaviour from the teacher.

On paper

Three candidate next tokens. The teacher predicts \(p_{\text{teacher}}=(\tfrac12,\tfrac14,\tfrac14)\) and the student \(p_{\text{student}}=(\tfrac14,\tfrac12,\tfrac14)\). Use \(\ln2\approx0.693\).

\[ \begin{aligned} \operatorname{KL} &=\tfrac12\ln2+\tfrac14\ln\tfrac12+\tfrac14\ln1\\ &=\tfrac14\ln2\approx0.173 \end{aligned} \]

Swapping the student's first two probabilities would match the teacher and make the loss 0. Unlike a one-hot label, the target also tells the student how much weight the teacher puts on the alternatives.

Longer version: 43 §19.

docs.title: 4.5 What is not public
docs.text:
• Exact data mixture and dedup thresholds.
  • Exact SFT/RL dataset sizes beyond the disclosed 3,995 verifier pairs.
  • Full reward model details.
  • Exact hyperparameters for the 14B run.
  • The precise filtering classifiers.

You can reproduce the recipe shape, not the exact model.

docs.title: 5. Qwen3-Coder: agentic code RL
docs.text:
Qwen3-Coder is built on Qwen3:

  • 7.5T tokens, 70% code.
  • 30B-A3B and 480B-A35B; 256K native, 1M with YaRN.
  • Code RL on verifiable tasks; synthetic test-case scaling.
  • Agent RL for multi-turn tool use: the model interacts with a repository, runs commands, observes failures and repairs.
  • Qwen2.5-Coder is used to clean and rewrite noisy code data.
  • Qwen3-Coder-30B-A3B: 48 layers, 32/4 heads, 128/8 experts, non-thinking.
  • Qwen3-Coder-Next: 80B total / 3B active, 256K, trained with executable, interaction-rich tasks.

The lesson: code capability at the frontier is execution-driven. Static next-token prediction is not enough; the model needs a verifier and multi-turn recovery.

docs.title: 6. Qwen3.5 / 3.6: hybrid linear attention
docs.text:
Qwen3.5 changes the architecture:

  • 3:1 hybrid: three Gated DeltaNet layers per one gated attention layer.
  • Sparse MoE: 512 experts, 17B active out of 397B (4.28%) in the flagship; dense 9B/27B variants.
  • Native multimodal: trained from scratch on interleaved text, image and video tokens.
  • 256K input, extendable to 1M.
  • Multi-token prediction.
  • RL at scale: million-agent environments, progressively harder tasks.

The GDN recurrence (see 32 — Mathematics §10):

\[ S_t = \alpha_t S_{t-1}(I-\beta_t k_t k_t^\top) + \beta_t v_t k_t^\top, \qquad o_t=S_t\,q_t, \]

with \(S_t\in\mathbb{R}^{d_v\times d_k}\).

On paper

Take \(d_k=d_v=2\) and a state that already stores two associations, key \(e_1\) to \(4e_1\) and key \(e_2\) to \(2e_2\): \(S_{t-1}=\operatorname{diag}(4,2)\). Write the new pair \(k_t=e_1=(1,0)\), \(v_t=(6,0)\) with \(\alpha_t=0.5\) and \(\beta_t=0.5\).

\[ \begin{aligned} I-\beta_tk_tk_t^\top&=\operatorname{diag}(0.5,\,1)\\ \alpha_tS_{t-1}(I-\beta_tk_tk_t^\top)&=\operatorname{diag}(1,\,1)\\ \beta_tv_tk_t^\top&=\operatorname{diag}(3,\,0)\\ S_t&=\operatorname{diag}(4,\,1) \end{aligned} \]

Reading with \(q_t=e_1\) gives \(o_t=(4,0)\): the \(e_1\) slot decayed from 4 to 2, then moved halfway to the new value 6. The \(e_2\) slot was not written, so it only decayed, from 2 to 1.

Longer version: 43 §11.

The 3:1 stack gives cheap long-context memory while keeping periodic full attention for retrieval. Qwen3.6 shares the architecture. Qwen3.8 is a newer generation with stronger coding/agentic results; it is not a 32 GB local training target.

Why this matters for you: Qwen3.5/3.6 are better models but harder to train in MLX due to the GDN kernels and backward pass. Qwen3-14B remains the reliable local base. If you rent a GPU, Qwen3.5-9B is the better quality/time trade.

docs.title: 7. Reproducing the recipe at small scale
docs.text:
You cannot reproduce 36T tokens or 14.8B parameters on a Mac. You can reproduce the shape:

Qwen stage Small-scale analogue 36T general pretraining 20–100B tokens on a 0.1–1B model STEM/code stage 10–30% code/math, higher-quality subset 32K long-context stage 4K–8K sequences on a small model Cold-start SFT 10k–100k verified reasoning traces Reasoning RL GRPO on math/code with exact verifiers Thinking fusion mixed think/no-think SFT General RL preference pairs + rule rewards Distillation teacher logits or on-policy samples

The exact numbers are in 35 — From zero; the 12B/14B budget is in 36 — Reproducing 12B–14B.

docs.title: 8. What to copy, what not to copy
docs.text:
Copy:

  • three-stage pretraining (general → reasoning → long context);
  • GQA + SwiGLU + RoPE + RMSNorm + QK-norm;
  • a large, deduplicated, decontaminated corpus;
  • verified cold-start data before RL;
  • GRPO with a real verifier;
  • thinking-mode fusion via chat template;
  • distillation for small models;
  • execution-driven agentic training.

Do not copy blindly:

  • the 36T token budget at small scale (Chinchilla-optimal is far less);
  • the exact LR/batch from a 14B run on a 100M model;
  • the full MoE routing without load-balancing and expert parallelism;
  • RL before the model can follow format and emit valid tools;
  • vendor benchmark claims as your target.

docs.title: 34 — How Gemma 4 was built
docs.text:
Last verified: 27 October 2026 against the Gemma 4 technical report (arXiv:2607.02770), the Google model cards, and the Hugging Face config/chat template.

Gemma 4 is Google DeepMind’s open-weight, natively multimodal family. The public report is unusually detailed about architecture, tokenizer, training infrastructure and post-training. This chapter reconstructs the design and the mathematics; exact data mixtures and hyperparameters remain undisclosed.

Read with: 37 — Architecture anatomy for the encoder-free 12B tensor shapes and 38 — Derivations and proofs for the RoPE/GQA/quantization math.

docs.title: 1. The family
docs.text:
Model Total params Effective / active Modalities Encoders Gemma 4 E2B 5.1B with embeddings 2.3B effective text, image, audio 150M ViT + 305M audio Gemma 4 E4B 8B with embeddings 4.5B effective text, image, audio 150M ViT + 305M audio Gemma 4 12B 11.95B dense text, image, audio none (encoder-free) Gemma 4 26B-A4B 25.2B 3.8B active text, image 550M ViT Gemma 4 31B 30.7B (31.3B with the ViT) dense text, image 550M ViT

All are Apache-2.0. The 12B is the model used in this handbook because it trains in 32 GB at 4-bit and has native vision/audio input without separate encoders.

The “E” in E2B/E4B means effective parameters: per-layer embeddings (PLE) store large lookup tables that are not all used per token, so the compute-relevant size is smaller than the stored size. Concretely, E2B’s 5.12B checkpoint holds 2.75B of embedding tables (a 0.40B token embedding and a 2.35B per-layer table); subtracting them leaves the 2.3B “effective” figure, of which 1.88B is the text decoder. 37 §4 decomposes both edge checkpoints.

docs.title: 2. The decoder architecture
docs.text:
Gemma 4 is a decoder-only transformer with:

  • pre-norm and post-norm RMSNorm;
  • QK-Norm;
  • GeGLU MLP;
  • RoPE on local layers, p-RoPE on global layers;
  • hybrid local sliding-window / global attention;
  • global layers reuse keys as values (K=V) in models above E4B — those layers have no v_proj;
  • in E2B/E4B only: per-layer embeddings (a 256-wide vector per token per layer), KV sharing in the last layers (20 of 35 in E2B, 18 of 42 in E4B reuse earlier K/V and cache nothing), and in E2B a double-wide MLP in those shared layers;
  • vocabulary 262,144, SentencePiece with split digits, preserved whitespace, byte-level fallback.

The block is:

\[ \begin{aligned} u &= x + \operatorname{Attn}(\operatorname{RMSNorm}_1(x)),\\ v &= u + \operatorname{MLP}(\operatorname{RMSNorm}_2(u)),\\ y &= \operatorname{RMSNorm}_{\text{post}}(v) \quad\text{(Gemma-style post-norm)}. \end{aligned} \]

The exact placement of post-norm is implementation detail; the point is that Gemma uses both normalisations, unlike Qwen3’s pure pre-norm.

On paper

One token with \(d=2\), \(x=(1,1)\), all norm gains 1 and \(\epsilon\approx0\). Since \(\operatorname{rms}(x)=1\), \(\operatorname{RMSNorm}_1(x)=x\). Suppose attention returns \((3,-1)\) and the MLP returns \((2,6)\).

\[ \begin{aligned} u&=(1,1)+(3,-1)=(4,0)\\ v&=(4,0)+(2,6)=(6,6)\\ \operatorname{rms}(v)&=\sqrt{(36+36)/2}=6\\ y&=(6,6)/6=(1,1) \end{aligned} \]

The two residual adds grew the stream from RMS 1 to RMS 6; the post-norm hands the next block a vector of RMS 1 again. A pure pre-norm block (Qwen3) would pass \((6,6)\) on.

docs.title: 3. Hybrid attention and p-RoPE
docs.text:
Gemma 4 uses a 5:1 local-to-global ratio (4:1 for E2B):

  • five layers of sliding-window attention with window \(W=1024\) (four layers and \(W=512\) on E2B; \(W=512\) on E4B);
  • one layer of full global attention.

Local attention:

\[ A_{ij}=0 \quad\text{if } j<i-W+1. \]

On paper

Toy window \(W=4\), query position \(i=6\), positions counted from 1. Keys after \(i\) are already hidden by the causal mask; the window also zeroes every key with

\[ j<i-W+1=6-4+1=3. \]

So the row for \(i=6\) keeps \(j=3,4,5,6\) (four keys, itself included) and zeroes \(j=1,2\). With the real \(W=1024\), token \(i=5{,}000\) sees \(j=3{,}977\) to \(5{,}000\), exactly 1,024 keys. Token 1 is out of reach of every local layer; only the global layers can still read it.

Longer version: 43 §12.

Global attention is standard causal attention. Global layers use:

  • K=V: one projection is reused for keys and values;
  • p-RoPE: only a fraction \(p=0.25\) of dimensions are rotated;
  • RoPE base \(10^6\) global, \(10^4\) local.

docs.title: 3.1 Why K=V
docs.text:
Standard attention stores both \(K\) and \(V\) in the cache. If \(K=V\):

\[ \text{KV cache} = L G d_h T b \]

instead of \(2LGd_hTb\) for those layers. Combined with p-RoPE and the local/global split, Gemma reports up to a 37.5% reduction in global KV cache.

On paper

The 4-layer experiment from §12 (3 local + 1 global): its \(L=1\) global layer has \(G=2\) KV heads of \(d_h=64\), and you cache \(T=4{,}096\) tokens in bf16 (\(b=2\) bytes).

\[ \begin{aligned} LGd_hTb&=1\cdot2\cdot64\cdot4{,}096\cdot2\\ &=1{,}048{,}576\text{ bytes}=1\text{ MiB} \end{aligned} \]

Without K=V the same layer stores \(2LGd_hTb=2\) MiB. Reusing one projection halves the global-layer cache exactly; the local layers are unaffected.

Longer version: 43 §7.

docs.title: 3.2 p-RoPE
docs.text:
For head dimension \(d_h\) and fraction \(p\):

\[ \tilde q = \big[R_{\theta}(q_{1:pd_h}),\; q_{pd_h+1:d_h}\big], \]

where \(R_\theta\) is the standard RoPE rotation. Only the first \(p d_h\) dimensions carry position; the rest are position-invariant. The global layers already integrate information over the full sequence, so rotating every dimension is unnecessary and can hurt long-context stability.

On paper

A toy head with \(d_h=8\) and \(p=0.25\): only \(pd_h=2\) dimensions rotate. Take \(q=(1,0,2,2,2,2,2,2)\) at position \(m=1\); the first pair turns by \(m\theta=1\) radian (\(\cos1\approx0.540\), \(\sin1\approx0.841\)).

\[ \begin{aligned} R_\theta(1,0)&=(\cos1,\ \sin1)\approx(0.540,\ 0.841)\\ \tilde q&\approx(0.540,\,0.841,\,2,2,2,2,2,2) \end{aligned} \]

The six untouched entries contribute the same amount to \(q\cdot k\) at any distance. In a Gemma 4 global head (\(d_h=512\)), \(0.25\cdot512=128\) dimensions rotate and 384 are position-free.

Longer version: 43 §8.

docs.title: 3.3 Cache math
docs.text:
For 12B: \(L=48\) (40 local + 8 global); local layers have \(G=8\), \(d_h=256\) and a 1,024-token window; global layers have \(G=1\) (num_global_key_value_heads) and \(d_h=512\). In bf16:

\[ \text{local cache} \approx 40 \cdot 2 \cdot 8 \cdot 256 \cdot 1024 \cdot 2 \approx 0.34\text{ GB}, \] \[ \text{global cache} \approx 8 \cdot 1 \cdot 512 \cdot T \cdot 2 \]

— one tensor per layer, because K=V. That is 268 MB at \(T=32{,}768\) (537 MB if K and V were stored separately) and 2.15 GB at 256K. At 32K the local term is still the larger one; the global term overtakes it at \(T=40{,}960\) and dominates long context, which is why K=V and int8 KV are what make 256K serving practical.

docs.title: 4. The encoder-free 12B
docs.text: This is the distinctive architectural choice.

docs.title: 4.1 Vision
docs.text:
Instead of a separate ViT, 12B takes 48×48×3 RGB patches and applies a single large matmul:

\[ z_{\text{patch}} = W_{\text{patch}}\,x_{\text{patch}} + b, \qquad W_{\text{patch}}\in\mathbb{R}^{d\times(48\cdot48\cdot3)}. \]

The patch embedder has ~35M parameters (a 26.5M projection plus the position table; the checkpoint holds 35.2M). Spatial information is added as 2D coordinate positional embeddings directly to patch representations, followed by LayerNorm:

\[ \tilde z = \operatorname{LayerNorm}(z + e_{\text{2D}}). \]

On paper

One 48×48 RGB patch flattens to \(48\cdot48\cdot3=6{,}912\) numbers, and the 12B’s width is \(d=3{,}840\). The checkpoint’s 2D position table \(e_{\text{2D}}\) has shape \(1{,}120\times2\times3{,}840\).

\[ \begin{aligned} W_{\text{patch}}&:\ 3{,}840\cdot6{,}912=26{,}542{,}080\\ e_{\text{2D}}&:\ 1{,}120\cdot2\cdot3{,}840=8{,}601{,}600\\ \text{sum}&\approx35.1\text{M} \end{aligned} \]

So the ~35M is the whole patch embedder: about three quarters is the matmul and one quarter the position table. The bias and LayerNorms add only 0.03M more.

docs.title: 4.2 Audio
docs.text:
Raw audio is segmented into 40ms chunks at 16kHz, giving 640-dimensional vectors:

\[ 640 = 16{,}000 \times 0.04. \]

Each chunk is projected directly into the LLM embedding space:

\[ z_{\text{audio}} = W_{\text{audio}}\,x_{\text{audio}} + b. \]

Audio is temporal, so no extra positional encoding is added. The 305M conformer encoder used by E2B/E4B is discarded entirely in 12B.

On paper

One second of 16 kHz audio is 16,000 samples, cut into 640-sample (40 ms) chunks:

\[ 16{,}000/640=25\ \text{tokens per second}. \]

A 30-second voice note therefore costs \(30\cdot25=750\) tokens of context. The projection \(W_{\text{audio}}\) is \(3{,}840\times640=2{,}457{,}600\approx2.46\)M weights, under 1% of the 305M conformer it replaces.

docs.title: 4.3 Why it matters
docs.text:
• fewer parameters and less memory fragmentation;
  • one decoder trained on all modalities;
  • the whole stack can be fine-tuned in one pass;
  • but the runtime must implement the gemma4_unified architecture, not an older Gemma loader.

For a text-only MLX LoRA, the vision/audio weights are stripped; the language model still trains normally.

docs.title: 5. Vision and audio encoders (other sizes)
docs.text:
Model Vision Audio E2B/E4B 150M ViT, patch 16, variable aspect ratio, axial 2D-RoPE, 2D absolute pos 305M USM-based conformer, 40ms Mel chunks 12B none (35M patch embedder) none (640-d projection) 26B-A4B / 31B 550M ViT no audio

The vision encoders support variable resolution with a token budget of 70, 140, 280, 560 or 1120 tokens. Higher budgets preserve detail for OCR/document parsing; lower budgets are faster for classification/video frames.

The encoders are frozen during pretraining in the non-unified models. Only the projection and the LLM are trained. In 12B, the projection is trained with the LLM from scratch.

docs.title: 6. Tokenizer
docs.text:
Gemma 4 uses the Gemini-style SentencePiece tokenizer:

  • 262k vocabulary;
  • split digits;
  • preserved whitespace;
  • byte-level encoding fallback;
  • 140+ languages;
  • control tokens for turns, tools, thinking, images and audio.

The vocabulary is much larger than Qwen3’s 151,669. That improves compression for multilingual/code text, but increases the embedding/output cost:

\[ P_{\text{emb}} = Vd = 262{,}144 \times 3{,}840 \approx 1.01\text{B} \]

for 12B (tied). The output softmax at every token is also over 262k classes, which is a real inference cost.

docs.title: 7.1 Data
docs.text:
• Large-scale web documents, code, images and audio.
  • Cutoff date: January 2025.
  • 140+ languages.
  • Filtering for benchmark decontamination, unsafe content, recitation and personal information.
  • Exact token count and mixture are not disclosed.

docs.title: 7.2 Objective
docs.text:
Standard next-token prediction:

\[ \mathcal{L} = -\frac{1}{T}\sum_{t=1}^{T}\log p_\theta(x_t\mid x_{<t}). \]

For multimodal sequences, image/audio tokens are interleaved with text tokens and the same objective applies; the model learns to predict the next text token conditioned on the modality tokens. The encoders (when present) are frozen, so the gradient flows through the projection and the decoder.

On paper

A 4-token caption after an image. The image tokens are context, so \(T=4\) counts only the caption, whose true tokens get probabilities \(\tfrac12,\tfrac18,\tfrac12,\tfrac18\). Use \(\ln2\approx0.693\).

\[ \begin{aligned} \mathcal{L}&=\tfrac14\big(\ln2+3\ln2+\ln2+3\ln2\big)\\ &=2\ln2\approx1.386 \end{aligned} \]

The perplexity is \(e^{\mathcal{L}}=4\): on average the model is as unsure as a fair pick among four tokens.

Longer version: 43 §1.

docs.title: 7.3 Infrastructure
docs.text:
Gemma 4 is trained on TPU v5p and TPU v6e:

Model TPU Chips Data shards Seq shards Replicas E2B v6e 4,096 16 8 32 E4B v6e 6,144 16 16 24 12B v5p 12,288 16 16 48 26B-A4B v6e 6,144 16 16 24 31B v6e 10,240 16 16 40

The stack uses JAX/Pathways, GSPMD partitioning, ZeRO-3 optimizer sharding, and slice-granularity elasticity to keep training alive when a TPU slice fails. This is the kind of infrastructure a from-scratch 12B requires; a single Mac cannot substitute.

docs.title: 7.4 Quantization-aware training
docs.text:
Gemma 4 ships quantized checkpoints trained with QAT:

  • mobile: per-channel int2/int4 weights + int8 activations;
  • Q4_0: blockwise 4-bit weights;
  • a scalar scale per block to keep activations in fp16 range.

Memory for 12B:

Format Weights KV at 32K bf16 24.0 GB — Q4_0 7.65 GB 0.28 GiB (int8; 302 MB)

QAT matters because post-training quantization of a 12B model can degrade reasoning; training with simulated quantization preserves quality.

docs.title: 8. Multi-token prediction drafter
docs.text:
Gemma 4 trains a small autoregressive MTP drafter for speculative decoding:

  • input: last-layer activations from the main model + token embeddings;
  • a 4-layer transformer block cross-attends to the main model’s KV cache;
  • predicts future tokens sequentially;
  • no separate MTP prefill;
  • 12B drafter: ~400M parameters;
  • 26B/31B drafter: model dimension 1024, three local + one global layer;
  • E2B/E4B use top-k cluster projection to reduce the final matmul from \(d\times262{,}000\) to \(d\times4096\).

Speculative decoding accepts the longest correct prefix; the speedup depends on the acceptance rate \(\alpha\). The drafter is a separate checkpoint, not part of the main model’s parameter count in the usual sense.

docs.title: 9. Instruction tuning
docs.text: Gemma 4 uses a Gemma-3-like post-training recipe with a new thinking mode.

docs.title: 9.1 Data filtering
docs.text:
• remove personal information;
  • remove unsafe/toxic model outputs;
  • remove mistaken self-identification;
  • deduplicate;
  • include attribution, hedging and refusal examples to reduce hallucination;
  • preserve factuality without degrading other metrics.

docs.title: 9.2 Thinking
docs.text:
Thinking is enabled by <|think|> at the start of the system prompt. The model emits:

<|channel>thought
...reasoning...
<channel|>final answer

When thinking is disabled, models other than E2B/E4B still emit an empty thought block. Multi-turn history should contain final answers only, except tool-call turns where thinking is preserved.

docs.title: 9.3 PT vs IT formatting
docs.text:
All models share the tokenizer, but:

  • pretrained models end generation with <eos>;
  • instruction-tuned models end with <turn|>;
  • fine-tuning either type requires adding the respective end token.

This is a common source of broken Gemma fine-tunes: train with the wrong EOS and the model never learns to stop.

docs.title: 9.4 Function calling
docs.text:
Gemma 4 has native function calling with:

  • OpenAI-style tool schemas;
  • <|tool_call>call:name{key:<|"|>value<|"|>}<tool_call|>;
  • <|tool_response>...<tool_response|> results;
  • tool-call ids resolved to function names.

The template rejects string arguments; they must be mappings. This is the single biggest difference from Qwen tool data.

docs.title: 10. Safety and responsibility
docs.text:
Gemma 4 is developed with Google’s safety policies:

  • CSAM and exploitation filtering;
  • dangerous content, self-harm, sexually explicit, hate, harassment;
  • PII filtering and recitation risk reduction;
  • safety evaluations and train-time mitigations;
  • responsible open-model release with usage policies.

The technical report also discusses governance, assessment and residual risk. Open weights do not remove the need for your own scope/policy layer if you build an agent.

docs.title: 11. What is disclosed vs not
docs.text:
Disclosed:

  • architecture, layer counts, heads, vocabulary, context;
  • tokenizer design;
  • training hardware and sharding;
  • QAT and MTP;
  • post-training filtering categories;
  • benchmark results;
  • safety approach.

Not disclosed:

  • exact token count and data mixture;
  • exact optimizer hyperparameters and LR schedule;
  • exact SFT/RL dataset sizes;
  • reward model details;
  • full data sources and dedup thresholds;
  • exact pretraining compute in FLOPs.

A reproduction can match the architecture and pipeline shape, not the exact model.

docs.title: 12. Reproducing Gemma’s ideas at small scale
docs.text:
Gemma choice Small-scale experiment 5:1 local/global 4-layer model with 3 local + 1 global K=V global share K/V projection, measure quality/cache p-RoPE 0.25 compare full RoPE vs 25% on a long-context task GeGLU swap SwiGLU for GeGLU in a 100M model encoder-free 12B small ViT-free patch projector on a toy image-caption task QAT quantize a 100M model to int8/int4 and measure perplexity MTP drafter train a 2-layer draft head, measure acceptance rate thinking channel SFT a small model on thought + answer traces

These are research experiments, not a path to a 12B model on a laptop. The practical path is 29 — Gemma fine-tuning: adapt the released weights.

docs.title: 35 — From zero: training a small model you can actually build
docs.text:
Last verified: 25 October 2026. The arithmetic is standard; the hardware numbers are estimates and must be replaced with measurements.

You cannot train a Qwen3-14B or Gemma 4 12B from scratch on one Mac. What you can do is build a small model that uses the same architecture and training recipe, learn the whole pipeline, and then decide whether to rent a GPU for a larger run.

This chapter is the honest path:

  1. compute the budget;
  2. choose a small architecture;
  3. train a tokenizer;
  4. build a clean corpus;
  5. run a stable pretraining job;
  6. evaluate it;
  7. post-train it;
  8. scale only if the small run works.

docs.title: 1. What “from zero” costs
docs.text:
Training compute is approximately

\[ C \approx 6ND, \]

where \(N\) is parameters and \(D\) is training tokens. The factor 6 is forward (2) plus backward (4) FLOPs per parameter per token.

On paper

Step 1 of the learning path in §8: a 10M-parameter model on 1B tokens.

\[ C\approx6\cdot10^{7}\cdot10^{9}=6\times10^{16}\ \text{FLOPs} \]

At the M1 Pro’s 1.5 TFLOP/s effective (the table below), that is \(6\times10^{16}/(1.5\times10^{12})=40{,}000\) s, about 11 hours: an overnight run. The first table row works the same way: \(6\cdot125\text{M}\cdot20\text{B}=1.5\times10^{19}\) FLOPs, 250 times more.

Longer version: 43 §15.

docs.title: 1.1 Worked examples
docs.text:
Model Tokens FLOPs One M1 Pro (1.5 TFLOP/s effective) 8×A100 (35% MFU) Cost at $2/GPU-h 125M 20B \(1.5\times10^{19}\) ~116 days ~0.2 days ~$76 336M 20B \(4.0\times10^{19}\) ~309 days ~0.5 days ~$205 1.2B 20B \(1.5\times10^{20}\) ~1,124 days ~1.9 days ~$741 1.2B 100B \(7.3\times10^{20}\) ~15 years ~9.6 days ~$3,700 14B 36T \(3.2\times10^{24}\) ~67,000 years ~9.3 days on 10,000 H100s (40% MFU) ~$4.5M

The last row is Qwen3-14B’s disclosed token count and uses 10,000 H100s, not 8×A100s. It is not a laptop project. Even the 1.2B/20B run needs a serious GPU and a clean data pipeline.

The M1 Pro number is intentionally brutal: local training is for LoRA adapters, not pretraining. The rest of this handbook is about adapters for a reason.

docs.title: 1.2 Chinchilla is a lower bound, not a target
docs.text:
Chinchilla-style compute-optimal training uses roughly

\[ D \approx 20N. \]

A 1.2B model would need ~24B tokens to be compute-optimal. But models that will be served many times are often overtrained far beyond 20 tokens/parameter because inference cost dominates. Qwen3-14B at 36T is ~2,438 tokens/parameter; that is a deliberate inference-quality trade, not a mistake. For your first small model, 20–100 tokens/parameter is a reasonable range; more tokens usually help if data quality holds.

docs.title: 2. Choose an architecture
docs.text:
For a first model, use a Llama-style decoder:

  • RMSNorm (pre-norm);
  • RoPE;
  • GQA;
  • SwiGLU;
  • no biases;
  • tied embeddings for small models;
  • vocabulary 32k–64k.

Why this shape: it is simple, well-supported, and close enough to Qwen to port lessons. Gemma’s GeGLU/local-global/p-RoPE stack is a second experiment, not a first build.

docs.title: 2.1 Three sizes
docs.text:
Name Layers \(d\) Heads KV heads FFN Params Tokens Use tiny-100m 12 768 12 4 2,048 ~125M 20B CPU/1 GPU learning run small-300m 24 1,024 16 4 2,816 ~336M 20–40B one or two GPUs small-1b 24 2,048 16 4 5,632 ~1.2B 20–100B 8×A100-class

The parameter column assumes a tied 64,000-token vocabulary. With 32,000 tokens the same stacks are ~100M, ~303M and ~1.15B — at this size the vocabulary choice moves the total by up to 20%.

Parameter formula:

\[ P \approx L\left(2d^2 + 2dG d_h + 3d d_{\text{ff}}\right) + Vd \]

for tied embeddings and \(H d_h=d\).

On paper

The tiny-100m row: \(L=12\), \(d=768\), \(G=4\), \(d_h=64\), \(d_{\text{ff}}=2{,}048\), tied, with a 64,000-token vocabulary. Per layer:

Projection Count Q and O, \(d\times d\) each \(2\cdot768^2=1{,}179{,}648\) K and V \(2\cdot768\cdot4\cdot64=393{,}216\) MLP \(3\cdot768\cdot2{,}048=4{,}718{,}592\) one layer 6,291,456 \[ \begin{aligned} 12\cdot6{,}291{,}456&=75{,}497{,}472\\ Vd=64{,}000\cdot768&=49{,}152{,}000\\ P&\approx124.6\text{M} \end{aligned} \]

That is the table’s ~125M. With a 32,000-token vocabulary the same stack is ≈100M: at this size the embedding is 39% of the model.

Longer version: 43 §14.

Use:

python scripts/estimate_pretraining.py --preset small-1b --vocab 64000 --tokens 20e9 \
  --gpus 8 --peak-tflops 312 --mfu 0.35 --cost-per-gpu-hour 2

This prints 1.21B parameters, 1.9 days and $741 — the §1.1 row. The small-1b and tiny-100m presets default to a 32,000-token vocabulary; without --vocab 64000 the same command prints 1.15B and $701. Replace the defaults with your GPU’s peak and a measured MFU.

docs.title: 3. Train a tokenizer
docs.text:
You need a tokenizer before you can tokenize the corpus. A practical recipe:

  1. Sample 1–10 GB of clean, deduplicated text from the same distribution as the corpus.
  2. Train SentencePiece BPE or Unigram with vocabulary 32k–64k.
  3. Enable byte fallback so no character is unknown.
  4. Split digits (split_digits=true) for math/code.
  5. Preserve whitespace if code is important.
  6. Add special tokens: BOS, EOS, PAD, UNK, turn separators, tool tokens.
  7. Measure compression on held-out text and code.
spm_train \
  --input=tok_sample.txt \
  --model_prefix=tok32k \
  --vocab_size=32000 \
  --model_type=bpe \
  --byte_fallback=true \
  --split_digits=true \
  --character_coverage=0.9995

Do not reuse a tokenizer from a different model family unless you are doing continued pretraining. A mismatched tokenizer breaks the embedding and the compression assumptions.

docs.title: 4. Build the corpus
docs.text: A small model is dominated by data quality, not architecture.

docs.title: 4.1 Sources
docs.text: Source Use License FineWeb / FineWeb-Edu general web ODC-BY / CC-BY The Stack v3 code ODC-BY, per-file licenses OpenWebMath / proof-pile math check each Wikipedia facts CC-BY-SA Books (public domain) long-form public domain arXiv (where permitted) STEM metadata/licenses vary Your own domain corpus specialization your rights

docs.title: 4.2 Pipeline
docs.text:
raw → language ID → text extraction → normalization
    → exact dedup → MinHash near-dedup
    → quality filter (classifier or heuristics)
    → toxicity/PII filter
    → benchmark decontamination (13-gram overlap)
    → mixture → tokenize → shard

Rules:

  • Deduplicate before tokenizing; duplicated tokens waste compute.
  • Decontaminate against every benchmark you will report.
  • Keep a held-out split by source/domain, not random rows.
  • Record provenance and licenses per shard.
  • Mix code/math/general deliberately; do not let one source dominate by volume.
  • Curriculum: general first, then higher-quality/STEM/code, then long-context annealing.

A reasonable first mixture for a general small model: 70% web, 15% code, 10% math, 5% books/reference. For a code model, invert toward code; for a domain model, add 10–30% domain data.

docs.title: 5.1 Starting hyperparameters
docs.text:
Setting 125M 336M 1.2B Tokens 20B 20–40B 20–100B Sequence 2,048 2,048–4,096 4,096–8,192 Batch tokens 0.5M 1M 2M Peak LR 6e-4 3e-4 2e-4 Min LR 10% of peak 10% 10% Warmup 2% 2% 1–2% Weight decay 0.1 0.1 0.1 Grad clip 1.0 1.0 1.0 AdamW β 0.9 / 0.95 0.9 / 0.95 0.9 / 0.95 Precision bf16 bf16 bf16

These are starting points, not laws. At small scale, the LR can be higher; at large scale, lower. Use a short LR sweep on a 1B-token subset before the full run.

docs.title: 5.2 Expected loss
docs.text:
At initialisation, a uniform model has

\[ \mathcal{L}_0 \approx \ln V. \]

For \(V=32{,}000\), that is ~10.4. A healthy run drops quickly toward 3–4 and then slowly. A loss stuck near \(\ln V\) means the model is not learning (LR, data, mask, or bug). A sudden spike means instability (LR, bad batch, numerical issue).

docs.title: 5.3 Training loop
docs.text:
Install the optional dependencies first:

uv pip install -r requirements-pretrain.txt

The reference implementation is:

python scripts/train_tiny_transformer.py \
  --data data/tiny/corpus.txt \
  --out runs/tiny \
  --dim 256 --layers 6 --heads 8 --kv-heads 2 --ffn 768 \
  --seq 256 --batch 16 --steps 2000 \
  --lr 3e-4 --eval-every 100

It implements byte-level tokens, RMSNorm, RoPE, GQA, SwiGLU, causal cross-entropy, AdamW, cosine schedule, gradient clipping, validation and sampling. It is a teaching implementation, not a substitute for a production trainer.

For a real run, use:

  • PyTorch FSDP or Megatron-LM/NeMo for multi-GPU;
  • FlashAttention-⅔ for long sequences;
  • activation checkpointing to trade compute for memory;
  • bf16 with fp32 master weights;
  • gradient accumulation to reach the target batch;
  • distributed checkpointing and resumable data loaders;
  • deterministic data order per run for reproducibility.

docs.title: 5.4 Memory math
docs.text:
Training memory is roughly:

\[ \text{bytes} \approx \underbrace{2N}_{\text{bf16 weights}} + \underbrace{12N}_{\text{AdamW fp32 states}} + \underbrace{2N}_{\text{gradients}} + \text{activations}. \]

That is ~16 bytes/parameter before activations for full fine-tuning. A 1.2B model needs ~19 GB for weights/optimizer alone; activations add more. FSDP/ZeRO shards these states across GPUs. LoRA avoids most of it by freezing the base.

docs.title: 6. Evaluate before scaling
docs.text:
Minimum evaluation:

Test What it catches Held-out perplexity basic learning, data leak MMLU / ARC / HellaSwag general knowledge GSM8K / MATH subset reasoning HumanEval / MBPP code Long-context needle context extension Toxicity / safety prompts unsafe behaviour Memorisation probes recitation risk

Report the tokenizer, data cutoff, contamination check and exact prompts. A small model’s MMLU will be low; that is expected. The question is whether the curve is healthy and whether the data pipeline works.

Plot loss vs tokens and fit a scaling law:

\[ L(N,D) = E + \frac{A}{N^\alpha} + \frac{B}{D^\beta}. \]

If the curve is flat, more tokens will not save you; fix the data or the architecture.

On paper

Suppose your small runs fit \(E=1.7\), \(A=5{,}000\), \(B=50{,}000\) and \(\alpha=\beta=0.5\). These are made-up round constants so the square roots come out exact; Chinchilla’s fit has \(\alpha\approx0.34\), \(\beta\approx0.28\). Start at 100M parameters and 2.5B tokens:

\[ L=1.7+\frac{5{,}000}{10^{4}}+\frac{50{,}000}{5\times10^{4}}=3.2 \]

Now spend 4× the compute (\(6ND\)) two ways:

Run \(A/\sqrt N\) \(B/\sqrt D\) \(L\) 100M, 2.5B tokens 0.5 1.0 3.20 400M, 2.5B tokens 0.25 1.0 2.95 100M, 10B tokens 0.5 0.5 2.70

Here the data term is the larger one, so 4× the tokens beats 4× the parameters. No run gets below \(E=1.7\), the irreducible loss.

docs.title: 7. Post-train the small model
docs.text:
A base model is not an assistant. The minimum post-training:

  1. SFT on 10k–100k high-quality instruction/response pairs.
  2. Preference optimisation (DPO/ORPO) on chosen/rejected pairs.
  3. Verifiable RL (GRPO) on math/code with exact answers.
  4. Safety tuning and refusal/scope examples.
  5. Distillation from a larger teacher if you have one.

Losses:

\[ \mathcal{L}_{\text{SFT}} = -\sum_{t\in\text{completion}}\log p_\theta(x_t\mid x_{<t}), \]

On paper

Prompt What is 2+2?, completion 4<eos>. The prompt tokens are masked; the model gives the two completion tokens probabilities \(\tfrac14\) and \(\tfrac12\). Use \(\ln2\approx0.693\).

\[ \mathcal{L}_{\text{SFT}}=-\big(\ln\tfrac14+\ln\tfrac12\big)=3\ln2\approx2.08 \]

However badly the model predicts the user’s words, they add nothing: the gradient only teaches the answer.

\[ \mathcal{L}_{\text{DPO}} = -\log\sigma\left( \beta\log\frac{\pi_\theta(y_w\mid x)}{\pi_{\text{ref}}(y_w\mid x)} -\beta\log\frac{\pi_\theta(y_l\mid x)}{\pi_{\text{ref}}(y_l\mid x)} \right). \]

On paper

Take \(\beta=0.5\) and use \(\sigma(\ln a)=a/(1+a)\). At the start \(\pi_\theta=\pi_{\text{ref}}\), both log-ratios are 0 and \(\mathcal{L}_{\text{DPO}}=-\ln\sigma(0)=\ln2\approx0.693\). After some steps the policy makes the chosen answer twice as likely as the reference does, and the rejected one half as likely:

\[ \begin{aligned} z&=0.5\big(\ln2-\ln\tfrac12\big)=\ln2\\ \sigma(\ln2)&=\tfrac{2}{1+2}=\tfrac23\\ \mathcal{L}_{\text{DPO}}&=-\ln\tfrac23=\ln1.5\approx0.405 \end{aligned} \]

The loss falls only as the gap between chosen and rejected grows, and both sides are measured relative to the frozen reference.

GRPO is in 33 — How Qwen was built §4.4.

For a small model, SFT + DPO is usually enough; GRPO only makes sense when you have a verifier and a base that can already emit valid formats.

docs.title: 8. A realistic learning path
docs.text:
Step Model Data Hardware Goal 1 10M 1B tokens CPU/1 GPU pipeline works 2 125M 10–20B 1–8 GPUs loss curve, tokenizer 3 336M 20–40B 8 GPUs scaling, eval 4 1.2B 20–100B 8–64 GPUs real base model 5 3B 100B+ 64–256 GPUs serious model 6 12–14B 10–36T 1k–10k GPUs frontier replication

Do not skip steps. Each step exposes a different failure: data pipeline, tokenizer, stability, parallelism, evaluation.

docs.title: 9. What not to do
docs.text:
• Do not train 12B from scratch on a Mac. It is not a matter of patience; the memory and compute do not fit.
  • Do not train on raw web text without dedup/decontamination. You will waste compute and overfit.
  • Do not compare loss across tokenizers. Compare task metrics.
  • Do not use a 14B LR on a 100M model. Scale the LR and batch.
  • Do not run RL before SFT. Format errors make reward meaningless.
  • Do not report benchmark numbers without contamination checks.
  • Do not ignore data licensing. A model is a derivative of its data.
  • Do not skip small-scale ablations. They are cheaper than a failed 1B run.

docs.title: 10. If you want “similar to Qwen/Gemma” without pretraining
docs.text:
The practical alternatives, in order of cost:

  1. LoRA/QLoRA on the released model — this handbook. Best quality per dollar.
  2. Continued pretraining on domain data — moderate cost, needs GPUs.
  3. Distillation from a larger teacher into a smaller student — good for narrow domains.
  4. Model merging — cheap, limited.
  5. From scratch — only if you need a new tokenizer, architecture, language or license, and you have a real budget.

“Similar” usually means similar behaviour, not similar initialisation. Fine-tuning gets you behaviour; from-scratch gets you architecture control.

docs.title: 36 — Reproducing a 12B–14B model from scratch
docs.text:
Last verified: 25 October 2026. This chapter is a planning document, not a claim that a 12B run is practical for an individual. It separates the architecture (reproducible) from the data and compute (not reproducible at home).

The previous chapter built a 100M–1B model. This one scales the same recipe to the size of Qwen3-14B, Qwen2.5-Coder-14B and Gemma 4 12B. The goal is not to clone a checkpoint; it is to understand what a real 12B–14B pretraining project requires, and to choose the cheapest path to your actual goal.

docs.title: 1. The three target configurations
docs.text:
Qwen3-14B Qwen2.5-Coder-14B Gemma 4 12B Parameters 14.8B 14.7B 11.95B Layers 40 48 48 \(d\) 5,120 5,120 3,840 FFN 17,408 13,824 15,360 Heads / KV 40 / 8 40 / 8 16 / 8 Head dim 128 128 256 (global 512) Vocab 151,669 151,646 262,144 Tied embeddings No No Yes Context 32K train / 128K YaRN 128K 256K Norm RMSNorm + QK-norm RMSNorm RMSNorm pre+post + QK-norm MLP SwiGLU SwiGLU GeGLU Attention full, GQA full, GQA 5:1 local/global, K=V, p-RoPE

These are different models. “12B–14B” is a parameter band, not an architecture.

docs.title: 1.1 Parameter count
docs.text:
For a dense decoder:

\[ P \approx L\left(2d^2 + 2dG d_h + 3d d_{\text{ff}}\right) + (1+\mathbf{1}[\text{untied}])\,Vd. \]
  • Qwen3-14B: \(P\approx14.77\text{B}\).
  • Qwen2.5-Coder-14B: \(P\approx14.7\text{B}\).
  • Gemma 4 12B: \(P\approx11.7\text{B}\) by this formula, which assumes \(Hd_h=d\) — false for Gemma (4,096 local and 8,192 global against \(d=3{,}840\)). The exact text-decoder count is 11.91B (37 §1.3); the model card says 11.95B.

On paper

Qwen3-14B: \(L=40\), \(d=5{,}120\), \(G=8\), \(d_h=128\), \(d_{\text{ff}}=17{,}408\), untied, with the checkpoint’s padded \(V=151{,}936\). Per layer:

Projection Count Q and O, \(d\times d\) each \(2\cdot5{,}120^2=52.43\)M K and V \(2\cdot5{,}120\cdot8\cdot128=10.49\)M MLP \(3\cdot5{,}120\cdot17{,}408=267.39\)M one layer 330.30M \[ \begin{aligned} 40\cdot330.30\text{M}&=13.21\text{B}\\ 2Vd=2\cdot151{,}936\cdot5{,}120&=1.56\text{B}\\ P&\approx14.77\text{B} \end{aligned} \]

The two vocabulary tables are about 10.5% of the model; the 40 MLPs hold 72%.

Longer version: 43 §14.

Use scripts/estimate_pretraining.py to check your own config.

docs.title: 2.1 The formula
docs.text:
\[ C \approx 6ND, \qquad \text{GPU-hours} = \frac{C}{\text{peak FLOP/s}\times\text{MFU}\times3600}. \]

For Qwen3-14B with \(D=36\text{T}\):

\[ C = 6 \times 14.77\times10^9 \times 36\times10^{12} \approx 3.2\times10^{24}\ \text{FLOPs}. \]

At 40% MFU on 10,000 H100-class GPUs (989 TFLOP/s dense BF16 peak; NVIDIA's 1,979 TFLOP/s figure is with sparsity, and 494.5 is the dense TF32 peak):

\[ \begin{aligned} \text{GPU-hours}&\approx2.24\times10^6\\ \text{wall time}&\approx9.3\ \text{days}\\ \text{cost}&\approx\$5.6\text{M} \end{aligned} \]

at $2.50/GPU-hour, before failures, data, evaluation and staff.

On paper

A run you could rent: a 1B model on 20B tokens on A100s (312 TFLOP/s dense BF16 peak), 35% MFU, $2/GPU-hour.

\[ \begin{aligned} C&=6\cdot10^{9}\cdot2\times10^{10}=1.2\times10^{20}\\ \text{per GPU-hour}&=312\times10^{12}\cdot0.35\cdot3600\\ &\approx3.93\times10^{17}\ \text{FLOPs}\\ \text{GPU-hours}&\approx\frac{1.2\times10^{20}}{3.93\times10^{17}}\approx305 \end{aligned} \]

That is about $610, or 38 hours on eight GPUs. The Qwen3-14B run above needs about 27,000 times this compute.

Longer version: 43 §15.

docs.title: 2.2 What changes the number
docs.text:
• MFU: 25% vs 45% is nearly a 2× cost difference.
  • Sequence length: long-context attention adds \(O(LT^2Hd_h)\) and lowers MFU.
  • Model FLOPs: MoE uses active parameters for compute but stores all experts.
  • Failures: add 20–50% for restarts, checkpoints and stragglers.
  • Data: pipeline compute and storage are separate.
  • Post-training: 5–20% additional compute, more for RL.

docs.title: 2.3 Chinchilla vs production
docs.text:
Chinchilla-optimal for 14B is roughly

\[ D\approx20N\approx280\text{B tokens}. \]

Qwen3-14B uses 36T, ~129× more. That is not a waste: a model served billions of times should be trained far past compute-optimal because inference cost dominates. For a one-off research model, 20–100 tokens/parameter is a saner starting point; for a product, overtrain.

docs.title: 3. Data: the hard part
docs.text: A 14B model at 36T tokens is a data project first.

docs.title: 3.1 Volume
docs.text:
• 36T tokens at ~4 bytes/token in uint32 shards is ~144 TB before compression.
  • Raw text, dedup indexes, quality scores and checkpoints add more.
  • You need a storage cluster, not a laptop.

docs.title: 3.2 Pipeline
docs.text:
crawl / licensed corpora
  → extraction (HTML, PDF, code, books)
  → language ID
  → normalization
  → exact dedup (hash)
  → near-dedup (MinHash/SimHash)
  → quality filter (classifier + heuristics)
  → toxicity/PII filter
  → benchmark decontamination
  → domain/mixture tagging
  → tokenize → shard → shuffle

docs.title: 3.3 Mixture
docs.text:
Qwen3 discloses domains but not weights: web, code, STEM, reasoning, books, multilingual, synthetic. Qwen2.5-Coder discloses a 70% code / 20% text / 10% math final mixture. Gemma 4 discloses web/code/images/audio and a Jan 2025 cutoff, not weights.

For a 14B general model, a reasonable starting mixture is:

Domain Share Web (filtered) 55–65% Code 15–20% Math/STEM 10–15% Books/reference 5–10% Multilingual 5–10% Synthetic/instruction 2–5%

For a code model, invert toward code; for a domain model, add 10–30% domain data.

docs.title: 3.4 Curriculum
docs.text:
A three-stage curriculum is the public Qwen3 pattern:

  1. General — most tokens, 4K context.
  2. Reasoning/STEM/code — higher-quality subset, faster LR decay.
  3. Long context — 32K sequences, hundreds of billions of tokens, RoPE base/ABF/YaRN.

Gemma 4 follows a Gemma-3-like pretraining recipe with a multimodal mixture and long-context design in the architecture. The exact curriculum is not public.

docs.title: 3.5 Data quality beats quantity
docs.text: At 14B scale, a 10% quality improvement is worth more than a 10% token increase. Budget 50% of the project for data: collection, cleaning, dedup, decontamination, mixture experiments and lineage.

docs.title: 4.1 Hardware
docs.text:
A 14B dense pretraining run needs:

  • 64–1,024 GPUs for a serious run; 1,000+ for a frontier token count;
  • high-bandwidth interconnect (NVLink/InfiniBand);
  • fast shared storage (parallel filesystem);
  • checkpoint storage;
  • a scheduler with preemption and restart.

A 12B/14B model does not fit on one 80 GB GPU for full training: weights (28 GB bf16) + optimizer (168 GB fp32 Adam) + gradients (28 GB) + activations exceed it. You need sharding.

docs.title: 4.2 Parallelism
docs.text:
Technique What it shards When Data parallel (DP) batch always FSDP / ZeRO-½/3 optimizer, gradients, parameters dense models Tensor parallel (TP) matrix dimensions within a node, high bandwidth Pipeline parallel (PP) layers across nodes Sequence/context parallel sequence long context Expert parallel (EP) experts MoE

Typical 3D setup: TP within a node, PP across nodes, DP/FSDP across the rest. MoE adds all-to-all communication for expert routing, which is often the bottleneck.

docs.title: 4.3 Precision
docs.text:
• bf16 weights/activations for training;
  • fp32 master weights and Adam states;
  • fp32 layernorm/softmax where needed;
  • gradient accumulation to reach the global batch;
  • activation checkpointing for memory;
  • FlashAttention for long sequences.

docs.title: 4.4 Throughput
docs.text:
Measure tokens/sec/GPU on a short run, then extrapolate:

\[ \text{wall time} = \frac{D}{\text{tokens/sec/GPU}\times\text{GPUs}}. \]

On paper

A short run of the 14B on 1,000 GPUs measures 4,000 tokens/sec/GPU, so the cluster processes \(4\times10^{6}\) tokens per second.

\[ \begin{aligned} \frac{280\times10^{9}}{4\times10^{6}}&=70{,}000\ \text{s}\approx19.4\ \text{h}\\ \frac{36\times10^{12}}{4\times10^{6}}&=9\times10^{6}\ \text{s}\approx104\ \text{days} \end{aligned} \]

Chinchilla’s 280B tokens (§2.3) take under a day; Qwen3’s 36T take about three and a half months. A measurement 20% lower stretches either run by 25%, because time scales with 1/throughput.

Do not trust vendor FLOPS alone. A 14B model at 2K context might do 3,000–8,000 tokens/sec/GPU on modern hardware depending on MFU and parallelism; at 32K it is much lower.

docs.title: 5. Stability
docs.text:
Large runs fail for boring reasons:

  • loss spikes from bad data or high LR;
  • attention logit explosion (QK-norm helps);
  • MoE expert collapse;
  • numerical overflow in fp16 (use bf16);
  • checkpoint corruption;
  • data loader imbalance;
  • network stragglers.

Mitigations:

  • QK-norm (Qwen3, Gemma 4);
  • pre-norm residual;
  • gradient clipping 1.0;
  • LR warmup 1–2%;
  • z-loss on logits;
  • skip/yield bad batches;
  • rollback to the last good checkpoint;
  • monitor grad norm, loss scale, expert load, throughput;
  • deterministic restart with the same data order.

A 14B run without a rollback plan is a gamble.

docs.title: 6. Post-training
docs.text: Pretraining gives a base model. The assistant behaviour comes from post-training.

docs.title: 6.1 SFT
docs.text:
• 100k–1M+ instruction/response pairs (Qwen2.5 disclosed 1M+).
  • Code, math, general, multilingual, tool use, safety.
  • Mask the prompt; train the completion.
  • Pack sequences for efficiency; watch cross-example contamination.

docs.title: 6.2 Reasoning cold start
docs.text:
• math/code/logic problems with verified answers or tests;
  • filter unverifiable and too-easy queries;
  • long-CoT traces in the target format.

docs.title: 6.3 RL
docs.text:
• GRPO with rule-based verifiers for math/code;
  • general RL with rule, model and human rewards;
  • agentic RL with tools and environment feedback;
  • KL to a reference policy, entropy control, large batch.

docs.title: 6.4 Distillation
docs.text:
For smaller models, distill the flagship:

\[ \mathcal{L}_{\text{KD}} = \operatorname{KL}\left(p_{\text{teacher}}\|p_{\text{student}}\right) \]

on teacher or on-policy student samples. Qwen3 reports distillation at ~1/10 the GPU hours of the four-stage RL recipe for small models.

On paper

Four candidate tokens. The teacher is split between the first two, \(p_{\text{teacher}}=(\tfrac12,\tfrac12,0,0)\); an untrained student is uniform, \(p_{\text{student}}=(\tfrac14,\tfrac14,\tfrac14,\tfrac14)\). Terms where the teacher’s probability is 0 contribute 0. Use \(\ln2\approx0.693\).

\[ \operatorname{KL}=2\cdot\tfrac12\ln\frac{1/2}{1/4}=\ln2\approx0.693 \]

The student lowers this only by moving the half it spends on tokens 3 and 4 onto the teacher’s two choices; at \((\tfrac12,\tfrac12,0,0)\) the loss is 0.

Longer version: 43 §19.

docs.title: 6.5 Safety
docs.text:
• red-team before release;
  • refusal/scope data;
  • PII and toxicity filters;
  • evaluation cards;
  • usage policy and license.

Post-training is 5–20% of compute but most of the product quality.

docs.title: 7. Team and timeline
docs.text:
A realistic 12B–14B from-scratch project:

Role Count Data engineering 5–15 Training/infra 5–15 Research/architecture 3–8 Evaluation 3–8 Safety/legal 2–5 Product 2–4

Timeline: 6–12 months for a first competitive model, longer for frontier quality. Data work starts first and never stops.

A single skilled engineer can reproduce the architecture and a small model; they cannot reproduce the data pipeline and compute of a 14B frontier run alone.

docs.title: 8. Alternatives, in order of cost
docs.text:
Path Cost Quality When LoRA/QLoRA on released weights $0–100 local high for a domain this handbook Continued pretraining $1k–100k medium-high new domain/language Distillation $1k–50k good for narrow tasks teacher available Model merging ~$0 modest two compatible adapters From scratch 1B $1k–10k low general, good learning research/education From scratch 14B $5M+ frontier-ish company-scale

“Similar to Qwen/Gemma” almost always means fine-tune the released model, not retrain it. The architecture knowledge is useful for debugging, data design and small-scale research; it is not a shortcut around compute.

docs.title: 9. Legal and ethical constraints
docs.text:
• Dataset licenses: ODC-BY, CC-BY, MIT, Apache-2.0, other.
  • Code licenses: per-file; keep provenance.
  • Web data: copyright, robots, terms of service.
  • PII and GDPR: lawful basis, deletion, minimization.
  • Model licenses: Apache-2.0 (Qwen, Gemma 4) permits commercial use; dataset licenses may not.
  • Safety: dual-use, cyber, bio, chemical; publish with care.
  • Attribution and model cards.

A model is a derivative of its data. “Open weights” does not mean “any data is fine”.

docs.title: 10. Checklist
docs.text:
Before committing:

  • Why from scratch? (new tokenizer/architecture/language/license)
  • Compute budget and MFU measured.
  • Data volume, licenses, dedup and decontamination.
  • Tokenizer trained and compression measured.
  • Architecture config and parameter count verified.
  • Parallelism plan and interconnect.
  • Checkpoint/restart plan.
  • Evaluation suite and contamination checks.
  • Post-training plan and safety.
  • Team and 6–12 month timeline.
  • Cheaper alternative considered (LoRA/continued pretraining/distillation).

If most boxes are empty, do not start a 14B run. Use 29 — Gemma fine-tuning or 24 — React fine-tuning instead.
