docs.title: 37 — Architecture anatomy: from config.json to tensors
docs.text:
Last verified: 27 October 2026.

32 — Mathematics gives the equations. This chapter connects them to the actual files, shapes and design choices in Qwen3-14B, Qwen2.5-Coder-14B and Gemma 4 12B. It is the page to read when you want to know why a checkpoint uses so much memory, what a config key changes, or where a fine-tune actually attaches.

docs.title: 1. One block, one tensor
docs.text:
A decoder is a stack of \(L\) blocks around a residual stream of shape

\[ X\in\mathbb{R}^{B\times T\times d}, \]

where \(B\) is batch, \(T\) sequence length and \(d\) hidden size. The block is

\[ \begin{aligned} U &= X + \operatorname{Attn}(\operatorname{Norm}_1(X)),\\ Y &= U + \operatorname{MLP}(\operatorname{Norm}_2(U)). \end{aligned} \]

On paper

One token (\(B=T=1\)) with \(d=2\): \(X=(2,2)\), RMSNorm with gain 1 and \(\epsilon\approx0\). Suppose attention returns \((5,-1)\) and the MLP returns \((-1,1)\).

\[ \begin{aligned} \operatorname{Norm}_1(X)&=(2,2)/2=(1,1)\\ U&=(2,2)+(5,-1)=(7,1)\\ \operatorname{Norm}_2(U)&=(7,1)/5=(1.4,\,0.2)\\ Y&=(7,1)+(-1,1)=(6,2) \end{aligned} \]

The MLP reads \((1.4,0.2)\), a vector of RMS 1, even though \(U\) itself has RMS \(\sqrt{(49+1)/2}=5\). The sub-layers only add to the stream, and \(Y\) keeps the \(1\times1\times2\) shape of \(X\).

Longer version: 43 §4.

The residual stream is the only path that connects the first embedding to the last logits. Attention and MLP are reads from and writes to that stream. This is why:

  • every block has the same input/output shape \(B\times T\times d\);
  • you can stack 40 or 48 blocks without changing the interface;
  • LoRA can be inserted into projections without changing the residual shape;
  • activation memory scales with \(L\times B\times T\times d\), not with parameter count alone.

docs.title: 1.1 Shape trace for Qwen3-14B
docs.text:
With \(B=1\), \(T=2{,}048\), \(d=5{,}120\), \(H=40\), \(G=8\), \(d_h=128\), \(d_{\text{ff}}=17{,}408\):

Tensor Shape Notes token ids [1, 2048] int32/int64 embedding [1, 2048, 5120] \(Vd\) table lookup normed input [1, 2048, 5120] RMSNorm Q [1, 40, 2048, 128] \(H d_h=5120\) K, V [1, 8, 2048, 128] \(G d_h=1024\) attention scores [1, 40, 2048, 2048] \(O(BHT^2)\) attention output [1, 2048, 5120] concat heads, \(W_O\) MLP gate/up [1, 2048, 17408] two projections MLP output [1, 2048, 5120] down projection logits [1, 2048, 151936] \(V\) per position

The logits tensor is enormous: \(1\cdot2048\cdot151{,}936\approx311\text{M}\) values. In fp32 that is 1.24 GB; in bf16 0.62 GB. This is why training uses fused cross-entropy and why long-context training is memory-bound even before attention.

On the 32 GB Mac this is why max_seq_length is the first knob to turn. The fp32 logits grow linearly with \(T\): 2.49 GB at 4,096 tokens and 4.98 GB at 8,192, before a single attention score is stored.

docs.title: 1.2 Shape trace for Gemma 4 12B
docs.text:
With \(B=1\), \(T=2{,}048\), \(d=3{,}840\), \(H=16\), \(G=8\), local \(d_h=256\), global \(d_h=512\), \(d_{\text{ff}}=15{,}360\):

Tensor Shape Notes token ids [1, 2048] int32/int64 embedding [1, 2048, 3840] tied with the LM head Q (local) [1, 16, 2048, 256] \(H d_h=4096\ne d\) K, V (local) [1, 8, 2048, 256] \(G=8\); cache capped at window 1024 Q (global) [1, 16, 2048, 512] \(H d_h=8192\) K=V (global) [1, 1, 2048, 512] one KV head; a single tensor serves as K and V local scores [1, 16, 2048, 2048] masked to window 1024 global scores [1, 16, 2048, 2048] every sixth layer logits [1, 2048, 262144] \(V\) per position

The output logits for Gemma are even larger: \(1\cdot2048\cdot262{,}144\approx537\text{M}\) values. The 262k vocabulary is a real inference cost, not a footnote.

Look at the global K=V row: one head of width 512 in bf16 is \(512\cdot2=1{,}024\) bytes, so each global layer caches exactly 1 KB per token. Eight global layers at 32,768 tokens is \(8\cdot32{,}768\cdot1\text{ KB}=268.4\text{ MB}\), the global term in §2.1. Reading the shape table correctly is the KV-cache calculation.

docs.title: 1.3 Parameter budget
docs.text:
scripts/inspect_architecture.py decomposes the checkpoint:

Component Qwen3-14B Gemma 4 12B attention / local layer 62.91M 47.19M attention / global layer — 64.88M MLP / layer 267.39M 176.95M total / local layer 330.32M 224.15M total / global layer — 241.84M layers 40 full 40 local + 8 global embedding 777.91M 1,006.63M LM head 777.91M (untied) 0 (tied) total (text decoder) 14.77B 11.91B checkpoint / model card 14.8B 11.96B / 11.95B 4-bit weights (approx.) ~8.3 GB ~7.65 GB

Gemma’s global layers use num_global_key_value_heads = 1 and global_head_dim = 512, so their attention block is larger than a local layer (64.88M vs 47.19M). They are also K=V: the key projection doubles as the value, so a global layer has q_proj, k_proj and o_proj but no v_proj — the checkpoint confirms it. Counting a value projection there adds 15.7M weights that do not exist; counting all 48 layers as local gives 11.77B and undercounts by ~0.14B.

The google/gemma-4-12B-it checkpoint holds exactly 11,959,730,224 parameters: 11.907B of text decoder plus 52.4M of multimodal embedders (a 35M vision patch embedder and the vision/audio input projections). Norms are only 0.7M. The model card rounds the total to 11.95B.

Gemma’s larger vocabulary costs ~1.0B parameters in the embedding; Qwen’s untied head costs another ~0.78B. The MLP is the largest per-layer block in both models: 81% of Qwen3-14B’s layer parameters and 79% of a Gemma 4 12B local layer’s.

This is why LoRA often targets both attention and MLP projections: the MLP holds most of the capacity.

docs.title: 1.4 Activation memory
docs.text:
Activation memory is roughly

\[ M_{\text{act}}\approx L\,B\,T\,d\,(c_{\text{attn}}+c_{\text{mlp}}) \]

before checkpointing, where \(c_{\text{attn}}\) and \(c_{\text{mlp}}\) depend on the implementation (number of intermediates kept for backward). For Qwen3-14B at \(B=1,T=2048,d=5120,L=40\), the residual stream alone is

\[ 40\cdot1\cdot2048\cdot5120\cdot2\text{ bytes}\approx0.84\text{ GB} \]

in bf16; attention scores add \(BHT^2\) per layer, which is much larger if materialised. Gradient checkpointing trades compute for memory by recomputing activations; it does not change the weights or the KV cache.

Which term dominates depends on the regime:

  • Full fine-tuning with AdamW: the optimizer state. fp32 master weights plus two moments are 12 bytes per parameter — 177 GB for Qwen3-14B, against 29.5 GB of bf16 weights.
  • LoRA/QLoRA: the base weights are quantized and frozen (~8.3 GB at 4-bit) and the optimizer state is tiny (adapter only), so activations, which scale with \(LBTd\), decide whether a run fits. That is why sequence length is the first knob to reduce.
  • Long context without a fused kernel: the \(BHT^2\) attention scores. For Qwen3-14B they are 336 MB per layer at 2K but 86 GB per layer at 32K in bf16, which is why FlashAttention never materialises them.

docs.title: 2. GQA shapes and the cache
docs.text:
For \(H\) query heads and \(G\) KV heads:

\[ Q\in\mathbb{R}^{B\times H\times T\times d_h},\qquad K,V\in\mathbb{R}^{B\times G\times T\times d_h}. \]

Each KV head is shared by \(H/G\) query heads. The attention score tensor is still \(B\times H\times T\times T\), but the cache is \(B\times G\times T\times d_h\).

docs.title: 2.1 Cache formula
docs.text:
\[ \text{KV bytes}=2\cdot L\cdot G\cdot d_h\cdot T\cdot b. \]

Qwen3-14B at \(T=32{,}768\), bf16:

\[ 2\cdot40\cdot8\cdot128\cdot32{,}768\cdot2=5.37\text{ GB}. \]

Gemma 4 12B is hybrid, so the single-formula number is only an upper bound:

\[ 2\cdot48\cdot8\cdot256\cdot32{,}768\cdot2=12.88\text{ GB}. \]

The real cache is

\[ \underbrace{L_{\text{local}}\cdot2G_{\text{local}}d_{h,\text{local}}Wb}_{\text{local, capped at }W} + \underbrace{L_{\text{global}}\cdot G_{\text{global}}d_{h,\text{global}}Tb}_{\text{global, }K=V}. \]

With \(L_{\text{local}}=40\), \(G_{\text{local}}=8\), \(d_{h,\text{local}}=256\), \(W=1024\), \(L_{\text{global}}=8\), \(G_{\text{global}}=1\), \(d_{h,\text{global}}=512\), bf16:

\[ 2\cdot40\cdot8\cdot256\cdot1024\cdot2 = 335.5\text{ MB} \] \[ 8\cdot1\cdot512\cdot32{,}768\cdot2 = 268.4\text{ MB} \]

Total at 32K: 604 MB, not 12.9 GB. At 256K the local term is unchanged and the global term is 2.15 GB, so the cache is 2.48 GB. Int8 KV halves both. This is the actual reason a 12B model can serve 256K context; the sliding window and the single global KV head do the work.

docs.title: 2.2 Why GQA matters
docs.text:
Model Q heads KV heads Ratio Cache vs MHA Qwen3-14B 40 8 5:1 ⅕ Qwen2.5-Coder-14B 40 8 5:1 ⅕ Gemma 4 12B (local) 16 8 2:1 ½ Gemma 4 12B (global) 16 1 16:1 1/16 Gemma 4 E4B (local and global) 8 2 4:1 ¼ Gemma 4 E2B (local and global) 8 1 8:1 ⅛

A 5:1 GQA model has one fifth of the KV cache of an MHA model with the same \(d_h\). That is the difference between serving 32K and 128K on one machine.

docs.title: 3.1 Qwen3 dense
docs.text: All 40 layers are full causal GQA. Cost per layer is \(O(T^2)\) for scores and \(O(T)\) cache. This is simple, predictable and easy to train. Long context is handled by RoPE base/ABF/YaRN and by training a long-context stage, not by changing the attention pattern.

docs.title: 3.2 Gemma 4 12B
docs.text:
48 layers in a repeating 5 local + 1 global pattern:

  • local: sliding window \(W=1024\), RoPE;
  • global: full attention, \(K=V\), p-RoPE \(p=0.25\), base \(10^6\).

The local layers do most of the work at \(O(TW)\); the global layers recover long-range retrieval. This is a hybrid architecture: not pure attention, not pure linear attention.

docs.title: 3.3 Qwen3.5 / 3.6
docs.text:
A different hybrid: 3 Gated DeltaNet + 1 gated attention per group. The GDN layers are linear-time with a fixed state; the full-attention layer recovers precise retrieval. This is closer to Mamba/DeltaNet than to Gemma’s sliding window.

Pattern Per-layer cost Cache Strength Full attention \(O(T^2)\) \(O(T)\) exact retrieval, simple Sliding window \(O(TW)\) \(O(W)\) cheap local context GDN / linear \(O(T)\) \(O(1)\) very long context, streaming Hybrid local/global mixed mixed balance Hybrid GDN/attention mixed mostly \(O(1)\) long context + retrieval

docs.title: 4. The edge models: Gemma 4 E2B and E4B
docs.text: E2B and E4B are not shrunken 12Bs. Four mechanisms change how their parameters, compute and cache behave, and each one is a key in config.json and a visible shape in the checkpoint. Everything below was read from the configs and safetensors headers of google/gemma-4-E2B-it, google/gemma-4-E4B-it and google/gemma-4-12B-it, and from the Hugging Face Transformers gemma4 implementation, on 27 October 2026; scripts/check_math_examples.py reproduces all three checkpoints to the parameter.

docs.title: 4.1 The configs side by side
docs.text: Key E2B E4B 12B hidden_size \(d\) 1,536 2,560 3,840 num_hidden_layers \(L\) 35 42 48 local : global (counts) 4 : 1 (28 + 7) 5 : 1 (35 + 7) 5 : 1 (40 + 8) sliding_window \(W\) 512 512 1,024 query heads \(H\) 8 8 16 KV heads, local / global 1 / 1 2 / 2 8 / 1 head dim, local / global 256 / 512 256 / 512 256 / 512 attention_k_eq_v false false true intermediate_size 6,144 (12,288 in shared layers) 10,240 15,360 hidden_size_per_layer_input 256 256 0 num_kv_shared_layers 20 18 0 use_double_wide_mlp true false false max_position_embeddings 131,072 131,072 262,144

docs.title: 4.2 Per-layer embeddings: what “effective” means
docs.text:
Next to the ordinary token embedding (\(V\times d\)), the edge models store a second table, embed_tokens_per_layer, of shape \([V,\;L\cdot256]\): for every token, a separate 256-wide vector for each layer. Each layer \(\ell\) receives an input \(p_\ell\) that combines that table row with a projection of the token embedding, and after attention and the MLP it adds a small gated correction to the residual stream:

\[ p_\ell=\tfrac{1}{\sqrt2}\Big(E_{\text{PLE}}[x]_\ell+\operatorname{RMSNorm}\big((W_{\text{proj}}\,e_x)_\ell\big)\Big)\in\mathbb{R}^{256}, \] \[ h\leftarrow h+\operatorname{RMSNorm}\Big(W_{\uparrow}\big(\operatorname{GELU}(W_{\downarrow}h)\odot p_\ell\big)\Big), \]

with \(W_{\downarrow}\in\mathbb{R}^{256\times d}\) and \(W_{\uparrow}\in\mathbb{R}^{d\times256}\) per layer (fixed scale factors omitted). The table is a lookup, not a matmul: it costs storage, not compute. For E2B it is \(262{,}144\cdot35\cdot256=2.35\text{B}\) parameters, but a token reads only \(35\cdot256=8{,}960\) of them — 17.5 KB in bf16.

That is the whole meaning of the “E”. Subtract the two embedding tables from the checkpoint and you get the model-card size:

Component (from the checkpoint) E2B E4B attention, all layers 278.4M 587.2M MLP, all layers 1,557.1M 3,303.0M PLE gates, projections and norms 41.3M 82.7M other norms and layer scalars 0.2M 0.4M text decoder compute 1.88B 3.97B token embedding (tied LM head) 402.7M 671.1M per-layer embedding table 2,348.8M 2,818.6M vision + audio encoders 475.7M 478.1M unused K/V weights of shared layers 18.9M 55.1M total in the checkpoint 5.12B 8.00B total minus the two tables 2.37B (card: 2.3B) 4.51B (card: 4.5B)

More than half of E2B’s file (53.7%) is embedding tables. For text-only work the per-token compute is \(\approx2\times(1.88+0.40)\text{B}=4.6\) GFLOPs for E2B and \(\approx2\times(3.97+0.67)\text{B}=9.3\) GFLOPs for E4B (the tied embedding still runs once as the LM head), against 23.8 GFLOPs for the 12B. As in the larger models, the MLP holds most of the capacity: 83% of the text decoder in both.

docs.title: 4.3 KV sharing: the last layers store nothing
docs.text:
The last num_kv_shared_layers layers do not compute keys or values. Each one reuses the K/V of the last earlier layer of the same type: in E4B, layers 24–41 reuse layer 22 (local) or 23 (global); in E2B, layers 15–34 reuse layer 13 or 14. Shared layers therefore have no k_proj/v_proj at run time — the checkpoints still ship those tensors (the “unused K/V” row above), and Transformers drops them on load.

Only the non-shared layers enter the cache: 20 local + 4 global for E4B, 12 local + 3 global for E2B. There is no K=V, so each cached global layer stores both K and V:

\[ \text{KV}=\sum_{\substack{\ell<L-S\\\text{local}}}2\,G\,d_h\,\min(T,W)\,b \;+\sum_{\substack{\ell<L-S\\\text{global}}}2\,G_g\,d_{h,g}\,T\,b . \] bf16 cache global bytes per token at 32K at 128K Gemma 4 E2B \(3\cdot2\cdot1\cdot512\cdot2=6\) KB 208 MB 812 MB Gemma 4 E4B \(4\cdot2\cdot2\cdot512\cdot2=16\) KB 558 MB 2.17 GB Gemma 4 12B \(8\cdot1\cdot1\cdot512\cdot2=8\) KB (K=V) 604 MB 1.41 GB

The local terms are small and constant (6.3 MB, 21 MB and 335.5 MB). The surprise is the last column: at 128K the E4B cache is larger than the 12B’s. The 12B stores one K=V head per global layer; E4B stores two heads, with separate K and V. A smaller model does not mean a smaller cache — the global-layer shape decides. Without KV sharing (a runtime that ignores num_kv_shared_layers) E4B would need 0.98 GB at 32K and E2B 0.48 GB; sharing saves 43% and 57%.

docs.title: 4.4 The double-wide MLP and the 4:1 pattern
docs.text: With use_double_wide_mlp, E2B’s 20 KV-shared layers get twice the MLP width (12,288 instead of 6,144). The capacity saved by not projecting K/V goes back into the MLP: 1,132M of E2B’s 1,557M MLP parameters live in those 20 layers. E2B also uses a 4:1 local:global pattern (seven global layers in 35) instead of 5:1, and both edge models halve the sliding window to 512 tokens.

docs.title: 4.5 Shape trace for Gemma 4 E4B
docs.text:
With \(B=1\), \(T=2{,}048\):

Tensor Shape Notes token ids [1, 2048] int32/int64 embedding [1, 2048, 2560] tied with the LM head per-layer inputs [1, 2048, 42, 256] one 256-vector per layer, from the PLE table + projection Q (local) [1, 8, 2048, 256] \(H d_h=2048\ne d\) K, V (local, layers 0–23) [1, 2, 2048, 256] \(G=2\); cache keeps the last 512 Q (global) [1, 8, 2048, 512] \(H d_h=4096\) K, V (global, layers 0–23) [1, 2, 2048, 512] separate K and V K, V (layers 24–41) — reused from layer 22 or 23 MLP gate/up [1, 2048, 10240] GeGLU logits [1, 2048, 262144] \(V\) per position

docs.title: 4.6 What this means on the Mac
docs.text:
• Size on disk is not size in compute. A 4-bit E4B is ~4 GB of weights, but over 40% of it is lookup tables; per token it computes like a ~4B dense model, not an 8B one.
  • Adapters can only attach where weights run. In the reference implementation the shared layers have no k_proj/v_proj, so LoRA there reaches q_proj, o_proj and the MLP. Run scripts/check_lora.py to see which modules your runtime actually adapts.
  • Long context is cheap on E2B, not on E4B. E2B serves 128K in 0.8 GB of cache; E4B needs 2.2 GB, more than the 12B. Quantising the cache to int8 halves either.
  • Inspect before downloading: python scripts/inspect_architecture.py --hf google/gemma-4-E4B-it --seq 131072 models PLE, KV sharing and the double-wide MLP.

docs.title: 5. Reading config.json
docs.text:
The config is the contract. These keys determine shapes:

Key Meaning Effect hidden_size / d_model \(d\) residual width, attention/MLP input num_hidden_layers \(L\) depth, activation memory, cache layers intermediate_size \(d_{\text{ff}}\) MLP width, parameter count num_attention_heads \(H\) query heads num_key_value_heads \(G\) KV heads; absence means MHA head_dim \(d_h\) per-head width; may differ from \(d/H\) vocab_size \(V\) embedding and logits tie_word_embeddings tied input/output share weights max_position_embeddings context RoPE cache / training length rope_theta RoPE base long-context extrapolation rms_norm_eps \(\epsilon\) numerical stability sliding_window \(W\) local attention window layer_types list local/global/hybrid pattern num_experts \(E\) MoE total experts num_experts_per_tok \(k\) active experts moe_intermediate_size expert FFN expert width attention_k_eq_v K=V global layers have no v_proj; one cached tensor num_kv_shared_layers \(S\) last \(S\) layers reuse earlier K/V: no K/V projections, no cache hidden_size_per_layer_input PLE width per-layer embedding table \([V, L\cdot P]\) (edge models) use_double_wide_mlp — KV-shared layers get a 2× MLP (E2B)

docs.title: 5.1 Traps
docs.text:
• head_dim may be absent. Then \(d_h=d/H\). Qwen2.5-Coder-14B has head_dim: null; \(5120/40=128\).
  • Gemma has global_head_dim. Local layers use 256, global use 512. A single \(d_h\) underestimates global attention.
  • Reported vocab vs padded vocab. Qwen3 reports 151,669 but the checkpoint pads to 151,936; Qwen2.5-Coder reports 151,646 and pads to 152,064. The padded rows are unused but allocated.
  • max_position_embeddings is not the training length. Qwen3 trains at 32K and extends to 128K with YaRN; Gemma 4 supports 256K but you train at 2K–3K.
  • tie_word_embeddings changes parameter count by \(Vd\). For Gemma 4 12B that is ~1.0B.
  • MoE configs have two FFN sizes. intermediate_size may be the dense/shared FFN; moe_intermediate_size is per expert.
  • layer_types is the architecture. Ignoring it turns a hybrid model into the wrong compute model.
  • K=V means no v_proj. Counting one in the 12B’s global layers adds 15.7M weights that do not exist.
  • An “E” size is not a compute size. E2B’s 5.1B checkpoint is 54% embedding tables; its text decoder computes with 1.88B. See §4.2.
  • KV-shared layers ship unused weights. The E2B/E4B files contain k_proj/v_proj for shared layers (18.9M / 55.1M) that are never used; do not count them, and do not expect a cache for those layers.

docs.title: 5.2 Inspect a checkpoint before downloading
docs.text:
python scripts/inspect_architecture.py --hf Qwen/Qwen3-14B --seq 32768
python scripts/inspect_architecture.py --preset gemma4-12b --seq 32768
python scripts/inspect_architecture.py --preset gemma4-e4b --seq 131072
python scripts/inspect_architecture.py --hf Qwen/Qwen3-30B-A3B --seq 4096

The script prints:

  • parameter count per component and total;
  • active parameters for MoE;
  • GQA ratio;
  • KV cache at a chosen context;
  • training/inference FLOPs for a batch.

It reads only config.json; no weights, no PyTorch.

docs.title: 6. Design choices and why they exist
6.1 Depth vs width
docs.text:
Given a parameter budget, depth and width trade off:

  • deeper: more sequential computation, better compositional reasoning, harder to train (residual scaling, QK-norm);
  • wider: more parallel compute, larger matrices, better GPU utilisation, more KV cache per layer.

Qwen3-14B is 40 layers at \(d=5120\); Qwen2.5-Coder-14B is 48 layers at the same width but a smaller FFN (13,824 vs 17,408). Gemma 4 12B is 48 layers at \(d=3840\) with a wider FFN (15,360). There is no universal optimum; data and training stability decide.

docs.title: 6.2 GQA ratio
docs.text: Higher \(H/G\) saves cache but can hurt quality. 5:1 is a common compromise; Gemma 4 12B uses 2:1 because its head dimension is larger and it relies on hybrid attention for long context. Do not “optimise” GQA after pretraining; it is an architecture choice.

docs.title: 6.3 Vocabulary
docs.text:
A larger vocabulary:

  • compresses text better (fewer tokens);
  • costs \(Vd\) embedding parameters and \(V\) softmax per token;
  • can improve multilingual/code coverage.

Qwen’s 151k and Gemma’s 262k reflect different multilingual/code priorities. A 262k vocab is ~1B parameters at \(d=3840\) when tied; at \(d=5120\) it would be ~1.34B.

docs.title: 6.4 Activation
docs.text:
SwiGLU vs GeGLU:

\[ \operatorname{SwiGLU}=W_d(\operatorname{SiLU}(W_gx)\odot W_ux), \] \[ \operatorname{GeGLU}=W_d(\operatorname{GELU}(W_gx)\odot W_ux). \]

Both have three matrices. The difference is the nonlinearity; empirical results are close, and the choice is usually inherited from the pretraining family. Do not swap activation in a fine-tune; it changes the architecture.

On paper

One hidden unit (\(d_{\text{ff}}=1\)) with gate \(W_gx=1\), up value \(W_ux=2\) and \(W_d=1\). Use \(\sigma(1)\approx0.7311\) (\(e\approx2.718\)) and the normal CDF \(\Phi(1)\approx0.8413\), so \(\operatorname{SiLU}(1)=\sigma(1)\) and \(\operatorname{GELU}(1)=\Phi(1)\).

\[ \begin{aligned} \operatorname{SwiGLU}&=0.7311\cdot2\approx1.462\\ \operatorname{GeGLU}&=0.8413\cdot2\approx1.683 \end{aligned} \]

With a negative gate \(W_gx=-1\), \(\operatorname{SiLU}(-1)=-0.2689\) and \(\operatorname{GELU}(-1)=-0.1587\), giving \(-0.538\) and \(-0.317\). GELU lets more of a positive gate through and less of a negative one; Gemma’s tanh approximation of GELU agrees to three decimals.

Longer version: 43 §9.

docs.title: 6.5 Normalization
docs.text:
• Pre-norm (Qwen3): stable deep training, residual path is identity.
  • Pre+post-norm (Gemma 4): extra normalization after the residual add; can improve representation quality but needs careful init.
  • QK-norm (Qwen3, Gemma 4): normalizes queries/keys per head, bounding attention logits and stabilising large LR.

docs.title: 6.6 Positional encoding
docs.text:
• RoPE (Qwen3, Qwen2.5, Gemma local): relative, no learned table.
  • p-RoPE (Gemma global): rotate only \(p d_h\) dimensions; cheaper and more stable at long context.
  • ABF/YaRN/DCA (Qwen3 long context): adjust base frequency and attention scaling to extend beyond training length.

docs.title: 6.7 MoE
docs.text:
MoE decouples total parameters from active compute:

\[ N_{\text{active}}\approx N_{\text{attn}}+N_{\text{router}}+\frac{k}{E}N_{\text{experts}}+N_{\text{embed}}. \]

Qwen3-30B-A3B stores 30.5B and activates 3.3B per token. The cost is routing, load balancing, all-to-all communication and memory for all experts. For a single 32 GB machine, a 30B MoE at 4-bit is ~17 GB and inference-only; training is not a realistic local path.

On paper

Qwen3-30B-A3B: 48 layers, \(d=2{,}048\), 32 query and 4 KV heads of \(d_h=128\) (so \(Hd_h=4{,}096\ne d\)), \(E=128\) experts of width 768, \(k=8\), untied \(V=151{,}936\).

Term Per layer × 48 layers \(N_{\text{attn}}\): \(2\cdot2{,}048\cdot4{,}096+2\cdot2{,}048\cdot4\cdot128\) 18.87M 0.906B \(N_{\text{router}}\): \(2{,}048\cdot128\) 0.26M 0.013B \(N_{\text{experts}}\): \(128\cdot3\cdot2{,}048\cdot768\) 603.98M 28.99B \(N_{\text{embed}}\): \(2Vd\), untied — 0.622B \[ \begin{aligned} \tfrac{k}{E}N_{\text{experts}}&=\tfrac{8}{128}\cdot28.99\text{B}=1.812\text{B}\\ N_{\text{active}}&\approx0.906+0.013+1.812+0.622\\ &\approx3.35\text{B} \end{aligned} \]

Stored, all four rows add up to \(\approx30.5\)B; per token only 3.35B are used. Those are the 30.5B and 3.3B above.

Longer version: 43 §10.

docs.title: 7. What fine-tuning changes — and what it doesn’t
docs.text:
Thing Pretraining LoRA fine-tune Tokenizer fixed fixed Architecture fixed fixed Attention pattern fixed fixed KV cache fixed fixed Base weights trained frozen (usually 4-bit) Adapters — low-rank \(BA\) in projections Sequence length 32K–256K 2K–3K (memory budget) Batch millions of tokens 8–16 examples effective Objective next-token masked completion Chat template learned must match

Consequences:

  • LoRA does not give the model a longer context; it only trains on longer sequences.
  • num_layers: 24 selects the last 24 blocks; it does not change the model’s depth at inference. The adapter is applied to those blocks.
  • max_seq_length is a training memory setting, not the model’s native context.
  • Quantizing the base changes the weights, not the architecture.
  • A different chat template can break a good adapter; see 06 — Data format.

docs.title: 8. Architecture checklist
docs.text:
Before training or serving:

  • config.json parsed and parameter count matches the model card (within padding).
  • GQA ratio and head dimension confirmed.
  • Vocabulary and tied embeddings confirmed.
  • Attention pattern (full/local/hybrid) understood.
  • KV cache at target context estimated.
  • max_position_embeddings vs training length separated.
  • MoE total vs active parameters separated.
  • Edge models: per-layer embedding tables and KV-shared layers separated from compute and cache.
  • Chat template rendered once with tools.
  • num_layers and max_seq_length chosen from memory, not habit.
  • The adapter target modules checked with scripts/check_lora.py.

docs.title: 38 — Derivations and proofs
docs.text:
Last verified: 27 October 2026. These are the derivations behind 32 — Mathematics; they are written for someone who wants to implement or debug a model, not just read about one.

Notation follows chapter 32. \(B\) is batch, \(T\) sequence, \(d\) hidden size, \(H\) query heads, \(G\) KV heads, \(d_h\) head dimension, \(V\) vocabulary.

For numeric checks of every result in this chapter, see 43 — Worked examples.

docs.title: 1. Cross-entropy and its gradient
docs.text:
For one position with logits \(z\in\mathbb{R}^{V}\) and target \(y\in\{1,\dots,V\}\):

\[ p_j=\frac{e^{z_j}}{\sum_{k=1}^{V}e^{z_k}}, \qquad \mathcal{L}=-\log p_y. \]

On paper

After "The capital of France is", a three-token toy vocabulary {Paris, Lyon, Nice} gets logits \(z=(1,0,-1)\), and the target is Paris, \(y=1\). With \(e\approx2.718\) and \(e^{-1}\approx0.368\):

\[ \sum_k e^{z_k}=2.718+1+0.368=4.086 \] \[ p=(0.665,\;0.245,\;0.090) \] \[ \mathcal{L}=-\log 0.665=0.408 \]

Equal logits would give \(p_y=1/3\) and \(\mathcal{L}=\log 3=1.099\), so this model is already well ahead of a uniform guess.

docs.title: 1.1 Gradient
docs.text:
Write \(Z=\sum_k e^{z_k}\). Then

\[ rac{\partial \mathcal{L}}{\partial z_j} =- rac{1}{p_y} rac{\partial p_y}{\partial z_j}. \]

For \(j=y\):

\[ rac{\partial p_y}{\partial z_y} =p_y(1-p_y), \]

so

\[ rac{\partial \mathcal{L}}{\partial z_y}=-(1-p_y)=p_y-1. \]

For \(j e y\):

\[ rac{\partial p_y}{\partial z_j}=-p_y p_j, \]

so

\[ rac{\partial \mathcal{L}}{\partial z_j}=p_j. \]

Combining:

\[ oxed{ abla_z\mathcal{L}=p-e_y} \]

where \(e_y\) is the one-hot target. This is why the logits gradient is bounded: it is a probability vector minus a one-hot vector, with entries in \([-1,1]\).

On paper

Same logits \(z=(1,0,-1)\), target Paris (\(y=1\)), \(p=(0.665,0.245,0.090)\):

\[ abla_z\mathcal{L}=p-e_1=(-0.335,\;0.245,\;0.090) \]

The entries sum to 0. Finite-difference check on the Lyon logit: since \(\mathcal{L}=\log\sum_k e^{z_k}-z_y\), moving \(z_2\) to \(\pm0.1\) changes only the sum, to \(4.1913\) and \(3.9910\) (\(e^{0.1}\approx1.10517\), \(e^{-0.1}\approx0.90484\)):

\[ egin{aligned} rac{\log(4.1913/3.9910)}{0.2}&= rac{\log1.0502}{0.2}\ &=0.2449 \end{aligned} \]

That matches \(p_2=1/4.0862=0.2447\); the gap in the last digit comes from the finite step. Longer version: 43 §2.

docs.title: 1.2 Softmax Jacobian
docs.text:
For the full vector:

\[ \frac{\partial p_i}{\partial z_j}=p_i(\delta_{ij}-p_j), \]

or in matrix form:

\[ J=\operatorname{diag}(p)-pp^\top. \]

The Jacobian is symmetric positive semidefinite with rank \(V-1\) (the all-ones direction is in the null space because probabilities sum to 1). This is the mathematical reason softmax is stable to optimize but cannot represent a full-rank linear map.

On paper

Take \(p=(0.5,0.25,0.25)\), the softmax of logits \((\log2,0,0)\). Then \(\operatorname{diag}(p)=\tfrac1{16}\operatorname{diag}(8,4,4)\), and \(pp^\top\) has entries \(p_ip_j\):

\[ J=\frac{1}{16}\begin{pmatrix}4&-2&-2\\-2&3&-1\\-2&-1&3\end{pmatrix} \]

Every row sums to 0, so \(J\mathbf{1}=0\): adding the same number to all logits changes nothing. Row 1 is minus the sum of rows 2 and 3, so the rank is \(2=V-1\). Finite-difference check of \(J_{11}=p_1(1-p_1)=0.25\): nudging \(z_1\) by \(\pm0.1\) gives \(p_1=0.52498\) and \(0.47502\), a slope of \(0.2498\).

docs.title: 1.3 Numerical stability
docs.text:
Computing \(e^{z_j}\) directly overflows for large logits. Subtract the maximum:

\[ p_j=\frac{e^{z_j-m}}{\sum_k e^{z_k-m}}, \qquad m=\max_k z_k. \]

This is algebraically identical and keeps the largest exponent at 1. The log-sum-exp form is

\[ \log\sum_k e^{z_k}=m+\log\sum_k e^{z_k-m}. \]

On paper

Logits \(z=(1000,999,998)\). Computing \(e^{1000}\) directly overflows every float format: fp32 and bf16 top out near \(3.4\times10^{38}\approx e^{88.7}\), fp64 near \(e^{709.8}\). With \(m=1000\) the shifted logits are \((0,-1,-2)\), and \(e^{-1}\approx0.3679\), \(e^{-2}\approx0.1353\):

\[ \sum_k e^{z_k-m}=1+0.3679+0.1353=1.5032 \] \[ p=(0.665,\;0.245,\;0.090) \] \[ \begin{aligned} \log\sum_k e^{z_k}&=1000+\log1.5032\\ &=1000.408 \end{aligned} \]

These are exactly the probabilities of \(z=(1,0,-1)\) above, because every logit moved by 999. The loss for the first token is \(1000.408-1000=0.408\), also unchanged.

A z-loss penalizes large logits:

\[ \mathcal{L}_z=\lambda\left(\log\sum_k e^{z_k}\right)^2, \]

which keeps the softmax denominator near 1 and reduces loss spikes in large-vocabulary models.

On paper

Use \(\lambda=10^{-4}\), the PaLM value. The logits \((1,0,-1)\) and \((1000,999,998)\) give the same probabilities and the same cross-entropy, 0.408, but their log-sum-exps are 1.408 and 1000.408:

\[ 10^{-4}\cdot1.408^2=0.000198 \] \[ 10^{-4}\cdot1000.408^2=100.08 \]

Cross-entropy cannot tell the two apart; the z-loss pushes the second back toward \(\log\sum_k e^{z_k}\approx0\). This matters in practice: bf16 numbers near 1000 are spaced 4 apart, so 1000, 999 and 998 would all round to 1000.

docs.title: 2. Attention forward and backward
docs.text:
For one head, with \(Q\in\mathbb{R}^{T\times d_h}\), \(K,V\in\mathbb{R}^{T\times d_h}\):

\[ S=\frac{QK^\top}{\sqrt{d_h}}+M, \qquad P=\operatorname{softmax}(S), \qquad O=PV. \]

\(M\) is the causal mask: \(M_{ij}=0\) for \(j\le i\), \(-\infty\) otherwise.

On paper

Two tokens, \(d_h=4\), so \(\sqrt{d_h}=2\). Token 2 has query \(q_2=(1,1,1,1)\); the keys are \(k_1=(2,2,0,0)\) and \(k_2=(0,0,1,-1)\):

\[ S_{2\cdot}=\tfrac12\,(q_2\cdot k_1,\;q_2\cdot k_2)=(2,\;0) \]

With \(e^2\approx7.389\):

\[ P_{2\cdot}=\Big(\tfrac{7.389}{8.389},\;\tfrac{1}{8.389}\Big)=(0.881,\;0.119) \]

With values \(v_1=(1,0,0,0)\) and \(v_2=(0,1,0,0)\), \(O_2=0.881\,v_1+0.119\,v_2=(0.881,0.119,0,0)\). Token 1 has \(S_{12}=-\infty\) from the mask, so \(P_{1\cdot}=(1,0)\) and \(O_1=v_1\): the first token can only read itself.

docs.title: 2.1 Forward complexity
docs.text:
• \(QK^\top\): \(T^2d_h\) multiply-adds.
  • softmax: \(O(T^2)\).
  • \(PV\): \(T^2d_h\).
  • per head: \(O(T^2d_h)\); for \(H\) heads and \(L\) layers: \(O(LHT^2d_h)=O(LT^2d)\).

The KV cache makes autoregressive decoding \(O(T)\) per token instead of \(O(T^2)\), because only the new query attends to cached keys/values.

On paper

Qwen3-14B has \(d_h=128=2^7\) and \(H=40\) query heads. For a prompt of \(T=4{,}096=2^{12}\) tokens, one head's \(QK^\top\) costs

\[ T^2d_h=2^{24}\cdot2^{7}=2^{31}\approx2.15\times10^{9} \]

multiply-adds, about \(8.6\times10^{10}\) for the 40 heads of one layer. With a cache, the next token needs only one query row against the \(T\) cached keys:

\[ T\,d_h=2^{12}\cdot2^{7}=2^{19}=524{,}288 \]

per head, \(2^{12}=4{,}096\) times less than recomputing the whole score matrix.

docs.title: 2.2 Backward
docs.text:
Given \(dO\):

\[ dP=dO\,V^\top, \qquad dV=P^\top dO. \]

For each row \(i\) with softmax row \(p_i\), let \(s_i=\sum_j dP_{ij}p_{ij}\). Then

\[ dS_{ij}=p_{ij}\left(dP_{ij}-s_i\right), \]

or in matrix form \(dS=P\odot(dP-s\mathbf{1}^\top)\), where \(s\) is the column vector of \(s_i=dP_i\cdot p_i\), so \((s\mathbf{1}^\top)_{ij}=s_i\). Subtract each row’s probability-weighted \(dP\), then multiply elementwise by \(P\). Then

\[ dQ=\frac{dS\,K}{\sqrt{d_h}}, \qquad dK=\frac{dS^\top Q}{\sqrt{d_h}}. \]

The mask sets \(dS_{ij}=0\) for \(j>i\). In practice, FlashAttention fuses these steps and never materialises the \(T\times T\) matrix in global memory; it recomputes tiles in the backward pass. That is why long-context training is feasible at all.

On paper

Back-propagate row 2 of the forward example above, \(p_2=(0.881,0.119)\), with upstream gradient \(dO_2=(1,-1,0,0)\). Then \(dP_2=(dO_2\cdot v_1,\;dO_2\cdot v_2)=(1,-1)\) and

\[ s_2=1\cdot0.881-1\cdot0.119=0.762 \] \[ \begin{aligned} dS_2&=\big(0.881\cdot0.238,\;0.119\cdot(-1.762)\big)\\ &=(0.210,\;-0.210) \end{aligned} \]

Check with the softmax Jacobian of §1.2: for two entries \(J=p_1p_2\begin{pmatrix}1&-1\\-1&1\end{pmatrix}\), so \(J\,dP_2=2p_1p_2\,(1,-1)\) and \(2\cdot0.881\cdot0.119=0.210\). Then, with \(\sqrt{d_h}=2\):

\[ \begin{aligned} dq_2&=\tfrac12\,(0.210\,k_1-0.210\,k_2)\\ &=(0.210,\;0.210,\;-0.105,\;0.105) \end{aligned} \]

Longer version: 43 §5.

docs.title: 2.3 Why scale by the square root of the head dimension
docs.text:
If \(q_i,k_i\) are independent with mean 0 and variance 1, then

\[ \operatorname{Var}(q\cdot k)=\sum_{i=1}^{d_h}\operatorname{Var}(q_i k_i)=d_h. \]

Dividing by \(\sqrt{d_h}\) gives unit variance, keeping the softmax in a regime where gradients are informative. Without it, logits grow with \(d_h\), softmax saturates, and gradients vanish.

On paper

Let every \(q_i\) and \(k_i\) be \(\pm1\) with equal odds, so each product \(q_ik_i\) is \(\pm1\): mean 0, variance 1. For \(d_h=2\) the four equally likely sums are \(2,0,0,-2\):

\[ \operatorname{Var}(q\cdot k)=\tfrac14\,(4+0+0+4)=2=d_h \]

For Qwen3's \(d_h=128\) the raw scores have standard deviation \(\sqrt{128}\approx11.3\). Two keys one standard deviation apart would get softmax weights 0.99999 and 0.00001; after dividing by 11.3 the gap is 1 and the weights are 0.731 and 0.269.

docs.title: 3. RMSNorm gradient
docs.text:
For \(x\in\mathbb{R}^{d}\):

\[ r=\sqrt{\frac{1}{d}\sum_{i=1}^{d}x_i^2+\epsilon}, \qquad y_i=\gamma_i\frac{x_i}{r}. \]

On paper

Take \(d=4\), \(x=(1,-1,3,5)\), \(\gamma=(1,1,1,1)\) and Qwen3's \(\epsilon=10^{-6}\), which is negligible here:

\[ r=\sqrt{\tfrac14\,(1+1+9+25)}=\sqrt9=3 \] \[ \begin{aligned} y&=\big(\tfrac13,-\tfrac13,1,\tfrac53\big)\\ &=(0.333,-0.333,1,1.667) \end{aligned} \]

The mean of \(y_i^2\) is \(\tfrac14\cdot\tfrac{36}{9}=1\): RMSNorm rescales the vector to unit root-mean-square without subtracting its mean (here 2).

For \(i\ne j\):

\[ \frac{\partial y_i}{\partial x_j} =\gamma_i x_i\cdot\left(-\frac{1}{2}\right)r^{-3}\cdot\frac{2x_j}{d} =-\frac{\gamma_i x_i x_j}{d r^3}. \]

For \(i=j\):

\[ \frac{\partial y_i}{\partial x_i} =\frac{\gamma_i}{r}-\frac{\gamma_i x_i^2}{d r^3}. \]

Combining:

\[ \boxed{ \frac{\partial y_i}{\partial x_j} =\frac{\gamma_i}{r}\left(\delta_{ij}-\frac{x_i x_j}{d r^2}\right) } \]

The Jacobian is \(\operatorname{diag}(\gamma)/r\) times a rank-one update of the identity. It is cheap to compute and does not center the input, which is the main difference from LayerNorm.

On paper

Take \(d=2\), \(x=(1,7)\), \(\gamma=(1,1)\), \(\epsilon=0\). Then \(r=\sqrt{(1+49)/2}=5\) and \(dr^2=50\):

\[ \begin{aligned} J&=\tfrac15\begin{pmatrix}1-\frac{1}{50}&-\frac{7}{50}\\-\frac{7}{50}&1-\frac{49}{50}\end{pmatrix}\\ &=\begin{pmatrix}0.196&-0.028\\-0.028&0.004\end{pmatrix} \end{aligned} \]

Check 1: \(Jx=(0.196-7\cdot0.028,\;-0.028+7\cdot0.004)=(0,0)\), as it must be, because scaling \(x\) leaves \(y\) unchanged. Check 2: moving \(x_1\) to 1.1 and 0.9 gives \(r=\sqrt{25.105}\approx5.0105\) and \(\sqrt{24.905}\approx4.9905\), so \(y_1=0.21954\) and \(0.18034\), a slope of \((0.21954-0.18034)/0.2=0.1960=J_{11}\). Longer version: 43 §4.

docs.title: 4. RoPE is relative: proof
docs.text:
For a 2D pair \((x_{2i},x_{2i+1})\), define

\[ R_{\theta}= \begin{pmatrix} \cos\theta & -\sin\theta\\ \sin\theta & \cos\theta \end{pmatrix}. \]

RoPE applies \(R_{t\omega_i}\) to the pair at position \(t\). The key identity is

\[ R_a^\top R_b=R_{b-a}. \]

Proof: rotation matrices commute and compose by adding angles:

\[ R_a^\top R_b=R_{-a}R_b=R_{b-a}. \]

For a query at \(t\) and key at \(s\):

\[ q_t=R_{t\omega}W_qx_t, \qquad k_s=R_{s\omega}W_kx_s. \]

Then

\[ q_t^\top k_s =x_t^\top W_q^\top R_{t\omega}^\top R_{s\omega}W_kx_s =x_t^\top W_q^\top R_{(s-t)\omega}W_kx_s. \]

The dot product depends only on \(s-t\), not on absolute positions. That is the relative property.

On paper

Use a toy frequency \(\omega=\pi/2\), a quarter turn per position, so every cosine and sine is 0 or \(\pm1\), and fix the content vectors \(W_qx=(1,0)\) and \(W_kx=(2,1)\). Recall \(R_\theta(a,b)=(a\cos\theta-b\sin\theta,\;a\sin\theta+b\cos\theta)\). The query sits at position \(t\), the key at \(s\):

\(t,\,s\) \(q_t\) \(k_s\) \(q_t^\top k_s\) 1, 3 \((0,1)\) \((1,-2)\) \(-2\) 2, 4 \((-1,0)\) \((2,1)\) \(-2\)

Both pairs are two positions apart, and the right-hand side gives the same number directly: \((1,0)\cdot R_{\pi}(2,1)=(1,0)\cdot(-2,-1)=-2\). At distance 1 the score changes: \((1,0)\cdot R_{\pi/2}(2,1)=(1,0)\cdot(-1,2)=-1\).

docs.title: 4.1 Base frequency
docs.text:
\[ \omega_i=\text{base}^{-2i/d_h}. \]

For \(i=0\), \(\omega=1\) (fast rotation); for \(i=d_h/2-1\), \(\omega=\text{base}^{-1+2/d_h}\) (slow). A larger base makes the slow dimensions rotate even more slowly, which helps long-context extrapolation. Qwen3 raises the base from \(10^4\) to \(10^6\) in the long-context stage and applies YaRN/DCA scaling.

On paper

Qwen3 uses \(d_h=128\). For the middle pair, \(i=32\), the exponent is \(2i/d_h=64/128=1/2\), so \(\omega_{32}=\text{base}^{-1/2}\):

base \(\omega_{32}\) positions per full turn, \(2\pi/\omega_{32}\) \(10^4\) 0.01 628 \(10^6\) 0.001 6,283

Pair 0 has \(\omega_0=1\) at any base and turns once every \(2\pi\approx6.28\) positions. Going from \(10^4\) to \(10^6\) slows the middle pair 10× and the slowest pair (\(i=63\)) about 93×.

docs.title: 4.2 p-RoPE
docs.text:
Gemma 4 rotates only the first \(p d_h\) dimensions:

\[ \tilde q=\big[R_{\theta}(q_{1:pd_h}),q_{pd_h+1:d_h}\big]. \]

The unrotated dimensions are position-invariant. This reduces the number of rotary operations and, more importantly, avoids imposing position on dimensions that global attention uses for content. The report uses \(p=0.25\).

On paper

Toy head with \(d_h=8\) and \(p=0.25\): only the first \(pd_h=2\) entries form a rotated pair. With \(q=(1,0,2,-1,0,3,1,1)\) and a quarter-turn angle \(\theta=\pi/2\):

\[ \tilde q=(0,1,\;2,-1,0,3,1,1) \]

The last six entries contribute the same amount to a query–key dot product at every distance. A Gemma 4 global layer has \(d_h=512\), so \(0.25\cdot512=128\) dimensions (64 pairs) carry position and 384 carry content only.

docs.title: 5. GQA equivalence and cache
docs.text:
GQA can be viewed as MHA with tied KV projections. For a group of \(H/G\) query heads sharing one KV head:

\[ K_h=K,\quad V_h=V \quad\text{for all }h\text{ in the group}. \]

The attention output for each query head is still computed independently:

\[ O_h=\operatorname{softmax}\left(\frac{Q_hK^\top}{\sqrt{d_h}}\right)V. \]

On paper

One KV head stores \(k_1=(1,1,0,0)\), \(k_2=(0,0,1,1)\), \(v_1=(1,0,0,0)\), \(v_2=(0,1,0,0)\) and serves two query heads, \(q_a=(2,2,0,0)\) and \(q_b=(0,0,2,2)\), with \(\sqrt{d_h}=2\). Their scores are \((2,0)\) and \((0,2)\), so with \(e^2\approx7.389\):

\[ \begin{aligned} O_a&=0.881\,v_1+0.119\,v_2\\ O_b&=0.119\,v_1+0.881\,v_2 \end{aligned} \]

Same cache, two different outputs. Averaging the queries first, \(\bar q=(1,1,1,1)\), would give scores \((1,1)\) and the single output \(0.5\,v_1+0.5\,v_2\), which is not what GQA computes.

So GQA is not averaging queries; it shares the keys and values. The cache saving is exact:

\[ \text{cache}_{\text{GQA}}=\frac{G}{H}\text{cache}_{\text{MHA}}. \]

The quality cost is empirical, not a theorem. 5:1 is common because it retains most of MHA’s quality at 20% of the cache.

On paper

Qwen3-14B has \(H=40\), \(G=8\), \(d_h=128\), 40 layers and a bf16 cache (2 bytes). One token's K and V in one layer:

\[ \text{MHA: }2\cdot40\cdot128\cdot2=20{,}480\text{ bytes} \] \[ \text{GQA: }2\cdot8\cdot128\cdot2=4{,}096\text{ bytes} \]

That is \(8/40=20\%\). Over 40 layers GQA needs 160 KiB per token, so a 16,384-token context takes 2.5 GiB; MHA would take 12.5 GiB of a 32 GB Mac's memory. Longer version: 43 §7.

docs.title: 6. SwiGLU and GeGLU derivatives
docs.text:
For

\[ y=W_d\big(\operatorname{SiLU}(W_gx)\odot W_ux\big), \]

let \(a=W_gx\), \(b=W_ux\), \(g=\operatorname{SiLU}(a)=a\sigma(a)\), and let \(\bar y=\partial\mathcal{L}/\partial y\) be the upstream gradient. The correct backward pass is

\[ \frac{\partial\mathcal{L}}{\partial a} =\left(W_d^\top\bar y\right)\odot b\odot g'(a), \qquad g'(a)=\sigma(a)+a\sigma(a)\big(1-\sigma(a)\big), \] \[ \frac{\partial\mathcal{L}}{\partial b} =\left(W_d^\top\bar y\right)\odot g. \]

On paper

One token, two hidden units: suppose \(a=W_gx=(0,2)\), \(b=W_ux=(3,1)\) and \(W_d=(1,1)\), so \(y\) is a scalar. With \(\sigma(2)\approx0.881\), \(g=\operatorname{SiLU}(a)=(0,\;1.762)\) and

\[ y=1\cdot(0\cdot3)+1\cdot(1.762\cdot1)=1.762 \]

Backward with \(\bar y=1\), so \(W_d^\top\bar y=(1,1)\); \(g'(0)=0.5\) and \(g'(2)=0.881+2\cdot0.881\cdot0.119=1.091\):

\[ \frac{\partial\mathcal{L}}{\partial a}=(3\cdot0.5,\;1\cdot1.091)=(1.5,\;1.091) \] \[ \frac{\partial\mathcal{L}}{\partial b}=(0,\;1.762) \]

The closed first gate outputs 0 yet still gets gradient 1.5, so it can learn to open. Finite-difference check on \(a_2\): with \(\sigma(2.1)\approx0.89090\) and \(\sigma(1.9)\approx0.86989\), \(\operatorname{SiLU}(2.1)=1.8709\) and \(\operatorname{SiLU}(1.9)=1.6528\), so \((1.8709-1.6528)/0.2=1.0905\), against \(g'(2)=1.0908\). Longer version: 43 §9.

Do not confuse the scalar derivative \(g'(a)\) with the vector gradient: the upstream gradient \(W_d^\top\bar y\) must be multiplied elementwise by \(b\) and \(g'(a)\). The gate’s derivative has the extra \(a\sigma(a)(1-\sigma(a))\) term, which is why SiLU is smooth and avoids the dead-unit behaviour of ReLU. GeGLU replaces \(\operatorname{SiLU}\) with \(\operatorname{GELU}\):

\[ \operatorname{GELU}(a)=a\Phi(a), \qquad \Phi(a)=\frac12\left(1+\operatorname{erf}\left(\frac{a}{\sqrt2}\right)\right). \]

Both have three matrices, so the parameter count is the same; the difference is the nonlinearity and its gradient.

On paper

About 68.27% of a standard normal lies within \(\pm1\), so \(\operatorname{erf}(1/\sqrt2)=0.6827\) and

\[ \operatorname{GELU}(1)=\tfrac12\,(1+0.6827)=0.841 \] \[ \operatorname{GELU}(-1)=-\tfrac12\,(1-0.6827)=-0.159 \]

Compare \(\operatorname{SiLU}(1)=\sigma(1)=0.731\) and \(\operatorname{SiLU}(-1)=-0.269\): the same shape with slightly different values, so GeGLU and SwiGLU differ only in the gate's values and slope.

docs.title: 7. MoE routing and load balancing
docs.text:
For \(E\) experts, router logits \(r=W_rx\), and top-k set \(\mathcal{T}\):

\[ g_i=\frac{\exp(r_i)}{\sum_{j=1}^{E}\exp(r_j)}, \qquad y=\sum_{i\in\mathcal{T}}\frac{g_i}{\sum_{j\in\mathcal{T}}g_j}E_i(x). \]

The router gradient flows only through the selected experts and the renormalisation. If one expert is selected for most tokens, the others receive no gradient and collapse further.

On paper

\(E=4\) experts, top-\(k=2\), router logits \(r=(1,0.5,0,-1)\). With \(e^{0.5}\approx1.6487\), the exponentials are \((2.7183,1.6487,1,0.3679)\), summing to 5.7349:

\[ g=(0.474,\;0.287,\;0.174,\;0.064) \]

Experts 1 and 2 win. In the renormalised weights the full sum cancels, leaving only their own exponentials:

\[ \frac{(2.7183,\;1.6487)}{2.7183+1.6487}=(0.622,\;0.378) \]

So \(y=0.622\,E_1(x)+0.378\,E_2(x)\). Experts 3 and 4 held 24% of the router probability but get no gradient from this token. Longer version: 43 §10.

docs.title: 7.1 Auxiliary load-balancing loss
docs.text:
With \(f_i\) the fraction of tokens routed to expert \(i\) and \(P_i\) the mean router probability:

\[ \mathcal{L}_{\text{bal}}=\alpha E\sum_{i=1}^{E}f_iP_i. \]

If routing is uniform, \(f_i=P_i=1/E\), so \(\mathcal{L}_{\text{bal}}=\alpha\). If routing collapses, \(f_iP_i\) is large for the dominant expert, increasing the loss. The gradient pushes probability mass toward underrepresented experts.

On paper

Take \(E=4\), top-1 routing, and Qwen3-30B-A3B's coefficient \(\alpha=0.001\). In a batch of 8 tokens, 7 go to expert 1 and 1 to expert 2, so \(f=(0.875,0.125,0,0)\), and the mean router probabilities are \(P=(0.6,0.2,0.1,0.1)\):

\[ \sum_i f_iP_i=0.875\cdot0.6+0.125\cdot0.2=0.55 \] \[ \mathcal{L}_{\text{bal}}=0.001\cdot4\cdot0.55=0.0022 \]

That is 2.2 times the balanced value \(\alpha=0.001\). Treating \(f\) as fixed counts, \(\partial\mathcal{L}_{\text{bal}}/\partial P_i=\alpha Ef_i\) is 0.0035 for expert 1 and 0 for experts 3 and 4, so the gradient lowers expert 1's probability fastest.

Qwen3 uses a global-batch version so specialisation can vary across a batch while staying balanced globally. The exact implementation (capacity factor, token dropping, expert bias) is not fully public.

docs.title: 7.2 Active compute
docs.text:
For \(k\) active experts out of \(E\):

\[ N_{\text{active}}\approx N_{\text{attn}}+N_{\text{router}} +\frac{k}{E}N_{\text{experts}}+N_{\text{embed}}. \]

For Qwen3-30B-A3B: \(E=128\), \(k=8\), so only 6.25% of expert parameters run per token. That is why it stores 30.5B but generates at ~3.3B speed.

On paper

Check both numbers against the Qwen3-30B-A3B config: 48 layers, \(d=2048\), 128 experts of width 768, 32 query and 4 KV heads of size 128, and an untied 151,936-token vocabulary. One expert in one layer has \(3\cdot2048\cdot768=4.72\)M weights, so all experts hold \(4.72\text{M}\cdot128\cdot48=29.0\)B, of which \(\tfrac{8}{128}\cdot29.0=1.81\)B run per token. Attention is 0.91B, embeddings plus LM head 0.62B, routers 0.01B:

\[ \begin{aligned} N_{\text{active}}&\approx0.91+0.01+1.81+0.62\\ &=3.35\text{B} \end{aligned} \]

Counting every expert instead gives \(0.91+0.01+29.0+0.62=30.5\)B stored.

docs.title: 8. Gated DeltaNet as online gradient descent
docs.text:
The delta rule updates an associative memory \(S\in\mathbb{R}^{d_v\times d_k}\), which maps a key to a value (the convention of the Gated DeltaNet paper), by correcting its prediction error for the current key/value:

\[ \mathcal{L}(S)=\frac12\|S k_t-v_t\|_2^2. \]

The gradient is

\[ \nabla_S\mathcal{L}=(S k_t-v_t)k_t^\top. \]

A gradient step with rate \(\beta_t\) gives

\[ S_t=S_{t-1}-\beta_t(S_{t-1} k_t-v_t)k_t^\top. \]

Gated DeltaNet first decays the state by \(\alpha_t\):

\[ S'=\alpha_tS_{t-1}, \]

then corrects:

\[ S_t=S'-\beta_t(S' k_t-v_t)k_t^\top. \]

Substituting \(S'\):

\[ \boxed{ S_t=\alpha_tS_{t-1} +\beta_t\big(v_t-\alpha_tS_{t-1} k_t\big)k_t^\top } \]

and

\[ o_t=S_t\, q_t. \]

This is exactly the recurrence in chapter 32. \(\alpha_t\) is a forget gate; \(\beta_t\) is the learning rate for the current association. In the actual GDN layer \(k_t\) is L2-normalised and \(\beta_t\in(0,1)\), which keeps the rank-one update bounded; without normalisation, a large \(\|k_t\|^2\) can make \(I-\beta_tk_tk_t^\top\) unstable.

On paper

Take \(d_k=2\) and a scalar value (\(d_v=1\)), so \(S\) is just two numbers. The memory holds \(S_{t-1}=(2,0)\): key \((1,0)\) returns value 2. A unit key \(k_t=(0.6,0.8)\) arrives with \(v_t=1\), \(\alpha_t=0.5\), \(\beta_t=0.5\):

\[ \alpha_tS_{t-1}k_t=0.5\cdot(2\cdot0.6+0\cdot0.8)=0.6 \] \[ \begin{aligned} S_t&=(1,0)+0.5\,(1-0.6)\,(0.6,0.8)\\ &=(1.12,\;0.16) \end{aligned} \]

Read back with \(q_t=k_t\): \(o_t=S_tk_t=0.672+0.128=0.8\). The decayed memory predicted 0.6, the target was 1, and \(\beta_t=0.5\) moved the answer exactly halfway. The two-step route gives the same state: \(S'=(1,0)\), then \(S'-0.5\,(0.6-1)(0.6,0.8)=(1.12,0.16)\). Longer version: 43 §11.

docs.title: 8.1 Why it is not just “linear attention”
docs.text:
Linear attention keeps only the write, with no decay and no correction:

\[ S_t=S_{t-1}+v_tk_t^\top, \]

which never erases. (Setting \(\alpha_t=\beta_t=1\) in the boxed update does not give this; it gives the ungated delta rule, which still erases.) The delta rule subtracts the component of the state already aligned with \(k_t\), so a new value overwrites the old association instead of accumulating. Gating adds exponential forgetting. The combination improves in-context retrieval, which is exactly what pure linear attention lacks.

On paper

Same memory \(S_{t-1}=(2,0)\), key \(k_t=(0.6,0.8)\), value \(v_t=1\). The old memory answers \(S_{t-1}k_t=1.2\) for this key. Linear attention only adds:

\[ S_t=(2,0)+1\cdot(0.6,0.8)=(2.6,\;0.8) \]

It reads back \(2.6\cdot0.6+0.8\cdot0.8=2.2\): the old 1.2 and the new 1 pile up. The delta rule with \(\alpha_t=\beta_t=1\) writes only the error \(1-1.2=-0.2\):

\[ S_t=(2,0)-0.2(0.6,0.8)=(1.88,-0.16) \]

It reads back \(1.128-0.128=1.0\): the new value has replaced the old one.

docs.title: 8.2 Chunkwise parallel form
docs.text:
The per-token transition is

\[ S_t=\alpha_tS_{t-1}(I-\beta_tk_tk_t^\top)+\beta_tv_tk_t^\top. \]

On paper

The numbers from the §8 example again: \(S_{t-1}=(2,0)\) as a row, \(k_t=(0.6,0.8)\), \(v_t=1\), \(\alpha_t=\beta_t=0.5\). The matrix \(k_tk_t^\top\) has entries 0.36, 0.48, 0.48, 0.64:

\[ I-0.5\,k_tk_t^\top=\begin{pmatrix}0.82&-0.24\\-0.24&0.68\end{pmatrix} \] \[ \begin{aligned} &0.5\,(2,0)\begin{pmatrix}0.82&-0.24\\-0.24&0.68\end{pmatrix}\\ &=(0.82,\;-0.24) \end{aligned} \]

Adding \(\beta_tv_tk_t^\top=(0.3,0.4)\) gives \((1.12,0.16)\), the same state as the boxed form.

The matrix \((I-\beta_tk_tk_t^\top)\) is a rank-one update of the identity. It is a Householder reflection only when \(k_t\) is unit norm and \(\beta_t=2\); in GDN it is a damped rank-one update. A product of such updates over a chunk can be written as

\[ \prod_{t=1}^{C}(I-\beta_tk_tk_t^\top)=I-K^\top W K, \]

where \(K\) stacks the chunk’s keys and \(W\) is a triangular matrix computed from the \(\beta\)’s and the dot products between the chunk’s keys (the WY representation). This turns the sequential recurrence into matrix multiplications over a chunk, which is why GDN can train in parallel despite being recurrent at inference.

On paper

A chunk of two keys, \(k_1=(1,0)\) and \(k_2=(0.6,0.8)\), both with \(\beta=0.5\). Multiplying the two factors in the order the recurrence applies them:

\[ \begin{aligned} &\begin{pmatrix}0.5&0\\0&1\end{pmatrix}\begin{pmatrix}0.82&-0.24\\-0.24&0.68\end{pmatrix}\\ &=\begin{pmatrix}0.41&-0.12\\-0.24&0.68\end{pmatrix} \end{aligned} \]

Expanding instead gives \(I-\beta_1k_1k_1^\top-\beta_2k_2k_2^\top+\beta_1\beta_2(k_1\cdot k_2)\,k_1k_2^\top\): the identity minus a combination of the \(k_ik_j^\top\), whose coefficients 0.5, 0.5 and \(-0.25\cdot0.6=-0.15\) are the entries of \(W\). Numerically:

\[ \begin{aligned} &I-0.5\,k_1k_1^\top-0.5\,k_2k_2^\top+0.15\,k_1k_2^\top\\ &=\begin{pmatrix}0.32&-0.24\\-0.24&0.68\end{pmatrix}+\begin{pmatrix}0.09&0.12\\0&0\end{pmatrix} \end{aligned} \]

This is the same matrix. With orthogonal keys the cross coefficient would vanish and \(W\) would be diagonal.

The exact WY construction is implementation detail; the key point is that training is chunk-parallel while inference is \(O(1)\) per token.

docs.title: 9. Sliding-window cache
docs.text:
For a local layer with window \(W\), position \(t\) attends to \([\max(0,t-W+1),t]\). The cache only needs the last \(W\) keys/values:

\[ \text{local cache}=2G d_h W b \]

per layer, independent of \(T\). For Gemma 4 with \(W=1024\), \(G=8\), \(d_h=256\), bf16:

\[ 2\cdot8\cdot256\cdot1024\cdot2=8.4\text{ MB per layer}. \]

Forty local layers ≈ 335 MB, versus gigabytes for full attention at 32K. The global layers still grow with \(T\), but there are only eight of them.

docs.title: 10. Speculative decoding speedup
docs.text:
A draft model proposes \(\gamma\) tokens. The target verifies them in one forward pass and accepts the longest correct prefix. If each draft token is accepted independently with probability \(\alpha\), the expected number accepted is

\[ \mathbb{E}[\text{accepted}]=\sum_{i=1}^{\gamma}\alpha^i =\frac{\alpha(1-\alpha^\gamma)}{1-\alpha}. \]

If the draft costs \(c\) times a target step, the approximate speedup is

\[ \text{speedup}\approx \frac{1+\mathbb{E}[\text{accepted}]}{1+\gamma c}. \]

For \(\alpha=0.8\), \(\gamma=4\), \(c=0.1\):

\[ \mathbb{E}=0.8+0.64+0.512+0.4096=2.36, \qquad \text{speedup}\approx\frac{3.36}{1.4}=2.4. \]

The formula explains why speculative decoding helps most when the draft is cheap and the acceptance rate is high. A bad draft can be slower than no draft.

docs.title: 11. Quantization error
docs.text:
For symmetric uniform quantization with \(k\) bits and scale

\[ s=\frac{\max_i|w_i|}{2^{k-1}-1}, \]

the quantized value is

\[ q=\operatorname{clamp}\left(\operatorname{round}\left(\frac{w}{s}\right),-2^{k-1}+1,2^{k-1}-1\right), \qquad \hat w=sq. \]

The rounding error satisfies

\[ |w-\hat w|\le\frac{s}{2}. \]

On paper

Four weights from one row, \(w=(0.46,-1.4,0.13,0.95)\), stored in 4 bits: \(2^{k-1}-1=7\), so \(s=1.4/7=0.2\).

\(w\) \(w/s\) \(q\) \(\hat w\) \(w-\hat w\) 0.46 2.3 2 0.4 0.06 −1.4 −7 −7 −1.4 0 0.13 0.65 1 0.2 −0.07 0.95 4.75 5 1.0 −0.05

Every error is at most \(s/2=0.1\). The row is stored as four 4-bit integers plus one scale. Longer version: 43 §16.

For a block of \(B_c\) weights, using a per-block scale \(s_b\) reduces the maximum error because each block’s range is smaller:

\[ s_b=\frac{\max_{i\in b}|w_i|}{2^{k-1}-1}. \]

This is why Q4_0 (blockwise) is better than a single per-tensor scale.

On paper

Give the same row a second block of small weights, \(w=(0.05,-0.07,0.02,0.03)\). With the shared scale \(s=0.2\), every \(|w/s|\) is below 0.5, so \(q=(0,0,0,0)\) and the block is erased, with errors up to 0.07. Its own scale is

\[ s_b=\frac{0.07}{7}=0.01 \]

so \(w/s_b=(5,-7,2,3)\): exact here, and never off by more than \(s_b/2=0.005\), twenty times tighter than 0.1. The price is one extra scale per block; Q4_0 uses blocks of 32 weights.

docs.title: 11.1 QAT straight-through estimator
docs.text:
Quantization is not differentiable at the rounding step. QAT uses

\[ \frac{\partial\hat w}{\partial w}\approx 1 \]

in the backward pass (straight-through estimator), so the model learns weights that are robust to the quantization error. Gemma 4 uses QAT for its int2/int4 mobile and Q4_0 checkpoints.

On paper

Take \(w=0.46\) from the row above (\(s=0.2\), \(\hat w=0.4\)), an upstream gradient \(\partial\mathcal{L}/\partial\hat w=2\) and a learning rate of 0.1. The straight-through estimator passes the gradient through unchanged:

\[ w\leftarrow0.46-0.1\cdot2=0.26 \] \[ \hat w=0.2\cdot\operatorname{round}(1.3)=0.2 \]

The full-precision weight moved smoothly, and \(\hat w\) dropped one step once \(w\) crossed the rounding boundary at 0.3. The true derivative of round is 0 almost everywhere, so without the STE \(w\) would never move.

docs.title: 12. Scaling-law fit
docs.text:
A common form is

\[ L(N,D)=E+\frac{A}{N^\alpha}+\frac{B}{D^\beta}. \]
  • \(E\) is the irreducible loss.
  • \(A/N^\alpha\) is the finite-model term.
  • \(B/D^\beta\) is the finite-data term.

On paper

Use toy constants rounded from the Chinchilla fit (\(E\approx1.69\), \(A\approx406\), \(B\approx411\)): \(E=1.7\), \(A=B=400\), and \(\alpha=\beta=1/3\) so the roots are easy. For a 1B model on 64B tokens, \(N^{1/3}=1{,}000\) and \(D^{1/3}=4{,}000\):

\[ L=1.7+\frac{400}{1{,}000}+\frac{400}{4{,}000}=2.2 \]

An 8× larger model (\(N^{1/3}=2{,}000\)) gives \(1.7+0.2+0.1=2.0\); 8× more data instead (\(D^{1/3}=8{,}000\)) gives \(1.7+0.4+0.05=2.15\). Neither can get below \(E=1.7\).

To fit:

  1. train several small models with different \(N\) and \(D\);
  2. record final loss;
  3. fit \(E,A,B,\alpha,\beta\) by least squares in log space;
  4. extrapolate cautiously.

The fit is only valid in the explored range. It does not tell you that 36T tokens will beat 10T for a specific model; it tells you the trend under the same data distribution and recipe.

Chinchilla’s compute-optimal allocation is approximately

\[ N^{*} \propto C^{0.5},\qquad D^{*}\propto C^{0.5}, \]

with \(D\approx20N\). Production models often overtrain because inference cost dominates.

On paper

Combine \(D\approx20N\) with the \(6ND\) estimate from §13: \(C\approx6N\cdot20N=120N^2\). For a budget of \(C=1.2\times10^{22}\) FLOPs:

\[ N=\sqrt{C/120}=\sqrt{10^{20}}=10^{10} \]

That is 10B parameters trained on \(20N=200\)B tokens. Four times the compute doubles both (\(\sqrt4=2\)): 20B parameters on 400B tokens. Qwen3-14B (14.8B parameters) saw 36T tokens, about 2,400 per parameter or roughly 120 times the Chinchilla ratio. It is overtrained on purpose, because a smaller model is cheaper to serve.

docs.title: 13. Exact FLOPs
docs.text:
The \(6ND\) estimate counts matrix multiplications but not attention scores. A more complete forward+backward estimate per layer is

\[ C_{\text{layer}}\approx \underbrace{6\,(2dHd_h+2dGd_h)\,T}_{\text{projections}} +\underbrace{12\,H\,d_h\,T^2}_{\text{attention scores/values}} +\underbrace{18dd_{\text{ff}}T}_{\text{MLP}} \]

for a dense block (the exact constants depend on whether biases/norms are counted). With full-width K and V (\(Hd_h=Gd_h=d\)) the projection term is the familiar \(24d^2T\); with Qwen3-14B’s grouped-query attention it is \(14.4d^2T\). The attention term uses the total query width \(H d_h\), not \(d\); they are equal for Qwen3-14B but not for Gemma’s global layers. The attention term is why long-context training is more expensive than \(6ND\) suggests.

For a 14B model at 32K, attention is a significant fraction of compute; at 2K, it is small. Always measure tokens/sec rather than trusting a formula.

On paper

For Qwen3-14B, \(Hd_h=40\cdot128=5{,}120=d\), \(Gd_h=8\cdot128=1{,}024\) and \(d_{\text{ff}}=17{,}408\). Divide the attention term by the other two; \(T\) and one \(d\) cancel:

\[ \frac{12\,dT^2}{(12d^2+12dGd_h+18dd_{\text{ff}})T} \] \[ =\frac{12T}{61{,}440+12{,}288+313{,}344}=\frac{T}{32{,}256} \] \(T\) attention / rest attention share 2,048 0.063 6% 32,768 1.02 50%

At 2K the scores add a small correction to the projection and MLP cost; at 32K they are half the layer.

docs.title: 14. AdamW bias correction
docs.text:
Adam keeps

\[ m_t=\beta_1m_{t-1}+(1-\beta_1)g_t, \qquad v_t=\beta_2v_{t-1}+(1-\beta_2)g_t^2. \]

At \(t=0\), \(m_0=v_0=0\), so the estimates are biased toward zero. The corrections are

\[ \hat m_t=\frac{m_t}{1-\beta_1^t}, \qquad \hat v_t=\frac{v_t}{1-\beta_2^t}. \]

On paper

First step for one LoRA weight: \(g_1=-0.2\), \(\beta_1=0.9\), \(\beta_2=0.999\), \(m_0=v_0=0\).

\[ m_1=0.1\cdot(-0.2)=-0.02 \] \[ v_1=0.001\cdot0.04=0.00004 \]

Both are far below the gradient \(-0.2\) and its square \(0.04\). Dividing by \(1-0.9=0.1\) and \(1-0.999=0.001\) gives \(\hat m_1=-0.2\) and \(\hat v_1=0.04\): exactly the gradient and its square.

The update is

\[ \theta_t=\theta_{t-1}-\eta_t \left( \frac{\hat m_t}{\sqrt{\hat v_t}+\epsilon} +\lambda\theta_{t-1} \right). \]

The \(\sqrt{\hat v_t}\) normalizes each parameter by its gradient scale, which is why AdamW is robust to heterogeneous gradients. Weight decay is decoupled from the adaptive step, unlike classic Adam.

On paper

Continue with \(\theta_0=0.5\), \(\eta=0.01\), \(\lambda=0.1\) and \(\epsilon\) negligible:

\[ \frac{\hat m_1}{\sqrt{\hat v_1}}=\frac{-0.2}{0.2}=-1 \] \[ \theta_1=0.5-0.01\,(-1+0.1\cdot0.5)=0.5095 \]

The first step has size \(\eta\) whatever the gradient's scale. Without the corrections, \(m_1/\sqrt{v_1}=-0.02/0.00632=-3.16\): a step more than three times too large. Longer version: 43 §17.

docs.title: 15. Worked numerical example
docs.text:
Suppose \(V=4\), logits \(z=(2.0,1.0,0.0,-1.0)\), and the target is the first token, index \(0\).

\[ e^z=(7.389,2.718,1.000,0.368),\quad Z=11.475. \] \[ p=(0.644,0.237,0.087,0.032). \] \[ \mathcal{L}=-\log(0.644)=0.440. \] \[ \nabla_z\mathcal{L}=p-e_0=(-0.356,0.237,0.087,0.032). \]

The gradient sums to zero (because probabilities sum to 1 and the target is one-hot). If the prediction were perfect (\(p=e_0\)), the gradient would be zero.

This is the entire training signal for next-token prediction: push the target logit up, push all others down proportionally to their probability.
