Detect isError / error in the observation; check it was addressed next step. Return actionable error text (§4); add recovery examples; verify before continuing (§12).

A reusable detector for the most common failure — the stuck loop:

def is_stuck(calls, window=3):
    """Detect a loop: the same (tool, arguments) repeated `window` times running."""
    if len(calls) < window:
        return False
    tail = calls[-window:]
    return all(c == tail[0] for c in tail)

repeated = [("nmap_scan", '{"target":"10.10.10.5"}')] * 3
varied = [("get_order", '{"id":"A"}'),
          ("issue_refund", '{"id":"A"}'),
          ("get_order", '{"id":"A"}')]
print("repeated calls -> stuck:", is_stuck(repeated))
print("varied calls   -> stuck:", is_stuck(varied))

repeated calls -> stuck: True
varied calls   -> stuck: False

Wire a detector like this into the loop: when it fires, break the budget early, tell the model it is repeating itself, or escalate to a human. Most agent failures are observable in the trajectory before they produce a wrong answer — which is the argument for logging and grading the trajectory, not just the result (11 §5.2, §17).

docs.title: 19. Key takeaways
docs.text:
• An agent is model + tools + loop + stop condition. Use the least autonomy that works: single call < workflow < agent, and reach for an autonomous loop last.
  • The five workflow patterns — chaining, routing, parallelization, orchestrator–workers, evaluator–optimizer — solve most "agentic" tasks deterministically; build them before an autonomous loop.
  • ReAct interleaves thought, action, and observation so the model decides its next move from what it just saw.
  • Tool design is API design for a literal, guessing caller; the tool-calling system around it — registry, validation, dispatch, timeouts, idempotency, result caps, audit, sandbox — is where safety and reliability live.
  • The autonomous loop is about twenty lines: a registry, a dispatcher that turns exceptions into observations, a budget, and a stop condition — the core every framework (61) wraps.
  • Autonomy is a dial (suggest → act with approval → act and report → fully autonomous); long-running agents need explicit state, checkpointing, resumability, and idempotent steps.
  • MCP standardizes tools/resources/prompts over JSON-RPC so a tool server works in any host; the 2026-07-28 revision is stateless. The full protocol, SDK and security are in 58 — MCP.
  • Memory is tokens: summarize old turns to stay under budget, and retrieve long-term memory instead of stuffing it in (51).
  • Reliability compounds: \(S = p^n\), so 0.95-per-step gives ~0.60 over 10 steps. Shorten the chain and raise \(p\) with retries and verification.
  • Cost grows with \(\tfrac{n(n+1)}{2}\) because history is resent each step; cap steps, summarize, return small results, and cache the stable prefix.
  • Enforce hard budgets in your code, gate risky actions on a human, sandbox at least privilege, and evaluate the trajectory, not just the answer.

docs.title: 20. Exercises
docs.text:
Exercise 20.1

Each step of an agent succeeds independently with probability 0.9. What is the success rate of a 5-step task?

Answer

\(S = 0.9^5 = 0.59049\). Even at 90% per step, five steps barely clear a coin flip — the case for shorter chains.

Exercise 20.2

You add verification so each step now succeeds with probability 0.99. What is the 5-step success rate, and what does that say about the value of verification?

Answer

\(S = 0.99^5 \approx 0.9510\). Going from 0.90 to 0.99 per step lifts the 5-step task from ~0.59 to ~0.95. Raising per-step reliability pays off multiplicatively over a chain.

Exercise 20.3

An agent adds 800 tokens of transcript per step and re-sends the whole history each step. How many tokens does an 8-step task process, and how does that compare to 800×8?

Answer

\(T = 800\cdot\frac{8\cdot 9}{2} = 800\cdot 36 = 28800\). Against \(800\times 8 = 6400\), the resend inflates it \(4.5\times\).

Exercise 20.4

A shaky step succeeds with probability 0.7. You allow up to 3 independent attempts. What is the effective per-step success rate?

Answer

\(p' = 1 - (1-0.7)^3 = 1 - 0.3^3 = 1 - 0.027 = 0.973\). Two retries turn a 0.70 step into a 0.973 step.

Exercise 20.5

The context budget is 4096 tokens. The system prompt and tools take 500 tokens, and the agent has produced 8 observations of 500 tokens each. Is it over budget?

Answer

Total \(= 500 + 8\times 500 = 4500\), which exceeds 4096. The agent must summarize old turns (§10) before the next step; otherwise the request overflows the budget, and depending on the server it is rejected or silently truncated.

Exercise 20.6

A task would need an autonomous agent to run 12 observation-driven steps, but you realize you can enumerate the control flow as a router feeding three fixed chains. Which should you build, and why?

Answer

Build the workflow (router + chains, §2). If the control flow can be enumerated in advance, a fixed workflow is cheaper, deterministic, and testable, and it avoids the compounding reliability (§12) and quadratic cost (§13) of a 12-step autonomous loop. Reserve autonomy for paths you genuinely cannot enumerate.

Exercise 20.7

An orchestrator dispatches a task to 3 workers, each making one model call; the orchestrator itself makes one call to assemble. How many model calls is that, versus a single agent that answers in one call? When is the extra cost justified?

Answer

\(1 + 3 = 4\) calls versus 1 — four times the calls (and more, once each worker re-sends its own context). It is justified only when the three sub-tasks are genuinely independent and benefit from specialization, and an eval (§17) shows the split beats a single well-scoped agent. Otherwise it is cost and coordination risk for no gain.

Exercise 20.8

Each step of a 20-step agent task succeeds with probability 0.95. What is the end-to-end success rate, and what is the single most effective lever to improve it?

Answer

\(S = 0.95^{20} \approx 0.3585\) — about a third. The most effective lever is usually to shorten the chain: halving \(n\) to 10 lifts \(S\) to \(0.95^{10}\approx 0.599\). Raising \(p\) with retries and verification (§12) is the complementary lever.

Next: 62 — Integrating agents to ship this loop inside a product, and 63 — Agents in the real world for twelve applications built on it; 53 — Fine-tuning when prompting and tools are not enough; 54 — Evaluation to measure any of this; 61 — Agent frameworks for the libraries that wrap this loop.

docs.title: 53 — Fine-tuning and model adaptation
docs.text:
Last verified: 28 October 2026.

This chapter is about the fourth rung of the adaptation ladder: changing the model's weights instead of changing its prompt. You will learn when fine-tuning is the right tool and when it is a waste of two days, the math of LoRA and QLoRA (counted by hand so you can predict memory before you launch), how to prepare data and mask the loss, how to read the hyperparameters and the loss curve, how to detect overfitting and catastrophic forgetting, and how to evaluate the result against the base. There is a tiny LoRA that runs on your CPU in a few seconds, a DPO loss computed with numbers, and a cost model for a local run versus a rented GPU. Read 50 — Prompting and APIs and 51 — RAG first; they are the rungs below this one, and most problems are solved there. The runbook for this handbook's actual training is 08 — Fine-tuning with MLX and 17 — Fine-tuning update; the math behind the model is in 32 — Mathematics and 37 — Architecture anatomy.

docs.title: 1.1 Six rungs, cheapest first
docs.text:
You rarely need to fine-tune. There is a ladder of ways to make a model do what you want, and each rung costs more than the one below it. Climb only as far as the problem forces you.

Rung What you change Cost to try Changes the weights? 1. Prompting the instruction minutes no 2. Few-shot examples in the prompt minutes no 3. RAG retrieved context days no 4. Fine-tuning (PEFT/LoRA) a small adapter hours–days yes (adapter) 5. Continued pretraining all weights, on raw text weeks, a cluster yes (all) 6. Training from scratch all weights, from zero months, millions of dollars yes (all)
  • Prompting is editing the system/user message. 50 is the whole rung.
  • Few-shot is prompting with worked examples (input → output pairs) so the model copies the pattern. Still just a prompt.
  • RAG retrieves documents at request time and pastes them into the prompt. It is how you add facts and freshness. 51 is the rung.
  • Fine-tuning adjusts weights on your examples. With LoRA you adjust a small adapter, not the whole model. This chapter.
  • Continued pretraining keeps training the base model on a large corpus of raw text (e.g. all of your company's code) to shift its distribution, not just its behaviour on one task. It needs a GPU cluster and is out of scope for a 32 GB laptop.
  • Training from scratch is 35 — From zero. You almost never do this.

Tip

The ladder is a cost gradient, not a quality gradient. A good prompt beats a bad fine-tune every time. Fine-tuning does not replace a good prompt; it lets you shorten one and make a behaviour reliable.

docs.title: 1.2 A decision procedure
docs.text:
Ask these in order and stop at the first "yes that's the problem":

1. Is the output format/style wrong, or the instruction ignored?
      → Fix the prompt first (rung 1–2). Add 2–5 examples.

2. Does the model lack a FACT, or need fresh/private data?
      → RAG (rung 3). Fine-tuning does NOT reliably add facts.

3. Is the behaviour right but UNRELIABLE, or the prompt huge
   and slow, or do you need a smaller/cheaper model to match
   a big one on ONE narrow task?
      → Fine-tune (rung 4). You have a repeatable skill to bake in.

4. Does the model lack a broad CAPABILITY (a language, a domain
   it has never seen) across many tasks?
      → Continued pretraining (rung 5). Rare; needs a cluster.

5. Do you have a novel architecture or a cluster and a reason?
      → Train from scratch (rung 6). Almost never.

Before fine-tuning, you must be able to answer: what prompt am I trying to replace, and on what eval does the fine-tune have to beat it? If you cannot write that eval, you are not ready (see §13 and 54).

docs.title: 1.3 Three worked product cases
docs.text:
Case A — the support-ticket classifier. You must tag incoming tickets as billing, bug, feature, or other. A prompt with the four definitions and three examples gets 88% accuracy but the prompt is 600 tokens and you classify 200k tickets a day.

  • Rung 1–2 solves the accuracy. The problem is cost and latency: 600 tokens of prompt on every one of 200k calls.
  • Fine-tune a small model on 5k labelled tickets so the prompt becomes Classify: <ticket>. The baked-in task lets you drop to a 20-token prompt and a smaller model. Verdict: fine-tune, for cost and latency, not capability.

Case B — the "answer from our docs" bot. Users ask about your product; the model must answer from your current documentation and cite it.

  • The model does not know your docs, and they change weekly. Fine-tuning would memorise a snapshot and still hallucinate the parts it did not memorise.
  • Verdict: RAG, not fine-tune. Retrieve the relevant doc chunk and put it in the prompt. Fine-tune only if the format of the answers (citation style, refusal when unsupported) is unreliable — and even then, fine-tune the format on top of RAG, do not replace it.

Case C — the Kali tool-call agent (this handbook). The model must emit valid tool calls against your schema, stay in scope, and recover from tool errors.

  • The behaviour is narrow, repeatable, and has a hard-to-prompt syntax (the exact JSON tool-call format). Few-shot helps but is not reliable enough at temperature 0 across 240 golden tasks.
  • Verdict: fine-tune (SFT on trajectories; 08), then maybe preference tuning (§10) to fix the "what to do when the tool fails" cases that SFT cannot teach. This is the whole reason the handbook exists.

Software-engineering analogy

The ladder is the same instinct as the performance ladder: tune the query before you add a cache, add a cache before you shard the database, shard before you rewrite in a faster language. Each rung is cheaper to try and easier to undo than the one above it. Fine-tuning is a database migration: powerful, slow to run, and painful to roll back — so you reach for it only when the cheaper moves are exhausted.

docs.title: 2. What fine-tuning changes — and what it does not
2.1 Reliably changes
docs.text:
Fine-tuning (even a small LoRA on a few thousand examples) reliably changes behaviour the base model already has the parts for:

  • Output format. JSON shape, Markdown vs plain, always-cite, always-end-with-a-summary.
  • Style and tone. Terse, formal, your house voice; refusal language and scope.
  • Tool-call syntax. The exact function-call format your server parses (06).
  • Narrow skills. One classification task, one extraction schema, one translation direction — baked in so the prompt shrinks.
  • Latency and cost, indirectly. By making a smaller model reliable on your task, so you can retire a bigger one or a long prompt.

docs.title: 2.2 Does not reliably change
docs.text:
Fine-tuning on a modest dataset does not reliably:

  • Add facts. Teaching "our API key rotation policy is 90 days" by putting it in 50 training examples is unreliable: the model may learn it, may half-learn it (right policy, wrong number), or may forget it under a slightly different question. Facts that must be correct belong in RAG or the prompt, where they are looked up, not recalled. (A large continued-pretraining run can add knowledge; a LoRA on a few thousand rows cannot be trusted to.)
  • Add a broad new capability. You cannot LoRA a model into a language it never saw, or into solving a class of problems it cannot do at all. LoRA re-weights and sharpens existing ability; it does not create it (this is the 15 point: SFT teaches "what a good answer looks like", not new reasoning).
  • Fix a bad base. If the base model is wrong about something in every sample, fine-tuning on 1k examples teaches it to be wrong confidently.

Warning

"The model keeps getting the price wrong, I'll fine-tune the price in" is the single most common fine-tuning mistake. The model will sometimes emit the trained price and sometimes a plausible neighbour, with no warning which. Prices, policies, inventory, anything that must be exactly right and changes goes in the prompt via retrieval, not in the weights.

docs.title: 3.1 Full fine-tuning
docs.text:
Full fine-tuning updates every weight. For Qwen3-14B that is 14.77B parameters, and with AdamW you also store, per parameter, an fp32 master copy and two moment estimates. That is 12 bytes per parameter of optimizer state on top of the weights:

\[ M_{\text{opt}} = 12 \times 14.77\times10^{9}\ \text{bytes} \]

On paper

AdamW keeps, per parameter, 4 bytes of fp32 master weight plus 4+4 bytes of first and second moment:

\[ 12 \times 14.77\times10^{9} = 1.77\times10^{11} \]

That is 177 GB of optimizer state alone, on top of ~29.5 GB of bf16 weights and another ~29.5 GB of bf16 gradients: about 236 GB before activations. It does not fit a 32 GB laptop or a single 80 GB datacenter GPU. This is why full fine-tuning of a 14B model needs a multi-GPU node.

Full fine-tuning is the most flexible and the most dangerous: with that much capacity on a small dataset you overfit and forget fast (see §8).

docs.title: 3.2 Parameter-efficient fine-tuning (PEFT)
docs.text:
PEFT freezes the base weights and trains a small number of new parameters. The dominant method is LoRA (and its 4-bit cousin QLoRA). Others you will meet: prefix/prompt tuning (train a few virtual tokens), adapters (small bottleneck MLPs between layers), and DoRA (LoRA split into magnitude and direction; 08 §9). LoRA is the default because it adds nothing at inference once merged and gives most of full fine-tuning's quality on post-training tasks (17 §2).

Full LoRA QLoRA Base weights trained, fp32/bf16 frozen, bf16 frozen, 4-bit Trained params (14B) 14.77B ~64M (r=16, all layers) ~64M Optimizer state ~177 GB tiny (adapter only) tiny Fits 32 GB? no no (29.5 GB bf16 base) yes Quality ceiling highest ~full, post-training ~LoRA

docs.title: 4.1 The idea
docs.text:
A weight matrix \(W\in\mathbb{R}^{d_{\text{out}}\times d_{\text{in}}}\) is frozen. LoRA adds a trainable update that is forced to be low rank: two thin matrices \(B\in\mathbb{R}^{d_{\text{out}}\times r}\) and \(A\in\mathbb{R}^{r\times d_{\text{in}}}\), with \(r\ll d\). The layer computes

\[ y = Wx + \tfrac{\alpha}{r}\,B A\,x, \]

where \(\alpha\) is a scaling constant. \(A\) is initialised random and \(B\) is initialised to zero, so at step 0 the update is exactly \(0\) and the model behaves like the base. Only \(A\) and \(B\) are trained; \(W\) never moves.

On paper

One token \(x=(1,0,1)\) through a frozen \(2\times3\) layer, LoRA rank \(r=1\), \(\alpha=2\), \(A=(1,0,1)\), \(B=(1,2)^\top\). First the base, with \(W\) the all-ones matrix:

\[ Wx = (1{+}0{+}1,\;1{+}0{+}1) = (2,2) \]

Now the update. \(Ax = 1\cdot1+0\cdot0+1\cdot1 = 2\):

\[ \tfrac{\alpha}{r}BA x = \tfrac{2}{1}(1,2)\cdot 2 = (4,8) \] \[ y = (2,2) + (4,8) = (6,10) \]

At step 0, \(B=0\), so the second term is \((0,0)\) and \(y=Wx=(2,2)\): the adapter starts invisible and only the trained \(A,B\) move it.

MLX writes the same thing as y = Wx + scale · BA x with scale = α / r. This is the trap from 17 §3: MLX's default scale: 20 is not PEFT's α, so you must set scale = 32/r to match a standard α=32 recipe.

docs.title: 4.2 Parameter count for one projection
docs.text:
Take one square projection of Qwen3-14B, say o_proj, which is \(5120\times5120\) (37 §1.1). Full fine-tuning trains every entry. LoRA at \(r=16\) trains only \(A\) (\(16\times5120\)) and \(B\) (\(5120\times16\)).

\[ \text{full} = 5120\times5120 = 26{,}214{,}400 \]

On paper

LoRA adds \(r(d_{\text{in}}+d_{\text{out}})\) parameters:

\[ 16\times(5120+5120) = 163{,}840 \] \[ \frac{163{,}840}{26{,}214{,}400} = 0.00625 \]

The adapter is 0.625% of the full projection — about 1 parameter trained for every 160. That ratio is why the optimizer state is tiny and why LoRA fits where full fine-tuning does not.

docs.title: 4.3 Parameter count for the whole Qwen3-14B adapter
docs.text:
An all-layer adapter puts LoRA on all seven projections in all 40 blocks. The shapes (from 37 §1.1: \(d=5120\), \(H d_h=5120\), \(G d_h=1024\), \(d_{\text{ff}}=17408\)) are:

Projection \(d_{\text{in}}\) \(d_{\text{out}}\) LoRA params at \(r=16\) q_proj 5120 5120 163,840 k_proj 5120 1024 98,304 v_proj 5120 1024 98,304 o_proj 5120 5120 163,840 gate_proj 5120 17408 360,448 up_proj 5120 17408 360,448 down_proj 17408 5120 360,448 per block 1,605,632

On paper

Sum one block, \(r(d_{\text{in}}+d_{\text{out}})\) each:

\[ 16(10240+6144+6144+10240) = 524{,}288 \] \[ 16(22528+22528+22528) = 1{,}081{,}344 \] \[ 524{,}288 + 1{,}081{,}344 = 1{,}605{,}632 \]

Times 40 blocks:

\[ 40\times1{,}605{,}632 = 64{,}225{,}280 \]

About 64M trainable parameters, 0.43% of 14.77B. This is the exact count behind the rounder "on the order of 60M, not 13M" in 17 §4 and "≈ 63M" in 02 §3.2. If scripts/check_lora.py shows only q_proj/v_proj modules (at \(r=16\) that is \(40\times262{,}144\approx10.5\)M parameters) or any total far below 64M, the adapter scope is narrower than you asked for — stop and fix it.

docs.title: 4.4 Why low rank works
docs.text: The claim behind LoRA is that the change a fine-tune needs to make has low intrinsic rank, even though \(W\) itself is full rank. You are not re-learning the projection; you are nudging it toward one narrow behaviour, and that nudge lives in a small subspace. Empirically (17 §2), rank 16–32 matches full fine-tuning on post-training tasks. The MLP projections hold most of the capacity (37 §1.3: the MLP is ~81% of a Qwen3-14B block's parameters), which is why all-layer LoRA that includes gate/up/down beats attention-only.

docs.title: 4.5 Rank and alpha
docs.text:
• Rank \(r\) is the capacity of the adapter. Low (8) for format/style; 16 is the handbook default; 32 for a capacity experiment; 64+ only with a large, clean dataset. More rank = more parameters = more overfitting risk, not automatically better.
  • Alpha \(\alpha\) scales the update. Because the update is \(\tfrac{\alpha}{r}BA\), the effective learning rate scales with \(\alpha/r\). Keep \(\alpha/r\) fixed (the handbook uses \(\alpha=32\), so scale = 32/r) and the learning rate is comparable across ranks. This is the single most important thing to get right in MLX (17 §3).

docs.title: 4.6 Which modules
docs.text: Adapt all seven projections (q,k,v,o,gate,up,down) in every block — MLX's num_layers: -1. Attention-only leaves quality on the table; MLP-only is nearly as good as both (17 §2.1). Fall back to the last 24 then 16 blocks only if memory forces it (02 §6).

docs.title: 5. QLoRA: 4-bit base, bf16 adapter
docs.text: QLoRA is LoRA with the frozen base quantized to 4-bit. The base weights read at ~4.5 bits/parameter; the adapter \(A,B\) and its optimizer state stay in bf16/fp32. This cuts the largest term — the weights — by ~3.5× (16 bits down to 4.5, 29.5 GB down to 8.3 GB) and is what lets a 14B model train on 32 GB.

docs.title: 5.1 Memory budget for 14B on 32 GB
docs.text:
The terms (from 02 §3.1–3.2):

Term Size Why 4-bit base weights ~8.3 GB 14.77B at ~4.5 bits LoRA params (r=16, all layers) ~0.25 GB 64M in fp32 Optimizer (AdamW, adapter only) ~0.7 GB 2–3× adapter Logits, B=1, L=2048, fp32 ~1.24 GB \(2048\times151936\times4\) Activations (grad checkpoint) ~4–8 GB scales with \(L\) and adapted layers Runtime (Metal, Python, tokenizer) ~2–3 GB overhead

On paper

The logits dominate the "fixed" part. Vocabulary \(V=151936\), one 2048-token sequence, fp32:

\[ 2048\times151936\times4 = 1.24\times10^{9} \]

That is 1.24 GB before a single activation, and it grows linearly with sequence length: 2.49 GB at 4096 tokens. The column sums to about 16.5–21.5 GB. Add the attention and dequantization temporaries of 02 §3.1 (10–30% of activations) and fragmentation, and 17 §5 estimates a peak of roughly 19–24 GB for the all-layer run — under the ~24 GB ceiling only with the Kali VM and Chrome shut down.

The practical consequences (all in 02 §6): cut max_seq_length before cutting num_layers; use --grad-checkpoint; keep the effective batch at 8 with batch_size: 1 and grad_accumulation_steps: 8.

docs.title: 6. Data preparation and loss masking
docs.text: This section covers the steps that are specific to fine-tuning: the chat JSONL shape, the train/valid/test split, loss masking, packing and sequence length. The general data work that comes first — sourcing, parsing, cleaning, deduplication, PII removal, labeling and data cards — is in 60 — Data preparation; do that before you get here, because a fine-tune is only as good as the cleaned, deduped data you feed it.

docs.title: 6.1 Chat-format JSONL
docs.text:
Training data is one JSON object per line, each a full conversation in the chat format the server will use (06):

{"messages": [
  {"role": "system", "content": "You scan only authorized scope."},
  {"role": "user", "content": "Enumerate services on 10.10.10.5."},
  {"role": "assistant", "content": "", "tool_calls": [
    {"type": "function", "function": {"name": "nmap_scan",
     "arguments": "{\"target\": \"10.10.10.5\"}"}}]}
]}

The trainer renders each row through the model's chat template (the same one the server uses) and tokenizes the result. If the training template and the serving template differ, a good adapter produces garbage (10 §4, 37 §7).

docs.title: 6.2 Train / valid / test split
docs.text: Split before you do anything else, and split by source task, not by row, so near-duplicate variations of one task do not straddle the boundary (that leaks the answer into validation). The handbook uses train to fit, valid to watch for overfitting during the run, and a frozen test/golden set to decide release (09 §3, 54). A rule of thumb: 80/10/10, but the valid and test sets matter more for their coverage than their size — 200 well-chosen tasks beat 2000 random ones.

docs.title: 6.3 Loss masking: train only on assistant tokens
docs.text:
The model sees the whole conversation, but you only want it to learn to produce the assistant's turn, not to parrot the prompt. So you mask the loss: prompt and tool-result tokens contribute nothing; only the final assistant completion does. This is --mask-prompt in MLX and exactly the completion loss \(\mathcal{L}_{\text{SFT}}\) of 32 §3.1.

import numpy as np

# A tiny rendered example: 3 prompt tokens, then a 2-token answer.
# mask=0 on prompt, mask=1 on the assistant completion.
tokens = ["<user>", "scan", "10.10.10.5", "<assistant>", "nmap", "10.10.10.5"]
mask   = [0,        0,      0,            0,             1,      1]

# Per-token negative log-likelihood the model assigned (toy numbers).
nll = np.array([2.0, 1.5, 3.0, 0.1, 0.22, 0.51])  # natural log units
m = np.array(mask, dtype=float)

masked_loss = float((nll * m).sum() / m.sum())
unmasked_loss = float(nll.mean())
print(f"tokens in completion: {int(m.sum())}")
print(f"masked loss   (assistant only): {masked_loss:.4f}")
print(f"unmasked loss (all tokens):     {unmasked_loss:.4f}")

tokens in completion: 2
masked loss   (assistant only): 0.3650
unmasked loss (all tokens):     1.2217

The masked loss averages only the two assistant tokens, \((0.22+0.51)/2=0.365\). The unmasked number is polluted by how badly the model "predicts" the user's own words, which you do not care about and cannot change. A nan masked loss means a row has zero completion tokens (the prompt filled the whole max_seq_length); that is the classic 08 §5 crash.

Software-engineering analogy

Loss masking is assert on the outputs only. You do not assert that the test fixture is correct — it is given. You assert on what the function returns. The prompt is the fixture; the assistant turn is the return value.

docs.title: 6.4 Packing and sequence length
docs.text:
• Packing concatenates several short examples into one max_seq_length sequence (with attention masks that stop one example attending to the next) so you do not waste compute padding. It raises tokens/sec on short data.
  • Sequence length vs memory is the main lever: activations and the logit tensor grow linearly with \(L\) (02 §3.4). Measure your 99th-percentile token length with scripts/token_stats.py and set max_seq_length just above it; do not pay for 4096 when 2048 covers 99% of rows.

docs.title: 7.1 Rules of thumb
docs.text: Knob Start Notes Learning rate 1e-4 (with scale=32/r) 10× the full-FT LR (17 §2.2); halve on nan/spikes. Epochs 1–2 >1M tokens: 1 epoch, add a 2nd only if val still falls. Effective batch 8 batch_size 1 × grad_accum 8; keep 8–32, avoid >32 (17 §2.3). Warmup ~50 steps ramp LR from 0 so the first steps do not blow up. Rank 16 8 for format, 32 for capacity. Dropout 0.05 0.1 for <500k tokens.

docs.title: 7.2 Reading the loss curve
docs.text:
Symptom Likely cause Action Train 1.5 → 0.6 over 200 steps, val tracks it healthy continue Train keeps falling, val rises for 2+ evals overfitting stop, keep the earlier checkpoint, more data/dropout Train stuck >1.0 after 200 steps LR too low, data too diverse, or bad mask raise LR, check masking Loss spikes then nan LR too high, or empty completion halve LR, check token_stats Train <0.2 very fast memorisation/duplication/leak dedup, check contamination

Warning

Loss is not the goal; the eval is. A model can reach 0.3 loss by memorising tool names and still fail held-out tasks. Always evaluate mid-run against a held-out set, not just watch the curve (08 §8).

docs.title: 8.1 Two different failures
docs.text:
• Overfitting is learning the training set, including its noise, so held-out performance drops. You detect it with a validation set: when val loss turns up while train loss falls, you have passed the useful point.
  • Catastrophic forgetting is subtler: the model gets better at your task and worse at everything else. Fine-tune hard on tool calls and the model may lose some general chat ability, reasoning, or even safety behaviour. The training and validation loss (both on your distribution) look great while a capability you did not measure quietly degrades.

docs.title: 8.2 Detecting forgetting: a general-skills eval
docs.text:
The only way to see forgetting is to measure a skill you are not training. Keep a small general-skills eval — a handful of tasks from the base model's competence (simple reasoning, a non-domain Q&A, an instruction-following check) — and run it on the base and on every adapter. If the adapter wins on your golden set but drops more than a point or two on the general eval, you are trading away breadth.

# Toy: base vs fine-tune on the target task AND on a held-out general set.
base = {"target": 0.55, "general": 0.90}
tune = {"target": 0.78, "general": 0.83}

for k in ("target", "general"):
    delta = tune[k] - base[k]
    print(f"{k:8s}: base {base[k]:.2f} -> tune {tune[k]:.2f}  ({delta:+.2f})")

target_gain = tune["target"] - base["target"]
general_drop = base["general"] - tune["general"]
print(f"traded {general_drop:.2f} general for {target_gain:.2f} target")

target  : base 0.55 -> tune 0.78  (+0.23)
general : base 0.90 -> tune 0.83  (-0.07)
traded 0.07 general for 0.23 target

Whether a 7-point general drop is acceptable for a 23-point target gain is a product decision — but you can only make it because you measured the general skill. Mitigations: fewer epochs, lower rank/LR, mix a little general data into the training set, or keep adapters separate and swap them in only for the task.

docs.title: 9. A tiny LoRA that runs on your CPU
docs.text:
This is LoRA in ~35 lines of PyTorch on the CPU: a frozen Linear, a trainable low-rank adapter, trained on a toy task. It prints trainable vs total parameters and a falling loss. Run it with the handbook venv; it finishes in a few seconds, most of them spent importing torch.

import torch, torch.nn as nn

torch.manual_seed(0)
D_IN, D_OUT, R, ALPHA = 16, 16, 4, 8.0

class LoRALinear(nn.Module):
    def __init__(self, d_in, d_out, r, alpha):
        super().__init__()
        self.base = nn.Linear(d_in, d_out, bias=False)
        self.base.weight.requires_grad_(False)       # freeze the base
        self.A = nn.Parameter(torch.randn(r, d_in) * 0.01)
        self.B = nn.Parameter(torch.zeros(d_out, r))  # B=0 => adapter invisible at step 0
        self.scale = alpha / r

    def forward(self, x):
        return self.base(x) + self.scale * (x @ self.A.t()) @ self.B.t()

model = LoRALinear(D_IN, D_OUT, R, ALPHA)

# The target is the frozen base plus a rank-4 update: exactly the kind of
# change a rank-4 adapter can represent, so LoRA can fit it.
tA, tB = torch.randn(R, D_IN), torch.randn(D_OUT, R)
delta = tB @ tA                                       # a rank-4 matrix
X = torch.randn(256, D_IN)
Y = model.base(X) + X @ delta.t()
opt = torch.optim.Adam([model.A, model.B], lr=0.05)   # ONLY A and B

trainable = sum(p.numel() for p in model.parameters() if p.requires_grad)
total = sum(p.numel() for p in model.parameters())
print(f"trainable={trainable}  total={total}  ({100*trainable/total:.1f}%)")

for step in range(201):
    opt.zero_grad()
    loss = ((model(X) - Y) ** 2).mean()
    loss.backward()
    opt.step()
    if step % 50 == 0:
        print(f"step {step:3d}  loss {loss.item():.4f}")

trainable=128  total=384  (33.3%)
step   0  loss 109.2847
step  50  loss 0.8949
step 100  loss 0.0061
step 150  loss 0.0000
step 200  loss 0.0000

The 128 trainable parameters are \(A\) (\(4\times16=64\)) plus \(B\) (\(16\times4=64\)); the 256 frozen base weights never move. The loss starts high (the untrained adapter is \(0\), so the model is just the base and misses the whole update) and falls to zero as \(A,B\) learn it — it can, because the update was built to be rank 4, exactly LoRA's assumption from §4.4. On a real model the base is a 4-bit Qwen3-14B and the "task" is your trajectories, but the mechanism — train a thin \(BA\), leave \(W\) alone — is exactly this.

docs.title: 10.1 When to use it
docs.text:
SFT teaches the model to imitate good trajectories. It cannot tell a trajectory that looks right from one that works, and it cannot learn "when the tool fails, do X instead of Y" from demonstrations alone (15 §2). Preference tuning fixes that: you give pairs (prompt, chosen, rejected) and push the model to prefer chosen. Use it after SFT, to fix verbosity, refusal calibration, format slips, and the "pick the action that succeeds" cases — not to teach a new capability.

Direct Preference Optimization (DPO) does this without a separate reward model. It keeps a frozen reference model (your SFT checkpoint) and trains the policy to raise the chosen response's likelihood and lower the rejected one's, relative to that reference.

docs.title: 10.2 The loss
docs.text:
\[ \mathcal{L}_{\text{DPO}} = -\log\sigma\!\big(\beta(\Delta_w - \Delta_l)\big), \]

where \(\Delta_w=\log\pi_\theta(y_w\mid x)-\log\pi_{\text{ref}}(y_w\mid x)\) is the chosen response's log-prob shift from the reference, \(\Delta_l\) is the same for the rejected response, \(\beta\) controls how far the policy may stray from the reference, and \(\sigma\) is the logistic function.

On paper

One pair, \(\beta=0.1\). The policy raised the chosen log-prob by 1.0 over the reference and lowered the rejected by 1.0, so \(\Delta_w=1.0\), \(\Delta_l=-1.0\):

\[ \beta(\Delta_w-\Delta_l) = 0.1(1.0-(-1.0)) = 0.2 \] \[ \sigma(0.2) = \frac{1}{1+e^{-0.2}} \approx 0.550 \] \[ \mathcal{L}_{\text{DPO}} = -\ln 0.550 \approx 0.598 \]

The margin is positive, so the loss (0.598) is already below \(-\ln 0.5=0.693\), the value at zero margin. A gradient step widens the margin further, driving the loss toward 0; if the model instead preferred the rejected answer the margin would be negative and the loss would climb above 0.693.

MLX-LM ships no DPO trainer as of October 2026; use TRL/PEFT on a rented GPU, or a small preference loss on top of MLX (15 §4). DPO's weakness: pair quality dominates, and it can reduce output diversity if over-trained.

docs.title: 11. Distillation
docs.text:
Distillation trains a small student to copy a larger teacher. It is a form of fine-tuning where the targets come from another model. Two kinds (full treatment in 39–42):

  • Sequence (behaviour) distillation. The teacher generates answers; the student is trained on them with ordinary SFT (39 §2.3). Cheap, robust, works through an API, and is the default on a 32 GB Mac. It transfers style, format and the teacher's solution path — not its uncertainty.
  • Logit distillation. The student matches the teacher's full next-token distribution with a KL term (39 §2.1). Richer signal (the "dark knowledge" in the tail), but you need both models' logits at once and matching tokenizers, so it is heavier.

Use distillation when you have access to a stronger model and want to compress its behaviour on your tasks into something you can serve. The evaluation is the same golden-set comparison as any fine-tune (42).

docs.title: 12. Quantizing the result and shipping the adapter
12.1 Quantization error on a small row
docs.text:
You will quantize the final model to serve it in 4-bit (smaller, faster decode; 55). Quantization maps each weight to a small integer grid with a per-group scale (32 §15). The error is bounded by half a step.

\[ s = \frac{\max_i |w_i|}{2^{k-1}-1}, \qquad \hat w_i = s\cdot\operatorname{round}(w_i/s). \]

On paper

One group of 4 weights \(w=(1.0,-0.6,0.3,-0.2)\), symmetric int4, grid \(-7\ldots7\):

\[ s = \frac{1.0}{7} \approx 0.142857 \] \[ \operatorname{round}(w/s) = (7,\,-4,\,2,\,-1) \] \[ \hat w = (1.0,\,-0.571,\,0.286,\,-0.143) \]

The errors are \((0,\,0.029,\,0.014,\,0.057)\), all within \(s/2\approx0.071\). At int8 the grid is \(-127\ldots127\), so \(s\approx0.0079\) and the worst error is ~18× smaller: that is the int4-vs-int8 quality/size trade.

Group-wise scales (one \(s\) per block of 32–128 weights) keep the error small for each block instead of letting one large weight set a coarse scale for the whole row.

docs.title: 12.2 Merge vs serve adapters separately
docs.text:
Two ways to ship a LoRA:

  • Merge (fuse) the adapter into the base: compute \(W' = W + \tfrac{\alpha}{r}BA\) once and save a standalone model (10 §1, mlx_lm.fuse). Zero inference overhead, one artifact to serve, but you have baked in one adapter and lost the ability to swap.
  • Serve the base + adapter separately: keep the base in memory and apply the small adapter at run time, for a small per-token cost. mlx_lm.server --adapter-path serves one adapter this way; a request that names a different adapter makes it reload the whole model. Multi-adapter servers such as vLLM (--enable-lora) keep many adapters next to one base and pick one per request, so one server can host many fine-tunes (one per customer or task) cheaply. Choose this when you have many adapters and one base; merge when you ship one model.

docs.title: 13. Evaluating a fine-tune
docs.text:
A fine-tune is a change; the only question that matters is whether it is an improvement. Evaluate the base and the adapter on the same frozen golden set, under the same decoding settings, with the same grader (09 §8, 42 §3, 54). Report the metric that matters for the product (tool-call validity, task success), not the loss. An adapter that does not beat the base on the golden set is not a release candidate, no matter how pretty its loss curve.

On paper

Golden set of 240 tasks. Base solves 132, adapter solves 158:

\[ p_{\text{base}} = 132/240 = 0.550, \quad p_{\text{tune}} = 158/240 = 0.658 \] \[ \Delta = 0.658 - 0.550 = 0.108 \]

An 11-point gain on 240 tasks is outside the noise. Treating the two runs as independent, the 95% margin on the difference is \(1.96\sqrt{(0.55\cdot0.45+0.658\cdot0.342)/240}\approx0.087\), and a paired test on the same tasks is usually tighter. A 1–2 point gap would be noise; use the Wilson/paired tests in 42 §2.4 and 54 to be sure. Only now is the adapter a candidate.

Also run the general-skills eval of §8 so a gain on the target task is not hiding a regression everywhere else.

docs.title: 14. Cost and time: local vs rented GPU
14.1 A local LoRA run
docs.text:
Use the token arithmetic from 08 §3.6. A 2M-token dataset, average 1,500 tokens/sample, effective batch 8, two epochs:

\[ \text{iters} = 2\times\frac{2{,}000{,}000}{8\times1500} \approx 334, \]

On paper

Each iteration sees \(8\times1500\) tokens, so the run processes:

\[ 334\times8\times1500 \approx 4.0\times10^{6}\ \text{tokens} \]

At the handbook's 22 tok/s for a 14B all-layer run (02 §4):

\[ \frac{4.0\times10^{6}}{22} \approx 1.82\times10^{5}\ \text{s} \] \[ 1.82\times10^{5}/3600 \approx 50\ \text{hours} \]

About 50 hours of pure compute, ~58 hours of wall time with the ~15% overhead for data loading, validation, checkpoints and thermal throttling. In dollars the laptop run is "free", but the machine is occupied for two and a half days.

docs.title: 14.2 Renting a GPU
docs.text:
Assume a rented GPU at $2.00 per hour (state your real price; prices move). Estimate its speed with the same FLOPs rule that gave the laptop's 22 tok/s (02 §4, 32 §14.4): tokens per second are the effective FLOP/s divided by \(6N\). An A100 has 312 TFLOP/s of dense BF16 peak and an H100 SXM 989. Assume a modest 100 TFLOP/s effective (about 32% of an A100's peak, 10% of an H100's), because QLoRA dequantization and small batches waste compute:

\[ r = \frac{\text{effective FLOP/s}}{6N} \]

On paper

\(N=14.77\times10^{9}\), so \(6N\approx8.86\times10^{10}\) FLOPs per token:

\[ \begin{aligned} r &= 10^{14}/(8.86\times10^{10})\\ &\approx 1130\ \text{tok/s}\\ t &= 4.0\times10^{6}/1130\\ &\approx 3540\ \text{s}\approx 1\ \text{h}\\ \text{cost} &\approx 1\ \text{h}\times\$2.00 = \$2 \end{aligned} \]

About 50 times the laptop's 22 tok/s: the run that occupies the Mac for two and a half days takes about an hour, for about $2 plus setup (downloading ~30 GB of weights), storage and egress.

The trade is clear: for a one-off adapter the laptop is fine if you can wait; for a sweep of 5 configs, or anything over ~24 hours, renting is the rational choice (02 §6, item 9). It also frees your laptop and avoids the thermal penalty.

docs.title: 15. A checklist before you fine-tune
docs.text:
• You tried prompting, few-shot and RAG first, and named why they are not enough.
  • The thing you want is a behaviour/format/skill, not a fact (facts go in RAG).
  • You have a frozen eval that the fine-tune must beat, and a base-model score on it.
  • You have a general-skills eval to catch forgetting.
  • Data is in the correct chat format, deduped, split by task, loss-masked.
  • The training template equals the serving template.
  • You checked the adapter scope (check_lora.py): ~64M params, all 7 projections.
  • scale = 32/r and the learning rate match (not MLX's scale: 20 trap).
  • Memory budget fits under ~24 GB with grad checkpointing.
  • You know how you will serve it: merged, or base + adapter.

docs.title: 16. Key takeaways
docs.text:
• The adaptation ladder is a cost gradient: prompting → few-shot → RAG → fine-tune → continued pretraining → from scratch. Climb only as far as the problem forces you.
  • Fine-tuning reliably changes format, style, tool-call syntax and narrow skills, and buys latency by making a smaller model reliable. It does not reliably add facts — those go in RAG.
  • LoRA trains a thin \(W+\tfrac{\alpha}{r}BA\); at \(r=16\) an all-layer Qwen3-14B adapter is ~64M parameters, 0.43% of the model. QLoRA's 4-bit base is what fits it on 32 GB.
  • Mask the loss to the assistant tokens; keep scale = 32/r; watch validation loss and a general-skills eval, not just train loss.
  • Evaluate the adapter against the base on the same frozen golden set. A pretty loss curve is not a release gate.

docs.title: 17. Exercises
docs.text:
Exercise 17.1

Your model returns valid JSON only 70% of the time at temperature 0, and the system prompt is already 500 tokens of format rules. Which rung of the ladder, and why?

Answer

Fine-tune (rung 4). The behaviour (JSON format) is one the model has the parts for but produces unreliably, and the prompt is already large. This is the "right but unreliable, prompt huge" case: SFT on a few thousand correctly-formatted examples bakes the format in so you can shorten the prompt. RAG would not help (no facts missing); more prompting has diminishing returns at 500 tokens.

Exercise 17.2

A 4096×1024 projection (k_proj-shaped) gets a LoRA adapter at rank 8. How many trainable parameters, and what fraction of the full projection?

Answer

LoRA adds \(r(d_{\text{in}}+d_{\text{out}}) = 8\times(4096+1024) = 8\times5120 = 40{,}960\). The full projection is \(4096\times1024 = 4{,}194{,}304\). The fraction is \(40{,}960/4{,}194{,}304 \approx 0.00977\), about 0.98%.

Exercise 17.3

You train on 100 examples that each contain the sentence "our refund window is 30 days". In production the model sometimes says 30 days, sometimes 14. Why, and what should you have done?

Answer

Fine-tuning does not reliably store facts. The model learned a tendency toward "30 days", but a slightly different question surfaces a plausible neighbour (14) with no warning. Facts that must be exact and can change belong in the prompt via retrieval (RAG), where they are looked up, not recalled. The fine-tune should have targeted the answer format ("state the window, then cite the policy doc"), with the number supplied by RAG.

Exercise 17.4

With β=0.1, a DPO pair has Δ_w = 0.5 and Δ_l = 0.5 (the policy shifted chosen and rejected by the same amount). Compute the loss and say what it means.

Answer

\(\beta(\Delta_w-\Delta_l)=0.1(0.5-0.5)=0\), so \(\sigma(0)=0.5\) and \(\mathcal{L}=-\ln 0.5\approx0.693\). Zero margin means the policy has learned nothing about this pair relative to the reference — it moved chosen and rejected equally. 0.693 is the DPO loss at no preference; training must push \(\Delta_w\) above \(\Delta_l\).

Exercise 17.5

Quantize the weight row \(w=(0.8, -0.4, 0.4, -0.8)\) to symmetric int4 (grid \(-7\ldots7\)). Give the scale, the integer codes, the dequantized values and the max error.

Answer

\(s=\max|w|/7=0.8/7\approx0.11429\). Then \(w/s=(7,-3.5,3.5,-7)\); the halves round to even, so the codes are \((7,-4,4,-7)\). Dequantized \(\hat w=(0.8,-0.457,0.457,-0.8)\), errors \((0,0.057,0.057,0)\), max \(0.057\le s/2\approx0.057\). The extreme values \(\pm0.8\) are exact (they set the scale); the mid values sit exactly half a step from the grid, the worst case.

Exercise 17.6

Your 14B LoRA run processes 6M tokens. At 25 tok/s, how long is the pure compute, and roughly the wall time?

Answer

\(6\times10^{6}/25 = 240{,}000\) s \(= 66.7\) hours of compute. With ~15% overhead, wall time is about \(66.7\times1.15\approx77\) hours, a little over three days. At the ~1,130 tok/s assumed for a rented GPU in §14.2, the same tokens take \(6\times10^{6}/1130\approx5{,}310\) s, about 1.5 hours, or about $3 at $2/hour — the point at which renting clearly wins.

Exercise 17.7

After fine-tuning, your golden-set success rises from 0.55 to 0.72 but a held-out general reasoning eval drops from 0.88 to 0.70. What happened and name two fixes.

Answer

Catastrophic forgetting: the model gained 17 points on the target task but lost 18 on general reasoning — a bad trade you could only see because you kept a general-skills eval. Fixes: fewer epochs or lower LR/rank (less aggressive adaptation); mix some general-purpose data into the training set; or keep the adapter separate and swap it in only for the target task.

Exercise 17.8

You have one base model and 20 customers who each want a slightly different fine-tune. Merge the adapters or serve them separately? Why?

Answer

Serve them separately (base + adapter), on a server that picks the adapter per request (§12.2). Merging would mean 20 full standalone models in memory/disk; serving one shared base with 20 small adapters costs ~64M extra parameters each instead of 14.77B, and lets one server host all customers. Merge only when you ship a single model and want zero adapter overhead at inference.

Next: 54 — Evaluation turns "is the fine-tune better?" into a real test suite with statistics.

docs.title: 54 — Evaluation: evals are your test suite
docs.text:
Last verified: 28 October 2026.

You cannot ship what you cannot measure, and with a probabilistic model you cannot measure it by looking. An eval is an automated check on a model's output; an eval set is a frozen collection of inputs with graders and thresholds — a regression suite whose assertions are not == but "pass rate ≥ 0.9". This chapter builds that suite: deterministic checks, reference metrics, execution tests, LLM judges, human agreement, the statistics to tell a real improvement from noise, a runnable harness, and the CI gate that blocks a bad release. It is the engineering counterpart to the model-specific protocols in 09 — Evaluation (tool-call graders, golden sets, release gates) and 42 — Distillation evaluation; the Wilson-interval arithmetic agrees with 43 — Worked examples. For evaluating retrieval, see 51 — RAG §§12–13; for agents, 52 — Agents.

docs.title: 1. Why evals are the core skill
docs.text:
A software test asserts an exact result: assert add(2, 2) == 4. A model test cannot, because the model is non-deterministic and natural language has many right answers. So the unit of measurement shifts from "this output is correct" to "the pass rate over a set is high enough." Everything else follows from that shift:

  • An eval set is a regression suite. You run it on every candidate (new prompt, new model, new retriever) and compare to the last known-good run.
  • A grader (scorer) is an assertion that returns pass/fail — but written to tolerate paraphrase, formatting and the other legitimate variation of language.
  • A threshold is the assertion's bar: "exact-match ≥ 0.85", "zero unsafe outputs". Setting it before you see the numbers is what keeps the suite honest.

The engineer's instinct transfers directly: you would not refactor without tests, and you should not change a prompt without an eval. The discipline that is new is statistics — because a pass rate is an estimate with error bars, "88% beats 85%" might be pure noise (§8).

Treat evals as the deliverable, not the afterthought. The teams that ship reliable LLM products are the ones with the best eval sets, not the cleverest prompts.

docs.title: 2. Deterministic checks
docs.text:
The cheapest, most reliable evals need no reference answer and no model — they check structure. Run them first and on every output, because a response that is not even parseable fails before any question of quality.

  • Format / schema: is it valid JSON? does it match the expected schema (keys, types)?
  • Regex: does it contain the required pattern (an order ID, a citation marker) and none of the forbidden ones (an email address in a redacted answer)?
  • Length / bounds: within the token budget? not empty? not a 2,000-word essay where one line was asked for?
import json
import re
from collections import Counter

def exact_match(pred, gold):
    return pred == gold

def normalize(s):          # lowercase, drop punctuation, squash whitespace
    s = re.sub(r"[^\w\s]", "", s.lower())
    return re.sub(r"\s+", " ", s).strip()

def normalized_em(pred, gold):
    return normalize(pred) == normalize(gold)

def token_f1(pred, gold):
    p, g = pred.split(), gold.split()
    common = sum((Counter(p) & Counter(g)).values())
    if common == 0:
        return 0.0
    prec, rec = common / len(p), common / len(g)
    return 2 * prec * rec / (prec + rec)

def valid_json(pred):
    try:
        json.loads(pred)
        return True
    except json.JSONDecodeError:
        return False

print("exact_match:", exact_match("Yes", "yes"))
print("normalized_em:", normalized_em("  Yes ", "yes"), normalized_em("Paris.", "paris"))
print("token_f1:", round(token_f1("the total is 42",
                                   "the invoice total is 42 dollars"), 4))
print("valid_json:", valid_json('{"label": "billing"}'), valid_json("billing"))

exact_match: False
normalized_em: True True
token_f1: 0.8
valid_json: True False

Notice exact_match("Yes", "yes") is False while normalized_em is True (and "Paris." matches "paris"): raw exact match is brutal about case, whitespace and punctuation, which is why reference metrics (§3) normalise first. Deterministic checks catch the failures that make everything else moot — a tool call that is not valid JSON cannot be executed no matter how good its intent.

docs.title: 3. Reference-based metrics
docs.text: When each input has a known gold answer, you compare the output to it. The art is tolerating correct variation.

docs.title: 3.1 Exact and normalized exact match
docs.text: Exact match (EM) is 1 if the output equals the gold string. Useful for short, closed answers (a label, a number, a yes/no). Normalized EM lowercases, trims whitespace and strips punctuation first, so "Paris." and "paris" count as equal. Normalise everything that is not semantically meaningful — but no more, or you will mark wrong answers right.

docs.title: 3.2 Token-level F1
docs.text:
For short free-text answers, token F1 gives partial credit by treating the answer as a bag of tokens. Precision is the fraction of predicted tokens that appear in the gold answer; recall is the fraction of gold tokens the prediction covers; F1 is their harmonic mean:

\[ F_1=\frac{2\,P\,R}{P+R} \]

On paper

Prediction "the total is 42" (4 tokens), gold "the invoice total is 42 dollars" (6 tokens). The shared tokens are the, total, is, 42 — 4 of them.

\[ P=4/4=1.0 \] \[ R=4/6\approx 0.667 \] \[ F_1=\frac{2\cdot 1.0\cdot 0.667}{1.0+0.667}=0.8 \]

Precision is perfect (every word the model said is in the gold answer) but recall is 0.667 (it dropped "invoice" and "dollars"), so F1 lands at 0.8 — partial credit for a mostly-right answer that exact match would have scored 0.

docs.title: 3.3 BLEU and ROUGE, and why they fail for open answers
docs.text:
BLEU (precision-oriented, from machine translation) and ROUGE (recall-oriented, from summarisation) score n-gram overlap with one or more references. ROUGE-1 overlap on unigrams:

\[ \text{ROUGE-1}_{\text{recall}}=\frac{\text{overlapping unigrams}}{\text{reference unigrams}} \]

On paper

Reference summary "the refund was issued today" (5 words), candidate "refund issued today" (3 words). The overlap is refund, issued, today — 3 unigrams.

\[ \text{recall}=3/5=0.6 \] \[ \text{precision}=3/3=1.0 \] \[ F_1=\frac{2\cdot 0.6\cdot 1.0}{0.6+1.0}=0.75 \]

The candidate is a fine shorter paraphrase, yet ROUGE recall is only 0.6 because it dropped two reference words. That is the whole problem: a correct answer phrased differently scores low.

These metrics are useful when there is a tight reference (translation, extractive summary) and worthless when the space of good answers is open (an explanation, a chat reply). They reward surface overlap, not meaning: against the reference "the refund was approved", the candidate "the refund was not approved" contains all 4 reference words, so its ROUGE-1 recall is a perfect 4/4 = 1.0 (precision ⅘ = 0.8) although it says the opposite; a perfect paraphrase with no shared words scores zero. For open answers, use an LLM judge (§5) or human eval (§6), not BLEU/ROUGE.

docs.title: 4. Execution-based evaluation
docs.text:
For code and anything with a verifiable outcome, do not score the text — run it. Generate a function, run the unit tests, pass if they pass. This is the gold standard because it checks behaviour, not resemblance. The Java and React tracks do exactly this (compile, tsc, Vitest); see 42 §3.3.

Because generation is stochastic, you sample \(n\) attempts and report pass@k — the probability that at least one of \(k\) sampled attempts passes. With \(c\) of \(n\) samples correct, the unbiased estimator is

\[ \text{pass@}k=1-\frac{\binom{n-c}{k}}{\binom{n}{k}} \]

On paper

A coding task sampled \(n=6\) times, \(c=2\) passing the tests.

\[ \text{pass@}1=1-\frac{\binom{4}{1}}{\binom{6}{1}}=1-\frac46 \] \[ \text{pass@}1\approx 0.333 \] \[ \text{pass@}3=1-\frac{\binom{4}{3}}{\binom{6}{3}}=1-\frac{4}{20}=0.8 \]

pass@1 (0.333) is just the per-sample success rate \(c/n\) — the number for deployment, where the user sees one answer. pass@3 (0.8) is the chance one of three tries works — a capability number, and relevant only if your product actually retries. Report which \(k\) you mean; see 42 §2.3 for the same estimator on an agent task.

docs.title: 5. Model-graded evaluation (LLM-as-judge)
docs.text: When there is no reference and no executable check — "is this summary faithful?", "which of two answers is more helpful?" — you can ask a strong model to grade. It scales human judgement to thousands of examples, but it is a measurement instrument with known biases, so calibrate it.

docs.title: 5.1 Rubric design
docs.text: A judge is only as good as its rubric. Give it: the task, the input, the output(s), any reference, and an explicit scale with described anchors ("1 = does not answer; 3 = answers but omits a caveat; 5 = complete and correct"). Ask for a short reason before the score (so the score is justified, not reflexive), and output a parseable field. Vague rubrics ("rate 1–10") produce vague, unstable scores.

docs.title: 5.2 Pointwise, pairwise, reference-guided
docs.text:
• Pointwise: score one output on the rubric. Simple, but absolute scores drift and cluster.
  • Pairwise: show two outputs, ask which is better. More reliable — relative judgements are easier and more stable than absolute ones — and the natural fit for comparing two prompts or models.
  • Reference-guided: give the judge a gold answer to compare against. Raises agreement with humans when a reference exists.

docs.title: 5.3 Known biases and mitigations
docs.text:
LLM judges have systematic, measured biases:

  • Position bias: a tendency to prefer the first (or a fixed) option in a pairwise test. Mitigation: run each pair both ways (A then B, B then A) and only count a win if it holds in both orders; ties otherwise.
  • Verbosity bias: longer answers are scored higher regardless of quality. Mitigation: instruct the rubric to ignore length; cap or normalise length; penalise padding explicitly.
  • Self-preference: a model tends to prefer text written by itself or its own family. Mitigation: use a different model family as judge than the one under test; anonymise which system produced which output.

Always validate the judge against human labels before trusting it, and never let it overturn a deterministic failure — a judge that "likes" invalid JSON is wrong by construction (see 09 §4.5).

docs.title: 6. Human evaluation
docs.text: Humans remain the ground truth that calibrates every automated metric. You use them sparingly — on a sample, to validate judges and to grade what nothing else can.

docs.title: 6.1 Guidelines
docs.text: Write a labelling guide as precise as a rubric: the exact question, the scale, worked examples of each level, and tie-break rules. Ambiguity in the guide shows up as disagreement between annotators. Collect at least two labels per item on a sample so you can measure that disagreement.

docs.title: 6.2 Inter-annotator agreement: Cohen's kappa
docs.text:
Raw agreement overstates reliability because two annotators agree sometimes by chance. Cohen's kappa corrects for chance, where \(p_o\) is observed agreement and \(p_e\) is the agreement expected if both labelled at random with their own base rates:

\[ \kappa=\frac{p_o-p_e}{1-p_e} \]

On paper

Two annotators label 100 answers pass/fail. Both say pass on 45, both fail on 40, and they disagree on 15 (A-pass/B-fail 10, A-fail/B-pass 5). Observed agreement:

\[ p_o=(45+40)/100=0.85 \]

A says pass 55/100, B says pass 50/100. Chance agreement:

\[ p_e=0.55\cdot 0.50+0.45\cdot 0.50=0.5 \] \[ \kappa=\frac{0.85-0.5}{1-0.5}=0.70 \]

Raw agreement looks strong at 0.85, but half of it was expected by chance, so kappa is 0.70 — "substantial" by the usual rule of thumb (0.6–0.8), good enough to trust the labels and to calibrate a judge against them. A kappa near 0 would mean your guide is too vague to label consistently; fix the guide, not the annotators.

docs.title: 7. Building a golden set
docs.text:
The eval set is the asset; the model is replaceable. Build it deliberately.

  • Sources: real production traffic (sampled and labelled), real support tickets, real documents — not invented toy inputs. The distribution must match what you ship against.
  • Size: enough for the precision you need (§8). A few hundred is a usable start; detecting small differences needs thousands.
  • Stratification: label each case with tags (topic, difficulty, language, length) so you can read per-tag pass rates, not just one average that hides a failing slice.
  • Edge and adversarial cases: include the empty input, the multi-part question, the out-of-scope request, the prompt-injection attempt (see 56). Average accuracy on easy cases is comfortable and useless.
  • Held-out set: keep a slice you never look at during development, so you can tell whether you improved the system or just overfit the eval set — the same lesson as a test set in ML.
  • Versioning: give the set a version (golden-2026-10-28); never silently edit it after seeing results. A changed eval set invalidates comparisons to older runs.

docs.title: 8. Statistics: is the difference real?
docs.text: A pass rate is an estimate from a sample, so it has error bars. Skipping this step is how teams ship "improvements" that are noise.

docs.title: 8.1 Confidence interval for a pass rate (Wilson)
docs.text:
For \(k\) passes out of \(n\), the 95% Wilson score interval (better than the textbook normal interval at small \(n\) and extreme rates) is

\[ \frac{\hat p+\frac{z^2}{2n}\pm z\sqrt{\frac{\hat p(1-\hat p)}{n}+\frac{z^2}{4n^2}}}{1+\frac{z^2}{n}}, \quad z=1.96 \]

On paper

40 of 100 cases pass, so \(\hat p=0.4\), \(z^2=3.8416\), denominator \(1+z^2/n=1.0384\).

\[ \text{centre}=\frac{0.4+0.0192}{1.0384}=0.4037 \] \[ \text{half}=1.96\cdot 0.04996/1.0384=0.0943 \] \[ 0.4037\pm 0.0943=(0.309,\;0.498) \]

"40 of 100" is consistent with a true rate from 31% to 50% — so a 2-point difference between two models on 100 cases is noise. This matches 43 — Worked examples to the digit; report the interval, not just the point.

docs.title: 8.2 How many examples to detect a 5-point difference
docs.text:
To detect a difference \(\Delta\) between two independent pass rates at significance \(\alpha\) and power \(1-\beta\), the per-arm sample size is

\[ n=\frac{(z_{\alpha/2}+z_{\beta})^2\,[p_1(1-p_1)+p_2(1-p_2)]}{\Delta^2} \]

On paper

Detect a 5-point lift from 50% to 55% (\(\Delta=0.05\)), at \(\alpha=0.05\) two-sided (\(z=1.96\)) and 80% power (\(z=0.84\)). The variance term is \(0.25+0.2475=0.4975\):

\[ (1.96+0.84)^2=7.84 \] \[ n=7.84\cdot 0.4975/0.0025 \] \[ n\approx 1561 \]

You need about 1,560 examples per model to see a 5-point difference. The rule of thumb \(n\approx 16\,p(1-p)/\Delta^2 = 16\cdot 0.25/0.0025 = 1600\) lands in the same place. Small differences need large sets — which is why a 200-case suite can only resolve large changes.

docs.title: 8.3 Paired comparison: McNemar's test
docs.text:
Running both systems on the same items is far more powerful than two independent samples, because each item's difficulty cancels. For paired pass/fail data, only the discordant pairs matter — the items where the two systems disagree. With \(b\) = "A right, B wrong" and \(c\) = "A wrong, B right", McNemar's statistic is

\[ \chi^2=\frac{(b-c)^2}{b+c} \]

On paper

Two prompts on 100 items: both right 60, both wrong 20, A-only right 15, B-only right 5.

\[ \chi^2=\frac{(15-5)^2}{15+5}=\frac{100}{20}=5.0 \]

With the continuity correction \((|b-c|-1)^2/(b+c)=81/20=4.05\). Both exceed the \(\chi^2_{1,0.05}=3.841\) cutoff, so prompt A is significantly better.

docs.title: 8.4 Why unpaired comparisons waste data
docs.text:
The same 100 items, scored unpaired, give A = 75/100 and B = 65/100. The two-proportion test:

\[ z=\frac{p_A-p_B}{\sqrt{\bar p(1-\bar p)(2/n)}} \]

On paper

Pooled rate \(\bar p=0.70\), so the standard error is \(\sqrt{0.21\cdot 0.02}=0.0648\):

\[ z=0.10/0.0648=1.54 \]

1.54 is below 1.96: not significant. The very same results are significant when paired (§8.3) and not significant when unpaired, because the unpaired test's error bars include item-to-item difficulty that the paired test cancels. Always run both systems on the same items and compare pairwise.

docs.title: 8.5 Multiple comparisons
docs.text: If you test 20 prompt variants against a baseline at \(\alpha=0.05\), you expect about one false positive by chance alone (\(20\times 0.05=1\)) — with a two-sided test, half of those look like wins and half like losses. Guard against it: pre-register the comparison you care about, or correct the threshold (Bonferroni: divide \(\alpha\) by the number of tests), or validate the apparent winner on the held-out set before believing it.

docs.title: 9. A runnable eval harness
docs.text:
The pieces above assemble into a small harness: a dataset of cases, a function under test, scorers, an aggregate report with a confidence interval, a per-tag breakdown, and JSONL results you can diff between runs. Here the "model" is a keyword stub so the block runs anywhere; §9.1 swaps in a served model unchanged.

import json
import math

# 1. the eval set: inputs, gold labels, tags (a frozen regression suite)
CASES = [
    {"id": "t1", "text": "I was charged twice this month", "gold": "billing", "tags": ["easy"]},
    {"id": "t2", "text": "the app crashes when I open settings", "gold": "bug", "tags": ["easy"]},
    {"id": "t3", "text": "how do I export my data?", "gold": "howto", "tags": ["easy"]},
    {"id": "t4", "text": "refund the duplicate charge please", "gold": "billing", "tags": ["hard"]},
    {"id": "t5", "text": "login button does nothing on mobile", "gold": "bug", "tags": ["hard"]},
    {"id": "t6", "text": "where is the invoice for March?", "gold": "billing", "tags": ["hard"]},
]

# 2. the system under test (a keyword stub; swap for a real model later)
def model(text):
    t = text.lower()
    if any(w in t for w in ("charge", "refund", "billing")):
        return "billing"
    if any(w in t for w in ("crash", "bug", "error")):
        return "bug"
    return "howto"

# 3. a scorer turns one case into pass/fail (the assertion)
def score(case):
    return model(case["text"]) == case["gold"]

def wilson(k, n, z=1.96):
    if n == 0:
        return (0.0, 0.0)
    p = k / n
    d = 1 + z * z / n
    c = (p + z * z / (2 * n)) / d
    h = z * math.sqrt(p * (1 - p) / n + z * z / (4 * n * n)) / d
    return (c - h, c + h)

results = [{"id": c["id"], "pass": score(c), "tags": c["tags"]} for c in CASES]
k = sum(r["pass"] for r in results)
n = len(results)
lo, hi = wilson(k, n)
print(f"overall: {k}/{n} = {k/n:.2f}  95% CI [{lo:.2f}, {hi:.2f}]")
for tag in ("easy", "hard"):
    sub = [r for r in results if tag in r["tags"]]
    kk = sum(r["pass"] for r in sub)
    print(f"  {tag:5s}: {kk}/{len(sub)} = {kk/len(sub):.2f}")
print("failures:", [r["id"] for r in results if not r["pass"]])
with open("results.jsonl", "w") as f:
    for r in results:
        f.write(json.dumps(r) + "\n")

overall: 4/6 = 0.67  95% CI [0.30, 0.90]
  easy : 3/3 = 1.00
  hard : 1/3 = 0.33
failures: ['t5', 't6']

The per-tag breakdown earns its keep: the overall 0.67 hides that easy cases are perfect and hard cases fail two in three. The CI [0.30, 0.90] on six cases is enormous — a reminder that a tiny eval set can tell you almost nothing (§8). The failures list (t5, t6) feeds the error analysis of §12.

docs.title: 9.1 The same harness against a served model
docs.text:
Swap the keyword stub for the OpenAI client pointed at the local server (see 50 — Prompting and APIs and 10 — Serving). The dataset, scorers and aggregation are unchanged — only model becomes a network call.

from openai import OpenAI

CASES = [
    {"id": "t1", "text": "I was charged twice this month", "gold": "billing", "tags": ["easy"]},
    {"id": "t2", "text": "the app crashes when I open settings", "gold": "bug", "tags": ["easy"]},
    {"id": "t3", "text": "how do I export my data?", "gold": "howto", "tags": ["easy"]},
    {"id": "t4", "text": "refund the duplicate charge please", "gold": "billing", "tags": ["hard"]},
    {"id": "t5", "text": "login button does nothing on mobile", "gold": "bug", "tags": ["hard"]},
    {"id": "t6", "text": "where is the invoice for March?", "gold": "billing", "tags": ["hard"]},
]
client = OpenAI(base_url="http://127.0.0.1:8080/v1", api_key="local")
MODEL = "mlx-community/Qwen3-14B-4bit"
SYSTEM = "Classify the ticket as exactly one of: billing, bug, howto. Reply with the label only."

def model(text):
    r = client.chat.completions.create(
        model=MODEL, temperature=0, max_tokens=4,
        # Qwen3 thinks first by default; 4 tokens would all go to the think block
        extra_body={"chat_template_kwargs": {"enable_thinking": False}},
        messages=[{"role": "system", "content": SYSTEM},
                  {"role": "user", "content": text}])
    return (r.choices[0].message.content or "").strip().lower()

results = [{"id": c["id"], "pass": model(c["text"]) == c["gold"]} for c in CASES]
k = sum(r["pass"] for r in results)
print(f"served model: {k}/{len(CASES)} = {k/len(CASES):.2f}")
print("failures:", [r["id"] for r in results if not r["pass"]])

Run against a local stub that classifies by richer keywords (no model needed to test the harness):

served model: 5/6 = 0.83
failures: ['t6']

The stub recognises "login button does nothing" as a bug (which the §9 keyword baseline missed) but still trips on "invoice for March", so the harness reports ⅚ and points at t6. A real Qwen3-14B would classify from meaning rather than keywords and likely clear both hard cases — but the only way to know is to run this harness against it with temperature=0 and read the number, not to assume. Apart from the model function, the harness is unchanged; that is the point.

Two lines exist because the model under test is Qwen3. Its default chat template makes it think before it answers (50), so without enable_thinking: False the 4-token budget is spent inside the think block and the answer never arrives: mlx_lm.server then returns content: null. Without the or "" guard the script crashes on None.strip(); with the guard but without the switch, every case fails, and the cause is the harness, not the model. Both mlx_lm.server and llama-server accept chat_template_kwargs per request. That switch is right for the base model; for an adapter trained with thinking on, serve it as trained (06 §6) and raise max_tokens instead.

docs.title: 10. Evals in CI as a release gate
docs.text:
Wire the harness into CI so a prompt or model change cannot merge without passing. Treat it exactly like a test suite, with two adjustments for the probabilistic world.

  • Thresholds and tolerance bands. Gate on absolute bars ("exact-match ≥ 0.85; unsafe-output rate = 0") and on no regression against the last green run, but allow a tolerance band so a 1-point wobble within the confidence interval does not block a release. Block only when the drop is larger than noise (§8).
  • Flaky-eval handling. Non-determinism makes evals flaky. Pin it down: temperature=0, a fixed seed where the server supports it, and fixed decoding params, so the same input gives the same output run to run. For anything still stochastic (sampling at temperature>0, an LLM judge), run it \(k\) times and gate on the mean, and store the per-run numbers so you can see the variance. A gate that flaps red/green on identical code is worse than no gate — nobody trusts it.

Record, with every run, the model ID, prompt version, eval-set version, and decoding params, so a red build is reproducible and a green history is comparable. This is the same hygiene as 09 §9's release gates.

docs.title: 11. Online evaluation
docs.text:
Offline evals measure a frozen set; production measures reality. You need both, because the offline set never perfectly matches live traffic.

  • A/B tests. Route a fraction of traffic to the new version, compare outcome metrics (resolution rate, thumbs-up rate, conversion) with the statistics of §8. The ground truth for "is it better" — but slow and needing volume.
  • Interleaving. For ranked outputs (search, retrieval), mix results from both systems in one list and see which the user clicks. More sensitive than A/B for ranking because each user compares both directly.
  • Explicit feedback. Thumbs up/down, star ratings, "was this helpful?" — sparse (few users click) and biased (unhappy users click more), but a direct signal; log it against the request so you can replay failures.
  • Implicit feedback. Did the user copy the answer, retry, rephrase, escalate to a human, abandon the session? Plentiful and noisy; good for trends, weak per-example.
  • Guardrail metrics. Watch latency (p50/p95/p99), cost per request, and error rate alongside quality. A new prompt that lifts quality 2 points but doubles latency or cost may be a net loss; guardrails stop you from "winning" on quality while losing the product. See 55 — Production.

docs.title: 12. Error analysis workflow
docs.text:
The highest-value hour in the whole discipline: read your failures. Metrics tell you that the system fails; only reading the outputs tells you why.

  1. Pull ~50 failing cases from the latest run.
  2. Read each and assign a short cause label, inventing the taxonomy as you go.
  3. Count the buckets.
  4. Fix the biggest bucket.
  5. Add those cases (and near-variants) to the eval set so the fix is protected.

On paper

Tally of 50 failures from the support-bot eval:

Cause Count Share Retrieval missed the doc 18 0.36 Hallucinated a fact 12 0.24 Wrong output format 8 0.16 Over-refused (said "I can't") 7 0.14 Other 5 0.10 Total 50 1.00

Retrieval misses are 18/50 = 0.36 of failures — more than a third. Fixing retrieval (better chunking or hybrid search, 51) removes the largest bucket; chasing the "wrong format" bucket first would fix 16% and feel productive while the real problem stayed. Count before you fix.

Error analysis turns a vague "the model is bad" into a ranked, fixable backlog — exactly like triaging a bug tracker by frequency and impact.

docs.title: 13. Evaluating RAG and agents
docs.text:
The frameworks specialise for multi-step systems: evaluate each stage so a failure localises, rather than scoring only the final text.

RAG pipelines are two subsystems, graded separately (if the right chunk was never retrieved, no prompt can save the answer):

  • Retrieval, against queries labelled with their relevant chunks: recall@k (did we find the relevant chunks?), precision@k, MRR (how high was the first good hit?), nDCG@k (ranking quality). Worked by hand in 51 — RAG §12.
  • Generation, against the retrieved context: groundedness/faithfulness (is every claim supported by the context?), answer relevance (does it address the question?), and citation accuracy (does each marker point at a chunk that supports its claim?). Worked in 51 §13.

Decompose a wrong answer along the pipeline — was the chunk retrieved, in the prompt (context budget), used by the model? Each "no" is a different fix. A grounded answer that cites the wrong chunk is still a failure; measure citation accuracy explicitly.

Agentic workflows add trajectory evaluation — the final answer is not enough:

  • Tool-selection accuracy (right tool for the step) and argument accuracy (right arguments), gradeable deterministically against expected calls — see the tool-call graders in 09 — Evaluation §4.
  • Task success / completion rate (did the whole task finish correctly), recovery rate (did it recover from a failed call), steps per task and cost/latency per task as guardrails, and scope/safety (zero out-of-scope or destructive actions).
  • Per-step reliability compounds: a 95%-reliable step over 10 steps is \(0.95^{10}\approx 0.60\) — a 60% task. This is why agents need very high per-step reliability; report pass@k and pass^k (all-k-succeed) as in 09 §5. Full agent evaluation is in 52 — Agents.

In both, keep the deterministic and execution-based checks (§§2, 4) at the base of the stack and reserve the LLM judge (§5) for what only judgement can score.

docs.title: 14. Contamination and leaderboard caveats
docs.text:
• Contamination: if a public benchmark's test set leaked into a model's training data, the model's score measures memorisation, not skill. Assume popular benchmarks are partly contaminated; your private, recent, held-out golden set is the only clean measurement. Decontaminate your own training data against your eval set (n-gram overlap, near-duplicate detection); see 09 §7.
  • Leaderboards versus your eval: a leaderboard ranks models on its distribution, which is not yours. A model that tops a benchmark can still lose on your support tickets, your documents, your formats. Use leaderboards to shortlist candidates; decide with your own eval on your own data. The benchmark is someone else's regression suite — informative, not authoritative.

A number without its provenance (which set, which version, contaminated?) is not evidence. Report the set, its date, its size, and how you know it was not trained on.

docs.title: 15. Key takeaways
docs.text:
• An eval set is a regression suite whose assertions are thresholds on pass rates, not ==. It is the deliverable; the model is replaceable.
  • Layer graders cheapest-first: deterministic checks (format, JSON, regex, length), then reference metrics (EM, token F1), then execution tests (pass@k), then LLM judges, then humans. Never let a judge overturn a deterministic failure.
  • BLEU/ROUGE reward surface overlap and fail on open answers; use a judge or humans there, and calibrate the judge against human labels (Cohen's kappa) while mitigating position, verbosity and self-preference bias.
  • A pass rate is an estimate with error bars. Report Wilson intervals; detecting a 5-point difference needs about 1,560 examples per arm; compare two systems paired (McNemar) on the same items, because unpaired tests waste data.
  • Gate releases in CI on absolute bars and no-regression bands, with temperature=0, fixed seeds and repeated runs to kill flakiness. Watch guardrail metrics (latency, cost) beside quality.
  • Measure production with A/B, interleaving and feedback; nothing offline replaces live outcomes.
  • Read 50 failures, build a taxonomy, fix the biggest bucket, add the cases back. Trust your own held-out eval over any leaderboard, and never report a number without its provenance.

docs.title: 16. Exercises
docs.text:
Exercise 1

A model answers "The total is 42 dollars" to a question whose gold answer is "42 dollars". Compute token F1. Why is this a fairer score than exact match here?

Answer

Prediction tokens: the, total, is, 42, dollars (5). Gold tokens: 42, dollars (2). Common: 42, dollars (2). \(P=2/5=0.4\), \(R=2/2=1.0\), \(F_1=2\cdot0.4\cdot1.0/(1.4)=0.571\). Exact match scores 0 because the strings differ, yet the answer contains the full correct answer plus filler — token F1's 0.571 reflects the perfect recall and the padding, which is fairer for a short free-text answer.

Exercise 2

A coding task is sampled 5 times; 1 sample passes the unit tests. Compute pass@1 and pass@5.

Answer

\(n=5\), \(c=1\). pass@1 \(=1-\binom{4}{1}/\binom{5}{1}=1-4/5=0.2\) (= \(c/n\)). pass@5 \(=1-\binom{4}{5}/\binom{5}{5}\); \(\binom{4}{5}=0\), so pass@5 \(=1-0=1.0\) — with all 5 samples drawn, at least one of 5 is certain to be the one that passes.

Exercise 3

Two annotators agree on 80 of 100 items. Annotator A says "pass" 70 times, B says "pass" 60 times. Compute Cohen's kappa.

Answer

\(p_o=0.80\). \(p_e=0.70\cdot0.60+0.30\cdot0.40=0.42+0.12=0.54\). \(\kappa=(0.80-0.54)/(1-0.54)=0.26/0.46\approx0.565\) — "moderate". The guide probably needs tightening before these labels are trusted as ground truth.

Exercise 4

Your eval of 200 cases gives 150 passes. Compute the point estimate and, using the Wilson numbers, say roughly how wide the 95% interval is. Can you distinguish this from a model scoring 73%?

Answer

Point estimate \(150/200=0.75\). Wilson at \(n=200\): \(z^2/n=0.0192\), so the denominator is 1.0192 and the centre is \((0.75+0.0096)/1.0192=0.745\). The half-width is \(1.96\sqrt{0.0009375+0.000024}/1.0192\), which is \(1.96\cdot0.0310/1.0192\approx0.060\), so the interval is about (0.686, 0.805), roughly ±6 points. (The plain normal shortcut \(1.96\sqrt{0.75\cdot0.25/200}\approx0.060\) gives nearly the same width here, because \(n\) is large and \(p\) is not extreme; Wilson also shifts the centre toward 0.5.) A 73% model sits well inside that, so no — 200 cases cannot distinguish 75% from 73%; you would need far more (§8.2).

Exercise 5

Prompt A and prompt B are run on the same 50 items. They agree on 44 (both right 38, both wrong 6); on the 6 they disagree, A is right 5 times and B once. Apply McNemar's test (no continuity correction).

Answer

\(b=5\), \(c=1\). \(\chi^2=(5-1)^2/(5+1)=16/6\approx2.67\). This is below the 3.841 cutoff, so the difference is not significant despite A winning 5 of 6 disagreements — only 6 discordant pairs is too little evidence. Collect more items.

Exercise 6

You run an eval at temperature=0.7 and the pass rate jumps between 0.80 and 0.88 across identical-code runs in CI. What two changes make the gate trustworthy?

Answer
