A very broad retrieval toolkit — chunking, many index types, rerankers, query transformations, hundreds of data connectors (LlamaHub); Workflows are a clean, typed orchestration primitive; strong for RAG and document agents. Minuses. Large surface and fast-moving APIs (the 0.x versioning tells you breaking changes are expected); the agent layer is younger than the retrieval layer; for a non-RAG tool loop it is more machinery than you need. Use it when. Retrieval is central; you want batteries-included RAG with an agent on top. Avoid it when. No documents are involved — a lighter library wires tools with less. Local models. Yes — OpenAILike(api_base=…, is_function_calling_model=True) with additional_kwargs={"extra_body": …} for enable_thinking. MCP. Yes, via llama-index-tools-mcp (McpToolSpec). Licence. MIT.

docs.title: 6.2 Haystack
docs.text:
What and who. Haystack (deepset) is a mature, production-oriented framework for search and RAG pipelines that added agents and tools. Version 3.4.1 (haystack-ai) here.

Mental model. You build a pipeline of typed components connected by explicit edges — retrievers, generators, rankers, and an Agent component that runs a tool loop. The pipeline graph is serializable (to YAML), so the same definition runs in notebook and production.

Minimal example (run against the stub; haystack-ai 3.4.1):

from haystack.components.agents import Agent
from haystack.components.generators.chat import OpenAIChatGenerator
from haystack.dataclasses import ChatMessage
from haystack.tools import tool
from haystack.utils import Secret

BASE = "http://127.0.0.1:8080/v1"
MODEL = "mlx-community/Qwen3-14B-4bit"


@tool
def get_order(order_id: str) -> dict:
    """Look up an order by id; returns status, amount and tracking_id."""
    return {"order_id": order_id, "status": "shipped", "amount": 129.99,
            "tracking_id": "TRK42", "_stub": "order_lookup_ok"}


@tool
def get_shipping_status(tracking_id: str) -> dict:
    """Look up the shipping status for a tracking id."""
    return {"tracking_id": tracking_id, "carrier": "UPS",
            "status": "in_transit", "eta": "2026-11-02",
            "_stub": "shipping_lookup_ok"}


generator = OpenAIChatGenerator(
    model=MODEL, api_base_url=BASE,
    api_key=Secret.from_token("local"),
    generation_kwargs={"temperature": 0,
                       "extra_body": {"chat_template_kwargs":
                                      {"enable_thinking": False}}})
agent = Agent(chat_generator=generator,
              tools=[get_order, get_shipping_status])
agent.warm_up()
result = agent.run(messages=[ChatMessage.from_user("Where is my order A1001?")])
print(result["messages"][-1].text)

Order A1001 shipped via UPS (tracking TRK42) and is in transit, ETA 2026-11-02. Amount charged: $129.99.

Strengths. Explicit, typed, serializable pipelines that are genuinely production-minded; strong retrieval heritage; stable, predictable component contracts; clean local-model support. Minuses. The pipeline/component model is more verbose for a simple agent; a smaller agent ecosystem than LangChain/LlamaIndex; fewer "magic" conveniences (which some teams consider a feature). Use it when. Production RAG/search with a need for explicit, serializable, testable pipelines. Avoid it when. You want a one-liner agent, or you are not doing retrieval. Local models. Yes — OpenAIChatGenerator(api_base_url=…, generation_kwargs={"extra_body": …}). MCP. Yes, via mcp-haystack (MCPToolset; stdio / SSE / Streamable HTTP). Licence. Apache-2.0.

docs.title: 7. Typed / lightweight agent libraries: Pydantic AI & Agno
7.1 Pydantic AI
docs.text:
What and who. Pydantic AI, from the Pydantic team, brings the "FastAPI feel" to agents: typed, validated, minimal. It reached 1.0 in September 2025 and is on the 2.x line now (2.63.0 here).

Mental model. An Agent is typed on its dependencies and its output. Tools are plain decorated functions whose signatures become schemas; structured outputs are Pydantic models, validated (and retried) automatically. The library stays close to the request — no hidden orchestration graph.

Minimal example (run against the stub; pydantic-ai 2.63.0):

import os
os.environ["PYDANTIC_AI_NO_BANNER"] = "1"
from pydantic_ai import Agent
from pydantic_ai.models.openai import OpenAIChatModel, OpenAIChatModelSettings
from pydantic_ai.providers.openai import OpenAIProvider

BASE = "http://127.0.0.1:8080/v1"
MODEL = "mlx-community/Qwen3-14B-4bit"

model = OpenAIChatModel(
    MODEL, provider=OpenAIProvider(base_url=BASE, api_key="local"))
settings = OpenAIChatModelSettings(
    extra_body={"chat_template_kwargs": {"enable_thinking": False}})
agent = Agent(model, model_settings=settings)


@agent.tool_plain
def get_order(order_id: str) -> dict:
    """Look up an order by id; returns status, amount and tracking_id."""
    return {"order_id": order_id, "status": "shipped", "amount": 129.99,
            "tracking_id": "TRK42", "_stub": "order_lookup_ok"}


@agent.tool_plain
def get_shipping_status(tracking_id: str) -> dict:
    """Look up the shipping status for a tracking id."""
    return {"tracking_id": tracking_id, "carrier": "UPS",
            "status": "in_transit", "eta": "2026-11-02",
            "_stub": "shipping_lookup_ok"}


result = agent.run_sync("Where is my order A1001?")
print(result.output)

Order A1001 shipped via UPS (tracking TRK42) and is in transit, ETA 2026-11-02. Amount charged: $129.99.

Strengths. Excellent typing and validation; small, legible surface; native structured output with validate-and-retry (50); first-class observability through Pydantic Logfire (OpenTelemetry); model-agnostic. Minuses. Fewer batteries than the big ecosystems (you add retrieval yourself); durable execution comes through integrations with Temporal, DBOS and Prefect rather than a built-in checkpointer; multi-agent support is lighter than LangGraph's; younger than the incumbents. Use it when. You want strict typing/validation and a thin, readable agent — the natural step up from the baseline for a Python service. Avoid it when. You need heavy built-in RAG, visual tooling, or a built-in graph checkpointer with time travel. Local models. Yes — OpenAIChatModel + OpenAIProvider(base_url=…), with OpenAIChatModelSettings(extra_body=…) for enable_thinking. MCP. Yes, native MCP client support. Licence. MIT.

docs.title: 7.2 Agno
docs.text:
What and who. Agno (formerly Phidata, renamed in early 2025; repo agno-agi/agno) is a performance-focused agent library, version 3.1.11 here. The 2.x line added AgentOS, a FastAPI-based runtime for serving agents.

Mental model. A single Agent object bundles a model, tools, memory and knowledge (vector retrieval); Agno's own benchmarks stress low per-agent memory and fast instantiation. Scale out with teams; serve with AgentOS.

Minimal example (run against the stub; agno 3.1.11). Note the leanest wiring in this chapter — plain functions, no decorators:

from agno.agent import Agent
from agno.models.openai.like import OpenAILike

BASE = "http://127.0.0.1:8080/v1"
MODEL = "mlx-community/Qwen3-14B-4bit"


def get_order(order_id: str) -> dict:
    """Look up an order by id; returns status, amount and tracking_id."""
    return {"order_id": order_id, "status": "shipped", "amount": 129.99,
            "tracking_id": "TRK42", "_stub": "order_lookup_ok"}


def get_shipping_status(tracking_id: str) -> dict:
    """Look up the shipping status for a tracking id."""
    return {"tracking_id": tracking_id, "carrier": "UPS",
            "status": "in_transit", "eta": "2026-11-02",
            "_stub": "shipping_lookup_ok"}


model = OpenAILike(id=MODEL, base_url=BASE, api_key="local",
                   extra_body={"chat_template_kwargs": {"enable_thinking": False}})
agent = Agent(model=model, tools=[get_order, get_shipping_status],
              telemetry=False)
resp = agent.run("Where is my order A1001?")
print(resp.content)

Order A1001 shipped via UPS (tracking TRK42) and is in transit, ETA 2026-11-02. Amount charged: $129.99.

Strengths. Very low ceremony (the leanest wiring here, §16); built-in memory, knowledge/retrieval and session storage; AgentOS gives a serving runtime out of the box; broad model support including OpenAI-compatible. Minuses. Smaller community than LangChain/LlamaIndex; the all-in-one Agent object can feel implicit; the Phidata→Agno rename means older tutorials reference the dead package. Use it when. You want a batteries-included single-agent (or small-team) app with memory and a serving layer, with minimal code. Avoid it when. You need the largest integration catalogue, or first-class graph checkpointing and time-travel. Local models. Yes — agno.models.openai.like.OpenAILike(base_url=…, extra_body=…). MCP. Yes, via agno.tools.mcp.MCPTools (requires the mcp package). Licence. Apache-2.0.

docs.title: 8. Vendor agent SDKs
docs.text: A model or cloud vendor's own agent layer. Expect excellent support for that vendor's models and features, and variable support for everything else.

docs.title: 8.1 OpenAI Agents SDK
docs.text:
What and who. The OpenAI Agents SDK (openai-agents, 0.24.0 here) is OpenAI's lightweight agent framework; the experimental Swarm repository now points to it as Swarm's production-ready successor. It is provider-agnostic: besides OpenAI's Responses API it has an OpenAIChatCompletionsModel that points at any OpenAI-compatible endpoint.

Mental model. Primitives are Agents (a model plus instructions and tools), handoffs (one agent delegates to another), guardrails (input/output validation) and sessions (conversation state). Built-in tracing to the OpenAI dashboard (disable it for local work). Newer releases add sandbox agents, which work inside a container over long time horizons.

Minimal example (run against the stub; openai-agents 0.24.0). Use the chat-completions model so it targets mlx_lm.server, and disable tracing:

from agents import (Agent, Runner, function_tool, ModelSettings,
                    OpenAIChatCompletionsModel, set_tracing_disabled)
from openai import AsyncOpenAI

BASE = "http://127.0.0.1:8080/v1"
MODEL = "mlx-community/Qwen3-14B-4bit"
set_tracing_disabled(True)


@function_tool
def get_order(order_id: str) -> dict:
    """Look up an order by id; returns status, amount and tracking_id."""
    return {"order_id": order_id, "status": "shipped", "amount": 129.99,
            "tracking_id": "TRK42", "_stub": "order_lookup_ok"}


@function_tool
def get_shipping_status(tracking_id: str) -> dict:
    """Look up the shipping status for a tracking id."""
    return {"tracking_id": tracking_id, "carrier": "UPS",
            "status": "in_transit", "eta": "2026-11-02",
            "_stub": "shipping_lookup_ok"}


client = AsyncOpenAI(base_url=BASE, api_key="local")
model = OpenAIChatCompletionsModel(model=MODEL, openai_client=client)
agent = Agent(name="support", model=model,
              tools=[get_order, get_shipping_status],
              model_settings=ModelSettings(extra_body={
                  "chat_template_kwargs": {"enable_thinking": False}}))

result = Runner.run_sync(agent, "Where is my order A1001?")
print(result.final_output)

Order A1001 shipped via UPS (tracking TRK42) and is in transit, ETA 2026-11-02. Amount charged: $129.99.

Strengths. Small, clean primitives; handoffs and guardrails are well designed; strong tracing; native MCP; works with local endpoints via the chat-completions model. Minuses. Best features (the Responses API, hosted tools, the trace dashboard) assume OpenAI's platform; local use means opting out of some of them; younger than the incumbents. Use it when. You are on OpenAI, or want a minimal vendor-blessed loop and can point it at a local model. Avoid it when. You want deep, vendor-neutral durable execution or the biggest integration catalogue. Local models. Yes — OpenAIChatCompletionsModel(openai_client=AsyncOpenAI(base_url=…)); ModelSettings(extra_body=…) passes enable_thinking. MCP. Yes, native (MCPServerStdio, MCPServerStreamableHttp). Licence. MIT.

docs.title: 8.2 Microsoft Agent Framework (and the AutoGen / Semantic Kernel story)
docs.text:
What and who. The Microsoft Agent Framework (agent-framework on PyPI; also .NET) is Microsoft's unified agent stack, generally available since April 2026 (1.0.0 reached PyPI on 2 April 2026; 1.23.0 by late October). The same teams built it as the successor to both AutoGen and Semantic Kernel:

  • AutoGen (the research-oriented multi-agent framework) is archived. Its README says Microsoft no longer provides bug fixes, security fixes, new features or support, advises against production use, and points to the Agent Framework and a migration guide.
  • Semantic Kernel (the enterprise SDK) is still supported: Microsoft committed to fixing critical bugs and security issues for at least one year after the Agent Framework's GA (so into at least April 2027), while most new features go to the Agent Framework. Its README now presents the Agent Framework as its successor and links a migration guide.

So for new projects the answer is the Microsoft Agent Framework; treat AutoGen and Semantic Kernel as legacy you migrate from — AutoGen urgently, since it no longer gets security fixes.

Mental model. It combines Semantic Kernel's enterprise plumbing (connectors, plugins, telemetry, .NET parity) with AutoGen's multi-agent patterns (group chat, hand-offs, workflows), under one API with OpenTelemetry built in.

Minimal example. Not shown here (this framework's sweet spot is Azure/.NET integration; it is documented, not benchmarked, in this chapter). In the 1.x Python API you wrap a chat client in an agent — Agent(client=OpenAIChatCompletionClient(model=…, base_url=…), instructions=…, tools=[…]), or client.as_agent(...) — and await agent.run("…"); see the official docs at https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/agent-framework/ for a current snippet.

Strengths. Enterprise-grade (observability, identity, Azure integration); .NET and Python parity; the consolidation ends the "AutoGen vs Semantic Kernel" confusion. Minuses. Newest of the majors (GA only in 2026); heaviest when used outside the Microsoft/Azure ecosystem; migration work for existing AutoGen/SK code. Use it when. A Microsoft/Azure shop, .NET in the mix, or you were on AutoGen/Semantic Kernel. Avoid it when. A small Python-only service with no Azure footprint — lighter libraries fit better. Local models. Yes — OpenAIChatCompletionClient(base_url=…), with default_options={"extra_body": {…}} on the Agent for enable_thinking. A quick check against this chapter's stub (agent-framework-core 1.23.0) made both tool calls with thinking off and printed the same answer. MCP. Yes, native MCP support. Licence. MIT.

docs.title: 8.3 Google Agent Development Kit (ADK)
docs.text:
What and who. Google's Agent Development Kit (google-adk, 2.13.0 here; also TypeScript, Go, Java and Kotlin) is Google's open-source agent framework, model-agnostic through adapters such as LiteLLM for non-Gemini models.

Mental model. Agents (LlmAgent) are composed into workflows with explicit runners, sessions and callbacks; it ships an evaluation harness and deployment paths to Google Cloud (its managed agent runtime, Cloud Run, GKE). It is session- and runner-centric, so even a one-shot needs a session.

Minimal example (run against the stub; google-adk 2.13.0 with the [extensions] extra plus mcp, so LiteLlm is available). It is the most verbose in this chapter because of the runner/session ceremony:

import asyncio
from google.adk.agents import LlmAgent
from google.adk.models.lite_llm import LiteLlm
from google.adk.runners import InMemoryRunner
from google.genai import types

BASE = "http://127.0.0.1:8080/v1"
MODEL = "mlx-community/Qwen3-14B-4bit"


def get_order(order_id: str) -> dict:
    """Look up an order by id; returns status, amount and tracking_id."""
    return {"order_id": order_id, "status": "shipped", "amount": 129.99,
            "tracking_id": "TRK42", "_stub": "order_lookup_ok"}


def get_shipping_status(tracking_id: str) -> dict:
    """Look up the shipping status for a tracking id."""
    return {"tracking_id": tracking_id, "carrier": "UPS",
            "status": "in_transit", "eta": "2026-11-02",
            "_stub": "shipping_lookup_ok"}


agent = LlmAgent(
    name="support",
    model=LiteLlm(model="openai/" + MODEL, api_base=BASE, api_key="local",
                  extra_body={"chat_template_kwargs": {"enable_thinking": False}}),
    tools=[get_order, get_shipping_status])
runner = InMemoryRunner(agent=agent, app_name="demo")


async def main():
    await runner.session_service.create_session(
        app_name="demo", user_id="u", session_id="s")
    msg = types.Content(role="user",
                        parts=[types.Part(text="Where is my order A1001?")])
    final = ""
    async for ev in runner.run_async(user_id="u", session_id="s",
                                     new_message=msg):
        if ev.is_final_response() and ev.content:
            final = ev.content.parts[0].text
    print(final)


asyncio.run(main())

Order A1001 shipped via UPS (tracking TRK42) and is in transit, ETA 2026-11-02. Amount charged: $129.99.

Strengths. Production-minded (sessions, evaluation, deployment to Vertex); strong multi-agent and workflow primitives; model-agnostic via LiteLLM; native MCP. Minuses. Verbose for simple cases (runner + session service even for one turn); best features point at Google Cloud; the 2.0 major release (May 2026) brought breaking changes recently (for example MCPToolset is now a deprecated alias of McpToolset). Use it when. On Google Cloud/Gemini, or you want the built-in eval and deployment path. Avoid it when. You want a two-line agent, or you have no Google-Cloud footprint. Local models. Yes — LiteLlm(model="openai/…", api_base=…, extra_body=…) (install google-adk[extensions] and mcp). MCP. Yes, native (McpToolset). Licence. Apache-2.0.

docs.title: 8.4 AWS Strands Agents
docs.text:
What and who. Strands Agents (strands-agents, 1.62.0 here; also TypeScript) is AWS's open-source, model-driven agent SDK, v1.0 since July 2025, with multi-agent primitives (graph, swarm) and A2A (agent-to-agent) support.

Mental model. "Model-driven": you give the agent a model, tools and a prompt, and let the model drive the loop; the SDK stays thin. Deep Bedrock integration, but model-agnostic — it has a first-class OpenAIModel for OpenAI-compatible endpoints.

Minimal example (run against the stub; strands-agents 1.62.0):

from strands import Agent, tool
from strands.models.openai import OpenAIModel

BASE = "http://127.0.0.1:8080/v1"
MODEL = "mlx-community/Qwen3-14B-4bit"


@tool
def get_order(order_id: str) -> dict:
    """Look up an order by id; returns status, amount and tracking_id."""
    return {"order_id": order_id, "status": "shipped", "amount": 129.99,
            "tracking_id": "TRK42", "_stub": "order_lookup_ok"}


@tool
def get_shipping_status(tracking_id: str) -> dict:
    """Look up the shipping status for a tracking id."""
    return {"tracking_id": tracking_id, "carrier": "UPS",
            "status": "in_transit", "eta": "2026-11-02",
            "_stub": "shipping_lookup_ok"}


model = OpenAIModel(
    client_args={"base_url": BASE, "api_key": "local"}, model_id=MODEL,
    params={"temperature": 0,
            "extra_body": {"chat_template_kwargs": {"enable_thinking": False}}})
agent = Agent(model=model, tools=[get_order, get_shipping_status],
              callback_handler=None)
result = agent("Where is my order A1001?")
print(result.message["content"][0]["text"])

Order A1001 shipped via UPS (tracking TRK42) and is in transit, ETA 2026-11-02. Amount charged: $129.99.

Strengths. Clean, thin, model-driven design; Apache-2.0; strong AWS/Bedrock integration and OpenTelemetry tracing; native MCP; A2A support. Minuses. Newer ecosystem; best observability/deployment lean on AWS; "let the model drive" gives you less explicit control than a graph. Use it when. On AWS/Bedrock, or you want a thin, open, model-driven SDK that still speaks OpenAI-compatible. Avoid it when. You need explicit, auditable control flow or heavy built-in RAG. Local models. Yes — OpenAIModel(client_args={"base_url": …}, params={"extra_body": …}). MCP. Yes, native (strands.tools.mcp.MCPClient). Licence. Apache-2.0.

docs.title: 8.5 Claude Agent SDK
docs.text:
What and who. Anthropic's Claude Agent SDK (claude-agent-sdk for Python, @anthropic-ai/claude-agent-sdk for TypeScript) is the agent harness that powers Claude Code, renamed from the "Claude Code SDK" in September 2025 (old packages claude-code-sdk and @anthropic-ai/claude-code; the rename also renamed ClaudeCodeOptions → ClaudeAgentOptions, stopped using Claude Code's system prompt by default, and moved the docs). It runs the Claude Code binary as a library — file tools, bash, sub-agents, MCP, permissions, sessions, hooks — behind a programmatic API.

Mental model. Rather than a bare model loop, you drive the same agent harness a coding assistant uses: a rich built-in toolset, a permission system, sub-agents and MCP, orchestrated for you. It is built around Claude models and their tool protocol.

Minimal example. Not run here: it is designed around Claude models and the Claude Code harness, not an arbitrary OpenAI-compatible local endpoint, so it falls outside this chapter's "point it at mlx_lm.server" test. The documented Python shape is async for message in query(prompt=…, options=ClaudeAgentOptions(...)); see https://code.claude.com/docs/en/agent-sdk/overview for a current snippet.

Strengths. The broadest built-in toolset of the SDKs here (file read/write/edit, shell, web search, sub-agents); a detailed permissions model; the same harness Claude Code runs on. Minuses. Tied to Claude models — not a local-model framework; heavier and more opinionated than a generic loop; the recent rename means older material uses the old names. Use it when. You are building on Claude and want coding-assistant-grade tooling and sub-agents without rebuilding the harness. Avoid it when. You need to run on a local OpenAI-compatible model (use a vendor-neutral library instead). Local models. Not meaningfully — it targets Claude; a local Qwen behind an OpenAI-compatible endpoint is not its path. MCP. Yes, first-class (it is an MCP host). Licence. Use is governed by Anthropic's Commercial Terms of Service. The Python package's own source is MIT-licensed, but it runs a bundled Claude Code binary, and the TypeScript package is not open source.

docs.title: 9. Code-agent libraries: smolagents
docs.text:
What and who. smolagents (Hugging Face, 1.26.0 here) is a deliberately small agent library whose headline idea is the code agent: the model writes Python that calls your tools, instead of emitting JSON tool calls.

Mental model. A CodeAgent prompts the model to express each action as a snippet of Python — result = get_order(order_id="A1001") — which runs in a sandbox (local, or E2B/Modal/Docker/Pyodide). This composes multiple calls, loops and data handling in one step, at the cost of a much larger reasoning prompt and the need to sandbox code execution (56 — Safety). A ToolCallingAgent variant asks for ordinary JSON tool calls, which is what maps onto an OpenAI-compatible endpoint.

Minimal example (run against the stub; smolagents 1.26.0). The ToolCallingAgent is used because it requests native tool calls (the tools field, with tool_choice: "required") and finishes by calling a built-in final_answer tool. It replays the history to the model as plain text, though — an assistant turn Calling tools: … and a user turn Observation: … — not as tool messages. The CodeAgent headline mode is shown as a snippet afterward:

from smolagents import ToolCallingAgent, OpenAIServerModel, tool

BASE = "http://127.0.0.1:8080/v1"
MODEL = "mlx-community/Qwen3-14B-4bit"


@tool
def get_order(order_id: str) -> dict:
    """Look up an order by id.

    Args:
        order_id: the order identifier, e.g. A1001.
    """
    return {"order_id": order_id, "status": "shipped", "amount": 129.99,
            "tracking_id": "TRK42", "_stub": "order_lookup_ok"}


@tool
def get_shipping_status(tracking_id: str) -> dict:
    """Look up the shipping status for a tracking id.

    Args:
        tracking_id: the carrier tracking id, e.g. TRK42.
    """
    return {"tracking_id": tracking_id, "carrier": "UPS",
            "status": "in_transit", "eta": "2026-11-02",
            "_stub": "shipping_lookup_ok"}


model = OpenAIServerModel(
    model_id=MODEL, api_base=BASE, api_key="local",
    extra_body={"chat_template_kwargs": {"enable_thinking": False}})
agent = ToolCallingAgent(tools=[get_order, get_shipping_status], model=model,
                         verbosity_level=0)
print(agent.run("Where is my order A1001?"))

Order A1001 shipped via UPS (tracking TRK42) and is in transit, ETA 2026-11-02. Amount charged: $129.99.

The CodeAgent is the same two lines with a different class — CodeAgent(tools=[…], model=model) — but it needs a model fluent in code-writing and a sandbox for execution, so it is not exercised against the simple stub here. (Its first request was logged, though: it describes the tools inside an 8,814-character system prompt instead of sending a tools field.)

Strengths. The code-agent idea is powerful for multi-step data manipulation (fewer round trips); genuinely small and readable core; Hugging Face Hub integration; ToolCallingAgent gives a conventional path when you want it. Minuses. The injected system prompts are large — 3,544 characters for the ToolCallingAgent run above, 8,814 for a CodeAgent with the same two tools (§18.6) — which is real tokens and latency on a local model; executing model-written code demands a sandbox (56); smaller feature set than the big frameworks. Use it when. Tasks that benefit from the model composing code (data wrangling, multi-tool steps), and you can sandbox execution. Avoid it when. You cannot sandbox code, or the token/latency budget is tight on a local model, or you only need a simple JSON tool loop (the baseline is lighter). Local models. Yes — OpenAIServerModel(api_base=…, extra_body=…). The CodeAgent mode needs a model that writes good Python. MCP. Yes, via ToolCollection.from_mcp. Licence. Apache-2.0.

docs.title: 10. Prompt-optimization / programming: DSPy
docs.text:
What and who. DSPy (originated at Stanford NLP; MIT licence; a DSPy open-source team at Databricks and tight MLflow integration; 3.4.1 here) is a different animal: a framework for programming — not prompting — language models, where prompts are compiled from typed signatures and optimised against a metric.

Mental model. You declare signatures ("question -> answer" with typed fields) and compose modules (Predict, ChainOfThought, ReAct). An optimiser (e.g. MIPROv2, GEPA) then tunes the prompts and few-shot examples automatically against an eval set — you optimise a program the way you train a model, instead of hand-editing prompt strings. DSPy drives the model through its own structured text adapters, not native OpenAI tool calls.

Minimal example (run against a DSPy-format stub; dspy 3.4.1). The task is the same two-tool question via dspy.ReAct:

import dspy

BASE = "http://127.0.0.1:8080/v1"
MODEL = "mlx-community/Qwen3-14B-4bit"


def get_order(order_id: str) -> dict:
    """Look up an order by id."""
    return {"order_id": order_id, "status": "shipped", "amount": 129.99,
            "tracking_id": "TRK42", "_stub": "order_lookup_ok"}


def get_shipping_status(tracking_id: str) -> dict:
    """Look up shipping status for a tracking id."""
    return {"tracking_id": tracking_id, "carrier": "UPS",
            "status": "in_transit", "eta": "2026-11-02",
            "_stub": "shipping_lookup_ok"}


dspy.configure(lm=dspy.LM(
    "openai/" + MODEL, api_base=BASE, api_key="local",
    model_type="chat", temperature=0, cache=False,
    extra_body={"chat_template_kwargs": {"enable_thinking": False}}))
react = dspy.ReAct("question -> answer",
                   tools=[get_order, get_shipping_status], max_iters=4)
print(react(question="Where is my order A1001?").answer)

Order A1001 shipped via UPS (tracking TRK42) and is in transit, ETA 2026-11-02. Amount charged: $129.99.

Note

DSPy does not send native tool calls; its ChatAdapter asks the model to emit [[ ## field ## ]] blocks (next_thought, next_tool_name, next_tool_args, then a separate reasoning/answer extract step). The run above therefore used a DSPy-shaped stub that replies in that format; DSPy itself parsed the fields, called both tools, and fed their results back in the next prompt's trajectory (four requests: three ReAct steps and the extract). A real Qwen3-14B is expected to produce those field blocks when prompted by DSPy, though a model can break the format, in which case ChatAdapter falls back to its JSONAdapter; the value of DSPy is not the loop but the optimiser that would tune this program against a labelled set (54 — Evaluation).

Strengths. Turns prompt engineering into measurable optimisation; portable across models (re-compile for a new model); excellent when you have an eval set and want to squeeze quality; MLflow-native observability. Minuses. A genuinely different mental model with a learning curve; the structured-adapter format is particular; overkill if you do not have a metric to optimise against; not primarily a tool/agent-orchestration framework. Use it when. You have an eval set and want to optimise a pipeline's quality systematically, or move prompts between models without rewriting them. Avoid it when. You just need a tool loop, or you have no metric to compile against. Local models. Yes — dspy.LM("openai/…", api_base=…, extra_body=…) (via LiteLLM). MCP. Yes — dspy.Tool.from_mcp_tool wraps MCP tools. Licence. MIT.

docs.title: 11. Stateful and durable-execution platforms
docs.text: Two related needs: persistent agent state (the agent remembers across sessions) and durable execution (a long run survives crashes and restarts).

docs.title: 11.1 Letta (formerly MemGPT)
docs.text:
What and who. Letta (the company and framework that grew out of UC Berkeley's MemGPT research, renamed September 2024) is built around stateful agents with self-editing memory. Its current open-source code is Letta Code (letta-ai/letta-code, npm @letta-ai/letta-code, Apache-2.0): an agent harness with a terminal UI, an App Server you can self-host, channels and SDKs. The original Python API server ("Letta V1") is retired to an archive branch of letta-ai/letta. Letta Cloud, which stores agent state for you, is the default backend; a local backend is an option.

Mental model. The agent owns a structured, persistent memory (memory blocks plus searchable history), stored by the Letta backend and edited by the agent itself; you talk to that backend (Letta Cloud or your own App Server), which keeps the state, so agents live beyond a single process.

Minimal example. Not run here: Letta is server-centric (you run an App Server or use Letta Cloud and talk to it over its API/SDK), which is outside this chapter's single-process stub test. See https://docs.letta.com/ for the current client snippet.

Strengths. Persistent, self-editing memory is the core of the design, not an add-on; agents retain state across sessions and restarts; self-hostable and open. Minuses. The server/stateful model is heavier to operate than a library; the project's focus and APIs have moved quickly (MemGPT → Letta server → Letta Code); you adopt its memory abstraction. Use it when. Long-lived assistants that must remember users and facts across sessions. Avoid it when. Stateless request/response, or you do not want to run a stateful server. Local models. Yes, with limits — a local backend can use the built-in Ollama or LM Studio providers, and an OpenAI-compatible custom provider can be added with /connect (for a Cloud-hosted agent the endpoint must be reachable from the internet, not localhost). MCP. Yes on the Letta platform (register MCP servers; Streamable HTTP recommended), though for Letta Code its docs recommend skills instead of MCP. Licence. Apache-2.0 (Letta Code; Letta Cloud is a hosted service).

docs.title: 11.2 Durable-execution platforms (Temporal, DBOS, Inngest, Restate)
docs.text:
These are not agent frameworks; they are workflow engines you wrap an agent in so a long, multi-step run is crash-safe and resumable. The pattern: each model call and tool call is a durably-recorded step, so if the process dies mid-run it replays deterministically from the last completed step — the durable-execution version of 52's pause-and-resume.

  • Temporal — the mature, self-hostable/managed workflow engine; its SDKs now have agent-oriented helpers. Heavy but battle-tested.
  • DBOS — durable execution as a library backed by Postgres; lighter to adopt.
  • Inngest — event-driven durable functions, popular in the TypeScript world.
  • Restate — a newer durable-execution runtime.

Use them when a run lasts minutes to hours, must survive restarts, or needs exactly-once side effects. LangGraph's checkpointer covers much of this inside one process; a durable-execution platform covers it across process and machine failures. Verify each project's current licence before adopting (several mix open-source cores with commercial cloud tiers).

docs.title: 12. TypeScript frameworks
docs.text: If the product is a Next.js/Node app, do not shell out to Python — use a TS-native framework.

docs.title: 12.1 Mastra
docs.text:
What and who. Mastra is a TypeScript agent framework (agents, workflows, tools, memory, RAG, evals) built on top of the Vercel AI SDK's model layer. Core is Apache-2.0; enterprise features in the ee/ directory are under a separate source-available licence.

Mental model. A batteries-included TS equivalent of the big Python frameworks: typed agents with tools and memory, graph-like workflows, RAG and evals, plus a local dev playground. Model access goes through the Vercel AI SDK, so it reaches any provider the AI SDK supports — including local OpenAI-compatible servers.

Minimal example. Not run here (this chapter's harness is Python). The documented TS shape is new Agent({ model, tools }) with an AI SDK OpenAI-compatible provider pointed at a local baseURL; see https://mastra.ai/docs for a current snippet.

Strengths. Full-featured and TypeScript-native; good DX (playground, typed tools, workflows); rides the AI SDK's broad provider support; MCP support. Minuses. Younger than the Python incumbents; enterprise ee/ code is not Apache-2.0; smaller ecosystem. Use it when. A TS/Next.js product that needs real agent structure (workflows, memory, RAG) rather than just model calls. Avoid it when. You are in Python, or you only need a single model call in a web route (use the AI SDK directly). Local models. Yes — via the Vercel AI SDK's OpenAI-compatible provider with a local baseURL; pass provider options for enable_thinking. MCP. Yes. Licence. Apache-2.0 (core); ee/ under the Mastra Enterprise Licence.

docs.title: 12.2 Vercel AI SDK
docs.text:
What and who. The Vercel AI SDK (ai on npm, Apache-2.0; 7.x in October 2026) is a widely used TypeScript toolkit for building LLM UIs and tool-calling apps — the useChat/streaming layer for React and a provider-agnostic generateText/streamText/tool core.

Mental model. Not an agent-orchestration framework so much as the model + tool-calling + streaming layer for JS: generateText({ model, tools, stopWhen: isStepCount(5) }) runs a tool loop (the older maxSteps option was replaced by stopWhen in AI SDK 5; stepCountIs is the earlier name of isStepCount), and a ToolLoopAgent class packages the same loop; the UI hooks stream it to the browser. For heavier orchestration you layer Mastra (or your own loop) on top.

Minimal example. Not run here (Python harness). The documented shape is generateText({ model: local('mlx-community/Qwen3-14B-4bit'), tools: { getOrder, getShippingStatus }, stopWhen: isStepCount(5) }), where local = createOpenAICompatible({ name: 'local', baseURL: 'http://127.0.0.1:8080/v1' }) from @ai-sdk/openai-compatible; see https://ai-sdk.dev/docs for a current snippet.

Strengths. Widely used for streaming LLM UIs in React/Next.js; provider-agnostic; small and focused; tool-execution approval (needsApproval) for human-in-the-loop; MCP support (createMCPClient from @ai-sdk/mcp). Minuses. Deliberately not a full agent framework (no durable state, limited multi-agent) — you add structure yourself; its agent loop is simpler than LangGraph's. Use it when. Any TS/React app that calls models, streams responses, and does light tool calling. Avoid it when. You need heavy multi-agent orchestration or durable workflows (add Mastra or a durable-execution engine). Local models. Yes — @ai-sdk/openai-compatible with a local baseURL; keys you put under providerOptions.<provider name> (here providerOptions.local) are merged into the request body, which is how chat_template_kwargs gets through. MCP. Yes (createMCPClient from @ai-sdk/mcp; experimental_createMCPClient remains as an alias). Licence. Apache-2.0.

docs.title: 13. Low-code and visual builders
docs.text:
For non-engineers, or for fast internal automations, a drag-and-drop canvas beats code. The trade-off is less control, a runtime to operate, and licences that often restrict resale/multi-tenancy — read them before you build a product on one.

Tool What it is Status & licence (Oct 2026) n8n Workflow automation with AI nodes; huge integration catalogue Active. Source-available under the Sustainable Use License (fair-code) + a separate Enterprise License; internal use allowed, reselling/embedding restricted. Dify LLM-app platform (RAG, agents, prompt IDE) with a visual builder Active. Dify's "Open Source License": Apache-2.0 plus extra conditions (no multi-tenant service without written permission; keep the console logo and copyright), so not an OSI-approved licence. Langflow Visual builder for LLM/agent flows (LangChain-lineage) Active. MIT; owned by IBM (DataStax acquired Langflow in 2024, IBM acquired DataStax in May 2025). Flowise Visual LLM/agent builder Archived: the repository was archived (read-only) on 13 August 2026. Apache-2.0, but an archived project gets no fixes, so do not start new projects on it.

Mental model. You compose nodes on a canvas; each node is a model call, a tool, a condition or an integration; the platform runs and (usually) hosts it. Many can call local OpenAI-compatible endpoints by setting a custom base URL on the model node.

Use them when. Non-engineers own the automation, or you need a fast internal workflow with many SaaS integrations. Avoid them when. You need version control, testing, and code review on the logic (export is often lossy), or the licence conflicts with shipping it in your product. For a permissive licence, Langflow (MIT) is the clearest; n8n and Dify carry commercial restrictions; Flowise is archived — avoid for new work.

docs.title: 14. Local models: the thinking trap
docs.text: The handbook serves Qwen3-14B through mlx_lm.server (10 — Export and serving), an OpenAI-compatible endpoint. Two things about a local, thinking-capable model cut across every framework, so "local-model friendliness" is a real selection criterion — not an afterthought.

docs.title: 14.1 Qwen3 thinks by default
docs.text:
Qwen3 emits a reasoning block before its answer. Through an OpenAI-compatible server, a request without thinking control can return message.content = null, or content that starts with <think>…, and that can confuse naive tool-call parsing and answer extraction. The handbook convention is to pass chat_template_kwargs={"enable_thinking": False} in the request body (with the openai client: extra_body={"chat_template_kwargs": {"enable_thinking": False}}) when you want direct answers and tool calls — and to guard content or "" everywhere, because content can be None.

This demo (run against the stub, which imitates a server that leaves Qwen3's think block in content) shows the difference on the final answer:

import json
from openai import OpenAI

client = OpenAI(base_url="http://127.0.0.1:8080/v1", api_key="local")
MODEL = "mlx-community/Qwen3-14B-4bit"


def final_answer(extra):
    msgs = [
        {"role": "user", "content": "Where is order A1001?"},
        {"role": "assistant", "content": None, "tool_calls": [
            {"id": "t1", "type": "function", "function": {
                "name": "get_shipping_status",
                "arguments": '{"tracking_id": "TRK42"}'}}]},
        {"role": "tool", "tool_call_id": "t1",
         "content": json.dumps({"carrier": "UPS", "status": "in_transit",
                                "_stub": "shipping_lookup_ok"})},
    ]
    r = client.chat.completions.create(model=MODEL, messages=msgs,
                                       temperature=0, **extra)
    return (r.choices[0].message.content or "")


on = final_answer({})
off = final_answer(
    {"extra_body": {"chat_template_kwargs": {"enable_thinking": False}}})
print("default  :", repr(on[:22]))
print("no-think :", repr(off[:22]))

default  : '<think>\nThe task needs'
no-think : 'Order A1001 shipped vi'

With thinking on, this answer begins with a <think> block you must strip; with enable_thinking=False, it is the clean answer (the sentence itself is the stub's canned text). Servers that leave the think block in content behave like this stub. mlx_lm.server 0.32.2 instead moves the reasoning into a separate reasoning field (50 — Prompting and APIs), so there content stays clean, or is None on a turn that only called a tool or ran out of max_tokens while thinking. The thinking tokens are still generated either way, so you wait for them and they can use up a small max_tokens. Turning thinking off for tool loops and guarding None is the fix that works on every server (see 10 §4 for --chat-template-args, which sets it server-wide).

docs.title: 14.2 Can the framework pass extra body fields?
docs.text:
The practical question for each framework: does it let you pass chat_template_kwargs (or arbitrary request-body fields) through to a local OpenAI-compatible endpoint? Every Python framework run in this chapter can, and the exact call differs — this is the real local-model-friendliness criterion:

Framework How to pass enable_thinking=False Baseline (openai) create(..., extra_body={"chat_template_kwargs": {"enable_thinking": False}}) LangGraph / LangChain ChatOpenAI(..., extra_body={...}) LlamaIndex OpenAILike(..., additional_kwargs={"extra_body": {...}}) OpenAI Agents SDK ModelSettings(extra_body={...}) Pydantic AI OpenAIChatModelSettings(extra_body={...}) smolagents OpenAIServerModel(..., extra_body={...}) CrewAI LLM(..., extra_body={...}) Haystack OpenAIChatGenerator(generation_kwargs={"extra_body": {...}}) Agno OpenAILike(..., extra_body={...}) Strands OpenAIModel(params={"extra_body": {...}}) DSPy dspy.LM(..., extra_body={...}) (LiteLLM) Google ADK LiteLlm(..., extra_body={...}) (LiteLLM)

Tip

A framework that makes extra_body hard to reach, or that assumes non-null content, will fight a local thinking model. All twelve above (the baseline and eleven frameworks) sent enable_thinking: false on every request — the stub logged it — and returned the same answer; a framework where you cannot thread that field is a red flag for local-model work.

docs.text:

Versions are the ones actually installed and run for this chapter (the Microsoft Agent Framework, Claude Agent SDK, Letta and the TypeScript frameworks were not run in the chapter; their rows are from docs and PyPI/npm). docs.title: 16. Lines of code for the same task
docs.text:
Counted from the code blocks above, which are the real run_*.py files minus their module docstring (non-blank, non-comment lines; function docstrings count). Every row does the identical two-tool order task and returns the identical answer. The tool bodies are the same everywhere; the difference is the wiring.

Implementation SLOC Notes Agno 19 leanest: plain functions, one Agent DSPy 19 signature + ReAct (different protocol) LangGraph 22 one create_agent call Strands 23 @tool + OpenAIModel LlamaIndex 24 async FunctionAgent OpenAI Agents 25 @function_tool + ModelSettings Pydantic AI 25 @agent.tool_plain smolagents 26 @tool with Args: docstrings CrewAI 27 role + goal + task + crew Haystack 29 pipeline components + Secret Google ADK 34 runner + session ceremony Baseline (no framework) 43 you hand-write the tool schemas and the loop

The frameworks need between 44% (Agno, DSPy: 19 lines) and 79% (ADK: 34 lines) of the baseline's 43 lines, about half to two-thirds for most of them, mostly because they generate tool schemas from function signatures and own the loop.

On paper

The hand-rolled baseline is 43 lines of code; Agno does the same task in 19:

\[ 43 / 19 \approx 2.3 \]

So the baseline is about 2.3 times as long as the leanest framework; against LangGraph (22 lines) the ratio is \(43/22 \approx 1.95\), so LangGraph needs roughly half the lines. That saved code is the benefit; the costs are the abstraction you debug through and the upgrade treadmill of §1.2. ADK at 34 lines shows a framework can also add ceremony (runners, sessions) for a simple task.

docs.title: 17. How to choose: decision tree and scenarios
17.1 Decision tree
docs.text:
START: you have a model endpoint and a task.
│
├─ Is it a single call or a fixed, writable-in-advance workflow?
│     └─ YES → no framework (openai client + a function). [§2]
│
├─ One tool-calling feature inside an existing service?
│     └─ YES → no framework, or a typed/light library (Pydantic AI). [§7.1]
│
├─ TypeScript / Next.js product?
│     ├─ just model calls + streaming + light tools → Vercel AI SDK. [§12.2]
│     └─ real agent structure (workflows, memory, RAG) → Mastra. [§12.1]
│
├─ Retrieval over documents is the core?
│     └─ YES → LlamaIndex (RAG-first) or Haystack (prod pipelines). [§6]
│
├─ Long-running, resumable, human-approved workflow?
│     ├─ within one process → LangGraph (checkpointer + interrupt). [§4.1]
│     └─ across crashes/machines → + a durable-execution engine. [§11.2]
│
├─ Persistent memory across sessions is the point?
│     └─ YES → Letta. [§11.1]
│
├─ Genuinely separate roles with different tools (proven by an eval)?
│     └─ YES → CrewAI, or LangGraph for tighter control. [§5]
│
├─ You have an eval set and want to optimise prompts systematically?
│     └─ YES → DSPy. [§10]
│
├─ On a specific cloud/model vendor?
│     └─ OpenAI → OpenAI Agents; Google → ADK; AWS → Strands;
│        Azure/.NET → MS Agent Framework; Claude harness → Claude Agent SDK. [§8]
│
├─ Non-engineers building automations?
│     └─ YES → low-code (Langflow for MIT; n8n/Dify mind the licence). [§13]
│
└─ Else → start from the baseline; add a typed/light library when it hurts.

docs.text: Scenario Recommended Runner-up Why Single tool-calling feature in an existing service No framework (openai client) Pydantic AI One call + a for loop beats learning a framework; Pydantic AI if you want typing. RAG over company docs LlamaIndex Haystack Richest retrieval toolkit; Haystack if you want explicit, serializable pipelines. Multi-agent research assistant LangGraph CrewAI Explicit orchestration and state; CrewAI if role personas fit and speed matters. Local model on a 32 GB Mac Pydantic AI or baseline Agno Thin, typed, easy extra_body for enable_thinking; Agno for batteries + low overhead. Strict typing / validation Pydantic AI baseline + pydantic Native typed tools and validated structured output. Prompt optimisation against an eval set DSPy — The only framework here built for compiling/optimising prompts. Non-engineers building automations Langflow (MIT) n8n / Dify Permissive licence and a visual canvas; n8n/Dify if their integrations win — mind the licence. Enterprise Azure/.NET shop MS Agent Framework — .NET parity, Azure integration, OTel; the AutoGen/SK successor.

docs.title: 18. Cross-cutting concerns
docs.text: These apply whatever framework you pick (or none).

docs.title: 18.1 Observability
docs.text: You cannot operate what you cannot see. Three neutral facts: the industry is converging on the OpenTelemetry GenAI semantic conventions (standard span/attribute names for model and tool calls), so prefer frameworks that emit them; Langfuse, LangSmith (LangChain's) and Arize Phoenix are widely used tracing/eval backends, and most frameworks have an integration for at least one. Pydantic AI leans on Logfire, DSPy on MLflow, OpenAI Agents and Strands emit traces natively. Whatever you choose, capture per-step spans with token counts and latency, and wire them into production observability (55 — Production §observability).

docs.title: 18.2 Evaluation
docs.text: A framework does not make your agent correct — an eval does. Treat evals as tests whose assertions are thresholds (54 — Evaluation): a golden set of tasks, reference or LLM-judge scoring, run in CI. Several frameworks ship eval helpers (ADK, Mastra, DSPy's optimisers, LangSmith datasets), but the discipline matters more than the tool. Evaluate the whole system — model + prompt + tools + framework glue — not the model in isolation, exactly as 11 §9 evaluates the agent loop rather than the endpoint.

docs.title: 18.3 Testing agents built on frameworks
docs.text:
The techniques are framework-independent:

  • Mock the model. Replace the model with a scripted fake that returns fixed tool calls and answers (52 uses exactly this), so the loop, dispatch and parsing are tested deterministically with no network.
  • Record/replay. Capture real model responses once, then replay them in tests — fast, deterministic, and it catches regressions in your glue.
  • A stub endpoint. The approach this whole chapter used: a tiny OpenAI-compatible server that returns canned tool calls and answers (50 on the request shape). It let eleven frameworks and the baseline run the same task offline (DSPy against a variant that speaks its text format), and it is how you'd test a framework-based agent in CI without a GPU. Make the stub advance only when it sees your tools' real return values, as this one did, so a passing run proves the tools were called.
  • Test tools in isolation. Your get_order is ordinary code — unit-test it without the model.

docs.title: 18.4 Managing upgrades
docs.text: Given the churn (§1.2): pin exact versions (you saw create_react_agent move to create_agent between LangGraph/LangChain versions, Pydantic AI already on 2.x, DSPy on 3.x, ADK and Haystack with new major versions in 2026). Read release notes before bumping. And wrap the framework behind your own interface — a thin Agent class of yours that the rest of the app calls — so a breaking change or a framework swap touches one module, not the whole codebase (§19).

docs.title: 18.5 Security
docs.text:
Frameworks concentrate the risks of 56 — Safety and security, so they deserve extra care:

  • Hidden prompts are attack surface. The framework's injected system prompt is text you did not audit; indirect prompt injection from tool outputs still applies (56).
  • Tool permissions. A framework makes it easy to hand the model many tools; the fewer and more typed, the smaller the blast radius (11 §4, 52). Keep the policy layer in your code, not a prompt.
  • Code-execution agents need sandboxes. A CodeAgent (§9) runs model-written code; never run it unsandboxed. Use the framework's sandbox backends (E2B/Modal/Docker/Pyodide) and treat the output as untrusted.
  • Dependency risk. Hundreds of transitive packages are a supply-chain surface; review them.

docs.title: 18.6 Cost and token overhead
docs.text:
Framework system prompts cost real tokens on every call. Measured here (the stub logged each request): LangGraph, LlamaIndex, Haystack, Pydantic AI, Agno, OpenAI Agents and Strands sent no system prompt of their own; CrewAI sent a 124-character persona system message (plus task framing in the user turn) and ADK a 50-character one; DSPy's adapter sent a 2,265-character format prompt on each ReAct step, because the tool descriptions and field format live in its prompt rather than in a tools field. smolagents' ToolCallingAgent sent a 3,544-character system prompt, the largest of the runs, and its first request was 4,872 bytes versus the baseline's 602. A CodeAgent with the same two tools sends 8,814 characters.

On paper

smolagents' ToolCallingAgent sends a 3544-character system prompt. At about 4 characters per token, over the 3 model calls this task takes:

\[ \begin{aligned} \text{tokens} &\approx 3544 / 4 = 886\\ \text{per task} &\approx 3 \times 886 = 2658 \end{aligned} \]

Each call carries about 886 tokens of scaffolding, about 5% of a 16K window, and the task makes the model read about 2,700 of them in total. On a local model that is prefill time: at roughly 120 prompt tokens/s (Qwen3-14B 4-bit on an M1 Pro, 50), 886 tokens take about 7 s on any call that the server's prompt cache cannot serve.

On paper

The stub logged smolagents' first request at 4872 bytes and the baseline's at 602:

\[ 4872 / 602 \approx 8.1 \]

Eight times the bytes on the wire. Most of the 4,270 extra bytes are the 3,544-character system prompt; the rest is its final_answer tool and longer tool descriptions. Most frameworks add little; smolagents trades tokens for its reasoning scaffold. Measure yours — do not assume it is zero.

If you pay per token, that overhead has a price. Hosted-model prices move, so treat the number as an assumption, not a fact:

On paper

Assume $0.50 per million input tokens. With 2658 scaffold tokens per task and 100,000 tasks a day:

\[ \begin{aligned} \text{per task} &\approx 2658/10^6 \times 0.50 \approx 0.0013\\ \text{per day} &\approx 10^5 \times 0.001329 \approx 133 \end{aligned} \]

About $133 a day is the framework's system-prompt tax alone (before any prompt-cache discount), before your own prompt and the outputs. For a local model the cost is latency and context instead of dollars, but it is just as real.

docs.title: 19.1 From no framework to a framework
docs.text:
You start with the baseline (§2.1) and outgrow it (you need durable state, or multi-agent, or RAG). The migration is mechanical because the pieces map:

  • Your tool functions become the framework's tools (usually just a decorator or passing the function).
  • Your hand-written TOOLS schema is deleted — the framework generates it from signatures and docstrings. (So keep good type hints and docstrings even in the baseline.)
  • Your run() loop becomes the framework's agent/runner.
  • Your extra_body for enable_thinking moves to the framework's model-settings call (§14.2).

Migrate behind your eval (§18.2): the answers should stay correct (against the stub every framework above printed the identical output; against a real model the wording can change, which is why you check with the eval rather than a string compare), so the eval catches any regression the migration introduces.

docs.title: 19.2 From a framework back to no framework (or to another)
docs.text:
This is the one teams underestimate. If the framework's abstractions fight you, or it churns too hard, you may want out. It is painful only if you coupled to it everywhere. The defence is an adapter layer: define your own small interface, make it the only module that imports the framework, and keep everything else depending on your type. Here the adapter wraps Pydantic AI (§7.1); the shape is the same whatever you wrap:

import os
os.environ["PYDANTIC_AI_NO_BANNER"] = "1"
from typing import Protocol
from pydantic_ai import Agent
from pydantic_ai.models.openai import OpenAIChatModel, OpenAIChatModelSettings
from pydantic_ai.providers.openai import OpenAIProvider

BASE = "http://127.0.0.1:8080/v1"
MODEL = "mlx-community/Qwen3-14B-4bit"


class OrderAgent(Protocol):
    def answer(self, question: str) -> str: ...


def get_order(order_id: str) -> dict:
    """Look up an order by id; returns status, amount and tracking_id."""
    return {"order_id": order_id, "status": "shipped", "amount": 129.99,
            "tracking_id": "TRK42", "_stub": "order_lookup_ok"}


def get_shipping_status(tracking_id: str) -> dict:
    """Look up the shipping status for a tracking id."""
    return {"tracking_id": tracking_id, "carrier": "UPS",
            "status": "in_transit", "eta": "2026-11-02",
            "_stub": "shipping_lookup_ok"}


class PydanticAIOrderAgent:
    """The only class (in the only module) that touches the framework."""
    def __init__(self, tools):
        model = OpenAIChatModel(
            MODEL, provider=OpenAIProvider(base_url=BASE, api_key="local"))
        settings = OpenAIChatModelSettings(
            extra_body={"chat_template_kwargs": {"enable_thinking": False}})
        self._agent = Agent(model, tools=tools, model_settings=settings)

    def answer(self, question: str) -> str:
        return self._agent.run_sync(question).output


agent: OrderAgent = PydanticAIOrderAgent([get_order, get_shipping_status])
print(agent.answer("Where is my order A1001?"))

Order A1001 shipped via UPS (tracking TRK42) and is in transit, ETA 2026-11-02. Amount charged: $129.99.

The rest of your app depends on OrderAgent and your plain tool functions, not on Pydantic AI, LangGraph or CrewAI. Swapping frameworks — or dropping back to the baseline loop of §2.1 — then means writing one new class with the same answer method, with your eval proving the behaviour held. This also neutralises the upgrade churn of §18.4: a breaking change lands in one file.

Tip

Write the adapter on day one, even if you are sure of your framework choice. It costs about a dozen lines — the Protocol and the wrapper class above — and buys you an exit. The frameworks took 19 to 34 lines for this task; the wrapper adds only that dozen on top of whichever one you pick.

docs.title: 20. Key takeaways
docs.text:
• A framework is leverage you rent: it removes boilerplate (schema generation, the loop, state, streaming, tracing) and in exchange you debug through its abstractions and ride its upgrade treadmill. Justify every departure from the ~43-line baseline.
  • Most "agent" problems are a single call or a fixed workflow (52). Use the least autonomy — and the least framework — that solves the task.
  • Pick by category, then by fit: graph/state-machine (LangGraph), role multi-agent (CrewAI), data/RAG (LlamaIndex, Haystack), typed/light (Pydantic AI, Agno), vendor SDKs (OpenAI Agents, MS Agent Framework, Google ADK, AWS Strands, Claude Agent SDK), code-agent (smolagents), prompt-opt (DSPy), stateful (Letta), TypeScript (Mastra, Vercel AI SDK), low-code (Langflow/n8n/Dify; Flowise is archived).
  • Status changed in 2025–2026: AutoGen and Semantic Kernel → Microsoft Agent Framework (AutoGen archived, Semantic Kernel on critical and security fixes); LangChain 1.x runs on LangGraph; the Claude Code SDK → Claude Agent SDK; Flowise archived; Letta's server gave way to Letta Code.
  • Local, thinking models are a real criterion. Qwen3 thinks by default; pass chat_template_kwargs={"enable_thinking": False} and guard content or "". Every Python framework here can thread that through extra_body; one that can't is a red flag (§14).
  • Measure the overhead. System-prompt tokens are real (3,544 chars / ~886 tokens per call for smolagents here); so is lines-of-code; so is churn. Numbers beat vibes.
  • Wrap the framework behind your own interface and pin versions, so a breaking change or a framework swap touches one module (§19).
  • Licences matter for shipping: most libraries are MIT or Apache-2.0; n8n and Dify add commercial restrictions (source-available, and modified Apache-2.0); the Claude Agent SDK is under Anthropic's commercial terms; Flowise is archived.

docs.title: 21. Exercises
docs.text:
Exercise 21.1

You are adding "summarise this ticket and tag its priority" to an existing support service. Which framework do you reach for, and why?

Answer

None. That is a single model call (or a two-step extract-then-classify workflow), not an agent (52). The openai client plus the structured-output pattern (50) is fewer lines than learning a framework, has no hidden prompt, and you already own the service's deployment and state. Reach for a framework only when the decision procedure of §2.2 pulls you past step 2.

Exercise 21.2

The same two-tool order task is 43 lines in the no-framework baseline and 19 in Agno. Compute the ratio and say what the saved lines cost you.

Answer

\(43 / 19 \approx 2.3\). The baseline is about 2.3x larger, mostly because it hand-writes the TOOLS JSON schema and the loop, which Agno generates from signatures and owns internally. The saved lines cost you an abstraction layer to debug through, a hidden system prompt, a dependency tree, and an upgrade treadmill (§1.2). Worth it when you need the batteries; not worth it for a single call.

Exercise 21.3

Your agent, on a local Qwen3-14B, sometimes returns an empty or <think>…-prefixed answer through the framework. What are the two fixes, and how do you apply them in (a) the raw openai client and (b) LangGraph?

Answer

(1) Disable thinking by passing chat_template_kwargs={"enable_thinking": False}; (2) guard content or "" because content can be None. In the raw client: create(..., extra_body={"chat_template_kwargs": {"enable_thinking": False}}). In LangGraph: ChatOpenAI(..., extra_body={"chat_template_kwargs": {"enable_thinking": False}}). See §14; every Python framework here exposes extra_body by some name.

Exercise 21.4

smolagents' ToolCallingAgent system prompt measured 3,544 characters. Estimate the token overhead per task if the task takes 3 model calls, at ~4 characters per token.

Answer

\(3544 / 4 = 886\) tokens per call, and \(3 \times 886 = 2658\) tokens per task — about 2,700 tokens of scaffolding the model must read before it gets to the order data. Each call's 886 tokens are about 5% of a 16K window, and at roughly 120 prompt tokens/s of local prefill they add about 7 s to every call the prompt cache cannot serve (§18.6). A CodeAgent sends 8,814 characters, about 2,200 tokens per call; it can still be worth it when composing several tool calls in one code step saves round trips — measure both.

Exercise 21.5

A teammate proposes a three-agent CrewAI "crew" (researcher, writer, reviewer) for a task a single agent handles today. Each agent step succeeds with probability 0.98. What happens to reliability and cost, and what do you ask for before agreeing?

Answer

Reliability compounds down with more steps (52): a single call is \(0.98\), while a naive 5-step three-agent flow is about \(0.98^5 \approx 0.904\) — and each agent re-sends its own context, so cost and latency multiply. Ask for an eval (§18.2) showing the crew beats the single agent on the real task. If it does not, the extra agents are cost and coordination risk for nothing (52).

Exercise 21.6

You built on AutoGen a year ago. What is the current status, and what should you do?

Answer

AutoGen is archived: its README says Microsoft no longer provides bug fixes, security fixes, new features or support, and names the Microsoft Agent Framework (GA April 2026; agent-framework on PyPI) as its successor, with an AutoGen migration guide (§8.2). Without security fixes, staying put is a growing risk, so plan the migration as scheduled work: put an adapter around the AutoGen code first (§19.2), port behind your eval, then switch. (Had you built on Semantic Kernel instead, you would have more time: it still gets critical and security fixes for at least a year after the Agent Framework's GA.) This is the churn risk of §1.2 made concrete.

Exercise 21.7

Why is "wrap the framework behind your own interface" worth a dozen lines on day one?

Answer

Because it localises both risks of §1.2: a breaking upgrade or a decision to swap frameworks (or drop back to the baseline) touches one adapter module instead of the whole codebase (§19.2). The frameworks here took 19 to 34 lines for the task (the baseline 43); the wrapper adds about a dozen lines on top of any of them, and your eval proves behaviour held across the swap.

Exercise 21.8

You need RAG over company docs and a long-running, human-approved workflow around it. One framework, or two layers?

Answer

Two concerns, so consider two layers: a data/RAG framework for retrieval (§6 — LlamaIndex or Haystack) and a graph/state-machine for the durable, human-gated workflow (§4.1 — LangGraph's checkpointer + interrupt). LangGraph can call a LlamaIndex/Haystack retriever as a tool. If retrieval is simple, one framework with a retrieval integration may suffice; if the workflow is simple, add retrieval to a lighter agent. Let the dominant concern pick the primary framework, and keep both behind your adapter (§19.2).

Exercise 21.9

You want to ship a visual agent builder inside your commercial SaaS so customers can build flows. Which low-code tool's licence is safest, and which should you avoid?

Answer

Langflow is MIT, a permissive licence that allows embedding in a product. n8n (Sustainable Use License, source-available) and Dify (its "Open Source License": Apache-2.0 plus extra conditions) restrict reselling, multi-tenant use or embedding — read them before shipping, and get written permission or a commercial licence if needed. Flowise was archived on 13 August 2026 and gets no fixes — do not build new on it (§13).

Exercise 21.10

How did this chapter test eleven frameworks' agents (plus the baseline) without a GPU or a hosted model, and why does that generalise to testing your own framework-based agent?

Answer

With a stub OpenAI-compatible server that returns canned tool calls and a final answer, driven by sentinels — marker strings that only the tools' return values contain — so it advances only after each tool has really run (§2.1 note, §18.3); DSPy used a variant that speaks its text format. Each framework was pointed at it and printed the identical answer (the stub's canned sentence), offline and deterministically. The same technique tests your production agent: mock the model (or stub the endpoint), record/replay real responses, and unit-test the tools as ordinary code — so your CI exercises the loop and the glue without a model at all.

Next: 62 — Integrating agents for how any of these is wired into a product and 63 — Agents in the real world for twelve applications; 52 — Agents and tool use for the loop these frameworks wrap, 58 — MCP for the tool protocol they share, and 54 — Evaluation to prove any choice here is the right one.

docs.title: 62 — Integrating agents into applications
docs.text:
Last verified: 29 October 2026.

You have an agent loop that works in a script: a model, a handful of tools, a for loop with a step budget (52 §6). This chapter is about the distance between that script and a feature that many people use inside a real product. It covers the shapes an agent can take inside an application (an in-process call, a run service, a streaming chat UI, a queue worker, a batch job, a durable workflow, an agent used as a tool, a local harness), the run contract (request, record, events, states), state and sessions, identity and per-user tool scopes, how to connect tools, approvals inside a product UI, streaming, reliability, observability, cost control, testing, rollout, and a runnable minimal agent service built from the standard library. It does not re-teach the loop, the workflow patterns, autonomy levels, the reliability and cost math, or the idea of a budget and a human gate — those are 52 — Agents; the frameworks that package some of this are 61 — Agent frameworks; the serving stack, gateway and observability basics are 55 — Production. Every Python block here runs; where a model is needed, the code calls the handbook's local mlx_lm.server and was tested against a stub that imitates it, Qwen3 thinking mode included.

The one idea to carry through: an agent in a product is a long-lived, resumable, auditable job with a budget — not a function call. Design the job first; the model is one step inside it.

docs.title: 1. From a script to a feature
1.1 What changes
docs.text:
In the script, one person runs one task on their own machine, reads the output, and stops the process when it misbehaves. Inside a product every one of those assumptions breaks:

  • Many users at once. Runs overlap. Two users' transcripts must never mix; one user's runaway run must not starve the others. The loop becomes a worker pool with a queue.
  • Identity. The script used your credentials. In the product the agent acts on behalf of a user, with that user's permissions and nothing more (§5).
  • Latency budgets. A request handler has a timeout. An agent that takes 40 seconds cannot live inside a 10-second request; it becomes a run you create, poll or stream (§2, §8).
  • Failures are routine. The model times out, a tool returns 503, a worker restarts mid-run. A run must be resumable from its last step, and a retry must not refund twice (§4, §9).
  • Cost ceilings. The script's bill was yours. The product's bill is the sum over every user and every step, and a prompt-injected or looping agent is an unbounded spend without a hard budget enforced by the runtime, not by the prompt (§9.5, §11).
  • Observability. You can no longer read the terminal. Every run needs a trace, structured logs, and metrics that say whether the feature works (§10).
  • Change management. A prompt edit is a deploy. You need versions, canaries, a kill switch, and a plan for runs that are in flight when you ship (§13).

A software-engineering analogy: the script is a shell one-liner; the feature is a job system with a scheduler, a job table, retries, idempotency, auth, metrics and a dashboard. The agent loop is the job's body. Most of this chapter is job-system engineering you already know, applied to a body that is non-deterministic and that can act.

docs.title: 1.2 Integration readiness
docs.text:
Before shipping, check each row. "Script" is where most agents start; "feature" is where they must be.

Concern Script Feature Who runs it you, by hand any user, concurrently, via a product surface Credentials your own the user's, scoped per tool and per tenant (§5) Lifetime one process, one task a run record with a state machine, resumable (§3, §4) Failure stack trace in the terminal retries with idempotency; a failed state with a reason (§9) Budget max_steps steps, tokens, wall time and money, enforced by the runtime (§9.5) Side effects happen gated by approvals and an audit log (§5.4, §7) Output printed streamed as events; stored as a record (§3, §8) Cost your API key per-run and per-tenant ceilings, a monthly model (§11) Visibility you watch it one trace per run; dashboards; alerts (§10) Change edit and rerun versioned prompts and tools; shadow → canary → GA; kill switch (§13) Tests "it worked on my ticket" record/replay, tool contracts, golden trajectories, eval gates in CI (§12)

docs.title: 2. Integration shapes
docs.text: An agent can be wired into a product in eight recognizable shapes. Each has a diagram, a case where it fits, an example product, and trade-offs. Pick by the requirements in §2.9, not by habit.

docs.title: 2.1 In-process call inside a request handler
docs.text:
The agent runs synchronously inside an existing HTTP handler, with a small step budget, and returns with the response.

client ──POST /tickets/{id}/suggest──▶ handler
                                         │ loop ≤ 3 steps, ≤ 8 s
                                         ├─▶ model ─▶ tool ─▶ model
                                         ▼
client ◀────── 200 {suggestion} ───────┘

When: the task is short (1–3 steps), read-only or low-risk, and must fit the handler's timeout. Example: a "suggest a reply" button in a support console that looks up the order and drafts two sentences. Trade-offs: the simplest shape — no new infrastructure, no run table — but the handler's timeout is your hard budget, there is nothing to resume if the process dies, the user sees nothing until the end, and a slow model call ties up a request worker. Treat it as the single-call pattern of 52 §1 with one or two tool round trips, and nothing more.

docs.title: 2.2 An agent service with run ids
docs.text:
The product creates a run and gets an id back immediately; a worker executes it; the client polls the record or streams its events.

client ──POST /runs──▶ API ──▶ queue ──▶ worker pool ──▶ model / tools
   ▲        │ 202 {run_id}      │              │
   │        ▼                   ▼              ▼
   └──GET /runs/{id} ◀───── run store ◀── state, steps, events
   └──GET /runs/{id}/events (SSE)

When: runs take seconds to minutes, may need approvals, and must survive a client that disconnects. Example: "investigate this incident" in an on-call tool — the run takes two minutes, calls six tools, and the engineer comes back to the result. Trade-offs: you now own a run store, a queue, workers and a state machine (§3) — real engineering — but you gain resumability, budgets enforced centrally, auditing, cancellation, and one place to put every cross-cutting concern. This is the default shape for anything beyond §2.1, and §14 builds one.

docs.title: 2.3 A chat or assistant UI with streaming and visible tool calls
docs.text:
A conversation surface where each user turn starts a run, the run's events stream to the UI as they happen, and tool calls are shown as collapsible steps.

user turn ──▶ run ──▶ events: tool.called ─▶ "Looking up order A1001…"
                              tool.result ─▶ "charged twice, $20"
                              approval.required ─▶ [Approve refund $20] [Deny]
                              message.delta ─▶ "Refunded $20.00 on…"

When: the user is present, wants to see progress, and may be asked to approve. Example: a billing assistant inside the account page. Trade-offs: the best experience for interactive work and the natural home for approvals; but you must design what each event looks like, keep the conversation state across turns (§4.1), handle disconnects (§8.4), and resist streaming raw model reasoning to end users (§8.1). It is §2.2 plus a UI contract.

docs.title: 2.4 An event-driven worker on a queue
docs.text:
No user starts the run; an event does — a webhook, a "ticket created" message, a file landing in a bucket.

"ticket.created" ──▶ queue ──▶ worker: run(agent, ticket)
                                  │ writes: labels, a draft, a note
                                  ▼
                            ticket system ◀── (human reviews the draft)

When: the work is triggered by the system, not a person, and nobody is waiting on a screen. Example: every new ticket gets triaged — category, priority, a draft reply saved as an internal note for an agent to send or edit. Trade-offs: scales naturally with the queue and tolerates bursts; but with no user present, a bad action has no one to stop it — so writes are "suggest" or "act and report" level (52 §8), failures must page an operator, and you need dead-letter handling and idempotent consumption (the same event delivered twice must not run twice — §4.3).

docs.title: 2.5 Scheduled and batch agents
docs.text:
A scheduler fans out one run per item at a fixed time: nightly, hourly, weekly.

cron 02:00 ──▶ select 5,000 stale tickets ──▶ N workers ──▶ run per ticket
                                                   │ rate-limited, budgeted
                                                   ▼
                                             report: 4,870 ok, 130 failed

When: throughput matters more than latency and the work is embarrassingly parallel. Example: re-categorize the backlog after a taxonomy change; summarize every long thread older than 30 days. Trade-offs: cheapest per item (pack batches, run off-peak — 55 §17); but a bug multiplies by N before anyone looks, so run a sample first, cap the batch's total budget, and make every item's run idempotent so a re-run after a crash skips what is done.

docs.title: 2.6 A durable workflow engine
docs.text:
For runs lasting minutes to days with approvals in the middle, wrap the loop in a workflow engine that records every step durably and replays after a crash: Temporal, DBOS, Inngest, Restate, or LangGraph's checkpointer inside one process (61 §11.2).

workflow(run):
  step 1: model call      ──▶ recorded
  step 2: tool: get_order ──▶ recorded
  step 3: wait_for_signal("approval", timeout=24h)   ◀── human, hours later
  step 4: tool: issue_refund (exactly once)
  step 5: model call → done
       crash anywhere ──▶ restart replays 1..k from the log, continues at k+1

When: a run must survive restarts and deploys, wait hours for a human, and apply side effects exactly once. Example: a vendor-onboarding agent that gathers documents, waits for compliance sign-off, then creates accounts. Trade-offs: you get crash safety and long waits for free; you pay with determinism rules (the workflow body must replay identically, so model calls and tools live in "activities"), an engine to operate, and a learning curve. Use it when §2.2's "resume from the last checkpoint" is not enough.

docs.title: 2.7 Agent as a tool inside another agent or workflow
docs.text:
A whole agent is exposed as one tool with a typed input and output, and an orchestrator — another agent or a fixed workflow — calls it like any other function (52 §11).

orchestrator ──▶ tool: research_agent(question) ──▶ {answer, sources, cost}
             ──▶ tool: code_agent(spec)           ──▶ {diff, tests_passed}
             ──▶ synthesize

When: sub-problems are genuinely separable with different tools, and an eval shows the split helps. Example: a release-notes workflow that calls a "summarize this PR" agent per PR, then a fixed template. Trade-offs: clean boundaries and independent testing per sub-agent; but each nested agent has its own budget, its own failure modes and its own cost, so the outer run's budget must cap the sum (§9.5), and the inner agent's result must be structured and size-capped like any tool result (§6.1).

docs.title: 2.8 Local harnesses: IDE, CLI, the Kali agent
docs.text:
The agent runs on the user's machine or in their VM, with tools that touch local files, a shell, or a lab network. Coding assistants in an IDE, a CLI agent, and the handbook's Kali agent — a local Qwen3-14B driving typed tools behind a deterministic policy layer — are this shape (11 — The Kali agent, 11 §1).

user ◀──▶ harness (IDE / CLI) ──▶ model (local or remote)
              │ policy: scope, allow-list, confirm, audit
              ▼
          tools: files, shell, nmap_scan … (sandboxed)

When: the data and the actions live on the user's machine, and the user is the approver. Example: "fix the failing test" in an editor; "enumerate services on the in-scope host" in the lab. Trade-offs: the richest tools and the tightest human loop; but the harness runs with the user's local privileges, so the policy layer, allow-lists and audit log (11 §5) carry the whole safety story, and nothing is observable centrally unless the harness reports home.

docs.title: 2.9 Choosing a shape
docs.text:
Map requirements to shapes. When two shapes fit, pick the simpler one on the left.

Requirement In-process (2.1) Run service (2.2) Chat UI (2.3) Queue worker (2.4) Batch (2.5) Durable (2.6) Agent-as-tool (2.7) Local (2.8) Latency: answer in < 10 s yes poll/stream stream — — — — yes Duration: seconds–minutes ≤ 3 steps yes yes yes yes yes inside parent yes Duration: hours–days, survives restarts no checkpoints no with retries no yes no no Human approvals mid-run no yes yes no (nobody present) no yes via parent yes Volume: thousands of items no with workers no yes yes costly — no Side effects allowed read-only gated gated suggest / report idempotent only exactly-once parent's gate policy layer User is present yes optional yes no no optional — yes New infrastructure none store + queue + workers + UI contract queue scheduler engine — harness
