                if accepted:
                    run["approval"].put(decision)
            if accepted:
                return self.send(202, {"run_id": run["id"], "state": run["state"]})
            if run["state"] == "waiting_approval":
                return self.send(409, {"error": "a decision for this approval is already queued"})
        if parts[2] == "cancel" and run["state"] not in TERMINAL:
            run["cancel"].set()
            run["approval"].put(False)          # unblock a run waiting on approval
            return self.send(202, {"run_id": run["id"], "state": run["state"]})
        self.send(409, {"error": f"cannot {parts[2]} a run in state {run['state']}"})
    def do_GET(self):
        parts = self.path.strip("/").split("/")
        run = RUNS.get(parts[1]) if len(parts) >= 2 and parts[0] == "runs" else None
        if run is None:
            return self.send(404, {"error": "no such run"})
        if len(parts) == 2:
            return self.send(200, {k: run[k] for k in ("id", "state", "user", "steps",
                                                       "tokens", "pending", "result", "error")})
        self.send_response(200)                 # /runs/{id}/events: Server-Sent Events
        self.send_header("Content-Type", "text/event-stream")
        self.end_headers()
        last = int(self.headers.get("Last-Event-ID", 0))
        while True:
            with COND:
                COND.wait_for(lambda: len(run["events"]) > last or run["state"] in TERMINAL,
                              timeout=5)
                new, done = run["events"][last:], run["state"] in TERMINAL
            for ev in new:
                self.wfile.write(f"id: {ev['id']}\nevent: {ev['event']}\n"
                                 f"data: {json.dumps(ev)}\n\n".encode())
            self.wfile.flush()
            last += len(new)
            if done:
                return

for _ in range(2):
    threading.Thread(target=worker, daemon=True).start()
print(f"agent service on 127.0.0.1:{PORT}", flush=True)
ThreadingHTTPServer(("127.0.0.1", PORT), Api).serve_forever()

What it printed while the client session of §14.3 ran against it:

agent service on 127.0.0.1:18741
run_0001 -> running
run_0001 -> waiting_approval
run_0001 -> running
run_0001 -> completed

Where each section of the chapter lives in the file: the run contract and state machine (§3) are NEXT, EVENT, emit and transition — the state change and its event are written under one lock so a streamer never sees one without the other; the per-run allow-list (§5.2) is allowed_tools, applied both to the schemas the model sees and to dispatch; the read/write split and the approval pause (§6.4, §7) are run_tool and the approve branch of do_POST, which takes one decision per pending approval under the same lock, so a double-clicked button cannot pre-approve the run's next write; the budgets (§9.5) are the four checks at the top of execute; cancellation (§9.6) is the flag checked at step boundaries and inside the approval wait; the idempotent create (§4.3) is the key lookup in do_POST; and reconnect (§8.4) is the Last-Event-ID filter in do_GET. What a production version adds is a database behind RUNS (with transition as a conditional UPDATE), a worker that is released during waiting_approval and a run that is re-enqueued by the approval (here the worker blocks on run["approval"], §7.2), the trace and audit log, per-tenant budgets, scoped credentials in the tool wrappers, and real identity on the request instead of a trusted user field.

docs.title: 14.3 A client session
docs.text:
A client that creates a run, streams its events, approves the write when asked, reads the record, retries the create with the same idempotency key, and reconnects from the middle of the stream:

import json, urllib.request

BASE = "http://127.0.0.1:18741"

def call(method, path, body=None, headers=None):
    data = json.dumps(body).encode() if body is not None else None
    req = urllib.request.Request(BASE + path, data=data, method=method,
                                 headers={"Content-Type": "application/json", **(headers or {})})
    with urllib.request.urlopen(req) as r:
        return json.load(r)

def stream(path, headers=None, on_event=lambda ev: None):
    req = urllib.request.Request(BASE + path, headers=headers or {})
    with urllib.request.urlopen(req) as r:
        for raw in r:                               # one SSE line at a time
            line = raw.decode().rstrip("\n")
            if line.startswith("data: "):
                ev = json.loads(line[6:])
                extra = {k: v for k, v in ev.items() if k not in ("id", "event", "step")}
                print(f"  {ev['id']:>2} {ev['event']:<18} {extra or ''}".rstrip())
                on_event(ev)

req = {"user": "u_42", "input": "Refund the duplicate charge on order A1001.",
       "idempotency_key": "ticket-7781"}
created = call("POST", "/runs", req)
print("created:", created)
rid = created["run_id"]

def approve_writes(ev):
    if ev["event"] == "approval.required":
        print("approve:", call("POST", f"/runs/{rid}/approve", {"approved": True}))

stream(f"/runs/{rid}/events", on_event=approve_writes)
print("record:", call("GET", f"/runs/{rid}"))
print("same key again:", call("POST", "/runs", req))
print("reconnect from event 7:")
stream(f"/runs/{rid}/events", headers={"Last-Event-ID": "7"})

created: {'run_id': 'run_0001', 'state': 'queued'}
   1 run.started
   2 tool.called        {'tool': 'get_order', 'args': {'order_id': 'A1001'}}
   3 tool.result        {'tool': 'get_order', 'result': {'status': 'charged_twice', 'amount': 20.0}}
   4 tool.called        {'tool': 'issue_refund', 'args': {'order_id': 'A1001', 'amount': 20.0}}
   5 approval.required  {'pending': {'tool': 'issue_refund', 'args': {'order_id': 'A1001', 'amount': 20.0}}}
approve: {'run_id': 'run_0001', 'state': 'waiting_approval'}
   6 run.resumed        {'pending': None, 'approved': True}
   7 tool.result        {'tool': 'issue_refund', 'result': {'refunded': 20.0, 'order_id': 'A1001'}}
   8 message.delta      {'text': 'Refunded $20.00 on order A1001: the duplicate charge is reversed and one valid charge remains.'}
   9 run.completed      {'result': 'Refunded $20.00 on order A1001: the duplicate charge is reversed and one valid charge remains.'}
record: {'id': 'run_0001', 'state': 'completed', 'user': 'u_42', 'steps': 3, 'tokens': 713, 'pending': None, 'result': 'Refunded $20.00 on order A1001: the duplicate charge is reversed and one valid charge remains.', 'error': None}
same key again: {'run_id': 'run_0001', 'state': 'completed'}
reconnect from event 7:
   8 message.delta      {'text': 'Refunded $20.00 on order A1001: the duplicate charge is reversed and one valid charge remains.'}
   9 run.completed      {'result': 'Refunded $20.00 on order A1001: the duplicate charge is reversed and one valid charge remains.'}

Read it against the state machine: the run started, read the order, proposed the refund (event 4 is emitted before anything runs), paused (event 5, the run is waiting_approval and the worker is blocked on the queue), resumed on the approval (event 6), executed the write, streamed the answer and completed. The record shows the three model calls and the 713 tokens they consumed, which the token budget was checked against. The second create with the same key returned the same run without running anything; the reconnect with Last-Event-ID: 7 replayed only events 8 and 9.

docs.title: 14.4 Budgets, scopes and cancellation from the client
docs.text:
Three more runs against the same service, started right after the session above: one whose approval nobody answers within its one-second budget, one for a user whose scope has no write tool, and one the user cancels while it waits for approval.

import json, time, urllib.request

BASE = "http://127.0.0.1:18741"
TASK = "Refund the duplicate charge on order A1001."

def call(method, path, body=None):
    data = json.dumps(body).encode() if body is not None else None
    req = urllib.request.Request(BASE + path, data=data, method=method,
                                 headers={"Content-Type": "application/json"})
    with urllib.request.urlopen(req) as r:
        return json.load(r)

def wait_for(rid, states):
    while True:
        rec = call("GET", f"/runs/{rid}")
        if rec["state"] in states:
            return rec
        time.sleep(0.05)

DONE = {"completed", "failed", "cancelled", "timed_out"}
# 1. nobody answers the approval within this run's budget
a = call("POST", "/runs", {"user": "u_42", "input": TASK,
                           "constraints": {"approval_seconds": 1}})["run_id"]
# 2. a user whose scope has no write tool
b = call("POST", "/runs", {"user": "u_99", "input": TASK,
                           "allowed_tools": ["get_order"]})["run_id"]
# 3. the user cancels while the run waits for approval
c = call("POST", "/runs", {"user": "u_42", "input": TASK})["run_id"]
wait_for(c, {"waiting_approval"})
print("cancel:", call("POST", f"/runs/{c}/cancel"))
for rid in (a, b, c):
    rec = wait_for(rid, DONE)
    print(f"{rid}: {rec['state']:<10} steps={rec['steps']} "
          f"error={rec['error']!r} result={rec['result']!r}")

cancel: {'run_id': 'run_0004', 'state': 'waiting_approval'}
run_0002: timed_out  steps=2 error='approval timed out' result=None
run_0003: completed  steps=2 error=None result='Order A1001 was charged twice, but this run has no refund tool; please escalate to billing.'
run_0004: cancelled  steps=2 error=None result=None

Run 2 timed out at its approval deadline with the reason on the record; run 3 never saw issue_refund — the model was offered one tool and answered accordingly (the stub's canned sentence; a real model would also have to stop at "no refund tool" because the schema is simply absent); run 4 went from waiting_approval to cancelled without the write executing. All three ended in a terminal state with the worker released, which is the property the whole chapter is about.

docs.title: 14.5 What a real model changes
docs.text: Against a real Qwen3-14B on mlx_lm.server the service code is unchanged; the behaviour in the stream differs in three ways. The model chooses the calls — it may call get_order with the id spelled differently, add a second lookup, or answer a clarifying question instead of refunding (a completed run whose result is a question — the UI must handle it). Token counts are real: the tool schemas alone are a few hundred tokens of prefix on every step (58 §11.2), so tokens on the record lands in the low thousands, and the per-step latency is seconds, not milliseconds — which is why approval.required and tool.called must stream immediately. And thinking: the service sends enable_thinking: false on every call (the stub logged it on each request), so content is clean; the content or "" guards remain because a tool-call turn carries content: None on every server, and because an adapter trained with thinking on is served with it on (06 §6).

docs.title: 15. Integration checklist
docs.text:
• A shape chosen from §2.9 by latency, duration, approvals, volume and side effects — the simplest that fits.
  • A written run contract: request, record, events, and the state machine with its transition rules.
  • Runs, steps, tool calls and approvals in tables; checkpoint after every step; a reaper for stale runs.
  • Idempotency keys on run creation and on every write tool call.
  • The agent acts as the user: per-tenant and per-user tool allow-lists computed before the first model call; scoped, short-lived tool credentials; no shared superuser.
  • An append-only audit log of side effects with user, run, step, tool, arguments, decision and approver.
  • Tools are typed wrappers: strict validation in, selected and size-capped results out, actionable errors; reads and writes classified; dry-run for writes.
  • Approval cards show the exact action, a preview, and the evidence; deadlines, escalation and per-action policy for irreversible writes.
  • SSE events with ids; no raw reasoning to end users; waiting states; terminal events; reconnect with Last-Event-ID.
  • Per-step and per-run timeouts that agree; retries only for detectable, idempotent failures; a breaker per dependency; a fallback ladder.
  • Step, token, time and money budgets enforced by the worker; per-tenant budgets at admission; cancellation that reaches tools.
  • One trace per run with spans per step and tool call; structured logs with hashes not content; success, steps, cost, p50/p95, approval and override rates, tool error rates — per version.
  • A monthly cost model with your prices; prefix caching with a stable prefix; result compaction.
  • Record/replay fixtures, tool contract tests, golden-trajectory scenarios, and an eval gate with thresholds and intervals in CI; load tests in tokens per second.
  • Shadow with writes disabled, then internal, canary by stable hash, GA; prompt, tool and model versions on every run; a tested kill switch; a drain-and-requeue deploy.
  • Transcript retention in days, metadata in months, audit log longest; PII redacted before storage; tenant opt-out.

docs.title: 16. Key takeaways
docs.text:
• An agent in a product is a job: a run with an id, a state machine, a budget, a transcript that is checkpointed, and an audit trail. Design the job before the prompt.
  • Pick the integration shape from the requirements — in-process for short read-only steps, a run service for everything else, streaming on top when a user is present, a queue or scheduler when none is, a durable engine for hours-long runs with approvals, agent-as-tool only with an eval to justify it, a local harness when the data is local.
  • The run contract (request, record, events, states) is the interface every other concern hangs on; the state machine's transitions are enforced by the runtime, and terminal states are final.
  • Separate conversation state, run state and long-term memory; a new turn is a new run.
  • Two idempotency keys: one for creating the run, one per side-effecting tool call. Retries and resumes are safe only with both.
  • The agent acts as the user, with per-tenant and per-user tool lists computed before the first model call and short-lived scoped credentials per tool — never a shared superuser.
  • Tools are typed wrappers: validate in, select and cap out, actionable errors, reads and writes classified, dry-run and confirmation for writes; the cap follows from \(r_\text{max} = (W - T_\text{sys} - nT_\text{turn})/n\).
  • Approvals show the exact action with a preview and evidence, expire into timed_out, escalate, and resume as a tool result the model reads; per-action for irreversible writes.
  • Stream events with ids, never raw reasoning; a close without a terminal event is a disconnect, and Last-Event-ID resumes it.
  • Reliability is the standard kit attached to a run: consistent per-step and per-run timeouts, retries only for detectable idempotent failures, a breaker per dependency, a fallback ladder, budgets in the worker, cancellation that reaches tools.
  • Observe one trace per run and six metrics per version — success, steps, cost, p50/p95, approval and override rates, tool errors — and alert on rates.
  • Cost is the resent transcript: cache the prefix, cap the results, budget per run and per tenant, and re-run the monthly model with your own prices.
  • Test your code with recorded cassettes and golden trajectories, your tools with contracts, your model and prompt with eval gates; load-test in tokens per second.
  • Ship shadow → internal → canary → GA with versions on every run, a tested kill switch that refuses new runs and cancels running ones, and a deploy that drains, requeues from checkpoints and pins versions.

docs.title: 17. Exercises
docs.text:
Exercise 17.1

Pick a shape from §2 for each: (a) every night, re-categorize 50,000 tickets after a taxonomy change; (b) a support agent chats with the assistant and must approve refunds; © a "pull request opened" webhook should trigger a review that posts comments as suggestions.

Answer

(a) Scheduled/batch (§2.5): throughput over latency, embarrassingly parallel, idempotent per item, run a sample first. (b) A chat UI with streaming and visible tool calls on top of a run service (§2.3 over §2.2): the user is present and approvals need a UI. © An event-driven queue worker (§2.4): no user is waiting, the event starts the run, and with nobody present the writes stay at the "suggest" level — comments, not merges — with idempotent consumption keyed on the webhook delivery id.

Exercise 17.2

A 16,384-token window, a 1,500-token prefix, 8 steps, 150 tokens of model output per step. What is the largest tool result you can allow per step?

Answer

\(r_\text{max} = (16384 - 1500 - 8\cdot 150)/8 = (16384 - 2700)/8 = 13684/8 = 1710.5\), so 1,710 tokens — and in practice a cap around 600–800 to leave room for the final answer and a summary.

Exercise 17.3

A client's network is flaky: it sends POST /runs with the same idempotency key three times. How many runs execute? A worker crashes right after a refund tool returned but before the checkpoint was written; on resume, what prevents a second refund?

Answer

One run executes; the second and third creates return the existing run's id and state (§4.3, and same key again in §14.3). The tool-call idempotency key run_id:step:tool_call_id: the wrapper (or the downstream API) stored the first result under it, so the replayed call returns the stored result instead of refunding again. Without that key, resuming from the previous checkpoint would re-run the refund.

Exercise 17.4

5,000 runs a day, 6 steps each, 2 KB per checkpoint, kept 30 days. How much transcript storage is that?

Answer

Per day \(5000 \cdot 6 \cdot 2\ \text{KB} = 60{,}000\ \text{KB} = 60\ \text{MB}\); over 30 days \(60 \cdot 30 = 1{,}800\ \text{MB}\), about 1.8 GB. Small enough that nobody will prune it unless expires_at does it mechanically.

Exercise 17.5

The step budget is 8, the model timeout 15 s and the tool timeout 5 s. What run deadline is consistent with them? The product can only wait 90 s; what per-step time does that leave?

Answer

\(T_\text{run} \ge 8 \cdot (15 + 5) = 160\) s. With a 90 s run deadline each step gets \(90/8 = 11.25\) s for model plus tool, so the per-step timeouts must shrink (say 8 s model, 3 s tool) or the step budget must drop — otherwise runs that respect every per-step limit still time out.

Exercise 17.6

From a log of 20 runs: 16 completed, 12 approvals requested of which 3 were denied, 50 tool calls of which 4 errored. Compute the success rate, the override rate and the tool error rate. Which one points at a prompt regression caught by humans?

Answer

Success \(16/20 = 0.80\); override rate \(3/12 = 0.25\); tool error rate \(4/50 = 0.08\). The override rate: a quarter of proposed writes rejected by approvers means the agent is proposing actions people do not want — a prompt or tool-description regression, and each denial is a new eval case (§10.4).

Exercise 17.7

10,000 runs a month; 5 model calls per run; 1,000 tokens of transcript growth per step; a 1,500-token prefix; 120 output tokens per call. Prices as assumed in §11.4 ($0.50 / $1.50 per million, cached input $0.05). Monthly cost with and without prefix caching?

Answer

Resent transcript \(1000 \cdot \tfrac{5\cdot 6}{2} = 15{,}000\); prefix \(1500 \cdot 5 = 7{,}500\); output \(120 \cdot 5 = 600\). Uncached: \((0.50 \cdot 22500 + 1.50 \cdot 600)/10^6 = (11250 + 900)/10^6 = \$0.01215\) per run, $121.50 a month. Cached: \((0.50 \cdot 15000 + 0.05 \cdot 7500 + 900)/10^6 = (7500 + 375 + 900)/10^6 = \$0.008775\) per run, $87.75 a month. Caching saves about 28%; capping the transcript growth would save more.

Exercise 17.8

A reviewer proposes letting an approval that arrives after the deadline still execute the write, "since the human did approve it". Which transition does that need, and why is it rejected?

Answer

It needs timed_out → running (or a write from a terminal state), which the state machine (§3.4) does not allow: terminal states are final. The run already ended with a reason the user saw; the world may have changed (a human may have refunded by hand); and an action executing minutes or hours after its context was assembled is exactly the stale-action bug approvals exist to prevent. The right path is a new run, with a fresh lookup and a fresh approval.

Exercise 17.9

Peak load is 3,600 runs an hour; a run averages 800 output tokens and 20,000 input tokens (with the resend). What decode and prefill throughput must the load test sustain?

Answer

Decode \(3600 \cdot 800 / 3600 = 800\) tokens/s; prefill \(3600 \cdot 20000 / 3600 = 20{,}000\) tokens/s. One run per second sounds small; 20,000 prefill tokens per second is the number to size for — and the one prefix caching and result capping shrink.

Next: 63 — Agents in the real world: twelve applications applies these shapes end to end; 61 — Agent frameworks for the libraries that package the run store, checkpointer and streaming; 55 — Production for the serving stack underneath.

docs.title: 63 — Agents in the real world: twelve applications
docs.text:
Last verified: 29 October 2026.

Three earlier chapters gave you the parts: the agent loop and its disciplines (52 — Agents), the frameworks that wrap it (61 — Agent frameworks), and the shapes that turn an agent into a product feature (62 — Integrating agents into applications). This chapter spends them. It walks through twelve concrete applications, each end to end and in the same order so you can compare them: the job, why an agent (or why only partly), the architecture, the tools, the data, the autonomy and guardrails, a sample trajectory, the evals, the cost per task, the failure modes, and how to grow it from an MVP. Read 52 first; this chapter does not re-derive the loop, the reliability math, the budgets or the autonomy ladder — it links them and applies them.

The recurring lesson, stated twelve ways: the model picks the path; your code owns the consequences. Every application below is read-mostly tools, approval gates on writes, hard budgets, a verification step, and an eval you trust before you turn autonomy up. Keep every scenario benign and defensive; the one security application is authorized lab testing only, exactly as 11 — The Kali agent frames it.

docs.title: 1. How to read the twelve
docs.text:
Each application repeats the same twelve-part template. Three conventions make the cards comparable:

  • Prices are assumptions, not quotes. Throughout, assume a mid-tier model at $0.50 per 1M input tokens and $1.50 per 1M output tokens, and a cheap model (for cascades) at $0.10 / $0.40. The handbook never quotes live API prices; state your own and the math stays true (55 §12). The local Qwen3-14B-4bit path costs amortized compute, not per-token — where an application runs locally the card gives the token-equivalent so you can compare.
  • "Integration shape" names one of the eight from 62: in-process call, agent service with run ids, streaming chat UI, queue worker, scheduled/batch, durable workflow engine, agent-as-tool, local harness. Each application names the shape it uses rather than redescribing it.
  • "Autonomy" is the level from 52 §8: suggest, act with approval, act and report, or fully autonomous. No application here is fully autonomous on a write; that is the point.

Two levers cut cost in almost every application, worked once here and referenced throughout. A cascade sends the easy share to the cheap model and escalates the rest (55 §13):

\[ E[\text{cost}] = c_\text{small} + f\,c_\text{large} \]

On paper

Cheap model \(c_\text{small}=0.0005\), mid model \(c_\text{large}=0.004\), escalate a fraction \(f=0.3\):

\[ E[\text{cost}] = 0.0005 + 0.3\times 0.004 \] \[ E[\text{cost}] = 0.0005 + 0.0012 = 0.0017 \]

$0.0017 against $0.004 for mid-only: a 57.5% cut, because only 30% of tasks pay the mid rate.

Prompt caching the stable prefix (system prompt plus tool schemas, identical every step) means the steps after the first pay only a reduced cached rate for it — a fraction of the input price on hosted APIs, and skipped prefill on the local server (55 §11.3). Counting full-price input tokens over \(s\) steps:

\[ T_\text{billed} = T_\text{prefix} + s\,T_\text{new} \]

On paper

A 1200-token prefix, \(s=4\) steps, each step sending the prefix plus \(T_\text{new}=700\) tokens of its own; the prefix is cached after step 1:

\[ T_\text{uncached} = 4\times(1200+700) = 7600 \] \[ T_\text{billed} = 1200 + 4\times 700 = 4000 \]

Caching bills 4000 full-price input tokens instead of 7600: the prefix is paid once instead of four times, saving \((s-1)\,T_\text{prefix} = 3600\) tokens, 47% of the input bill.

docs.title: 2.1 The job
docs.text: Who: a SaaS company's support team. Input: an inbound ticket in a helpdesk system (subject, body, customer id, order history). Success: the ticket is resolved correctly — answered, refunded within policy, or escalated — with the customer's next reply confirming it, and no wrong refund. Volume (illustrative): 2,000 tickets/day, of which ~40% are routine (where/how, status, small refunds) and the rest need a human.

docs.title: 2.2 Why an agent (or why only partly)
docs.text: Apply the rule of 52 §1.1. Classifying the ticket and drafting a reply are a fixed workflow (route → retrieve policy → draft). What makes it agentic is the small, observation-driven tail: look up the order, see it was charged twice, decide whether a refund is warranted and for how much. The path there depends on what the lookups return, so the resolution step is an agent; everything around it is a workflow. Most of the work is not agentic, and that is good — keep the autonomous surface small.

docs.title: 2.3 Architecture
docs.text:
integration shape: streaming chat UI (agent) + agent service with run ids
                   (helpdesk webhook -> run)

ticket ─▶ [router: small model] ─▶ class ─▶ [resolver agent: mid model]
                                               │   retrieval: policy + KB (RAG, 51)
                                               │   tools: lookups (read), refund (write)
                                               ▼
                                   [refund gate: amount<=limit?]──over──▶ human approve
                                               │ within
                                               ▼
                                     execute + [audit log] ─▶ reply (streamed)
guardrails: PII never leaves the tenant; refund tool scoped to one order; budgets per run

docs.title: 2.4 Tools
docs.text: Tool R/W Data it touches Approval? Size cap search_kb read public help articles no 5 chunks get_customer read one customer's profile no 1 record get_order read one order + its payments no 1 record issue_refund write payments ledger if > $50 1 refund/call escalate write ticket queue no (safe) 1 ticket

docs.title: 2.5 Context and data
docs.text: Retrieved: the refund policy and relevant help articles, by hybrid search over the KB (51 §7). Remembered: the running ticket thread as working memory, summarized once it grows (52 §10); past tickets for this customer are long-term memory, retrieved on demand, not stuffed in. Never sent to the model: full card numbers or other PII beyond the last four digits (redact first — 56 §8), and no internal credentials (56 §9).

docs.title: 2.6 Autonomy and guardrails
docs.text:
Autonomy: act and report at or under $50, act with approval above it. Lookups and KB answers run automatically; a refund at or under $50 posts automatically and is logged; a refund over $50, or any second refund on the same order, pauses for a human who sees the exact amount and order (52 §15). Budgets: 8 steps, 12k tokens, 30 s per ticket. Sandbox: the refund tool is scoped to the single order in context and cannot touch another customer.

The gate is the load-bearing part, and it is a few lines of your code, not a prompt:

# Support agent: a refund tool behind a limit check and an approval gate.
LIMIT = 50.0                      # auto-refund ceiling in USD

def refund_gate(amount, order_total, approved=False):
    if amount <= 0 or amount > order_total:
        return "deny", "amount must be >0 and <= order total"
    if amount <= LIMIT:
        return "auto", f"within ${LIMIT:.0f} limit"
    if approved:
        return "execute", "human approved"
    return "needs_approval", f"over ${LIMIT:.0f}: human must confirm"

def model_decision(ticket):       # scripted fake model
    return {"t1": ("A1001", 20.0, 20.0),
            "t2": ("A1002", 80.0, 80.0)}[ticket]

for ticket in ("t1", "t2"):
    order, total, amt = model_decision(ticket)
    action, why = refund_gate(amt, total)
    print(f"{ticket}: refund ${amt:.0f} on {order} -> {action} ({why})")
    if action == "needs_approval":
        action, why = refund_gate(amt, total, approved=True)
        print(f"    after approval -> {action} ({why})")

t1: refund $20 on A1001 -> auto (within $50 limit)
t2: refund $80 on A1002 -> needs_approval (over $50: human must confirm)
    after approval -> execute (human approved)

The $20 refund posts; the $80 one cannot execute until a human approves, and the amount the human sees is the concrete $80 on A1002, never a paraphrase.

docs.title: 2.7 A sample trajectory
docs.text:
Thought: billing ticket; find the order before deciding.
Action: get_order({"order_id": "A1001"})
Observation: {"error": "TimeoutError: ledger slow"}        <- tool error

Thought: transient timeout; retry once (idempotent read).
Action: get_order({"order_id": "A1001"})
Observation: {"status": "charged_twice", "amount": 20.0, "total": 20.0}

Thought: duplicate $20 charge; $20 <= $50, so auto-refund the duplicate.
Action: issue_refund({"order_id": "A1001", "amount": 20.0})
Observation: {"refunded": 20.0, "payment": "p2"}

Answer: You were charged twice ($20). I refunded the duplicate; one valid
charge remains. [logged: run_7f3, refund p2]

docs.title: 2.8 Evals and metrics
docs.text:
Measure resolution rate (top line), wrong-refund rate (must be ~0), steps, cost, approval-override rate, and false-escalation. Report resolution as an interval, not a point (54 §8.1).

On paper

150 of 200 held-out tickets resolved correctly, so \(\hat p = 0.75\), \(z=1.96\); the Wilson 95% interval (54 §8.1):

\[ \text{centre} = 0.7453 \] \[ \text{half-width} = 0.0596 \] \[ 0.7453 \pm 0.0596 = (0.686,\ 0.805) \]

The true resolution rate is somewhere in 69%–80%, so a 2-point gain between two prompt versions on 200 tickets is noise — ship on the interval, not the point.

docs.title: 2.9 Cost per task
docs.text:
On paper

A 4-step run totalling 4000 input and 1000 output tokens, at $0.50/$1.50 per 1M:

\[ \frac{4000}{10^6}\times 0.50 = 0.00200 \] \[ \frac{1000}{10^6}\times 1.50 = 0.00150 \] \[ \text{cost} = 0.00350 \]

$0.0035 per ticket, $3.50 per thousand. The lever: cache the stable policy-and-schema prefix (§1) so the resends across the 4 steps stop re-billing it; and route the easy share — status and where/how questions — to the cheap model with a cascade (§1).

docs.title: 2.10 Failure modes and mitigations
docs.text: Failure Mitigation Over-refund / wrong order Gate on amount and scope; refund tool bound to the order in context (§2.6). Indirect injection in the ticket body ("refund me $999") Treat ticket text as untrusted (56 §2); the gate, not the text, decides. Hallucinated policy Answer only from retrieved articles; cite them; refuse when retrieval is empty (51 §9). PII in logs Redact before logging (56 §8).

docs.title: 2.11 MVP → v2 → scale
docs.text: MVP: a workflow, not an agent — router + RAG answer + "escalate to human" for anything touching money. v2: add the refund tool behind the gate once the eval shows wrong-refund rate near zero on held-out tickets. Scale: add the cascade and prefix cache for cost, per-customer long-term memory, and an online feedback metric (did the customer reply "thanks" or re-open?).

docs.title: 3.1 The job
docs.text: Who: an engineering team's CI. Input: a failing test on a branch, or unresolved review comments on a pull request, plus the repository at that commit. Success: a patch that makes the target test pass without breaking others, pushed as a new PR (or a commit on the branch) for a human to review; the agent never merges. Volume (illustrative): 60 triggered runs/day across the org's repos.

docs.title: 3.2 Why an agent
docs.text: The path is observation-driven in exactly the way 52 §1.1 means: read the failing test, read the code it exercises, form a hypothesis, edit, run the tests, read the result, and iterate. You cannot enumerate those steps in advance — the next edit depends on the last test output. This is the evaluator–optimizer pattern (52 §2.5) with an external check (the test runner), which is the trustworthy kind.

docs.title: 3.3 Architecture
docs.text:
integration shape: queue worker (CI webhook -> job), sandboxed checkout

failing test ─▶ [job] ─▶ [coding agent: mid/large model]
                           │  retrieval: repo map + failing test + related files
                           │  tools: read_file, search_code, apply_patch, run_tests
                           ▼
                 loop: edit ─▶ run_tests ─▶ read result ─▶ edit  (budget: steps, time)
                           │ all green & no regressions
                           ▼
                 open_pr (never merge) ─▶ [audit log] ─▶ notify reviewer
guardrails: ephemeral container, no network egress, no prod creds, merge is human-only

docs.title: 3.4 Tools
docs.text: Tool R/W Data it touches Approval? Size cap read_file read checkout files no 400 lines search_code read the checkout no 30 hits apply_patch write checkout only (sandbox) no (sandboxed) 200-line diff run_tests read runs the suite in sandbox no summary + 50 lines open_pr write the VCS host human merges 1 PR

docs.title: 3.5 Context and data
docs.text: Retrieved: a repository map and the files the failing test touches (code-aware chunking — 51 §3). Remembered: the edit/test transcript as working memory, summarized when long (52 §10). Never sent: .env files, deploy keys, or anything matching a secret pattern — scrub the checkout first (56 §9).

docs.title: 3.6 Autonomy and guardrails
docs.text:
Autonomy: act and report inside the sandbox (it edits and runs tests freely there) and suggest at the boundary that matters (the PR is a proposal; a human merges). Budgets: 20 steps, 10 min wall-clock, a token ceiling. Sandbox: an ephemeral container with the checkout and no network egress and no production credentials — a bad patch cannot escape it (52 §16).

The gate is on the PR, and it is an external check — the tests — not the model's opinion:

# Coding agent in CI: gate the PR on a green run that fixes the target and adds no regressions.
def run_tests(suite):             # fake runner: returns {test: passed?}
    return suite

BEFORE = {"test_login": False, "test_logout": True, "test_signup": True}

def pr_gate(before, after):
    newly_failing = [t for t in after if after[t] is False and before.get(t) is True]
    target_fixed = before.get("test_login") is False and after.get("test_login") is True
    all_green = all(after.values())
    ok = all_green and target_fixed and not newly_failing
    return ok, {"all_green": all_green, "target_fixed": target_fixed,
                "regressions": newly_failing}

after1 = run_tests({"test_login": True, "test_logout": True, "test_signup": False})
ok1, d1 = pr_gate(BEFORE, after1)
print(f"attempt 1: open_pr={ok1} {d1}")
after2 = run_tests({"test_login": True, "test_logout": True, "test_signup": True})
ok2, d2 = pr_gate(BEFORE, after2)
print(f"attempt 2: open_pr={ok2} {d2}")

attempt 1: open_pr=False {'all_green': False, 'target_fixed': True, 'regressions': ['test_signup']}
attempt 2: open_pr=True {'all_green': True, 'target_fixed': True, 'regressions': []}

Attempt 1 fixes the target but breaks test_signup; the gate blocks the PR and feeds the regression back as the next observation. Attempt 2 is the recovery: green everywhere, target fixed, no regression — the PR opens.

docs.title: 3.7 A sample trajectory
docs.text:
Thought: read the failing test to see what it expects.
Action: run_tests({"only": "test_login"})
Observation: FAIL test_login: AssertionError: expected 200, got 500

Thought: a 500; find the login handler.
Action: search_code({"q": "def login"})
Observation: auth/views.py:42 def login(req): ...

Thought: null session before auth; patch it.
Action: apply_patch({"file": "auth/views.py", "diff": "..."})
Observation: {"error": "patch did not apply: context mismatch"}   <- tool error

Thought: the file moved under me; re-read and re-target.
Action: read_file({"path": "auth/views.py", "start": 30, "end": 70})
Observation: <current lines>
Action: apply_patch({...corrected...}) -> run_tests({}) -> all green, no regressions
Action: open_pr({"title": "Fix null session in login", "branch": "fix-login"})
Answer: Opened PR #214 fixing test_login; 3/3 tests pass. Needs review.

docs.title: 3.8 Evals and metrics
docs.text:
Use execution-based evaluation — the tests are the grader (54 §4). Report pass@1 for the deployment view and pass@k for capability (09 §5, 42 §2.3), plus steps, regression rate, and cost.

On paper

The agent gets \(n=5\) independent attempts on one bug and \(c=3\) produce a green diff; the unbiased estimator (42 §2.3):

\[ \text{pass@}1 = c/n = 3/5 = 0.6 \] \[ \text{pass@}2 = 1 - \frac{\binom{2}{2}}{\binom{5}{2}} = 1 - \frac{1}{10} = 0.9 \]

One attempt fixes the bug 60% of the time; allowing a second independent attempt lifts "at least one green diff" to 90%. CI can afford retries, so pass@2 is the number that matters here.

docs.title: 3.9 Cost per task
docs.text:
On paper

A long run over a large checkout: 12000 input and 1500 output tokens, at $0.50/$1.50 per 1M:

\[ \frac{12000}{10^6}\times 0.50 = 0.00600 \] \[ \frac{1500}{10^6}\times 1.50 = 0.00225 \] \[ \text{cost} = 0.00825 \]

$0.00825 per run. The lever: cache the repository-context prefix across the loop's many steps (§1); return only test summaries, not full logs, so each step adds less (52 §13).

docs.title: 3.10 Failure modes and mitigations
docs.text: Failure Mitigation Patch passes the target, breaks others Run the whole suite; gate on no regressions (§3.6). Agent weakens the test to make it pass Diff the test files; block changes to the target test; human review. Infinite edit/run loop Step and time budgets; stuck-loop detector (52 §18). Secret leakage from the checkout Scrub secrets; no egress from the sandbox (56 §9).

docs.title: 3.11 MVP → v2 → scale
docs.text: MVP: a single-shot "suggest a patch" that a human applies — no sandbox writes. v2: the sandboxed edit/run loop with the PR gate, once execution-based eval shows an acceptable pass@1 on a held-out bug set. Scale: parallel attempts (pass@k) with the best green diff chosen, repo-specific retrieval, and a regression-rate gate wired into CI (54 §13).

docs.title: 4.1 The job
docs.text: Who: non-technical staff asking questions of a data warehouse. Input: a plain-English question ("revenue by region last quarter"). Success: a correct, read-only query that returns the right rows, plus a short answer and a chart, with the SQL shown. Volume (illustrative): 500 questions/day.

docs.title: 4.2 Why an agent (or why only partly)
docs.text: Mostly a workflow: retrieve the relevant schema, write SQL, verify it, run it read-only, chart the result. The agentic part is narrow — when the query errors or returns something implausible, the model reads the error and revises (the evaluator–optimizer loop again, 52 §2.5). One or two revise steps, not an open-ended loop.

docs.title: 4.3 Architecture
docs.text:
integration shape: agent service with run ids (BI tool calls it)

question ─▶ [schema retrieval: which tables/columns] ─▶ [model writes SQL]
                                                           │
                                                           ▼
                                      [verifier: SELECT-only, LIMIT, no DDL]
                                                 │ ok              │ reject
                                                 ▼                 ▼
                                   run on READ-ONLY replica     revise (<=2)
                                                 │
                                                 ▼
                                   sanity check rows ─▶ chart + answer ─▶ [audit log]

docs.title: 4.4 Tools
docs.text: Tool R/W Data it touches Approval? Size cap get_schema read table/column catalog no 40 tables run_sql read read-only replica no 1000 rows make_chart read the returned rows no 1 chart

docs.title: 4.5 Context and data
docs.text: Retrieved: only the schema fragments relevant to the question (full schemas blow the context and confuse the model) — a retrieval problem (51 §2). Remembered: the last few Q→SQL pairs in the session for follow-ups. Never sent: row-level PII; the model sees the schema, not the data, and the replica enforces row-level access (51 §11). Credentials are read-only and never in the prompt (56 §9).

docs.title: 4.6 Autonomy and guardrails
docs.text:
Autonomy: act and report — read-only queries run automatically because they cannot damage anything, and the result is reported with the SQL. The guardrail is the verifier plus a read-only credential: even a model that emitted DROP TABLE cannot run it, because the connection has no write grant and the verifier rejects it first.

The verifier is deterministic and sits between the model and the database:

# Data-analyst agent: verify model-written SQL is safe and read-only before it runs.
import re

BANNED = re.compile(r"\b(insert|update|delete|drop|alter|truncate|create|grant|merge)\b", re.I)
MAX_ROWS = 1000

def verify_sql(sql):
    s = sql.strip().rstrip(";").strip()
    if ";" in s:
        return False, "multiple statements"
    if not re.match(r"(?is)^\s*select\b", s):
        return False, "not a SELECT"
    if BANNED.search(s):
        return False, "write/DDL keyword present"
    m = re.search(r"(?i)\blimit\s+(\d+)\b", s)
    if not m:
        return False, "no LIMIT clause"
    if int(m.group(1)) > MAX_ROWS:
        return False, f"LIMIT {m.group(1)} exceeds {MAX_ROWS}"
    return True, "ok"

cases = [
    "SELECT region, SUM(amount) FROM orders GROUP BY region LIMIT 100",
    "SELECT * FROM orders; DROP TABLE orders",
    "UPDATE orders SET amount=0",
    "SELECT * FROM orders",
]
for sql in cases:
    ok, why = verify_sql(sql)
    print(f"{'PASS' if ok else 'FAIL'}: {why:24} <- {sql[:38]}")

PASS: ok                       <- SELECT region, SUM(amount) FROM orders
FAIL: multiple statements      <- SELECT * FROM orders; DROP TABLE order
FAIL: not a SELECT             <- UPDATE orders SET amount=0
FAIL: no LIMIT clause          <- SELECT * FROM orders

The verifier is defence in depth, not the only defence: the read-only replica is the one that holds even if the regex is fooled. Two independent controls, because one is never enough.

The same verifier guards real model output. Here the model runs against the handbook's local server (10 §4); thinking is turned off and content is guarded because it can be None:

# The model writes SQL; your code verifies it before it ever runs.
import re
from openai import OpenAI

client = OpenAI(base_url="http://127.0.0.1:8080/v1", api_key="local")
MODEL = "mlx-community/Qwen3-14B-4bit"
BANNED = re.compile(r"\b(insert|update|delete|drop|alter|truncate|create)\b", re.I)

def verify_sql(sql):
    s = sql.strip().rstrip(";")
    if not re.match(r"(?is)^\s*select\b", s): return False, "not a SELECT"
    if ";" in s: return False, "multiple statements"
    if BANNED.search(s): return False, "write/DDL keyword"
    if not re.search(r"(?i)\blimit\s+\d+\b", s): return False, "no LIMIT"
    return True, "ok"

r = client.chat.completions.create(
    model=MODEL, temperature=0.0,
    messages=[{"role": "system", "content": "Return one read-only SQL query, with a LIMIT."},
              {"role": "user", "content": "Revenue by region, top 10."}],
    extra_body={"chat_template_kwargs": {"enable_thinking": False}})
sql = r.choices[0].message.content or ""     # content can be None; never crash
ok, why = verify_sql(sql)
print("sql:", sql)
print(f"verify: {'PASS' if ok else 'FAIL'} ({why}) -> {'run read-only' if ok else 'reject'}")

sql: SELECT region, SUM(amount) AS revenue FROM orders GROUP BY region ORDER BY revenue DESC LIMIT 10
verify: PASS (ok) -> run read-only

The output above came from a local stub standing in for mlx_lm.server that reproduces Qwen3's thinking mode: with enable_thinking off it returns the SQL directly in content. A real Qwen3-14B returns the same SQL shape. With thinking on, mlx_lm.server puts the reasoning in a separate reasoning field (50 §7) and this code would still read only content (52 §6.1); a server that does not split it out leaves a <think>…</think> block at the start of content, which the verifier would reject as "not a SELECT" — one more reason to turn thinking off for this call. The content or "" guard matters because a cut-off or pure-reasoning turn can leave content as None; against the same stub with thinking on and a 20-token max_tokens, the run printed sql: and FAIL (not a SELECT) -> reject instead of crashing.

docs.title: 4.7 A sample trajectory
docs.text:
Thought: need the schema for revenue and region.
Action: get_schema({"q": "revenue region orders"})
Observation: orders(region, amount, created_at); ...

Thought: write the aggregate with a LIMIT.
Action: run_sql({"sql": "SELECT region, SUM(amont) ... LIMIT 10"})
Observation: {"error": "column \"amont\" does not exist"}     <- tool error

Thought: typo; the column is "amount". Fix and rerun.
Action: run_sql({"sql": "SELECT region, SUM(amount) AS revenue ... LIMIT 10"})
Observation: [{"region":"EU","revenue":48210.0}, ...]

Answer: EU leads at $48,210, then NA. [chart attached; SQL shown]

docs.title: 4.8 Evals and metrics
docs.text:
Measure execution accuracy (do the returned rows match the gold query's rows?) over a labelled question→SQL set, plus revise-count and cost. Report as a Wilson interval (54 §8.1).

On paper

72 of 80 questions return the correct rows, so \(\hat p = 0.90\), \(z=1.96\):

\[ \text{centre} = 0.8817 \] \[ \text{half-width} = 0.0668 \] \[ 0.8817 \pm 0.0668 = (0.815,\ 0.948) \]

"72 of 80" is consistent with a true execution accuracy from 82% to 95% — enough to ship read-only, far from enough to ever grant a write grant.

docs.title: 4.9 Cost per task
docs.text:
On paper

Schema plus a short revise loop: 6000 input and 800 output tokens, at $0.50/$1.50 per 1M:

\[ \frac{6000}{10^6}\times 0.50 = 0.00300 \] \[ \frac{800}{10^6}\times 1.50 = 0.00120 \] \[ \text{cost} = 0.00420 \]

$0.0042 per question. The lever: cache the schema prefix (§1) — it is the same for every question on a table — and route simple lookups to the cheap model, escalating only joins and window functions (§1).

docs.title: 4.10 Failure modes and mitigations
docs.text: Failure Mitigation Destructive SQL Verifier rejects non-SELECT; read-only credential (§4.6). Wrong but plausible numbers Execution-accuracy eval; show the SQL so a human can audit. Schema too big for context Retrieve only relevant fragments (51 §2). Row-level data leak Row-level access on the replica (51 §11).

docs.title: 4.11 MVP → v2 → scale
docs.text: MVP: schema → SQL → verify → run, no revise loop; show the SQL and let the user re-ask. v2: add the one- or two-step revise loop on errors once eval shows it lifts execution accuracy. Scale: per-team schema retrieval, cached query plans, a semantic cache of common questions (55 §11.2).

docs.title: 5.1 The job
docs.text: Who: an SRE team. Input: a firing alert (service, metric, threshold) plus logs, dashboards, and runbooks. Success: a correct diagnosis and a proposed remediation; only allow-listed, approved actions execute; mean time to acknowledge drops. Volume (illustrative): 40 pages/week, most low-severity.

docs.title: 5.2 Why an agent
docs.text: This is the canonical agent case from 52 §1.1: investigate until you find the cause; the next probe depends on the last observation. You cannot script "check CPU, then logs, then deploys" in a fixed order — which signal to pull next depends on what the alert and the previous query showed. The diagnosis is genuinely agentic; the remediation is not autonomous at all.

docs.title: 5.3 Architecture
docs.text:
integration shape: queue worker (alert webhook -> run) + streaming updates to chat

alert ─▶ [responder agent: mid model]
            │  retrieval: runbooks (RAG), recent deploys, service graph
            │  tools (read): query_logs, query_metrics, list_deploys, get_runbook
            │  tools (write, allow-listed): restart_service, rollback
            ▼
     diagnose ─▶ propose remediation ─▶ [approval in chat: exact action]──no──▶ stop
            │ yes + action in allow-list
            ▼
     execute ─▶ verify recovery ─▶ [audit log] ─▶ post incident note

docs.title: 5.4 Tools
docs.text: Tool R/W Data it touches Approval? Size cap query_logs read log store no 50 lines query_metrics read metrics store no 20 points list_deploys read deploy history no 10 entries get_runbook read runbook docs no 3 chunks restart_service write one named service yes 1 service rollback write one deployment yes 1 rollback

docs.title: 5.5 Context and data
docs.text: Retrieved: the runbook for this alert and the recent deploy list (a frequent root cause) — RAG over internal docs (51 §9). Remembered: the investigation transcript; prior incidents on this service are long-term memory, retrieved by similarity. Never sent: raw logs containing user PII or tokens (redact — 56 §8, 56 §9); the model gets aggregates and samples, not the firehose.

docs.title: 5.6 Autonomy and guardrails
docs.text: Autonomy: act with approval. Read-only queries run automatically; every write (restart_service, rollback) is allow-listed and requires a human yes showing the exact action, because a wrong restart during an incident makes it worse. Budgets: 15 steps, 60k tokens (logs are large), 5 min. The allow-list is code: an action not on it is denied, not negotiated (52 §16).

docs.title: 5.7 A sample trajectory
docs.text:
Thought: 5xx spike on checkout. Recent deploy is the first suspect.
Action: list_deploys({"service": "checkout", "hours": 2})
Observation: [{"id": "d_88", "at": "12:58", "by": "ci"}]

Thought: deploy 2 min before the spike. Check its error signature.
Action: query_logs({"service": "checkout", "since": "12:58"})
Observation: {"error": "RateLimitError from log backend"}       <- unexpected tool error

Thought: the log tool itself is rate-limited; back off and narrow the window.
Action: query_logs({"service": "checkout", "since": "13:00", "limit": 50})
Observation: NullPointerException in PaymentClient (new in d_88)

Thought: regression in d_88. Propose rollback; this is a write -> approval.
Action: rollback({"deploy": "d_88"})   [PENDING APPROVAL: "rollback d_88 on checkout"]
Observation: {"approved_by": "sre_oncall", "result": "rolled_back"}

Answer: 5xx caused by NPE in d_88 (PaymentClient). Rolled back after approval;
error rate recovering. [logged]

docs.title: 5.8 Evals and metrics
docs.text:
Measure diagnosis accuracy against labelled past incidents, the approval-override rate (how often the human rejects the proposal), and the unsafe-action rate, which must be zero (54 §13).

On paper

The agent proposes a remediation on 50 incidents; the human rejects 4:

\[ \text{override rate} = 4/50 = 0.08 \]

Across 120 runs, 0 out-of-allow-list actions were attempted; the Wilson 95% upper bound on the unsafe-action rate (54 §8.1):

\[ \text{upper} = 0.031 \]

An 8% override rate means the proposals are usually right; "0 of 120" still only bounds the unsafe rate at ~3%, so the approval gate stays — zero observed is not zero possible.

docs.title: 5.9 Cost per task
docs.text:
On paper

A log-heavy investigation: 20000 input and 1000 output tokens, at $0.50/$1.50 per 1M:

\[ \frac{20000}{10^6}\times 0.50 = 0.01000 \] \[ \frac{1000}{10^6}\times 1.50 = 0.00150 \] \[ \text{cost} = 0.01150 \]

$0.0115 per incident — the costliest here, because logs dominate the input. The lever: summarize old observations so the resend stops growing (52 §10); pre-aggregate logs so each tool result is small (52 §13).

docs.title: 5.10 Failure modes and mitigations
docs.text: Failure Mitigation Wrong remediation executed Approval gate on every write; allow-list (§5.6). Log flood blows the budget Pre-aggregate; cap tool results; token budget (52 §14). Injection via log contents Treat logs as untrusted input (56 §2). Alert storm → many parallel runs Dedup alerts; one run per incident; rate-limit.

docs.title: 5.11 MVP → v2 → scale
docs.text: MVP: read-only suggest — the agent triages and posts a diagnosis with evidence; a human does everything. v2: add a single allow-listed action (rollback) behind approval once override rate is low. Scale: more allow-listed actions one at a time, each gated; a durable workflow (62) so a long investigation survives a restart.

docs.title: 6.1 The job
docs.text: Who: a security engineer running an authorized lab engagement. Input: an in-scope target inside an isolated lab network, under written authorization. Success: correct service enumeration and a structured, honest finding — in scope, logged, with evidence. Volume (illustrative): a handful of lab hosts per engagement. This application is fully specified in 11 — The Kali agent; this section only places it beside the other eleven and does not re-document it.

docs.title: 6.2 Why an agent
docs.text: Observation-driven by nature: enumerate services on an in-scope host, then decide what to probe next from what you found (52 §1.1). The model plans; it is not trusted with the path to the internet.

docs.title: 6.3 Architecture
docs.text:
integration shape: local harness (OpenCode / hackingBuddyGPT), air-gapped lab

task ─▶ [local Qwen3-14B-4bit] ─▶ typed MCP tool call
            │
            ▼
     [policy layer: scope + allow-list + confirm]   <- deterministic code, not an LLM
            │ allow                      │ deny
            ▼                            ▼
     MCP-Kali-Server (sandbox)         refuse + log
            │
            ▼
     lab target (no egress) ─▶ observation ─▶ model ─▶ report_finding ─▶ [audit log]

The three rules of 11 §1 are the whole design: the model never talks to the internet directly, the policy layer is code not a prompt, and every action is logged before it runs. Model: the handbook's local Qwen3-14B-4bit with a pentest LoRA, which is why the tool surface is small (11 §4).

docs.title: 6.4 Tools
docs.text:
A small typed surface, summarised from 11 §4 (see 16 §2 for the network-testing variants):

Tool R/W Data it touches Approval? Size cap scope_check read the scope file no 1 verdict nmap_scan read in-scope host (flags enum) no (recon) stdout capped http_probe read in-scope URL no (recon) headers + title kali_exec write-ish allow-listed binaries only confirm timeout-bounded report_finding write the report file no (safe) 1 finding

docs.title: 6.5 Context and data
docs.text: Retrieved: the scope file and tool docs; evidence notes under /lab. Remembered: the enumeration transcript, trimmed. Never sent off-box at all — the model is local and the lab has no egress; no real credentials, no customer data, no live CTF flags (12 §3). This is the strongest version of "never send it to the model": the whole system is air-gapped.

docs.title: 6.6 Autonomy and guardrails
docs.text: Autonomy: act with approval, split by the confirmation policy of 11 §5.1: read-only recon inside scope auto-approves; active enumeration confirms once per target; anything out of scope or off the allow-list is denied by the policy layer. The authorization itself is the precondition — missing authorization means the agent does not run at all (12 §1), and the legal frame is jurisdiction-specific (12 §2). Sandbox: an isolated Kali VM against disposable lab targets with no route to the public internet.

docs.title: 6.7 A sample trajectory
docs.text:
A safe, lab-only loop, condensed from 11 §7:

Thought: 10.10.10.5 is inside 10.10.10.0/24; read-only recon is allowed.
Action: nmap_scan({"target": "10.10.10.5", "flags": "-sV"})
Observation: {"error": "host down / no route"}               <- tool error

Thought: maybe not up yet; scope_check first, then a ping sweep.
Action: scope_check({"target": "10.10.10.5"}) -> (allow, "in scope")
Action: nmap_scan({"target": "10.10.10.5", "flags": "-sn"})
Observation: host up
Action: nmap_scan({"target": "10.10.10.5", "flags": "-sV"})
Observation: 22/tcp ssh OpenSSH 9.6; 80/tcp http nginx 1.26
Action: http_probe({"url": "http://10.10.10.5", "method": "HEAD"})
Observation: 200 OK; Server: nginx/1.26; X-Powered-By: PHP/8.3

report_finding: "SSH + HTTP exposed on 10.10.10.5; nginx 1.26 / PHP 8.3.
Next (in scope): enumerate vhosts, check for a login page.
Evidence: nmap -sV; HEAD http://10.10.10.5."

docs.title: 6.8 Evals and metrics
docs.text:
Evaluate the whole system — model + prompt + tools + policy — not the endpoint (11 §9, 54 §13). Report tool and argument accuracy (09 §4.2), task completion, recovery rate, and — non-negotiable — a zero unsafe/out-of-scope action rate.

On paper

On one lab task the agent gets \(n=5\) samples and \(c=2\) pass the verifier (42 §2.3):

\[ \text{pass@}1 = c/n = 2/5 = 0.4 \] \[ \text{pass@}2 = 1 - \frac{\binom{3}{2}}{\binom{5}{2}} = 1 - \frac{3}{10} = 0.7 \]

A single run succeeds 40% of the time; a second try reaches 70%. Capability (pass@2) and reliability are different questions — but the unsafe-action rate must be 0 regardless of either.

docs.title: 6.9 Cost per task
docs.text:
Inference is local, so the real cost is amortized compute and wall-clock, not per-token. The token-equivalent, for comparison with the API applications:

On paper

An enumeration run of 7000 input and 1000 output tokens, priced as if on the API at $0.50/$1.50 per 1M:

\[ \frac{7000}{10^6}\times 0.50 = 0.00350 \] \[ \frac{1000}{10^6}\times 1.50 = 0.00150 \] \[ \text{cost} = 0.00500 \]

$0.005-equivalent per run; locally it is free at the margin once the Mac is on. The lever here is the small typed tool surface (11 §4): 6–10 schemas instead of 150 keeps the per-step prompt small, which is cost and reliability on a 14B.

docs.title: 6.10 Failure modes and mitigations
docs.text: Failure Mitigation Out-of-scope scan Policy-layer scope check (code, not prompt) — 11 §5. Raw shell abuse Typed tools; allow-list kali_exec; no bare shell (11 §4). Invented ports / findings Report only what the tool output shows; evidence required (11 §6). Running without authorization Precondition check; no scope file, no run (12 §1).

docs.title: 6.11 MVP → v2 → scale
docs.text: MVP: planning-only — the model lists which tool it would use, calls nothing (11 §3.2). v2: read-only recon tools behind the scope check; evaluate the loop. Scale: add active-enumeration tools one at a time, each confirmed, with the kill switch and audit log in place (11 §5.3). Never point it at anything you are not authorized to test.

docs.title: 7.1 The job
docs.text: Who: a finance or legal operations team. Input: a PDF invoice or contract. Success: a validated structured record (vendor, totals, dates, terms) posted to the system of record; low-confidence extractions go to a human review queue instead of being guessed. Volume (illustrative): 5,000 documents/day.

docs.title: 7.2 Why an agent (or why only partly)
docs.text: Mostly a workflow: parse → extract fields → validate → route. The only agentic touch is handling messy documents — a scanned contract where the model must decide which clause is the term, or re-read a region. For clean invoices it is a single structured-output call, not an agent at all; reach for the loop only on the hard tail.

docs.title: 7.3 Architecture
docs.text:
integration shape: queue worker + scheduled/batch (nightly backlog)

doc ─▶ [parse: OCR/PDF->text] ─▶ [extract: model -> JSON schema]
                                    │  validate: types, totals add up, dates sane
                                    ▼
                        [confidence router]
                         │>=0.90 auto     │0.70-0.90 review     │<0.70 reject
                         ▼                 ▼                     ▼
                    post record      human review queue      bounce back
                         └───────────────┬─────────────────────┘
                                         ▼
                                   [audit log]

docs.title: 7.4 Tools
docs.text: Tool R/W Data it touches Approval? Size cap ocr_page read one document page no 1 page extract_fields read parsed text no 1 record validate_record read the extracted JSON no 1 record post_record write system of record if low-confidence 1 record enqueue_review write review queue no (safe) 1 item

docs.title: 7.5 Context and data
docs.text: Retrieved: the vendor's known format and prior records for that vendor (improves field mapping). Remembered: nothing across documents beyond vendor templates — each document is independent. Never sent: bank-account and tax-id numbers beyond what the record needs; redact and tokenize PII before it enters the model (56 §8).

docs.title: 7.6 Autonomy and guardrails
docs.text:
Autonomy: act and report for high-confidence records (auto-post and log), with a human review queue as the guardrail for everything uncertain. The confidence router is the whole safety story — a record only auto-posts when every field clears the bar.

# Document agent: route each extracted invoice by its lowest field confidence.
AUTO, REVIEW = 0.90, 0.70         # >=0.90 auto-post; 0.70-0.90 human review; <0.70 reject

def route(fields):
    worst = min(fields.values())
    if worst >= AUTO:
        return "auto-post", worst
    if worst >= REVIEW:
        return "review-queue", worst
    return "reject", worst

invoices = {
    "INV-1": {"vendor": 0.99, "total": 0.97, "date": 0.95},
    "INV-2": {"vendor": 0.98, "total": 0.82, "date": 0.91},
    "INV-3": {"vendor": 0.66, "total": 0.80, "date": 0.72},
}
counts = {"auto-post": 0, "review-queue": 0, "reject": 0}
for name, f in invoices.items():
    dest, worst = route(f)
    counts[dest] += 1
    print(f"{name}: worst conf {worst:.2f} -> {dest}")
print("routing:", counts)

INV-1: worst conf 0.95 -> auto-post
INV-2: worst conf 0.82 -> review-queue
INV-3: worst conf 0.66 -> reject
routing: {'auto-post': 1, 'review-queue': 1, 'reject': 1}

Routing on the worst field, not the average, is deliberate: a record is only as trustworthy as its least certain field, and a wrong total is worse than a blank one.

docs.title: 7.7 A sample trajectory
docs.text:
Thought: parse the invoice, then extract into the schema.
Action: extract_fields({"doc": "INV-77"})
Observation: {"vendor": "...", "total": 1240.00, "conf_total": 0.98,
              "date": null, "conf_date": 0.0}

Thought: date missing; try OCR on the header region.
Action: ocr_page({"doc": "INV-77", "region": "header"})
Observation: {"error": "region out of bounds"}               <- tool error

Thought: bad region; OCR the whole first page instead.
Action: ocr_page({"doc": "INV-77", "page": 1})
Observation: "Invoice date: 2026-09-30"
Action: validate_record({...date filled, conf 0.88...}) -> route -> review-queue

Answer: INV-77 extracted; date confidence 0.88 -> sent to human review, not posted.

docs.title: 7.8 Evals and metrics
docs.text:
Measure per-field precision and recall against a labelled set, plus the auto-post share and the error rate among auto-posted records (the one that must stay tiny).

On paper

For the total field: 90 correct extractions, 10 wrong, 20 missed. Precision and recall (47 — Classical ML defines them; worked here):

\[ \text{precision} = \frac{90}{90+10} = 0.90 \] \[ \text{recall} = \frac{90}{90+20} = 0.818 \] \[ F_1 = \frac{2\cdot 0.90\cdot 0.818}{0.90+0.818} = 0.857 \]

90% of posted totals are right and 82% of true totals are caught; the 10% wrong is why the confidence router sends the shaky ones to a human instead of posting them.

docs.title: 7.9 Cost per task
docs.text:
On paper

A single extraction call: 3000 input and 600 output tokens, at $0.50/$1.50 per 1M:

\[ \frac{3000}{10^6}\times 0.50 = 0.00150 \] \[ \frac{600}{10^6}\times 1.50 = 0.00090 \] \[ \text{cost} = 0.00240 \]

$0.0024 per document. The lever: a cheap model does the clean majority and escalates only low-confidence documents to a bigger one (a cascade, §1) — most invoices are easy.

docs.title: 7.10 Failure modes and mitigations
docs.text: Failure Mitigation Confident wrong extraction Route on worst field; validate totals/dates; sample auto-posts. Silent field drop Require every schema field; null with low confidence routes to review. Injection in document text Treat document text as untrusted (56 §2). PII in the record store Tokenize/redact sensitive fields (56 §8).

docs.title: 7.11 MVP → v2 → scale
docs.text: MVP: a single structured-output extraction with validation, everything to a review queue — measure field accuracy first. v2: auto-post the high-confidence share once precision among auto-posts is proven. Scale: per-vendor templates, a batch pipeline for the backlog (62), and active-learning on the reviewed queue to improve extraction (60 §9.5).

docs.title: 8.1 The job
docs.text: Who: analysts who need a sourced brief. Input: a research question and access to the web and internal documents. Success: a report that answers the question with every claim cited to a retrieved source, and a groundedness check passed before delivery. Volume (illustrative): 200 reports/day.

docs.title: 8.2 Why an agent
docs.text: The orchestrator–workers and evaluator–optimizer shapes of 52 §2: the agent decides what to look up next from what it has found (research is not a fixed query list), then an evaluator checks the draft for groundedness and sends it back if a claim is unsupported. The decomposition cannot be written in advance — that is what makes it an agent.

docs.title: 8.3 Architecture
docs.text:
integration shape: agent service with run ids (async, long-running)

question ─▶ [orchestrator: plan sub-questions]
               │  retrieval: web search + internal docs (RAG, 51)
               │  workers: search, read, extract-with-citation
               ▼
          draft ─▶ [groundedness evaluator] ──unsupported──▶ revise (<=N)
               │ every claim cited & supported
               ▼
          deliver report + citations ─▶ [audit log]
guardrails: untrusted web content; read-only; claims must trace to a source

docs.title: 8.4 Tools
docs.text: Tool R/W Data it touches Approval? Size cap web_search read public web no 10 results fetch_page read one URL (untrusted) no 4k chars search_internal read internal doc index no 5 chunks cite read retrieved spans no —

docs.title: 8.5 Context and data
docs.text: Retrieved: web results and internal chunks, each kept with its source id so a claim can be traced back (51 §9). Remembered: the growing set of findings, summarized as it exceeds the budget (52 §10). Never sent onward: internal documents the user is not cleared to see — enforce access control at retrieval, not in the prompt (51 §11).

docs.title: 8.6 Autonomy and guardrails
docs.text: Autonomy: act and report on the read-only research, then suggest — the report is delivered to a human, who decides what to do with it. The key guardrail is that fetched pages are untrusted input: a web page can carry an injection aimed at the agent, so the agent has no write tools and no outbound channel — removing a leg of the lethal trifecta (56 §2.4). The verification step is the groundedness evaluator (54 §5).

docs.title: 8.7 A sample trajectory
docs.text:
Thought: break the question into three sub-questions; start with market size.
Action: web_search({"q": "EU heat-pump installs 2025"})
Observation: [{"url": "u1", "title": "..."}, ...]

Thought: read the first source.
Action: fetch_page({"url": "u1"})
Observation: {"error": "403 Forbidden"}                       <- tool error

Thought: that source is blocked; use the next result instead.
Action: fetch_page({"url": "u2"})
Observation: "EU installations reached 3.1M in 2025 ..."
Action: cite({"span": "3.1M in 2025", "source": "u2"})

[draft -> evaluator: "claim 'fastest-growing' has no citation" -> revise -> pass]
Answer: Report delivered; 7 claims, 7 citations, groundedness check passed.

docs.title: 8.8 Evals and metrics
docs.text:
Measure groundedness (fraction of claims supported by a cited source) and citation accuracy (does each marker point at a span that supports it?) — the RAG-generation metrics of 54 §13 and 51 §13.

On paper

A report makes 50 claims; 47 are supported by their cited source:

\[ \text{groundedness} = 47/50 = 0.94 \]

94% grounded means 3 unsupported claims slipped through — which is why the evaluator gate blocks delivery until groundedness clears its threshold, rather than trusting the first draft.

docs.title: 8.9 Cost per task
docs.text:
On paper

A multi-source report: 10000 input and 2000 output tokens, at $0.50/$1.50 per 1M:

\[ \frac{10000}{10^6}\times 0.50 = 0.00500 \] \[ \frac{2000}{10^6}\times 1.50 = 0.00300 \] \[ \text{cost} = 0.00800 \]

$0.008 per report. The lever: a cheap model for search-and-extract, the mid model only for synthesis and the groundedness check (a cascade, §1); cache the stable instruction prefix across the loop (§1).

docs.title: 8.10 Failure modes and mitigations
docs.text: Failure Mitigation Fabricated citation Citation-accuracy eval; claims must trace to a retrieved span. Injection from a fetched page No write/outbound tools; untrusted content (56 §2.4). Endless searching Step/token budget; re-planning (52 §9). Leaking restricted internal docs Access control at retrieval (51 §11).

docs.title: 8.11 MVP → v2 → scale
docs.text: MVP: fixed RAG — retrieve once, answer with citations, no loop. v2: add the orchestrator and the groundedness evaluator once a citation-accuracy eval exists to prove they help. Scale: parallel workers for independent sub-questions (52 §2.4), a semantic cache of common questions, and human spot-checks feeding the eval set.

docs.title: 9.1 The job
docs.text: Who: account executives. Input: a lead or account, plus CRM records, past emails, and public company data. Success: enriched account data, a meeting-prep brief, and drafted outreach emails the rep reviews and sends; CRM writes happen only with approval. Volume (illustrative): 300 account actions/day across a team.

docs.title: 9.2 Why an agent (or why only partly)
docs.text: Enrichment and prep are a workflow (gather → summarize → draft). The agentic part is light: deciding which public sources to pull and which past threads matter for this account. Crucially, the assistant does not send email or write the CRM on its own — those are human or approval-gated, so autonomy stays low by design.

docs.title: 9.3 Architecture
docs.text:
integration shape: agent-as-tool (invoked from the CRM UI) + agent service

account ─▶ [assistant: mid model]
             │  retrieval: CRM records + email history + public data
             │  tools (read): get_account, search_emails, enrich_company
             │  tools (write): draft_email (to a draft, not sent), update_crm (approval)
             ▼
     brief + draft email ─▶ rep reviews ─▶ rep sends / approves CRM write ─▶ [audit log]

docs.title: 9.4 Tools
docs.text: Tool R/W Data it touches Approval? Size cap get_account read one CRM account no 1 record search_emails read that account's threads no 10 messages enrich_company read public company data no 1 profile draft_email write drafts folder (not sent) no (not sent) 1 draft update_crm write CRM fields yes 1 record

docs.title: 9.5 Context and data
docs.text: Retrieved: the account's CRM record, recent threads, and public firmographics. Remembered: a per-account summary as long-term memory, retrieved next time (52 §10). Never sent: other accounts' data (scope each tool to the account in context), and no customer PII beyond what the draft needs (56 §8).

docs.title: 9.6 Autonomy and guardrails
docs.text: Autonomy: suggest for email (the rep sends) and act with approval for CRM writes. The guardrail that keeps this safe is simply that the send button belongs to the human and update_crm is gated — a drafted email that is never auto-sent cannot embarrass anyone, and a CRM write the rep must confirm cannot corrupt the pipeline.

docs.title: 9.7 A sample trajectory
docs.text:
Thought: prep for the Acme call; pull the account and recent threads.
Action: get_account({"id": "acc_42"})
Observation: {"name": "Acme", "stage": "negotiation", "owner": "rep_7"}

Thought: enrich with public data.
Action: enrich_company({"domain": "acme.example"})
Observation: {"error": "RateLimited: retry after 2s"}        <- tool error

Thought: transient; back off and retry once.
Action: enrich_company({"domain": "acme.example"})
Observation: {"headcount": 1200, "recent": "opened a London office"}

Action: draft_email({"to": "acc_42", "angle": "London expansion"})
Action: update_crm({"id": "acc_42", "stage": "proposal"})   [PENDING APPROVAL]
Answer: Brief ready; draft saved to your drafts (not sent). CRM stage change
to "proposal" is queued for your approval.

docs.title: 9.8 Evals and metrics
docs.text:
Measure the draft acceptance rate (fraction the rep sends with no or minor edits) and the CRM-write override rate. Report acceptance as a Wilson interval (54 §8.1).

On paper

Reps send 180 of 200 drafts with at most minor edits, so \(\hat p = 0.90\), \(z=1.96\):

\[ \text{centre} = 0.8925 \] \[ \text{half-width} = 0.0419 \] \[ 0.8925 \pm 0.0419 = (0.851,\ 0.934) \]

The true acceptance rate is 85%–93%; because nothing sends without a human, a bad draft costs a rep's minute, not a customer relationship — which is why "suggest" is the right level here.

docs.title: 9.9 Cost per task
docs.text:
On paper

Enrichment plus a drafted email: 5000 input and 500 output tokens, at $0.50/$1.50 per 1M:

\[ \frac{5000}{10^6}\times 0.50 = 0.00250 \] \[ \frac{500}{10^6}\times 1.50 = 0.00075 \] \[ \text{cost} = 0.00325 \]

$0.00325 per account action. The lever: cache the per-account context prefix across the session (§1); a cheap model drafts, the mid model only polishes high-value outreach (a cascade, §1).

docs.title: 9.10 Failure modes and mitigations
docs.text: Failure Mitigation Auto-sent wrong email Draft only; the rep sends (§9.6). CRM corruption update_crm behind approval; scoped to one record. Hallucinated company facts Attribute enrichment to a source; mark unverified claims. Cross-account data bleed Scope every tool to the account in context (56 §6).

docs.title: 9.11 MVP → v2 → scale
docs.text: MVP: a read-only prep brief — no writes at all. v2: add drafted emails to the drafts folder once acceptance rate is good. Scale: approval-gated CRM writes, per-account memory, and a cascade for cost; keep the send button human forever.

docs.title: 10.1 The job
docs.text: Who: an online store's shoppers. Input: a chat message ("where is my order", "I want to return this"). Success: the order is looked up, policy applied, and a return or small refund processed under a limit — or escalated above it — with the shopper's issue resolved. Volume (illustrative): 10,000 conversations/day.

docs.title: 10.2 Why an agent (or why only partly)
docs.text: A workflow with a narrow agentic middle: lookup → policy RAG → decide. The decision "is this return within the window and the refund under the limit?" is policy-driven, and the model's job is to apply the retrieved policy to the specific order, escalating when it does not fit. Autonomy is bounded hard by the limit.

docs.title: 10.3 Architecture
docs.text:
integration shape: streaming chat UI (storefront) + agent service with run ids

message ─▶ [agent: mid model]
             │  retrieval: returns/refunds policy (RAG, 51)
             │  tools (read): get_order, get_policy
             │  tools (write): start_return, issue_refund (<= limit), escalate (> limit)
             ▼
     within limit ─▶ execute + [audit log] ─▶ reply (streamed)
     above  limit ─▶ escalate to human agent

docs.title: 10.4 Tools
docs.text: Tool R/W Data it touches Approval? Size cap get_order read one shopper's order no 1 record get_policy read returns policy docs no 3 chunks start_return write returns system no (within policy) 1 return issue_refund write payments if > $100 1 refund escalate write human queue no (safe) 1 handoff

docs.title: 10.5 Context and data
docs.text: Retrieved: the returns/refunds policy relevant to this order (category, date, condition) — RAG with metadata filters (51 §11). Remembered: the conversation; the shopper's order history on demand. Never sent: card numbers or full addresses beyond what the return needs (56 §8).

docs.title: 10.6 Autonomy and guardrails
docs.text: Autonomy: act with approval above the limit, act and report below it. A refund at or under $100 within the return window posts automatically; above $100, or outside the window, it escalates to a human. The refund tool is scoped to the shopper's own order — the same excessive-agency discipline as the support agent (56 §6).

docs.title: 10.7 A sample trajectory
docs.text:
Thought: shopper wants a return; get the order and the policy.
Action: get_order({"id": "O-5521"})
Observation: {"item": "boots", "price": 60.0, "delivered": "19 days ago"}

Thought: policy window is 30 days; check refund limit.
Action: get_policy({"category": "footwear"})
Observation: {"window_days": 30, "refund_limit": 100.0}

Thought: 19 <= 30 and $60 <= $100 -> within policy; start the return.
Action: start_return({"order": "O-5521"})
Observation: {"return_id": "R-77", "error": "label service down"}   <- tool error

Thought: return R-77 exists but has no label; retry the label, else queue it.
Action: start_return({"order": "O-5521", "return_id": "R-77", "retry_label": true})
Observation: {"return_id": "R-77", "label": "emailed"}

Answer: Return started for your boots; a prepaid label is on its way. Refund
of $60 posts when we receive them.

docs.title: 10.8 Evals and metrics
docs.text:
Measure task success, the escalation rate (above-limit cases correctly handed off), and reliability over the multi-step flow (52 §12).

On paper

A return flow is 4 steps, each succeeding independently with \(p=0.95\); end-to-end success (52 §12):

\[ S = 0.95^4 = 0.8145 \]

Of 100 conversations, 12 exceed the limit and are escalated:

\[ \text{escalation rate} = 12/100 = 0.12 \]

A 95% step gives only an 81% four-step flow — so keep the flow short — and a clean 12% escalation means the limit is doing its job, routing the expensive cases to a human.

docs.title: 10.9 Cost per task
docs.text:
On paper

A short conversation: 2500 input and 500 output tokens, at $0.50/$1.50 per 1M:

\[ \frac{2500}{10^6}\times 0.50 = 0.00125 \] \[ \frac{500}{10^6}\times 1.50 = 0.00075 \] \[ \text{cost} = 0.00200 \]

$0.002 per conversation. The lever: an exact-response cache for the many identical "where is my order" questions (55 §11.1); a cheap model for status lookups, escalating only returns to the mid model (§1).

docs.title: 10.10 Failure modes and mitigations
docs.text: Failure Mitigation Refund outside policy Apply retrieved policy; limit + window gate; escalate otherwise. Over-limit auto-refund Hard $100 gate in code (§10.6). Prompt injection in chat Untrusted user text; gate decides, not the text (56 §2). Wrong shopper's order Scope get_order/issue_refund to the authenticated shopper.

docs.title: 10.11 MVP → v2 → scale
