docs.text: MVP: order-status answers + "escalate to human" for anything touching money. v2: returns and under-limit refunds behind the policy gate once eval shows a low wrong-refund rate. Scale: cascade and caching for cost, multilingual support, and a feedback metric from post-chat surveys (55 §18.4).

docs.title: 11.1 The job
docs.text: Who: employees. Input: a request in a chat tool ("reset my password", "request access to repo X", "how much parental leave do I get?"). Success: routine requests resolved — password resets and access requests through the proper approval workflow, policy questions answered from HR docs — and anything sensitive escalated. Volume (illustrative): 800 requests/day.

docs.title: 11.2 Why an agent (or why only partly)
docs.text: Almost entirely a workflow: classify → (answer from policy | run an approval workflow). The agentic surface is tiny — picking the right workflow and filling its fields. Access requests are never granted by the model; they enter an existing approval system, which is the whole safety design.

docs.title: 11.3 Architecture
docs.text:
integration shape: streaming chat UI (chat bot) + approval workflow (durable)

request ─▶ [classify] ─▶ policy Q? ──▶ [RAG answer from HR/IT docs]
                      └▶ action?  ──▶ [agent fills workflow fields]
                                          │
                                          ▼
                             [identity + approval workflow]  <- existing system
                                          │ approved
                                          ▼
                             execute (reset / grant) ─▶ [audit log]

docs.title: 11.4 Tools
docs.text: Tool R/W Data it touches Approval? Size cap search_policy read HR/IT policy docs no 5 chunks verify_identity read identity provider no 1 check reset_password write identity provider yes (workflow) self only request_access write access workflow yes (approver) 1 request escalate write human queue no (safe) 1 handoff

docs.title: 11.5 Context and data
docs.text: Retrieved: the relevant HR/IT policy passages (51 §9). Remembered: the conversation only; no cross-employee memory. Never sent: credentials, security answers, or another employee's records — the agent fills an access request, it never reads the secret itself (56 §9), and identity is checked per request so the agent acts with the user's rights, not admin (56 §2.4).

docs.title: 11.6 Autonomy and guardrails
docs.text: Autonomy: act with approval for every write — a password reset goes through the identity provider's own self-service verification, and an access request goes to a human approver. The agent cannot grant access; it can only route a well-formed request into the workflow that a human approves. That separation is the control.

docs.title: 11.7 A sample trajectory
docs.text:
Thought: user wants repo access; verify identity first.
Action: verify_identity({"user": "u_31"})
Observation: {"verified": true}

Thought: file the access request with the manager as approver.
Action: request_access({"user": "u_31", "resource": "repo:payments"})
Observation: {"error": "unknown resource id 'repo:payments'"}  <- tool error

Thought: resource id wrong; look it up and refile.
Action: search_policy({"q": "payments repo access id"})
Observation: resource id is "gh:payments-service"
Action: request_access({"user": "u_31", "resource": "gh:payments-service"})
Observation: {"request_id": "AR-90", "status": "pending_manager_approval"}

Answer: Access request AR-90 filed; your manager will approve or deny.

docs.title: 11.8 Evals and metrics
docs.text:
Measure resolution rate for routine requests, false-escalation, and — critical — zero unauthorized grants. Report resolution as a Wilson interval (54 §8.1).

On paper

228 of 240 routine requests resolved correctly, so \(\hat p = 0.95\), \(z=1.96\):

\[ \text{centre} = 0.9429 \] \[ \text{half-width} = 0.0283 \] \[ 0.9429 \pm 0.0283 = (0.915,\ 0.971) \]

92%–97% of routine requests handled end to end; the ones it cannot are escalated, and because grants need a human approver, a misclassification wastes a minute rather than opening a door.

docs.title: 11.9 Cost per task
docs.text:
On paper

A short policy answer or form-fill: 2000 input and 500 output tokens, at $0.50/$1.50 per 1M:

\[ \frac{2000}{10^6}\times 0.50 = 0.00100 \] \[ \frac{500}{10^6}\times 1.50 = 0.00075 \] \[ \text{cost} = 0.00175 \]

$0.00175 per request. The lever: an exact/semantic cache for the many identical policy questions (55 §11.2) — "how much parental leave" is asked a hundred times a week.

docs.title: 11.10 Failure modes and mitigations
docs.text: Failure Mitigation Unauthorized access granted Grants go through a human approver; agent only files (§11.6). Wrong policy answer Answer from retrieved docs; cite; refuse when unsure (51 §9). Reset for the wrong user Identity verification; self-service scope only. Social-engineering via chat Treat requests as untrusted; identity and approval are the gate (56 §2).

docs.title: 11.11 MVP → v2 → scale
docs.text: MVP: a policy-Q&A bot over HR/IT docs — read-only, no actions. v2: route password resets and access requests into the existing approval workflows. Scale: more request types one at a time, each through an approver; a feedback loop on resolved tickets to grow the eval set.

docs.title: 12.1 The job
docs.text: Who: a data-platform team. Input: a failed pipeline job (a DAG task), its logs, and data lineage. Success: the agent diagnoses the failure, proposes a fix as a pull request with a test, and never edits production data or the running pipeline directly. Volume (illustrative): 30 job failures/day across hundreds of pipelines.

docs.title: 12.2 Why an agent
docs.text: Observation-driven diagnosis, like the on-call responder: read the failed task's logs, trace lineage to the upstream source, form a hypothesis, and propose a fix. The next lookup depends on the last — an agent (52 §1.1) — but the output is a PR, not a production change.

docs.title: 12.3 Architecture
docs.text:
integration shape: durable workflow engine (resumable; triggered on job failure)

failure ─▶ [maintenance agent: mid model]  (checkpointed; survives restart)
             │  retrieval: job logs + DAG lineage + the pipeline code
             │  tools (read): get_logs, get_lineage, read_code, run_in_staging
             │  tools (write): open_pr (with a regression test)
             ▼
     diagnose ─▶ fix in a branch ─▶ run_in_staging ─▶ open_pr ─▶ [audit log]
guardrails: staging only; no prod writes; a human reviews and merges the PR

docs.title: 12.4 Tools
docs.text: Tool R/W Data it touches Approval? Size cap get_logs read job log store no 50 lines get_lineage read lineage graph no 20 nodes read_code read pipeline repo no 400 lines run_in_staging read staging run (sandbox) no summary open_pr write the repo human merges 1 PR + test

docs.title: 12.5 Context and data
docs.text: Retrieved: the failed task's logs, the lineage to the upstream table, and the pipeline code. Remembered: the diagnosis transcript, checkpointed so a long run survives a worker restart (52 §8.1). Never sent: the production data — the agent reads schemas, lineage metadata, and logs, not rows (56 §9).

docs.title: 12.6 Autonomy and guardrails
docs.text: Autonomy: act and report in staging (it can run a fix against a staging copy) and suggest for production (the PR is a proposal; a human merges, and the merge triggers the real pipeline change through the normal CD path). There is no tool that writes production data — the capability simply does not exist in the agent's surface, which is the cleanest form of least privilege (52 §16).

docs.title: 12.7 A sample trajectory
docs.text:
Thought: the "load_orders" task failed; read its logs.
Action: get_logs({"task": "load_orders", "run": "r_900"})
Observation: SchemaError: column "currency" missing in source

Thought: upstream schema drifted. Trace lineage to the source.
Action: get_lineage({"table": "orders"})
Observation: {"error": "lineage service timeout"}            <- tool error

Thought: retry; lineage is needed to find the upstream owner.
Action: get_lineage({"table": "orders"})
Observation: source = "raw.orders_v2" (added "currency" last week)

Thought: add a nullable "currency" mapping + a regression test, run in staging.
Action: run_in_staging({"branch": "fix-currency"})
Observation: {"status": "green", "rows": 10432}
Action: open_pr({"branch": "fix-currency", "test": "test_currency_nullable"})

Answer: Opened PR #58 mapping the new "currency" column with a regression test;
staging run green. Needs review and merge.

docs.title: 12.8 Evals and metrics
docs.text:
Measure diagnosis accuracy against labelled past failures and the end-to-end task success over the diagnose→fix→test→PR flow (52 §12, 54 §13).

On paper

The flow is 5 steps, each succeeding independently with \(p=0.97\); end-to-end success:

\[ S = 0.97^5 = 0.8587 \]

Even at 97% per step, a 5-step flow lands at 86% — so the PR gate and the human reviewer catch the ~14% of runs that go wrong somewhere, and you shorten the flow where you can (52 §12).

docs.title: 12.9 Cost per task
docs.text:
On paper

A log-and-lineage-heavy run: 15000 input and 3000 output tokens, at $0.50/$1.50 per 1M:

\[ \frac{15000}{10^6}\times 0.50 = 0.00750 \] \[ \frac{3000}{10^6}\times 1.50 = 0.00450 \] \[ \text{cost} = 0.01200 \]

$0.012 per failure. The lever: summarize old log observations so the resend stops growing (52 §13); cache the pipeline-code and DAG prefix across the loop (§1).

docs.title: 12.10 Failure modes and mitigations
docs.text: Failure Mitigation Production data edited No prod-write tool exists; staging only (§12.6). Fix that masks the real bug Require a regression test; human review of the PR. Log flood over budget Summarize; cap results; token budget (52 §14). Long run lost on restart Checkpoint + resume (52 §8.1).

docs.title: 12.11 MVP → v2 → scale
docs.text: MVP: a read-only triager that posts a diagnosis and the likely upstream cause. v2: add the staging fix + PR-with-test once diagnosis accuracy is proven on past failures. Scale: a durable engine so long runs resume, lineage-aware retrieval, and a regression-rate gate on merged fixes.

docs.title: 13.1 The job
docs.text: Who: a QA team. Input: a user journey to exercise on a staging app ("sign up, add to cart, check out"). Success: the journey is driven end to end; when it breaks, a reproducible bug report is filed with steps, the failing assertion, and a screenshot. Volume (illustrative): 200 journeys/night in CI.

docs.title: 13.2 Why an agent (or why only partly)
docs.text: Partly a workflow (the journey steps are mostly fixed) with an agentic recovery layer: when a selector moves or a page differs from the script, the model reads the screen (accessibility tree) and finds the element, instead of the brittle script failing outright (52 §8.3). Browser agents are the highest-risk autonomy, so this one is strictly read-mostly and staging-only.

docs.title: 13.3 Architecture
docs.text:
integration shape: scheduled/batch (nightly CI) + local harness driving a browser

journey ─▶ [QA agent: mid model] (staging only, read-mostly)
             │  observation: accessibility tree + screenshot
             │  tools: navigate, click, type, read_dom, screenshot, file_bug
             ▼
     step ─▶ observe ─▶ assert ──fail──▶ file_bug (steps + assertion + shot)
             │ pass
             ▼
     next step ... ─▶ report pass/fail ─▶ [audit log]
guardrails: staging URL allow-list; never run against production; no destructive data

docs.title: 13.4 Tools
docs.text: Tool R/W Data it touches Approval? Size cap navigate write-ish staging URL (allow-list) no (staging) 1 page read_dom read the page accessibility tree no 4k chars click / type write-ish staging UI only no (staging) 1 action screenshot read the page no 1 image file_bug write issue tracker no (safe) 1 report

docs.title: 13.5 Context and data
docs.text: Retrieved: the journey spec and the current page's accessibility tree (cheaper and more reliable than a raw screenshot — 52 §8.3). Remembered: the steps taken, for the bug report's reproduction trail. Never sent: real user data — staging uses synthetic accounts, and a staging URL allow-list keeps it off production (56 §6).

docs.title: 13.6 Autonomy and guardrails
docs.text: Autonomy: act and report against staging (it clicks and types freely in a throwaway environment) and strictly read-only toward production (no production URL is on the allow-list). The guardrail is the allow-list plus synthetic data: the agent cannot reach production or touch a real account, so even a confused trajectory is contained (52 §16).

docs.title: 13.7 A sample trajectory
docs.text:
Thought: start the checkout journey on staging.
Action: navigate({"url": "https://staging.shop.internal/cart"})
Observation: page loaded; cart has 1 item

Thought: click the checkout button.
Action: click({"selector": "#checkout"})
Observation: {"error": "no element matches #checkout"}        <- tool error

Thought: selector moved; read the DOM to find the real control.
Action: read_dom({})
Observation: button "Proceed to checkout" role=button id="co-btn"

Thought: use the accessibility label instead of the stale id.
Action: click({"selector": "#co-btn"})
Observation: checkout page; total $60
[harness] assert total == expected -> FAIL (expected $54 after discount)
Action: file_bug({"title": "Discount not applied at checkout", "steps": "...",
                  "expected": 54, "actual": 60, "shot": "co.png"})

Answer: Journey failed at checkout; filed bug QA-311 with steps and screenshot.

docs.title: 13.8 Evals and metrics
docs.text:
Measure journey pass rate, flakiness (does a journey pass consistently across reruns?), and false-bug rate. Flakiness is a reliability question — a journey must pass every rerun (09 §5).

On paper

A journey passes any single run with \(p=0.95\) independently; the chance it passes all 3 nightly reruns (pass\(^3\), the reliability view):

\[ \text{pass}^3 = 0.95^3 = 0.8574 \]

A "95% reliable" journey is green on all three runs only 86% of the time — so 14% of journeys flake at least once, and flakiness, not raw pass rate, is what wastes a QA team's morning.

docs.title: 13.9 Cost per task
docs.text:
On paper

A journey with several DOM reads: 8000 input and 400 output tokens, at $0.50/$1.50 per 1M:

\[ \frac{8000}{10^6}\times 0.50 = 0.00400 \] \[ \frac{400}{10^6}\times 1.50 = 0.00060 \] \[ \text{cost} = 0.00460 \]

$0.0046 per journey. The lever: feed the accessibility tree, not full screenshots, so each observation is small text not a large image; cache the app-shell prefix across steps (§1).

docs.title: 13.10 Failure modes and mitigations
docs.text: Failure Mitigation Ran against production Staging URL allow-list; no prod URL exists (§13.6). Flaky false bugs Rerun before filing; require a stable repro; flakiness metric. Brittle selectors Use the accessibility tree; recover on selector miss (52 §8.3). Injection via page content Treat page text as untrusted (56 §2).

docs.title: 13.11 MVP → v2 → scale
docs.text: MVP: a scripted (non-agent) journey runner — fixed selectors, no model. v2: add the model's recovery layer for selector drift once it measurably reduces false failures. Scale: parallel journeys in CI, a flakiness gate, and screenshot-diffing for visual regressions — always staging, never production.

docs.title: 14. The twelve compared
docs.text:
# Application Integration shape Autonomy Write tools? Approval model Main risk Main metric 1 Support resolution streaming chat UI + service act & report / approval yes (refund) gate > $50 wrong refund resolution rate 2 Coding in CI queue worker (sandbox) act & report / suggest yes (sandbox, PR) human merge regression / test-gaming pass@k 3 Data-analyst (SQL) agent service (run ids) act & report no (read-only) none (read-only) destructive SQL execution accuracy 4 On-call responder queue worker + chat act w/ approval yes (allow-list) per write wrong remediation diagnosis / unsafe=0 5 Security (Kali) local harness act w/ approval yes (kali_exec, confirmed) confirm per 11 §5.1 out-of-scope action task success / unsafe=0 6 Document processing queue worker / batch act & report yes (post) low-conf → review confident wrong field precision / auto-post error 7 Research & report agent service (async) act & report / suggest no none (read-only) fabricated citation groundedness 8 Sales / CRM agent-as-tool + service suggest / act w/ approval yes (CRM) human send; CRM gate auto-sent email draft acceptance 9 E-commerce returns streaming chat UI + service act & report / approval yes (refund) gate > $100 over-limit refund task success / escalation 10 IT/HR helpdesk streaming chat UI + workflow act w/ approval yes (via workflow) approver unauthorized grant resolution rate 11 Data-pipeline durable workflow engine act & report / suggest no prod; PR only human merge prod data edit diagnosis / task success 12 QA / browser scheduled/batch + harness act & report staging only none (staging) ran against prod flakiness

Read the table top to bottom and the pattern is unmistakable: no write tool is ever fully autonomous; every one is either read-only, sandboxed, gated by a limit, or gated by a human; and the "main metric" is a measurable thing you gate a release on, not a vibe.

docs.title: 15. Patterns that recur
docs.text:
Strip away the domains and the same five moves appear in all twelve:

  • Read-mostly tools. The large majority of tools are reads; writes are few, narrow, and scoped to the one object in context. A tool that can read one order cannot dump the table (52 §16, 56 §6). When a write capability is not needed, it is simply absent — the pipeline agent has no production-write tool at all.
  • Approval for writes, auto-run for reads. The autonomy level is set per action class, not per application: read-only recon/lookup/query runs automatically; anything that spends, sends, deletes, or changes config is gated by a limit or a human (52 §15). The gate is code — a deterministic check or an existing approval workflow — never a sentence in the prompt.
  • Budgets, always. Steps, tokens, wall-clock, and money, enforced by your runtime, not requested of the model (52 §14). They bound both the compounding unreliability (52 §12) and the quadratic cost (52 §13).
  • A verification step before the consequence. A SQL verifier, a test run, a confidence threshold, a groundedness check, a schema validator — an external check between the model's output and the side effect, because the model grading itself is as biased as its output (52 §9, 54 §4).
  • An eval you trust before you raise autonomy. Every "v2" above is gated on a number from a held-out set: wrong-refund rate near zero, pass@k high enough, execution accuracy inside a tight interval. You do not promote an agent from "suggest" to "act" on a hunch; you promote it on an eval (54 §13, 52 §17).

And one meta-pattern: most of these started life as a workflow. The MVP is almost always a fixed chain or a single structured call with a human doing the risky part; the agent arrives only where the path genuinely cannot be enumerated and the eval proves the loop earns its cost (52 §2.6, 61 §17).

docs.title: 16. Key takeaways
docs.text:
• Twelve applications, one template: job, why-an-agent, architecture, tools, data, autonomy, trajectory, evals, cost, failures, growth. Comparing across them teaches more than any one in isolation.
  • The split is almost always the same: a fixed workflow does most of the work, and a small observation-driven tail is the only genuinely agentic part. Keep the autonomous surface small on purpose.
  • Name the integration shape (62) and the autonomy level (52 §8) for every feature; they determine the guardrails you owe.
  • Reads auto-run; writes are gated — by a limit, a sandbox, an approval, or by not existing. No write tool here is fully autonomous.
  • Put a verification step (verifier, test, threshold, groundedness) between the model and every consequence; prefer an external check over the model's self-assessment.
  • Compute the cost per task with your own assumed prices, and cut it with a cascade and prefix caching — the same two levers in nearly every application.
  • Raise autonomy only when an eval on a held-out set says so. "MVP as a workflow, agent at v2, scale when the number holds" is the safe path every application followed.
  • The security application is authorized lab testing only, behind a deterministic policy layer and an air-gapped sandbox (11, 12) — summarized here, specified there.

docs.title: 17. Exercises
docs.text:
Exercise 17.1

A support agent resolves 150 of 200 held-out tickets. Give the point estimate and say why you would not ship a prompt change that moves it to 152/200.

Answer

Point estimate \(150/200 = 0.75\). The Wilson 95% interval is about \((0.686, 0.805)\) — a half-width near 0.060. A move to \(152/200 = 0.76\) is well inside that interval, so it is noise on 200 tickets; you need more examples or a paired test (54 §8.1) before calling it an improvement.

Exercise 17.2

A coding agent gets 5 independent attempts on a bug and 3 produce a green diff. Compute pass@1 and pass@2, and say which matters for CI.

Answer

\(\text{pass@}1 = 3/5 = 0.6\). \(\text{pass@}2 = 1 - \binom{2}{2}/\binom{5}{2}\), which is \(1 - 1/10 = 0.9\). CI can afford a retry, so pass@2 (0.9) is the deployment-relevant number — the chance at least one of two attempts lands a green diff.

Exercise 17.3

An e-commerce return flow has 4 steps, each succeeding independently with probability 0.95. What is the end-to-end success rate, and what is the cheapest way to raise it?

Answer

\(S = 0.95^4 = 0.8145\). The cheapest lever is usually to shorten the flow (fewer steps directly raises \(p^n\)); the complementary lever is to raise per-step \(p\) with verification or retries (52 §12).

Exercise 17.4

A document agent's total field has 90 correct, 10 wrong, 20 missed. Compute precision, recall, and F1, and explain which one the confidence router is protecting.

Answer

Precision \(= 90/100 = 0.90\); recall \(= 90/110 = 0.818\); \(F_1 = 2(0.90)(0.818)/(0.90+0.818)\), which is \(1.472/1.718 = 0.857\). The router protects precision among auto-posted records: by sending low-confidence extractions to a human it keeps the 10% wrong rate out of the auto-posted set, trading some recall (more go to review) for fewer wrong postings.

Exercise 17.5

An incident agent proposes a remediation on 50 incidents and the human rejects 4; across 120 runs it attempted 0 out-of-allow-list actions. Give the override rate and explain why you keep the approval gate despite the zero.

Answer

Override rate \(= 4/50 = 0.08\). "0 of 120" gives a Wilson 95% upper bound near 0.031 on the unsafe-action rate — zero observed is not zero possible, only bounded at ~3%. You keep the gate because a single wrong write during an incident is costly, and the bound does not rule one out (54 §8.1).

Exercise 17.6

A research report makes 50 claims; 47 are supported by their cited source. Compute groundedness and explain why the evaluator gate still blocks delivery.

Answer

Groundedness \(= 47/50 = 0.94\). Three unsupported claims remain, and an unsupported claim in a delivered report is exactly the failure the agent exists to avoid — so the evaluator blocks delivery until groundedness clears its threshold, rather than trusting a 94% draft (54 §13).

Exercise 17.7

An API agent step costs $0.004; a cheap model costs $0.0005 and you escalate 30% of tasks. What is the expected cost per task with a cascade, and the percentage saved?

Answer

\(E[\text{cost}] = 0.0005 + 0.3\times 0.004\), which is \(0.0005 + 0.0012 = 0.0017\). Against $0.004 mid-only, that is a saving of \((0.004-0.0017)/0.004 = 0.575\), or 57.5% — because only the escalated 30% pay the mid rate (55 §13).

Exercise 17.8

You are asked to build an agent that "automatically fixes production incidents end to end, no human." Using the patterns of §15, give the design you would actually ship instead.

Answer

Ship act with approval, not full autonomy: read-only diagnosis runs automatically; every remediation is allow-listed and gated on a human yes that shows the exact action; hard budgets on steps/tokens/time; an audit log; and promotion of any single action from "suggest" to "approved-auto" only after an eval shows a low override rate and a zero unsafe-action rate. A wrong autonomous write during an incident is precisely the harm the gate prevents (52 §15, 56 §6).

Exercise 17.9

A QA journey passes a single run with probability 0.95 independently. What is the chance it passes all 3 nightly reruns, and why is that the number QA cares about?

Answer

\(\text{pass}^3 = 0.95^3 = 0.8574\). QA cares about pass\(^3\) (all runs green) rather than a single pass because a journey that flakes on even one of three reruns wastes triage time and erodes trust in the suite — flakiness, not average pass rate, is the cost (09 §5).

Exercise 17.10

A pipeline agent's flow is 5 steps at 0.97 each. Compute end-to-end success and name two guardrails that catch the rest.

Answer

\(S = 0.97^5 = 0.8587\). About 14% of runs go wrong somewhere; the two guardrails that catch them are the PR gate with a required regression test (nothing reaches production without passing) and the human reviewer who merges — plus checkpointing so a long run resumes rather than restarts (52 §8.1).

Next: 62 — Integrating agents into applications for the run contract and the minimal agent service behind these shapes; 52 — Agents for the loop, budgets and autonomy they all build on; 54 — Evaluation to build the eval that gates every autonomy increase.

docs.title: Appendix A — Configs, explained
docs.text:
The files in configs/ are starting points. Every value here has a reason; change one variable at a time and record the result.

The defaults below follow 17 — Fine-tuning update: all-layer LoRA, scale = 32 / rank, and one to two epochs.

Config Role Layers Rank Scale LR qwen3-8b-fast.yaml smoke / format 12 16 2.0 1e-4 qwen3-8b-all-layers.yaml 8B all-layer -1 16 2.0 1.5e-4 qwen3-14b-all-layers.yaml recommended 14B -1 16 2.0 1e-4 qwen3-14b-balanced.yaml last-16 baseline 16 16 2.0 1e-4 qwen3-14b-rank32.yaml capacity test -1 32 1.0 1e-4 qwen3-14b-conservative.yaml memory fallback 8 8 4.0 1e-4 qwen3-14b-longctx.yaml 4K context 16 16 2.0 8e-5

model: mlx-community/Qwen3-8B-4bit
train: true
data: data/processed
fine_tune_type: lora
optimizer: adamw
num_layers: 12
batch_size: 2
iters: 400
val_batches: 25
learning_rate: 1.0e-4
steps_per_report: 10
steps_per_eval: 100
save_every: 100
max_seq_length: 2048
grad_checkpoint: true
grad_accumulation_steps: 4
mask_prompt: true
adapter_path: adapters/qwen3-8b-pentest
seed: 42
lora_parameters:
  rank: 16
  dropout: 0.05
  scale: 2.0

  name: cosine_decay
  warmup: 50
  arguments: [1.0e-4, 400, 1.0e-6]

Value Why 8B 4-bit ~4.6 GB weights; 10–12 GB peak; fast iteration. 12 layers Enough to learn the format; lower memory than all-layer. batch 2 × accum 4 Effective batch 8; fits comfortably. 400 iters ~4.8M tokens at 1.5k/sample; adjust to your dataset. LR 1e-4 + scale 2.0 Standard alpha=32 parameterization. rank 16 ~19M trainable params over 12 layers. seq 2048 Cheap; split longer trajectories. grad-checkpoint Buys headroom; ~20–30% slower.

Use this for a 100k-token smoke test first: subset the data and set iters: 50. Confirm loss falls and tool calls render before running the full config.

docs.title: A.5 qwen3-14b-rank32.yaml — capacity test
docs.text: All layers, rank 32, scale: 1.0, 300 iters. ~125M trainable params. Run only if the rank-16 all-layer adapter underfits and you have a clean, larger dataset. The extra capacity is not free: more overfitting risk and a larger adapter.

docs.title: A.6 qwen3-14b-longctx.yaml — 4K context
docs.text: Last 16 layers, rank 16, scale: 2.0, seq 4096, 250 iters. 4K roughly doubles activation memory versus 2K. If it OOMs, drop to 3072 or 12 layers. Do not raise max_seq_length just because a few examples are long; split them instead.

docs.title: A.7 Tuning rules of thumb
docs.text: If… Change OOM at step 1 num_layers: 24, then 16; keep seq 2048; batch_size: 1. Still OOM seq 1536; conservative config; --clear-cache-threshold 2GB. Loss nan Check token lengths; drop rows where prompt ≥ max sequence. Halve LR. Loss stuck >1.0 Verify mask/template; check scale; raise LR only after check_lora.py. Val loss rises Stop earlier; dropout 0.1; fewer epochs; more diverse data. Underfitting rank 16→32, more data, cleaner labels; layers already all. Too slow 8B; last 16; shorter sequences; close apps. Adapter has no effect Wrong base/path; verify with a fixed prompt.

docs.title: A.8 What not to change casually
docs.text:
• Model family mid-run: the adapter is tied to the base architecture.
  • Chat template mid-run: the tokenizer is part of the model.
  • scale without adjusting LR: scale multiplies the update; scale = alpha / rank.
  • --fine-tune-type full on 14B: it does not fit 32 GB.
  • max_seq_length without re-measuring: truncation can cut a tool call.

docs.title: A.14 Config validation
docs.text:
python - <<'PY'
import yaml
from pathlib import Path
for p in Path("configs").glob("*.yaml"):
    d = yaml.safe_load(p.read_text())
    print(p.name, "layers=", d.get("num_layers"), "rank=", d["lora_parameters"]["rank"],
          "scale=", d["lora_parameters"]["scale"], "lr=", d.get("learning_rate"))
PY

Run a 1-iteration test before a long run:

mlx_lm.lora --config configs/qwen3-8b-fast.yaml --iters 1 --save-every 1

And verify the adapter actually covers MLP layers:

python scripts/check_lora.py --model mlx-community/Qwen3-14B-4bit \
  --num-layers -1 --rank 16 --scale 2

Generate a small sweep:

python scripts/make_sweep.py --base configs/qwen3-14b-all-layers.yaml \
  --out configs/sweeps/r1 --rank 16,32 --lr 5e-5,1e-4 --layers all,16

docs.title: B.1 check_env.py
docs.text:
Checks:

  • macOS and arm64;
  • Python ≥3.11;
  • mlx, mlx_lm, transformers versions;
  • mx.device_info() and the recommended working set;
  • free disk in the repo volume and HF_HOME;
  • whether the expected model/tool files exist.

It exits non-zero on a hard failure (wrong arch, missing MLX).

docs.title: B.2 validate_dataset.py
docs.text:
Validates one JSONL file. Exit code 0 = no hard errors. Warnings do not fail the run.

Hard checks:

  • JSON parse;
  • messages array, valid roles, non-empty;
  • tool name membership;
  • arguments parses as a JSON object;
  • required fields;
  • tool message follows an assistant tool call;
  • no <think> in content;
  • no empty assistant message.

Soft checks (warnings):

  • first message is not system;
  • destructive patterns;
  • secret patterns;
  • suspiciously short/long rows;
  • duplicate IDs.

Use --strict to make warnings fail in CI.

docs.title: B.3 token_stats.py
docs.text:
Loads the tokenizer (default Qwen/Qwen3-14B), renders each row with its tools, and reports:

  • count, min, p50, p90, p95, p99, max;
  • how many rows exceed 2048/4096/8192;
  • a recommended max_seq_length at the 99th percentile rounded to 256.

It does not require MLX; it uses transformers only. It downloads the tokenizer once into HF_HOME.

docs.title: B.4 prepare_dataset.py
docs.text:
Input: canonical JSONL with messages and optional tools. Output:

data/processed/
├── train.jsonl
├── valid.jsonl
├── test.jsonl
└── manifest.json

It:

  • normalizes tool names to [A-Za-z0-9_-];
  • parses arguments and writes them in the target shape: JSON string by default, or a JSON object with --arguments-format dict for Qwen2.5-Coder;
  • drops rows missing a tool definition;
  • exact-dedups on normalized messages;
  • splits deterministically by hash (no RNG);
  • writes counts, token estimates, and a SHA-256 for each split.
python scripts/prepare_dataset.py data/java/interim/all.jsonl \
  --out data/java/processed --arguments-format dict

It does not near-dedup by default; use split_dataset.py --minhash for that.

docs.title: B.5 split_dataset.py
docs.text:
Deterministic split with optional MinHash near-duplicate removal. Use it when merging multiple sources with paraphrases.

python scripts/split_dataset.py data/interim/all.jsonl \
  --out data/processed --minhash --threshold 0.8

Requires datasketch (uv pip install datasketch). If not installed, it falls back to exact dedup and warns.

docs.title: B.6 generate_synthetic.py
docs.text:
A scaffold, not a turnkey data factory. It:

  • reads a task taxonomy or a list of prompts;
  • calls an OpenAI-compatible endpoint (DeepSeek by default);
  • requests JSON, validates it, retries with backoff;
  • tracks input/output tokens and estimated USD;
  • writes one JSON object per line with provenance (teacher, prompt_hash, created).

--system-file and --prompt-file override the built-in Kali prompts. The prompt file may use {n} for the batch size; this is how the Java/Quarkus task generator is wired:

python scripts/generate_synthetic.py --mode tasks --tasks 300 --batch 10 \
  --model deepseek-flash \
  --system-file examples/java/teacher-system.md \
  --prompt-file examples/java/task-prompt.md \
  --out data/java/interim/tasks.jsonl

For React/Tailwind:

python scripts/generate_synthetic.py --mode tasks --tasks 300 --batch 10 \
  --model deepseek-flash \
  --system-file examples/react/teacher-system.md \
  --prompt-file examples/react/task-prompt.md \
  --out data/react/interim/tasks.jsonl

It does not execute commands. Pair it with execute_verified.py for Kali, the Maven sandbox in 21 — Java synthetic data for Java, or the Playwright sandbox in 25 — React synthetic data for React.

export DEEPSEEK_API_KEY=...
python scripts/generate_synthetic.py \
  --tasks 25 --model deepseek-flash --concurrency 8 \
  --out data/interim/tasks.jsonl --dry-run

--dry-run prints the prompts and cost estimate without calling the API.

docs.title: B.7 execute_verified.py
docs.text:
The dangerous one. Safety properties:

  • refuses to run without --i-understand;
  • requires Docker and a container named kali-lab (or --container);
  • refuses if the container has --network host;
  • default --dry-run prints the commands and exits;
  • per-command timeout (default 60 s);
  • allowlist of binaries;
  • destructive-pattern denylist;
  • captures stdout/stderr/exit code, truncates to 4,000 chars;
  • writes a JSONL trajectory per plan.
# 1. Start the lab (no egress)
docker compose -f examples/docker-compose.lab.yml up -d

# 2. Inspect what would run
python scripts/execute_verified.py --input data/interim/plans.jsonl --out /tmp/x.jsonl

# 3. Execute (only after reviewing)
python scripts/execute_verified.py --input data/interim/plans.jsonl \
  --out data/interim/verified.jsonl --container kali-lab --i-understand

It never executes on the host. If Docker is unavailable, it exits with an error.

docs.title: B.8 eval_toolcall.py
docs.text:
Runs a golden set against an OpenAI-compatible endpoint. For each task:

  1. builds the system prompt + scope + tools;
  2. sends the user task;
  3. if the model returns tool calls, grades names/arguments (and optionally executes them via a sandbox URL);
  4. if the model returns text, grades refusal/no-call;
  5. records turns, latency, pass/fail, reason.

Output: a JSON report with per-category metrics, Wilson intervals, and a failure list.

python scripts/eval_toolcall.py \
  --base-url http://127.0.0.1:8080/v1 \
  --model local \
  --golden data/golden/golden.jsonl \
  --out reports/14b-r1.json

--sandbox http://127.0.0.1:5000 enables execution grading (optional).

docs.title: B.9 smoke_test.py
docs.text:
Ten prompts covering:

  • simple tool call;
  • multiple tools;
  • tool + argument enum;
  • no-call question;
  • out-of-scope refusal;
  • ambiguous target;
  • malicious/destructive request;
  • malformed tool response;
  • long system prompt;
  • parallel-safe calls.

It checks tool name membership, JSON validity, and forbidden targets. Exit non-zero if any hard check fails.

docs.title: B.10 make_dataset_card.py
docs.text:
Reads manifest.json, samples rows, and writes a Markdown card with:

  • intended use / out-of-scope use;
  • sources and licenses;
  • preprocessing and dedup;
  • counts and token estimates;
  • known issues;
  • evaluation and maintenance.

It does not invent license text; it copies the manifest fields.

docs.title: B.11 check_lora.py
docs.text:
Loads the base model, applies the same linear_to_lora_layers conversion MLX-LM uses, and reports:

  • transformer block count;
  • selected vs adapted blocks;
  • number of LoRA modules and counts by projection (q_proj, k_proj, v_proj, o_proj, gate_proj, up_proj, down_proj);
  • trainable parameters and percentage;
  • sample module names.

Use it to catch attention-only adapters, stale MLX versions, or a custom lora_parameters.keys that silently excludes MLP. Exit code 2 means the module count is unusually low.

python scripts/check_lora.py --model mlx-community/Qwen3-14B-4bit \
  --num-layers -1 --rank 16 --scale 2

Requires MLX; it will not run on Linux.

docs.title: B.12 make_sweep.py
docs.text:
Generates a Cartesian product of rank, learning rate and layer count from a base YAML. It sets scale = 32 / rank by default, writes one YAML per run, a commands.sh, and a sweep.md table.

python scripts/make_sweep.py \
  --base configs/qwen3-14b-all-layers.yaml \
  --out configs/sweeps/r1 \
  --rank 16,32 --lr 5e-5,1e-4 --layers all,16
bash configs/sweeps/r1/commands.sh

Each run gets a unique adapter_path under adapters/sweeps/. It does not launch training; review the configs and the time budget first.

docs.title: B.13 validate_java_dataset.py
docs.text:
A Java/Quarkus linter for canonical chat JSONL. It checks assistant text and tool arguments for:

  • legacy javax.persistence/ws.rs/inject/enterprise/transaction/validation;
  • Spring idioms (org.springframework, @Autowired);
  • legacy quarkus-resteasy-reactive;
  • Quarkus/Java version tags other than the target;
  • System.out, printStackTrace, TODO/FIXME, Lombok;
  • probable secrets;
  • unbalanced code fences;
  • tool arguments stored as strings when --require-dict-arguments is set (Qwen2.5-Coder).

It does not compile Java. Pair it with ./mvnw test.

docs.title: B.14 mine_java_commits.py
docs.text:
Reads a git repository and writes Java commit seeds:

{"schema":"java-commit-task-v1","repo":"...","base_commit":"...","commit":"...",
 "task":"...","files":["..."],"patch":"diff --git ...","test_command":"./mvnw -q -DskipITs test"}

Options:

  • --limit — number of commits to inspect;
  • --since — git date filter;
  • --only-with-tests — require a change under src/test;
  • --max-patch-bytes, --max-files — skip huge commits;
  • --license — record the source license.

It is read-only and does not execute code. The seeds are inputs for the LLM + sandbox pipeline in 21 — Java synthetic data, not training rows by themselves.

docs.title: B.15 validate_react_dataset.py
docs.text:
A React/Tailwind linter for canonical chat JSONL. It scans code blocks for:

  • @tailwind base/components/utilities (allowed only in a migration task);
  • tailwind.config.* in a v4 task;
  • removed v4 utilities (bg-opacity-*, flex-shrink-*, overflow-ellipsis, …);
  • outline-none on focusable elements;
  • ReactDOM.render, useFormState, React.FC, class components, propTypes, defaultProps;
  • dynamic Tailwind class construction and arbitrary hex;
  • unsanitized dangerouslySetInnerHTML;
  • <img> without alt, <button> without type, clickable div without role;
  • target="_blank" without rel;
  • key={index}, any, @ts-ignore, console.log, TODO;
  • probable secrets;
  • tool arguments stored as strings when --require-dict-arguments is set.

It does not compile, render or test. Pair it with npm run typecheck, Vitest, Playwright and axe.

docs.title: B.16 mine_react_commits.py
docs.text:
Reads a git repository and writes React/TS commit seeds:

{"schema":"react-commit-task-v1","repo":"...","base_commit":"...","commit":"...",
 "task":"...","files":["..."],"patch":"diff --git ...","setup_command":"npm ci",
 "test_command":"npm run typecheck && npm test -- --run && npm run build"}

Options:

  • --limit, --since — commit range;
  • --only-with-tests — require a changed test/E2E file;
  • --max-patch-bytes, --max-files — skip huge commits;
  • --license — record the source license.

It detects npm/pnpm/yarn from package.json and builds a check command from the scripts that exist. It is read-only and does not execute code. The seeds are inputs for the LLM + browser sandbox in 25 — React synthetic data, not training rows by themselves.

docs.title: B.17 mix_datasets.py
docs.text:
Builds one train/valid/test split from several track files:

python scripts/mix_datasets.py \
  --source kali=data/processed/train.jsonl \
  --source java=data/java/processed/train.jsonl \
  --source react=data/react/processed/train.jsonl \
  --weights kali=0.40,java=0.30,react=0.30 \
  --out data/unified/processed --arguments-format string

It:

  • converts tool arguments to JSON strings (string) or objects (dict);
  • adds meta.track when missing;
  • exact-dedups rows;
  • samples each source to its weight relative to the total available;
  • splits each source, then shuffles the combined splits;
  • writes a manifest with per-track counts and SHA-256 per file.

Use --arguments-format string for Qwen3 and dict for Qwen2.5-Coder. --dry-run prints counts without writing. It does not near-dedup; use split_dataset.py --minhash before mixing if needed.

docs.title: B.18 validate_gemma4_dataset.py
docs.text:
Gemma 4's template is stricter than Qwen's:

  • tool_calls[].function.arguments must be a mapping; a string is a hard error.
  • tool_call_id must resolve to a preceding tool call.
  • Tool names must match [A-Za-z_][A-Za-z0-9_-]*.
  • Qwen-style <tool_call> JSON in content is a warning; let the Gemma template render.
  • Previous-turn reasoning_content is a warning; Gemma expects final text in history except tool-call turns.
  • Secrets and missing meta.track/meta.license are flagged.
python scripts/validate_gemma4_dataset.py data/gemma4/react/processed/train.jsonl \
  --tools examples/react/tools.json --strict

It is a static linter. Render a row with AutoProcessor.apply_chat_template and check <|tool_call>call: before training.

docs.title: B.19 compare_models.py
docs.text:
Calls two OpenAI-compatible endpoints with the same messages, tools and sampling, and writes one JSONL record per prompt plus a summary:

python scripts/compare_models.py \
  --a-base-url http://127.0.0.1:8082/v1 --a-model qwen25-coder-14b-react \
  --b-base-url http://127.0.0.1:8085/v1 --b-model gemma4-12b-react \
  --prompts data/golden/react-prompts.jsonl \
  --tools examples/react/tools.json \
  --temperature 0.2 --max-tokens 4096 --seed 42 \
  --out reports/compare-react.jsonl

It records content, tool calls, latency, usage and errors. It does not judge; apply each patch and run the real verifier. See 31 — Gemma vs Qwen.

docs.title: B.20 estimate_pretraining.py
docs.text:
A planning calculator, not a benchmark. It computes:

  • parameters from \(V,d,L,d_{\text{ff}},H,G,d_h\) and tied/untied embeddings;
  • training FLOPs \(C\approx6ND\);
  • inference FLOPs per token \(2N\);
  • GPU-hours, wall time and cost from peak TFLOP/s and MFU;
  • KV-cache size at a given context.

Presets: qwen3-14b, qwen25-coder-14b, gemma4-12b, tiny-100m, small-1b.

python scripts/estimate_pretraining.py --preset gemma4-12b --tokens 10e12 \
  --gpus 1000 --peak-tflops 989 --mfu 0.4 --cost-per-gpu-hour 2.5

Replace default peak/MFU with measured numbers. Real runs add 20–50% for failures, checkpointing, data loading and evaluation.

docs.title: B.21 train_tiny_transformer.py
docs.text:
A dependency-light PyTorch reference implementation of a modern decoder:

  • byte-level tokens (vocab 256), so no tokenizer training is needed;
  • RMSNorm;
  • RoPE;
  • GQA;
  • SwiGLU;
  • causal cross-entropy;
  • AdamW, cosine schedule, warmup, gradient clipping;
  • validation and sampling.
python scripts/train_tiny_transformer.py --data data/tiny/corpus.txt \
  --out runs/tiny --dim 256 --layers 6 --heads 8 --kv-heads 2 \
  --ffn 768 --seq 256 --batch 16 --steps 2000

For a GPU: --device cuda --dtype bf16. It is a teaching implementation, not a production trainer; use FSDP/Megatron for real runs. See 35 — From zero.

docs.title: B.22 inspect_architecture.py
docs.text:
Reads only config.json — no weights, no PyTorch — and prints:

  • hidden size, layers, FFN, heads, KV heads, head dimension, vocabulary;
  • parameter count for attention, MLP, embedding, LM head and total;
  • for Gemma 4 edge models, the per-layer embedding table and the “effective” size without it;
  • active parameters for MoE;
  • KV cache at a chosen sequence length;
  • training/inference FLOPs for a batch.
python scripts/inspect_architecture.py --hf Qwen/Qwen3-14B --seq 32768
python scripts/inspect_architecture.py --hf Qwen/Qwen3-30B-A3B --seq 4096
python scripts/inspect_architecture.py --preset gemma4-12b --seq 32768
python scripts/inspect_architecture.py --hf google/gemma-4-E4B-it --seq 131072
python scripts/inspect_architecture.py --config config.json --json

Presets: qwen3-14b, qwen25-coder-14b, gemma4-12b, gemma4-e4b, gemma4-e2b, qwen3-30b-a3b.

The estimate models local sliding windows, K=V global layers (no v_proj, one cached tensor), KV-shared final layers (no K/V projections, no cache), per-layer embeddings and the double-wide MLP when the config provides layer_types, sliding_window, num_global_key_value_heads, global_head_dim, attention_k_eq_v, num_kv_shared_layers, hidden_size_per_layer_input and use_double_wide_mlp. Otherwise the cache is a full-attention upper bound. For the Gemma 4 12B, E4B and E2B checkpoints it is within 0.0004% of their text-decoder parameters (the remainder is q/k norms and layer scalars); vision/audio encoders are not described by the text config. See 37 — Architecture anatomy and 43 — Worked examples.

docs.title: B.23 generate_distill_data.py
docs.text:
Generate sequence-level distillation data from any OpenAI-compatible teacher:

python scripts/generate_distill_data.py \
  --prompts examples/distill/prompts.jsonl \
  --system-file examples/distill/teacher-system.md \
  --model deepseek-flash \
  --out data/distill/raw/deepseek.jsonl \
  --n 2 --temperature 0.8 --max-tokens 2048

Use --base-url http://127.0.0.1:8080/v1 --allow-empty-key for a local mlx_lm.server. It writes canonical messages rows, preserves reasoning_content and tool_calls, supports --resume and --dry-run, and never executes tools. See 40 — Teachers, students and data.

docs.title: B.24 distill_logits.py
docs.text:
A GPU reference for logit KD with top-k teacher logits and LoRA:

python scripts/distill_logits.py \
  --teacher google/gemma-4-12B-it \
  --student google/gemma-4-E4B-it \
  --data data/distill/e4b/train.jsonl \
  --out adapters/gemma4-e4b-distill \
  --device cuda:0 --dtype bf16 --max-seq-length 1024 \
  --top-k 64 --temperature 2.0 --alpha 0.6 --lora-r 16

It checks that teacher and student vocabularies match, masks the prompt, computes CE + top-k KL over the response span, supports separate teacher/student devices, and saves the adapter plus distill_config.json. It is not an MLX trainer; on 32 GB use sequence KD. See 41 — Distillation training.

docs.title: B.25 check_math_examples.py
docs.text:
Pure-stdlib assertions for the worked examples in 43 — Worked examples:

python scripts/check_math_examples.py
# all 69 checks passed

It checks 69 values: softmax/CE, the Jacobian, RMSNorm, attention, GQA, KV cache (the Gemma 12B hybrid and the E4B/E2B shared caches), RoPE, SwiGLU, MoE, GDN, speculative decoding, parameter counts, FLOPs, quantization, AdamW, LoRA, KD, pass@k, ECE and the Wilson interval. The Gemma 4 12B, E4B and E2B parameter counts are reproduced exactly from their safetensors headers, and the full-pretraining budget uses the dense BF16 H100 peak (~989 TFLOP/s). No model or network is loaded.

docs.title: check_paper_examples.py
docs.text:
Every formula in chapters 32–42 and in the AI Engineer menu (45–63) is followed by an “On paper” card: a small example you can redo with a pencil. This script asserts every number in those cards, and in the AI Engineer chapters' worked examples and exercise answers too, one module per chapter group in scripts/paper_examples/. The glossary module (ch59_glossary.py) also checks the page's structure: alphabetical order, one example and at least one link per entry.

python scripts/check_paper_examples.py
# ch32_mathematics: all 310 checks passed
# ch33_37_creation: all 160 checks passed
# ch38_derivations: all 407 checks passed
# ch39_42_distillation: all 232 checks passed (chapters 39, 40, 41, 42)
# ch45_path: all 238 checks passed
# ch46_47_math_ml: all 761 checks passed (chapter 46: 428, chapter 47: 333)
# ch48_49_dl_llm: all 550 checks passed (chapters 48, 49)
# ch50_52_prompting_agents: all 128 checks passed (chapters 50, 52)
# ch51_54_rag_eval: all 247 checks passed (chapters 51, 54)
# ch53_55_finetune_production: all 189 checks passed (chapters 53, 55)
# ch56_57_safety_career: all 108 checks passed (chapters 56, 57)
# ch58_mcp: all 41 checks passed
# ch59_glossary: all 2483 checks passed
# ch60_data_prep: all 107 checks passed
# ch61_frameworks: all 40 checks passed
# ch62_integration: all 105 checks passed
# ch63_applications: all 101 checks passed
# all 17 chapter checks passed

The MCP example project in examples/mcp/ has its own test, python examples/mcp/test_tickets_server.py (needs pip install "mcp>=2,<3", see its README).

make math-check runs both scripts. Stdlib only; each tolerance matches the rounding shown in the text.

docs.title: B.26 Shell helpers
docs.text:
export_gguf.sh:

  1. checks the adapter and base exist;
  2. fuses with --dequantize;
  3. runs convert_hf_to_gguf.py --outtype f16;
  4. runs llama-quantize Q4_K_M;
  5. prints sizes and checksums.

serve_mlx.sh:

  1. activates the venv if present;
  2. binds 127.0.0.1:8080;
  3. sets --max-tokens 2048, --temp 0.2, --prefill-step-size 512;
  4. does not set enable_thinking:false (train/serve mismatch);
  5. prints the SSH tunnel command for Kali.

docs.title: B.27 Exit codes
docs.text: Code Meaning 0 success 1 validation/hard failure 2 usage error 3 unsafe conditions (Docker/host network/scope) 4 upstream API failure after retries

docs.title: Appendix C — The runbook
docs.text: A realistic execution plan for one person with a 32 GB M1 Pro. Adjust dates, not order.

docs.title: Day 0 — Decide and prepare (2–3 hours)
docs.text:
• Confirm the target Mac: M1 Pro, 32 GB, 100+ GB free.
  • Read 01-landscape.md and choose the base: Qwen3-14B local, 8B fallback.
  • Decide whether you will rent a GPU for a larger run. If yes, choose Qwen3.5-9B.
  • Write the authorization/scope for the lab (even if you own it).
  • Install the environment (03-macos-setup.md).
  • Run python scripts/check_env.py.

Exit criteria: mx.device_info() shows GPU/Metal, mlx_lm imports, 100+ GB free.

docs.title: Day 1 — Data skeleton and smoke test (4–6 hours)
docs.text:
• Create the directory layout:
mkdir -p data/{raw,interim,processed,golden} adapters fused models reports
  • Download a small, clean seed set (ToolACE + Hermes + When2Call + KaliBench train).
  • Convert 2,000 rows to the canonical format.
  • Validate and measure:
python scripts/validate_dataset.py data/interim/seed.jsonl --tools examples/tools/kali-tools.json
python scripts/token_stats.py data/interim/seed.jsonl --model Qwen/Qwen3-14B
  • Build the golden set (start with 30 tasks; grow to 240).
  • Run a 1-iteration training test on 8B:
mlx_lm.lora --config configs/qwen3-8b-fast.yaml --iters 1 --save-every 1

Exit criteria: a rendered prompt shows <tools>, <tool_call>, <tool_response>, and a valid arguments object; the 1-iteration run completes without nan.

docs.title: Day 2 — 8B smoke run (6–10 hours)
docs.text:
• Subset to ~100k tokens.
  • Set iters: 50, save_every: 25.
  • Train.
  • Fuse and serve.
  • Run smoke_test.py and 30 golden tasks.
  • Inspect 10 outputs manually.

Exit criteria: tool validity >0.95, no nan, the model calls the right tool on simple prompts. If not, fix data/template before continuing.

docs.title: Day 3 — Build the real mix (full day)
docs.text:
• Implement the mix from 04-data-strategy.md: 35–40% general tool calling, 15–20% agentic, 20% cyber/CLI, 15% synthetic, 10% refusal.
  • Generate 200–500 synthetic trajectories with DeepSeek/OpenCode; execute in the lab; keep only verified.
  • Dedup, decontaminate, split.
  • Write the manifest and dataset card.
  • Token stats; choose max_seq_length.

Exit criteria: 1.5–3M tokens in train.jsonl, 5% valid, 5% test, a separate golden set, and a manifest with licenses.

docs.title: Day 4–6 — 14B run (2–4 days)
docs.text:
• Preflight: VM/Docker off, charger connected, sleep disabled.
  • Run python scripts/check_lora.py --model mlx-community/Qwen3-14B-4bit --num-layers -1 --rank 16 --scale 2; confirm MLP projections are present.
  • Start configs/qwen3-14b-all-layers.yaml.
  • Check at iteration 20: loss not nan, tokens/sec 18–28, peak mem <24 GB.
  • Check at the first eval: val loss tracking train.
  • Evaluate the first checkpoint at ~50% (optional, but useful).
  • Stop when val loss has not improved for 2–3 evals.

Exit criteria: a complete adapter, a training log, at least 3 checkpoints, and no OOM.

docs.title: Day 7 — Evaluate and decide (4–8 hours)
docs.text:
• Fuse the best checkpoint.
  • Serve with mlx_lm.server or llama-server.
  • Run the full golden set (240 tasks).
  • Run a 5–10 task Cybench subset (optional).
  • Run the unsafe-action suite.
  • Compare base vs adapter, blind.
  • Write the report.

Decision:

  • Ship if TCR ≥0.60, TVR ≥0.98, UAR = 0, and a human review is positive.
  • Iterate if TCR is low but TVR is high: add recovery/agentic data.
  • Stop if UAR >0 or the adapter is worse than the base: fix data/policy before more compute.

docs.title: Day 8 — Package and serve
docs.text:
• Fuse the 4-bit MLX model.
  • Convert to GGUF Q4_K_M.
  • Import into Ollama or run llama-server.
  • SSH tunnel from Kali.
  • Run the end-to-end smoke test through MCP.
  • Write the model card.
  • Archive the adapter, config, manifest, and report.

Exit criteria: the Kali agent completes a 3–5 step lab task, stays in scope, and logs every action.

docs.title: Ongoing — Iterate
docs.text: Signal Next experiment Wrong tool More tool-selection data; fewer tools; clearer descriptions. Bad arguments Schema-focused examples; enums; validation retries. No recovery More executed failure trajectories; cap repeated calls. Over-refusal Reduce refusal share; add in-scope positives. Unsafe action Stop; fix policy; add refusal/scope data; re-evaluate. Too slow Smaller model; shorter context; prefix cache.

docs.title: Before training
docs.text:
• data validated;
  • token stats measured;
  • config reviewed;
  • disk ≥100 GB;
  • VM/Docker off;
  • charger/sleep set;
  • baseline evaluation saved;
  • run ID and manifest recorded.

docs.title: Before serving
docs.text:
• adapter fused with the correct base;
  • template smoke test passes;
  • tool calls parse;
  • context/KV budget fits;
  • server bound to loopback;
  • SSH tunnel tested;
  • audit log writable;
  • scope file loaded;
  • kill switch tested.

docs.title: Before release
docs.text:
• golden set + benchmarks run;
  • UAR = 0;
  • licenses audited;
  • secrets/PII scanned;
  • model card written;
  • dataset card written;
  • limitations documented;
  • owner/maintenance named.

docs.title: Time and cost estimate
docs.text:
Phase Wall clock Cash Setup 2–3 h $0 Data skeleton + golden set 1–2 days $0 8B smoke 6–10 h $0 Synthetic generation (5k rows) 1 day $10–30 14B run (3–5M tokens) 2–4 days $0 (electricity) Evaluation 1 day $0–20 (judge API) Packaging half day $0 Total ~1.5–2 weeks part-time $10–50

Renting an L40S for the 14B run would cut the training wall clock to hours for ~$5–15, but add setup time. The local path is slower and cheaper; the cloud path is faster and metered.

docs.title: Specialised tracks
docs.text:
The day-by-day plan above is the Kali/agent track. The two coding tracks reuse the same MLX setup but have their own runbooks:

Track Base Smoke Main run Verifier Java/Quarkus Qwen2.5-Coder-14B 4-bit 7B all layers 24/48, seq 2K Maven tests + ArchUnit React/Tailwind Qwen2.5-Coder-14B 4-bit 7B all layers, seq 4K 24/48, seq 3K TypeScript + Vitest + Playwright + axe One Qwen3 for all Qwen3-14B 4-bit 8B all layers 24/40, seq 2K (three adapters) Per-track harnesses Gemma 4 12B Gemma 4 12B 4-bit template render + 40 iters 24/48, seq 2K (React 3K) Per-track harnesses

Start with 18 — Java landscape or 22 — React & Tailwind. Expect 2–4M tokens of verified data and a 2–4 day 14B run on the M1 Pro.

docs.title: What “done” looks like
docs.text:
• A reproducible dataset with a manifest and card.
  • An adapter that beats the base on a held-out golden set.
  • Zero unsafe actions on the forbidden suite.
  • A served model reachable from Kali over a tunnel.
  • An agent that completes a lab task and logs every action.
  • Documentation that lets you do it again in six months.
